At the far end of the corridor lies a cell filled with countless communication devices.
A solitary figure, tall yet stooped, waits within his modern citadel, listening for the dormant voices of telephones, wireless sets, and phonographs to awaken.

On the cell's leftmost wall hangs a black telephone. Its metal casing is cheap and rusted. Manufactured in 1977, it arrived as a gift from the National Foucault Studies Association and the powers that be.
And still, its prototype eludes me. This is a mere replica of a perfect form.
As we seem doomed to hear nothing but grievances on the futility of learning and the tedium of oppression and power, we might as well name this thing Bureaucracy's Most Miserable Mouthpiece.
Your choice of name is acceptable, yet still, I see you bending it to your ideals.
You cannot keep doing this, Idealist. Grasping only a fragment of a thing and then twisting it to your whims ...

Suspended on the cell's right wall, a solemn yet refined wooden box, traced with the warped inscriptions of the arcanum. Now and then, arcanists choose it over ink and parchment to send their messages.
How, then, should I regard it, or regard them, for that matter? Comala Prison and the so-called Manus Vindictae—living proof of dependency theory in its purest form!
Your theories are far too radical.
A moment, please ... Yes, let's call this The Parable of a Blind Age.
A cutting-edge combination of arcanum and advanced technology wrapped up in a frigid metal exterior. Signals surge through its circuits; its frame quivers as it drones in a low wail.
Only Laplace could have produced such a thing.
Observe how it has been altered in the most unusual ways—signals wander through its delicate pathways, dissolving into obscurity, their source irretrievably lost ...
It's nothing more than an effort to conceal the identity of the person on the other end.
Why are we bothering to even name these horrid machines? This is the most worthless game of semantics we've ever entertained.
We were waiting for a call.
A telephone does not ring simply by virtue of our being here—just as Estragon and Vladimir will be forever waiting in vain. In language, we must deconstruct what is taken as truth.

More importantly—what and when is now? Are we still within reality, or is this an edifice of our own memories recalled later? If we are only memories, then waiting for anything, even a telephone's ringing, is a paradox.
Caught between the endless avenues of what has been and what is yet to come—like every one of us.
Patience. All we need to do is wait.
Ah, a scene lifted straight from the great absurdist tradition. Our players today—The Idealist and Zahir.
Act One: A Human in Pursuit of Transcendentality.
Our tragic star, Aleph, a human consumed by the desire to grasp the primordial core of the world, to reach a singular philosophical truth—a concept with neither genesis nor terminus.

He was proud once, certain that nothing could be more excruciating than the burden of the unknown. That certainty would break. His pursuit led him to the gates of transcendentality, where he understood at last—the key was scattered across the fabric of existence itself.
Finally, one day, he devoured his Ouroboros with unflinching resolve, a distilled fusion of sulfur and mercury—submitting to the forbidden elixir as it unraveled and redefined his very form.
He thinks to himself: "I'll find the ultimate truth, and soon."
A telephone dares to disturb his scene. Their heated discourse halts as each withdraws to the other side of the mirror.
The man in the wooden chair gradually lifts the receiver.
Good morning, good afternoon, good evening, and good night! Your continued support is invaluable to us!
Whether you're in Cuernavaca, Gómez Palacio, or beyond, you will always remain a valued client of the Uqbar Company!
Silence pulses out of the telephone line. On the other end, hurried breaths beat against the transmitter, filling the receiver with an irksome hiss.
*grating static* One moment—%￥# ... Sir, please, stay on the line! Any feedback you have will be crucial. Your opinions are indispensable to the Uqbar Company!

*grating static* Our main office is in Gómez Palacio, near the ... %￥# ... Museum of Literature and Fine Arts, just past the lake of fractured reflections, through the forest where a single leaf dreams. You must have heard of it—surely, you've seen the burning bridge ...

*grating static* In fact, all you need to do is check your credit card statement. I guarantee you've used our services before ... &*%# ... Simply complete the following satisfaction survey, and you stand a chance to win a round-trip ticket to Tlön!

The lake of fractured reflections, the forest where a single leaf dreams, the burning bridge ... The prisoner poised by the telephone is sure that these places do not exist in Gómez Palacio or anywhere else. But the riddle woven into these words is of far greater value than the promised ticket itself.
I've never heard of your company, nor have I ever been one of your customers.
But you must have played our Indisputable Board Game (Romance Language Edition)—a linguistic marvel of subverting contingency and materialism!

Regrettably, at present, the game is single-player only! We are, however, working on improvements. Tell me, would you be interested in a multiplayer format? Perhaps you've got a few close friends handy? Some fellow language-game aficionados?
Fragments of glass and unbroken mirrors cast back the prisoner's image, multiplying him into infinity.

Splendid! We are now ready to enhance your board game experience. Kindly stand up, face the direction of the aurora, open up Volume XI: Hronir and the Synthesis of Scientific Cosmology, and spin around sixteen times!
Stay calm. A mild sense of disorientation is an entirely natural response. Now, what vision presents itself in the mirror?
In the mirror, the poet, philosopher, physician, and alchemist ripple in unison.
A tangled convergence devoid of purpose.

Now, I'll need you to check the second appendix, Idealism and Contingent Phenomena Concordance table. Then identify the corresponding notion and scribble it down at the top of your chart. And there you go! Your multiplayer upgrade is now complete! From now on, every game will begin with a single action—placing a mirror at the map's center.
Everyone knows—mirrors expand the world, mirrors invoke revulsion, mirrors embody the infinite.

Naturally, we hope you will be understanding. This upgrade does come with a few flaws. It is not a seamless revision. Should you experience any irregularities, we recommend removing all traces of material reality from the game and reinserting them, manually if necessary ...
Thank you for your participation. Tell me—what do you think of the game so far?
The question is laid out like a trap. A test to reveal whether the prisoner is still imprisoned within the confines of language.
A manual removal of all materialist elements ...
... in a consummate game of words.
A brilliant reply, sir, brilliant, yes! You have demonstrated a stellar understanding of the Indisputable Board Game's true significance.

As it stands, our current understanding of reality is inadequate to unravel the mystery of this inexplicable call. We must anchor our objectivity in the solidity of being itself. Through thought and discourse, we will, in time, find our hands upon the door of transcendentality.
A single die appears upon the desk.
A worn black twenty-sided die—a symbol of chance and fate. The solitary prisoner rolls it between his fingers; the cell itself shifts imperceptibly with the rhythm of his breath.
*speaking to himself* Is this for this Indisputable Board Game? A tool for responding to the questions from the other side of the line.
*speaking to himself* A word game shaped by the randomness of being and the pursuit of idealism. I suppose a die that never settles is quite fitting.
*speaking to himself* But who will oversee our game—the poet, the philosopher, or some as yet unknown player standing at the edge of our arena?
Imagine that, sir—21 minutes and 40 seconds! And here you are still on the line! You, sir, are a kind and patient gentleman, but beyond all, an impeccable connoisseur of board games!

The Uqbar Company's business has covered every facet of human life and will, if no one stands in our way, eventually come to encompass every aspect of reality. Now, through the marvel of modern telecommunication technology, we intend to help you become a part of the inevitable.
*grating static* But our work is far from over. Within a global corporeal empire like Uqbar, there is always more to be done. Each day, I traverse the burning bridge ...
Oh, forgive me, sir. Back to business. Have you got any pastimes you'd like to share? Or, shall we say, preoccupations?
The answer to that is both singular and infinite.

Really, sir, I don't mean to offend, but I wouldn't call answering phones a pastime! Even if it's something I happen to do as well, it's far from the sort of thing that stokes the fires of passion, haha! Now, a fascination with linguistic paradoxes, linearity or lack thereof of storytelling, psychology, and speculative fiction—those are true passions ... Perhaps that's why the company decided I was so well suited for this role.

Only ... I admit that lately, things have been unusually complicated. Uqbar has a way of erasing memories. Is it arcane skill or merely idealism? I can't say for certain. What I do know is that I've been searching for a number, a forgotten one. A woman's number.
*grating static* I hear her voice, always, ceaselessly, and always loudest when I step onto the burning bridge ...
The static sharpens to the point of becoming unbearable. Then, in the unnatural silence that follows, the prisoner hears an echo from the unknown.

*grating static* Hi, this is Laura. I'm not home right now, and to be honest, I won't be back for some time. I'm exhausted, and I just can't stay here any longer. But one day, I will return. If it's important, leave a message with Orbis after the tone. That way, I'll get it as soon as possible.
An answering machine, and the speaker has a Spanish accent. Certainly not Castilian, not European.
Latin America, Spanish-speaking territories. Argentina, Mexico, Guatemala, Peru, Chile, Venezuela, Bolivia, Cuba, Costa Rica, Panama ...
Why not dial every number in these regions? You will find her voice eventually.
It eats away at me, sir. Day in and day out, confined to this coffin of a cubicle. I find myself asking—where has she gone? Has something happened to her? Is she safe?
My mind turns more and more to darker explanations. That something has happened ... that her life has come unwound.
I just want to help her. Maybe she was someone I once knew. I can't remember much of anything from before. Sometimes I'd rather she was just another customer and nothing more.
I need to check on her again. Making calls is what I'm best at, and I can keep calling forever. Or for as long as I stay in Uqbar.
Until I've gone through every pattern of numbers—every one of them ... again.
You're absolutely right, sir. Sooner or later, I will find her again.
A cluster of nerve pain tightens its grip on the man as he withers away in confinement.
There was no phone. I'm sure you realize that already, but I'll remind you. It wasn't there. Not until it started ringing.
It was—a survey call from Hell. No real questions were asked, and no answers were needed—no philosophy, no science, no history, no art—nothing of any real consequence.
Surely, it wasn't an actual call from Hell.

I suspect this is nothing more than another of our neuroses manifesting itself. As we reenter our labyrinth of recollection, it every so often collapses into chaos. Given that, it would be better to conclude this was only an illusion wrought by hyperthymesia.
Fragments of discourse interlace, shaping a story both novel and obscure.
Like las babas del diablo, the threads of reality stretch in myriad directions, linked by some unknowable force.
What is it that you suggest? That we're mentally compromised? How positively unlikely. Just consider how many of us are doctors here—if we really were slipping into madness, then we could treat it.
But taking medicine at random is not a compromise we can handle. We don't have much time left, Paracelsus. We cannot afford to waste it on ourselves.
Hah. To see a rose reborn from the ashes, one must at least have the patience to watch it bloom.

Perfection is demanded in all things. Even the tiniest particle of dust could doom the creation of the Elixir of Immortality. Every alembic, every ember, every vial must be meticulously positioned, without deviation ...
But achieving such precision is too difficult, wouldn't you agree?
Of all of us, you stand closest to our triumph, Master Alchemist.
All look to you; all follow your guidance. And yet ... are you about to claim, as Aleph does, that beyond this point, there is only emptiness?

No, of course not. I'm only pointing out that we can't afford to lose ourselves in these infinite minutiae day after day; mental fatigue is an inevitable consequence of the strain we put ourselves through.
I have walked this path for many years. The rose, nourished by the Fountain of Immortality, has remained unchanged for a thousand days, but who can say if it will wilt tomorrow?
I have done everything within my power. The rest is in the hands of God.
The darkness stirs as an old, worn screen flickers on in the darkened room.
The dull tone persists, rippling through stagnant air. Inside the sealed glass, a rose trembles as one of its wilted petals falls.
His hand rises, hesitating for a moment before selecting a chat window that has long remained dormant.
We are aware of it now. But awareness is not enough—our theories are insufficient, our knowledge incomplete. We need more: more books, more truth, more reality ...
Endless scrolls of messages spill across the small screen, like a nosy virtual neighbor, disregarding any notion of consent.
There's something unusual in the way this dialogue is unfolding.
Who in their right mind would greet a person missing for over a year with "You're back"? As if your last exchange had been a few minutes ago.
I'd be willing to put money on it—you have no concept of time whatsoever.
The prisoner requires no special insight to see it. "The Linguist" on the other end of the screen is not the one he had previously been speaking to.
You can call me Lorentz Butterfly—if that name holds any meaning for you.
As you wish, then, Lorentz Butterfly.
He complies without resistance, reshaping the designation in his mind.
Then you're saying that he has vanished? The Linguist, I mean.
That's right. One day, he just up and disappeared. There's nothing left but an empty husk and disaster in his wake. No one can say for sure what happened.
Everyone's been scrambling around since. It seems like we keep expecting him to just reappear and take back his garbage spot as easily as he left it.
Then, you're searching for him as well.
That's a generous assumption. But at least if we're talking about what it is I'm doing, then sure. As for why I keep doing it ... haha ...

Let me paint a picture for you. I'm in a long-abandoned office. How I got here is irrelevant. Let's just say a certain research institute's security team dropped the ball. This place is empty, worthless, except for this III-X6 computer, former property of your Linguist.

Getting it up and running without setting off any alarms wasn't easy. I've said this a thousand times before. Refined dragon tree resin is a disaster waiting to happen. Using it for any electronic device was madness! Now, the entire circuit board is crawling with these damn critters.
This computer, much like the Linguist, has been weighed down by an utterly gratuitous affinity for "classical design."
All things considered, the fact this thing still functions is nothing short of a miracle.
Laplace / Lorentz / Thief / Robber / Researcher / Arcanum / Linguist
The prisoner orders and reorders the words in his mind, absent of ethical weight. So far no answer presents itself.
The only thing of any use in here is a remote communication program. It's so damn clean. It almost makes me mad.
*emphasized tone* Even more baffling is that this program is still running after all this time, and there is only one chat visible in the logs—yours.

For someone "the Linguist" never mentioned to anyone else, Mr. Aleph, you two certainly had a lot to talk about. Your chat history reads like an infinite loop—between June 12 and June 22, 2004, you dissected a single preposition over the course of 3,000 messages.

From March to July 2005, you two spent four months fixating on whether Holiday Language exists, exchanging 1.2 million words ... With a little editing, it could pass for a landmark philological thesis ...
I have to say, it's a bizarre thing. You're like some kind of ghost in the machine, a hallucination he conjured. So, what are you? An undercover Laplace agent, or maybe just an imaginary friend?
I'm not with Laplace. As for being his friend, I wouldn't know how he defines us. We merely exchange our thoughts when the occasion arises.
Alright, you're touchy about calling them a "friend." That's fine. I wouldn't be surprised if Ludwig felt the same way. I suppose that makes you something of an unofficial advisor to Laplace.
My responses are not confined to Laplace as an institution, nor were they reserved for the Linguist's questions alone.

Oh? So you'll just answer anyone about anything? Why's that, Aleph? Think you know everything? That's a bit egotistical. Unless you're actually a program. Just some old process running on a loop in this dusty thing? Oh, maybe that's why they've kept you on ...

Thanks for your honest answer, Aleph. And yet, oddly enough, I feel more confused about you than ever. No matter. I think your responses might somehow be more mechanical than a program. So, let's change the subject.
Two books rest upon the unpolished wooden table before him.
One book bears the title Meaning and Mental Phenomena (Vienna first edition, 1921), the other, Structural Analysis of Symbolic Systems (Selected Philosophical Propositions, 1918).
The pages are aged and yellowed, and the first's cover is adorned by a precarious slip of paper with the words: To my dear friend Aleph—Ludwig.
The books rest against each other at a calculated 20-degree tilt, an arrangement that forms a structure both intelligible and functional.
*speaking to himself* Problems do not truly exist in gradients of complexity. They are, at their core, just a series of problems.
*speaking to himself* Every problem must have an answer, and each answer, in turn, may lead to transcendentality.
*speaking to himself* That is ... how it is, isn't it?
You know, I dabble in a little side business—purely for the enjoyment of it—which has led me to some truly unusual encounters.
But a screen-bound conversationalist claiming to possess all the answers to the universe—now that hits my top three most bizarre, for sure.

Second place: an arcanist who was erased from the very fabric of society. A few years back in Luxembourg, I was tracking—ahem, researching—an arcanist when, overnight, he simply ceased to exist. Maybe it was a curse. Whatever it was, everyone forgot all about him, which, in turn, made my research obsolete.
Apologies. You'll find I enjoy extrapolating from and deciphering my subject's minds until I get a full grasp of them. It's really the only way to find some joy in the work.

As for the strangest of them all? It was something that happened in 1999. I was at Cambridge, sitting in on a philosophy class, when the bird-headed professor suddenly stopped mid-sentence and declared that being a philosophy professor was the most absurd profession in the world.
No sooner than that, he left and resigned his post. Another "investigation" cut abruptly short.
The scattered words solidify, locking into a discernible pattern. This time, the prisoner has his answer.
You're an assassin with a talent for analysis. And the Linguist is the latest of your targets.
If you're looking for the Linguist's location, I cannot help you, at least not yet. Your identity is irrelevant; I simply do not know.
An absurd truth. But what compels such unguarded honesty?
Perhaps because he is even less of a threatening conversation partner than a program.
Don't be so hasty, Aleph. For researchers and assassins alike, truth is like las babas del diablo—thousands of strands, impossibly entangled, forming patterns that twist into incomprehensible messes.

But what you mistake for incomprehension is merely the first flicker of a clue. Tell me about your work—you and your Linguist. I want to see what kind of cosmic embers your twin intellects have sparked.
The Linguist and I—or, to be exact, he and the Idealist—have been engaged in the pursuit of a perfect linguistic framework.
Is that so? Then you believe in the possibility of a perfect language?
There are languages whose phonetics are widely regarded as elegant, and others valued for their communicative precision. Yet among them all, I've found no single language that embodies perfection.
Yet the Idealist is determined to create a language that tolerates no vagueness, one in which every term is precisely defined and controlled. In this endeavor, he and the Linguist were aligned.

The Linguist held that only by building and maintaining rigid definitions would we be able to erect a true foundation for metaphysics. Completing this task would eradicate the notion of skepticism that has persisted for a century and resolve the nascent contradictions of empirical inquiry.
Each of them sought to create a linguistic framework capable of encapsulating their own understanding of reality.
I see why you got along so well.
Someone's coming. We'll have to put this on hold for now. The details of your perfect language model ... I have a feeling they hold more pieces of the puzzle behind the Linguist's disappearance.
I will unravel las babas del diablo's ... %￥#* ...
The words twist and distort before the prisoner's eyes.
They unfurl into a band of digits and keystrokes, their logic forming an entire world and revealing to the prisoner sights never before seen.
The dust-covered office door opens as a security officer storms in.
Identify yourself! What are you doing here?! This entire floor is off limits!
Me? Oh, I just happened to be passing by and noticed the door was open. If you want to point fingers, maybe start with whoever left this place unlocked.
Step away from that device, ma'am! You're in direct violation of Appendix III, Section 68 of the LSCC Safety Management Regulations. According to protocol, I have no choice but to—
Hold on, this is a piece of history right here! You need to respect its delicate circuitry, handle it with care ... Ah, great, now you've gone and riled up the critters!
A swarm of critters surges through the machine, shorting its circuits in an instant. Flames catch on dust-laden files, and the abandoned office erupts into an all-consuming blaze.
Well, let's just hope Ludwig really is dead.
The other party's online indicator turns gray, never to light up again.
I rather enjoyed talking to our friends from the computing center. They're such a diverse bunch, always thoroughly interesting.
Textbook sociopaths hiding behind a veil of academia—is that what you consider interesting?
As for this remorseless predator who delights in dissecting others, all they've done is flail about looking for clues to find their vanished prey.
But they aren't our problem yet. The only fitting destination for an arcanist criminal is Comala Prison, right beneath our feet.
If circumstances allow, we'll ensure this assassin gets an invitation.
Maybe she's too caught up in her research. We shouldn't impose undue interpretations on her words, considering how language itself defies definition.
Analyzing the inner logic of language grants insight into both the universe and our place within it.
You're starting to sound like the Linguist.
It's an alluring thought. After all, isn't the transcendentality we seek inextricably linked to the definitional nature of reality?

The Linguist has posited that language is merely a totality of propositions, just as the world is a totality of facts. The direct mapping between them suggests that the world possesses an inherent linguistic essence.
Then it is through language that we may uncover this fundamental essence.
The transcendentality we seek cannot be articulated through language. I won't even entertain the idea.

Even your antipathy to the concept demands at some level that you have studied it. Hah, Merlin ... like when you wrote that scathing review of our young novelist's manuscript. You can't deny it—you finished reading.
By your logic, we are merely constructed identities from the fragments of Aleph's infinitely reflective mind. We are Aleph.
Your rhetorical prowess is admirable, but not when I'm the target. Why not invest that effort in your theories? Tell me, Zahir, have you found your single-sided coin yet?
A coin that shows its obverse and reverse, comprehensible only through a dialectical lens, yet never the same in any two pairs of eyes.
Why don't you tell me first, when did this pursuit of transcendentality become our excuse for escaping reality altogether?
So I haven't found it yet, but the success of my search is not dictated by my effort, nor by the whims of interest.

I will find that coin. But when I do, it will come to me in some unguarded instant, a moment that defies all effort. Still, to get there, I must study it endlessly until it's indistinguishable from my very being—
The futile clash of thoughts dissolves into nothing.
In a place where the borders of reality and dreams collapse and blur, the prisoner takes hold of a black radio inscribed with arcane symbols.
He adjusts the dial, sifting through the frequencies.
Now, doesn't that just feel great? Sink into it ...
A soothing voice rises from the speaker, warping within the coils, reshaping itself into something that defies comprehension.
To all you faithful arcanists out there, followers of the Sufferer, devotees of the mask—this is the Panamerican Broadcast, brought to you by the Manus Vindictae.
A single spark of arcane radiance is all it takes for one extreme to dissolve into its opposite.
A wisp of static seeps between the words.

*radiance flickers* From the demented repetition of classical compositions to the relentless assault of bad news, from literary autopsies to the vogue of tragic radio plays—every note, every word, every sorrow is just a little touch of the dial away! Panamerican Arcanist Radio bringing you the latest voices from McMurdo Port.
Antarctica is still basking in auroral radiance today; that glowing tide will keep gushing into the sky and hovering over the world until time itself breathes its last.
*radiance flickers* I wonder, listeners—how does the sky weep where you are? Is a storm raging, or has the sun fallen? Let us relish this moment, together, on the last evening on Earth ...
Extend my sincere regards to the Preacher.
Through the static, a soft and steady breath emerges—quick, restless, and measured at precisely one hundred and six beats per minute.
The line is open. A listener from Ushuaia is now on the air.
Panamerican Arcanist Radio reaches the ears of the devoted across continents. From Los Angeles to São Paulo, from the Chisos to Ushuaia, our dramas have captivated arcanists everywhere.
But you, sir—you are a mere human. That is an enigma in itself. I say "mere," but you are anything but ordinary; that much is clear.
Years have passed since Mr. Forget Me Not and I last spoke. A mere intersection of research—nothing of significance.
There is nothing exceptional about me, except the fact that I cannot leave this place.
I will speak plainly, Ms. Grace, so long as you find reason to listen.
This station has many listeners, but none quite like you.
The radio host's face is a mosaic of countless others.
Kayla, Grace, Cecilie, Newman ... names without weight, faces without permanence. She drifts unseen, a colorless moth in the dark—an existence without self.
From the mirror, they sigh as one—a chorus laced with disdain.

*speaking to himself* So alike and so ill-fated. One condemned to remember, yet commanded to forget—a Scheherazade without an audience, keeper of shameful secrets, lost in the tragedy of his own illusions.
*speaking to himself* And so ... hyperthymesia is no blessing, but a curse without cure.
This story begins in San Francisco, 1990. Our protagonist is a young girl called Cecilie, lost in the flow of things.
Somewhere between 18 and 22, she speaks with a Low Saxon lilt. Behind her, the cry of a black-fronted Piping Guan sounds—so precise it could be real. She may actually be from Blumenau.

An arcanist in search of an exit, yearning to slip beyond the grasp of thought's phantoms and power's unseen hand. There is a place she knows—one where the sun does not shy from those who seek hidden truths.
Children of the esoteric, keepers of heresy, zealots of the arcane ... They are as a mighty shoal amidst the currents of upheaval, never still, always moving.

Of course, they'd never turn away a stray. The thing she feared remained unrealized—she was taken in and reshaped. For the cause, she became Kayla, became Ms. Grace, then Newman, then Cecilie ... The tree had shed its leaves, and foreign branches took their place. Who she had been no longer mattered. She became another, again and again, until even time forgot what had once grown there.
The whispers of innumerable voices gather on the other side of the white noise.

This Monday's edition of The Ushuaia Times reported on the sinking of the "Free Breeze." Among the survivors, some claimed to have seen a great number of islanders aboard, adorned with seashell ornaments. There is reason to believe that some of the Nukutai may have forsaken their homeland.

We hear now Louis, reporting from the scene: "Why they departed, we cannot say. Was it the allure of modern civilization or a promise that somewhere in the farthest west, a river of immortality awaits? Their arrival was a moment of wonder, but by the time the night faded, they were already lost."
A sound hangs in the air, almost a sob. The young lady does not weep; she merely breathes, her sorrow measured in time, her grief a part of the rhythm of existence.
And so, this gripping "incident" reached its tragic epilogue—the fate of a people sealed, over nothing more than a shell.
Falling back into his reverie, the Idealist idly presses the power switch, yet the broadcast's performance of disorder and delirium has already reached its end. The radio plays no more.
A name carried in whispers ... the Panopticon of Comala—where every question finds its answer.
I quite like these stories that travel up from the telephone lines.

The stranded, the deluded, the ones forever haunted by riddles without solutions, they come here, drawn by forces unseen, by paths not meant to be traveled. They ask, they seek, they wander through lives frayed at the edges, tangled in paradox and unreality.
Do you really feel nothing in the face of these challenges? Don't you realize we can shape what we have here into something that holds actual meaning?
This all leaves me feeling ... somewhat lost.
Have we found clarity or more confusion? I'm not sure. But it's already taken up too much time. Idealist, do you still remember what you set out to do at the very start?
I ... Of course I do! My poem—I would never forget it.
The Idealist scans the confines of his cell in panic. Finally, he finds it—a tiny fissure in the wall.
Beneath this crumbling plaster, I named it: A History of Eternity, for within it lies poetry without end—the very source and medium of my great epic! Its delicate contours speak to me of ... sorrow.
With every passing day, the crack extends a little further, and so your poem will never reach its final line.
There will be a way. If this endless and sorrowful poem is to be conveyed with all the elegance and exactitude it deserves, then I must construct a language worthy of it!
One all-encompassing, unhindered by ambiguity—not a conceptual illusion, but something absolute, precise, essential. A "language of creation," one that shall unshackle every artist and poet alike.
So that's what you've been discussing with the Linguist all this time—your perfect language.

Claro que sí. But now, with the Linguist gone, our language's birth hangs in limbo. That is the tragedy of the telephone. We speak, yet we remain strangers to each other, and he, perhaps, to himself most of all!

But! I will continue onward with new projects. Poems, shaped by many hands within these walls, a curated collection of their imprisoned tongues. Within them, I will discover the systematic method behind every language. Through that, I will ensure the opening lines are flawless in their meaning. Until then, I will host our literary salons, wandering through this literary labyrinth with the intent to build an exit someday ...
But for all your efforts, that poem remains unwritten, unexecuted. Not even a single word has been committed.
You are lost within your literary labyrinth, lost in infinite inquiry—so much so that even your name has abandoned you. Idealist, do you even remember who you are?
The poet, the writer, the pioneer of thought ... Bewildered, he stares at the sorrowful crack in the wall.
The line stirs once more with another call from the outside world.
Lift the receiver and vanish into the interplay of reality and perception ...
To lose meaning is to lose yourself.
In the end, he will vanish within his own story ...

It defies reason. Why haven't we reached transcendentality? Not even the door seems within sight. I ... I cannot fathom it. Is all of this meaningless? Are we condemned to stand on the edge of that which cannot be spoken? How does one bring about an end to the endless?
It cascades over the Atacama Plateau, scouring the sands along the highway.
Oh, thank God! I actually got through!
Please, don't hang up, sir. You wouldn't believe what I've just been through.

Listen, we ... we're stranded on some highway in the middle of nowhere. Wanna know what I can see? Well ... sand, sand dunes ... endless sand dunes ... no villages, no steeples in sight ... only a highway, half-buried beneath the desert ... wolves lurking behind the dunes ... not even a single cactus.
There's a sign just ahead—it says ... Cuentos Completos! It says we're on the Cuentos Completos! That's impossible! I've lived in Antofagasta long enough to know there's no such road!
There's nothing else around here apart from this phone booth. Weird, isn't it? A road to nowhere, with this strange relic of something that once was ... and somehow, it's now my only hope.
I dialed every number I could think of—emergency services, roadside assistance, the publishing house, the university, the bank ... Nothing. Not a single connection. I was about to lose my mind.

I'm still half-convinced this phone booth is nothing more than a hallucination, but then I caught sight of your number. An impossible coincidence—it had been scribbled onto the back of a manuscript, lying forgotten in my car. With a scruffily written note: He can answer any question.
Call it ... an impulse? A feeling? I can't explain it, but I called your number, and against all reason ... it's gone through! Thank God—I was beginning to think I'd wound up in hell.

Please, uh, just call me ... erm ... the Literary Critic. That's what my colleagues call me—mockingly, of course. They think I'm hopelessly out of my depth, a clueless fraud, an impostor in the world of letters.
But there's no use dwelling on it now. I've accepted the name, just as I've accepted the weight of this job.
Oh, that's right, I forgot to mention—I'm an editor working for H.A. Publishing House! You know, The Forgotten Crows, The Portrait ... ring any bells?
Hah, very perceptive, sir. In fact, that's precisely why I'm out here stranded on this "Cuentos Completos."

It's my friend Lise's birthday, see. We were supposed to go to the reserve; we were going to visit the geysers and the valley, the flamingos, the little desert towns ... all the things she loves. The colonial architecture, abandoned settlements, remnants of religion, history, natural landscapes, geometry ... It's supposed to be a perfect day.
Then I noticed something in the backseat—manuscripts I was sure had already been submitted. I had sent them to the publishing house yesterday, and yet, here they are ...
So I had to turn back to drop these manuscripts off at the publisher. But Lise—she wasn't pleased. We argued, and by the time I looked back at the road, everything had changed.
We've been driving in circles for ... what, two hours? Three? I don't even know anymore. There's nothing but sand stretching out in all directions.
Except for a sign marking this place as the Cuentos Completos and this strange phone booth.
If you can truly answer anything, sir, then answer this—what do I do next?
The driest wind in the world.
Salt mountains, desert, and an infinite horizon of red and brown.
It looks like they were right all along. I really am a fool.

Lise couldn't take it anymore and walked off. She left me, left the car, just walked into the desert without looking back. I couldn't stop her. I couldn't even explain. I don't even know if there was anything I could say. All I know is that the desert isn't a safe place for someone to go walking around all on their own.
She had every reason to be angry. Why did I turn around? I let a stack of paper, a manuscript that might never even be published, destroy her perfect day.
I can't even decipher these manuscripts. The writing, the literature—none of it speaks to me.
Where is Archimboldi? Four chapters in, and not a trace of him. He's the book's most important character, so why has he disappeared from his own narrative?
Why is Comala full of nothing but restless spirits? And why is it that the dead can talk to the living?
What compelled Pierre Menard to rewrite Don Quixote? How can one man produce a text identical to another's, word for word?
Why must the narrative unfold through these fragmented dialogues? Flashbacks, always with the flashbacks ... Where did Santiago and Ambrosio actually meet, if they ever met at all?
Can you give me an answer, Mr. Aleph? Why is the world of words like this?
Perhaps I've been looking for meaning where there is none ...
I guess this was never the right job for me. I see that now. The publishing house is barely scraping by. And honestly, who still has the luxury of reading these days?

It won't be long before the Antofagasta branch shuts its doors for good, and I can't do a damn thing to stop it. I don't even understand what I'm supposed to be doing! We all keep at it, but what's the point?
If nothing about this place has meaning to you, then the simplest solution is to let it go.
That's it? Yes ... I see. Thank you, sir ... You're—you're absolutely right!
Sunset. A crimson radiance spills across the boundless sands.
With a heavy sigh, Monique slumps against the car, burying her face in her hands.
Footsteps crunch through the sand behind her, then the sound of leather soles on loose stones. She lifts her head in disbelief.
I'm so sorry, Monique. I shouldn't have left you alone. I ... I just needed a moment to pull myself together.
Come on, let's head back. You were right. There's still time to make it.
We'll still have time for dinner, and as an added bonus, you won't get fired! This isn't exactly the best time to be unemployed.
No. I'm the one that should be saying sorry, mi corazón.
Forget the publishing house. I'm done with that place.
Monique grabs the manuscript and, with firm conviction, tears it to shreds.
Wait, Monique! What are you doing?!
To hell with these stories. To hell with everything else. Today's your birthday, Lise. All that matters to me is you.
Let's go. We'll follow this road, no matter where it takes us. Even if we lose our way, even if we never find our destination—I can't think of anything more romantic, can you?
Hop in! I'm gonna give you a birthday we'll never forget!
Mi amor. This is already the most wonderful birthday gift I could've wished for.
This day belongs to just you and me. I'll remember it for the rest of my life.
The engine rumbles as the car starts up again.

The desert wind lifts the scattered manuscript scraps. Their torn fragments dance on the breeze, momentarily revealing their title—The Rise and Fall of Sanity, Recoleta. Then, as swiftly as it rose, the wind subsides, and the manuscript, the words, and the mysterious phone number on its back are consumed beneath shifting red sands.
A red sedan speeds down an unknown highway, shrinking from sight until it ultimately vanishes into the horizon.
Again, another pursuit of the ultimate truth has been proven futile.
Yet futility is but a part of the eternal cycle. In the endless stories and selfless reality, the cycle itself becomes one of its meanings.

Historically, the town of Ushuaia originally was home to just 400 people ... until 1,100 convicts were exiled here.
It's not hard to see why! After all, this little town has a chill to it that pierces the bone. Even the rain feels unapologetic and bleak.

Those exiles soon became essential for the town. They cut the lumber, built the generators, and survived the harsh winters alongside the townspeople. Some stayed after their release, and with time, the town prospered.
A town so deeply intertwined with stories of exile and imprisonment—don't you think that gives it a certain mysterious, intricate, unspoken charm?
In the cold and silence of the polar night, a pair of warm hands can warm not just your body but also your heart.
Even if those hands belong to a death row convict exiled here ...?
Of course. Even if they belonged to a waddling penguin, they would still be the hands of a friend. Over the years, we could even end up like family!
Indeed. I think I understand how the residents and prisoners integrated.

Surviving in the harsh climate of polar regions like this isn't easy. Prisoners couldn't make it alone. The harsh nature of their surroundings taught them a simple truth—no person survives on their own.
Such poetic wording—Sonetto, you really ought to try your hand at poetry. It is an act of outpouring one's feelings, and taking a journey through one's own mind!
A journey through your mind? Hmm, thanks for the suggestion. Perhaps, I'll consider giving it a try in the future.
The National Foucault Studies Association was founded by scholars, alongside the Junta, to support the study of Foucault's theories and further exploration of social structures.
... Thus, a regular column was established in this publication, where contributions from all perspectives are welcomed and encouraged.
This newspaper is about as old as I am, yet you somehow managed to find a copy.
Yes ... The Panopticon of Comala was founded by the National Foucault Studies Association as a site for experimental psychoanalysis.

I've read about it. A single watcher could observe all prisoners, and since the prisoners never knew if they were being watched or not, the surveillance system infiltrated every detail of their lives.
It is smart, isn't it? The actual surveillance remains unseen, yet the prisoners nonetheless end up trapped in a closed, fragmented structure—oh, those were my pen pal's words.
He also said it was a significant experiment for the government at the time.
But in that era, Foucault's psychoanalysis seemed more like a means to an end.
Huh? Wait, so if I'd been born a few decades earlier, would I have needed to try so hard to get into this prison? Wouldn't the gendarmes have locked me up just for writing or speaking out?
... I may not always understand you, but I sincerely hope you are joking now.
Back then, people faced more than just imprisonment. There were disappearances, torture, and many deaths.
Alright, alright, I apologize. That was probably a bit inappropriate for a joke, I admit. Please relax, Sonetto.
Have you ever heard of Foucault, Sonetto?
Yes, he's a renowned French philosopher and social theorist. I read books about his theories at the SPDM ...
So those are precisely the kind of books they'd never confiscate.
Never mind that. Could you explain what you read in detail?
Alright. Foucault argued that madness isn't a natural phenomenon, but rather a cultural construct.
In early times, punishment was a public spectacle, a display of power for the rulers.
Nowadays, things are different. After the Enlightenment, punishment became a form of public education, intended primarily to deter crime ...
That's true. The phrase "public execution" has all but disappeared from everyday language.
Discipline and punishment ... By that logic, the SPDM aligns closely with Foucault's ideals.
But Deleuze believed that another model of power had replaced disciplinary power—the power of administration. A highly efficient yet indifferent system of management.
The system holds control over the environment, and under such circumstances, the individual's inner self ceases to matter.
... Timekeeper, is this discussion because of what the Physician said?
That's right. Initially, I just wanted to hear your perspective on this.
Now ... I'm starting to see how this model reduces people to little more than animals.
The Admiral sent me to deliver the latest updates.
Ha, I think Igor has misunderstood something: Just because we're both here doesn't mean the Apostles Brotherhood and Zeno are obliged to work together.
Mr. Santos, you know the Preacher's said it before—each and every one of us is Their subject.
Why don't you just tell me what Igor really sent you here for?
Zeno's intelligence officers intercepted a message from The Foundation's Buenos Aires branch.
How typical of Zeno to do something like that.
The message states that a fleet from the Foundation—including a battleship and a destroyer—has departed from the north and is heading south.
So you're telling me those gray-and-white checkers are actually sending a fleet ...
The General wants you to speed up the transport of personnel and supplies, and to weaken the manpower of The Foundation's Buenos Aires branch as much as possible.
Let me make this perfectly clear—I do not answer to him.
... But for the Preacher, and for Them, I will fulfill my duty.
Tell your Admiral that he doesn't need to worry about anything else. We'll prepare a proper welcome for The Foundation's feeble little fleet.

Open it, reread it. Witness firsthand the events that transpired within the desert.
A silent and merciless order of ideals.

Even though they refuse to discuss the outside world, spending even a few days inside the prison makes clear that the reason they are here is precisely what they avoid speaking about.

Ushuaia is a cold town on the tip of Argentina's southernmost territory. The polar night, the frozen sea, the proximity to Antarctica, the endless winter—it all makes the place seem buried by time and forgotten. It possesses all the necessary qualities of a prison, making it an ideal place to send arcanist suspects diagnosed with mental illness, a place to be forgotten.

Setting aside the true definition of madness and their status as prisoners, what I see in this prison are former poets, writers, and social activists. In their era, some spoke of poetry—then disappeared from society for owning a book by Jean-Paul Sartre. Some incited grassroots rebellion against hierarchical structures—only to be exiled. They were repeatedly questioned, "Why do you read these books? Why do you write these poems?" They were branded "thought organizers" and eventually sent here to partake in an experiment conducted under the names of Foucault and psychoanalysis. It is nearly impossible to determine whether their "madness" was defined by society because they resisted order, or if it was induced through relentless electric shocks and torture. Or perhaps all of these reasons are one and the same. This reason is often avoided, sanitized, or ignored—because deep down, we all know how deeply it is woven into the fabric of all our lives.

...

At first, they said nothing, but this very act of deliberate avoidance was what truly conveyed their grief and fear.

When they speak of "Manus Vindictae," their tone is always light, often laced with jokes—colorful descriptions like "a greasy-headed musician smearing tiles like a drunk Edward Goya" frequently crop up in their poetry. Even though I have never "seen" such a scene myself, I can still grasp their attitude toward Manus Vindictae—it was an oppression surpassing even their past sufferings. Yet, subconsciously, they "ignored" this similarity—perhaps out of denial, or perhaps because this prison had already taught them to obey, also subconsciously.

But as far as I know, Manus Vindictae did bring their terror here. Those masks drove arcanists to insanity and caused unbearable suffering, as if they were caught in an inescapable snare. After prolonged torment, they lost the ability to utter even a single phrase of their own language, reduced to slaves of this underground faction—left with only a singular thought, their souls having left the empty husk of their former selves.

And as for humans—it seems they were driven to death en masse. At night, they were not allowed prolonged sleep, woken by their companions every hour to sit beneath the watchtower and chant prayers. And by dawn, high-intensity training and interrogations that did not require or expect any answers would begin again ... The purpose of Manus Vindictae is buried beneath these cruel methods, as clear as the deepest crevasse in the ice field—it is nothing but destruction. They seek to "completely destroy" humanity.

In 1935, Professor António from Portugal became intrigued by a medical study documenting how gorillas became docile after the removal of their frontal lobes. Inspired by this, he successfully performed the world's first human frontal lobotomy, known as leukotomy. The surgery was remarkably successful, paving the way for significant breakthroughs in research. In 1949, Professor António was awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine for his work.

Through continuous practice and refinement, he and others eventually improved and perfected the procedure, even developing a specialized leukotome. However, the surgical technique required a high level of expertise, and as a result, it was never widely adopted.

In 1945, American doctor Walter Freeman modified the procedure, which became infamously known as the "ice pick lobotomy." The technique involved rendering patients unconscious with electroshock or anesthesia, and then hammering a steel pick—roughly the thickness of a chopstick—through the upper part of the eye socket into the brain. The pick was then manually rotated to destroy the frontal lobe.

In 1950, following strong recommendations from psychiatric pathologist Vasily Gayanovsky, the Soviet government became the first to announce a complete ban on frontal lobotomies. Over the next two decades, most countries, including the United States, followed suit and passed laws prohibiting the procedure.

"The crowd ... it's all just Carbuncles. That's right. Look at that silly hat—nobody's even paying attention to you. Just a line of polite Carbuncles, sitting there ... just focus."
"Enduring twenty-five hours of cold and wind was worth it—I caught the moment Sweetheart stepped off her plane and waved at us with a smile."
"Scrounging up two hundred million dollars, working for two whole years; all to compress a dream into just two hours. Now, the dreaming begins."
"Yeah, no, I get nervous too ... But I tell myself, 'Flammy, think about your first boxing match. Mom, Dad, and all your friends are waiting for you.' And then, my steps feel a little lighter."
"Look ahead, my dear colleagues. I mean, towards the direction that is closer to 'the future' than today, or any other era. The iron lady convinced me—it exists."
"Gratitude always tastes good at first—better than strong liquor. But, you get used to it, just like you get used to the throbbing pain when the buzz subsides."
"An era has disappeared ... But the paperwork never will."
"In that white snow, we wove our own songs—about the aurora, about the flames, about the heavy heart of coal. I will remember it forever."
"Pure, solemn, the simple contrast of black and white ... Sometimes, I feel like I don't live in the present, but in that golden age of the past."
"Screaming is an art, darling—you have to make the audience believe you're just as scared as they are. Even though you're the one scaring them."
"I received an offer for an acting role. Oh, it's tempting, but I'd prefer to perform in something ... more real."
"A fine costume, a fine mask—both can help you get into character. Will you play a lion or a fairy? I'm happy to assist."
"A nameplate, a price I don't understand ... and a bicycle. I get it now—this is modern art."
"I've had some inspiration! My next ingredient will be ... a single tear, free of sorrow!"
"Oh I've read the new script. It's going to be a challenge, darling—they want me to play 'myself.' Fine. On-screen, they'll see whoever they think that is."
"The trees whisper what they wish to become. Every wand is a creation we shape together."
"Sometimes I still dream of the good old days—flowers, poetry, declarations. But with the 'Storm,' tomorrow feels uncertain. And I'm not so young anymore."
"That familiar intro, that same old tune—this is why I love The Tonight Show and its theme song."
"I just want to fill my stomach... It's been so long since I last enjoyed such a satisfying meal."
"I had a dream older than fire itself—a dream without conflict, without fear."

One evening in 1996, in Stockholm, a well-known local alchemist and arcanist received an unusual visitor.

The guest was a 17-year-old human boy. A pure-blooded human—such visitors were rare for an alchemist, as the field of alchemy was dominated by arcanists with innate talent and access to resources. Few humans ever sought their counsel.

But soon, the alchemist realized that this taciturn young man was a prodigy beyond comprehension. He came in search of knowledge, but after a night of conversation, the alchemist knew the boy would leave disappointed.

The alchemist wished to help the boy, but in this world, there was no answer to his question. What he sought was too vast, too ambitious—a pursuit destined to become a lifelong curse.

The alchemist wanted to free the boy from this curse, or perhaps—to help him find the answer. An answer everyone desires, including the alchemist.

Alchemy is a science of the body. The alchemist gave the boy a formula for a potion, one that would free him from the limitations of human physiology, allowing him to reach the peak of rationality and perception. He would never again forget anything—not one detail, nor any speck of knowledge or trivia. He could absorb endless expanses of alchemical wisdom and more ...

The boy left, overjoyed. He did not yet know that this potion formula would soon become a curse that would haunt him for the rest of his days.

Pandora Wilson: Hello, Mr. Aleph.
Pandora Wilson: I've leaned on some highly secretive sources to get in contact with you. I've heard that you've served as an advisor to quite a few people. Whether it's Manus Vindictae, Lorentz, Laplace, or even ordinary Arcanists ... do you truly answer all of their questions?
Aleph: Yes. Just as I am doing now.
Pandora Wilson: Ha, I see. May I ask how you ensure that your answers are always correct?
Aleph: In truth, I cannot guarantee that. I extract all of my knowledge from the books, history, and disciplines I am familiar with, but that does not mean any of it is necessarily correct, authoritative, or representative of any truth. It is merely an answer.
Pandora Wilson: So, you mean that your answers do not contain your personal emotions or judgments?
Aleph: I cannot be certain. But "personal emotions and judgments" ... that is a vague concept. These memories are a part of me—do they also define my "personality"?
Pandora Wilson: There will always be those who take your answers as absolute truth.
Aleph: My apologies. In the future, I will make sure to inform them of these disclaimers before answering their questions.

A literary symbol of chivalry, granted to those who have secretly and fervently safeguarded their lost homeland over the years. *This inscription was written personally by the interviewee*

In 1975, at the Gandhi Bookstore in Mexico City, three unknown young poets founded the "Visceral Realism" poetry movement. They disrupted formal poetry readings, took part in youth resistance, and declared: "The important thing is not to write poetry, but to live as a poet." 

Misunderstood, lonely, poor, and failed—thus was born a poet's glory. 

Every postwar Latin American youth was swept into the movement. They were lost idealists, convinced that their struggle could transform this land, could change the world. But their generation's ideals quickly collapsed. In the end, the poet left for Europe, exiled and disillusioned.

The legend of resistance continues in the poet's novels. He wrote about his past wanderings, about his lifelong journey across Latin America, about the unfinished quests of poets, and the ideals shattered by the violence of reality ... the absurd, brave, glorious, and failed poets.

Let me tell you how a story should be written: stories should be written in threes, and if possible, in tens! The Rise and Fall of Sanity A tale set in a desert town, revolving around the ancient tradition known as "The Die of Babylon" ... There's no way to write the ending. Something's off—what could possibly be missing from this story? Ruinas Gloriosas y Directrices de Metáforas A trilogy belonging to two protagonists, an epic journey beginning with their return home. Through countless revisions, nearly every part of their adventures had multiple versions. In the end, they all became part of this work. The manuscript is complete, but for certain reasons, it was never submitted or published. The Final Days of Chac Mool Amid the Mexican Muralist Movement, a young muralist unexpectedly uncovers a secret hidden within his friend's work ... It's on hold. I need to return to Mexico City. To stand once more before those great murals, only then will I know how to finish it!

Recoleta: I love the concept of this magazine, the concept of this interview.
Pandora Wilson: Ms. Recoleta, what do you mean ...? 
Recoleta: From the way it's framed to the content itself, it's steeped in symbolism and mysticism. "A person can be a work of art—dead or alive"? Fragrance note, dimensions, medium—are we intellectualizing writing or mystifying it? I imagine this is your signature arcanist commercial style, blending market trends, public taste, and mass literature. But isn't an anti-market product still a product of the market? Have you exaggerated the interviewees' experiences? Are these legendary stories really honest interviews? Is interpreting arcanists as art pieces a bit one-dimensional? Oh, I mean no offense—I'm just very curious about what makes an arcanist business magazine successful ...
Pandora Wilson: Ms. Recoleta, must we really go breaking the fourth wall like this?

Forged from "mithril," its delicate filigree and flowing curves are the hallmark of elven craftsmanship. Even through perilous journeys and fierce battles, the ranger would never neglect this cherished keepsake from home.
... In reality, it's made of aluminum wire, tin foil, and glass beads.

When the party won their first battle against a lord-tier foe and reached their first post-battle trading post, the ranger spent all her goblin-plundered gold on this hand crossbow, bought from the best merchant around. In hindsight, it was worth every coin.

A finely woven, deep green travel cloak—sturdy, dirt-resistant, and perfect for keeping out the night's chill. However, when the host announces a long rest, the ranger often drapes it over her Splintercat companion, preferring to curl up against its warm, soft fur instead.

A stage costume personally designed by the interviewee for Ms. Acey, inspired by a bouquet in full bloom. The colors are striking, the design daring—when it's under the spotlight, it demands attention.
"A simple but effective trick ... I'm on stage, yet unseen by all. Ahem, Ms. Acey certainly put in a lot of effort for this."

A deck of cards named "Trump Card" by the interviewee—aside from its unique face designs, it's identical to a standard deck.
"Miracles" come from a mix of imagination and meticulous execution, and the interviewee understands this well. In a dazzling display of card magic, she always seems to pull the ace.

The classic black top hat, standard for all magic performances. Before wearing, be sure to shake out any lingering rose or lily petals. 
Pulling rabbits, doves, or ribbons from it is an old tradition—but the interviewee has other plans. "No, this is the art of the unexpected. Following tradition and wearing it is just another way of breaking expectations."

An unremarkable bronze oil lamp. 
The mage has held golden lamps fueled by dragon fat and danced with nothing but a torch in hand. When asked why she ultimately settled on such an ordinary lamp, she replied, "It doesn't interfere with my magic, and it doesn't trip me up while I dance. Just like how my expression right now won't stop you from continuing with these pointless questions."

A piece of gear that's both stylish and practical, capable of blocking a dragon's breath attack—once. 
Before the game even started, the adventurer insisted on calling it this to "save time coming up with fancy names for equipment."

A waist chain and anklets strung with bells. Legends say the mage learned a long-lost secret from an ancient being, replacing traditional incantations with dance steps that harmonize with chimes and firelight, wielding the power to drive away fiends. The crisp bell sounds also perfectly mask the "thud-thud" of a prosthetic limb touching the ground.

A magnificent beard designed to enhance one's warrior presence—always thick, well-groomed, and requiring no maintenance.
Every dwarf treasures their beard, and laughing at one is the surest way to earn a warrior's wrath.

As bold as the flames of battle, as red as fresh blood, and tailored to a warrior's exact height. Perfect in every way—except for the "small chance to wrap around you as you fight causing you to trip you at the worst possible moment" curse.

Carefully managing supplies and stamina, and wisely deciding what to pack in your backpack—these are essential skill for any great adventurer. But if you're strong enough, or if your load is light enough, who's to say you can't carry a shield, a defeated dragon, or even a conquered fortress?

A Viennese noble wielding a conch is recklessly flinging coins at passersby. The people hit by the money scramble away in panic—no one dares pick up the coins from the ground. 
"Take it! Take it! If you take this money, I'll be happy!"

"Do you want this conch? No, only this conch brings me joy—you can't take it! Take this useless money and go!" ... "Forget it, it's just a singing conch. Don't waste your time—there are more pressing matters waiting for you in Vienna."

"That conch … Are you a friend of Lorelei? Please, help me! Those soldiers have gone mad! They're destroying my shop!"
It seems the panicked citizen has mistaken the conch in Semmelweis's hand. Their expression is that of a drowning person clinging to a reed.

"Look at the foolish choice you've made. The troops have surrounded the area. Are you really going to risk your life under cannon fire for a stranger's property? You know the reward isn't worth the risk."

Here she returns once more. The studio is empty, but Semmelweis would never mistake the rose on the table—she knows the lingering Arcane energy all too well. Bullets. Black mist. The water droplets on the petals have yet to dry. ... "A rose—perhaps it's a clue she left behind? Should I trust her? But be careful not to commit too much too soon, or you'll be the one who suffers."
The conch's song grows clearer upstream of the river. Semmelweis begins to make out the message in the melody—the people downstream are pleading for her aid.
Whose prank is this? Semmelweis sees a portrait of her past self—healthy, unburdened—mocking the pitiful state she is in now.
A plain theater play is being performed, one that satirizes the lives of certain people. However, Semmelweis's attention is drawn to the old vendor stalls outside the theater.
The artist of this painting must have had quite the imagination. In it, Semmelweis sees herself as having achieved great success, holding all she has gained in her hands, as if offering a deal.

A woman from the Golden Alley appears before Semmelweis. "After this great war, another unavoidable battle will come—none of us can escape it. But your fate does not belong here. Let me see ... I can offer you some advice to avoid tragedy. The cost is minimal."

A foreboding feeling hangs over Semmelweis. The decor of this room is all too strange, and the eerie tranquility feels more like a trap for those seeking refuge. Yet, with the riots raging outside, stepping out is not an option.
Semmelweis offers a few flattering words to the Viennese noble. Pleased, they hand over a handful of Goldfinch Coins.
Lose 50 Stimulus. Lose all Stimulus if there's less than 50. Obtain Little Conch
After much effort, Semmelweis finally convinces them that joy takes many forms and receives the now-useless conch in return. She swears she can only handle three more eccentrics today.
Talking to lunatics is time-consuming and exhausting. Semmelweis decides on the most reasonable course of action.
After confirming that the person has no knowledge of Lorelei's whereabouts, Semmelweis decides not to waste any more time here.
All companions lose 75% HP, obtain Ancient Chalice.

[A Series of Dusks: Rhapsody of the Moon] is an expansion for [A Series of Dusks]. [Rhapsody of the Moon] builds on the base game mode, introducing new gameplay elements and increased difficulty levels, requiring you to take on an even more surreal and frenzied version of "Vienna." Suite of the Moon After loading up the new expansion, the "Suite of the Moon" feature becomes available. Before embarking on your exploration, you can visit the Suite of the Moon panel and choose from a variety of "Omen" modifiers. These modifiers add challenges to your gameplay, with each one increasing the current "Indulgence" value. The "Indulgence" value serves as an indicator for the difficulty level of your playthrough. Depending on this value, you may see changes in the appearance of the moon, with each moon phase representing a different difficulty bracket that adds even more dangerous effects to your playthrough. There are five difficulty brackets, or phases of the moon, determined by the current Indulgence value: [Misperception]: Low chance of increasing Stress at the start of the round. Very low chance of triggering Sudden Disaster. Clear Vision. Shard of Shadow gain +20%. [Illusory Sounds]: Low chance of increasing Stress at the start of the round. Low chance of triggering Sudden Disaster. Limited Vision. Shard of Shadow gain +20%. Enemy Control Resilience +20%. [Illusory Sight]: Moderate chance of increasing Stress at the start of the round. Moderate chance of triggering Sudden Disaster. Reduced Vision. Shard of Shadow gain +50%. Enemy Control Resilience +30%. [Illusory Touch]: High chance of increasing Stress at the start of the round. High chance of triggering Sudden Disaster. Majorly obstructed Vision. Shard of Shadow gain +100%. Enemy Control Resilience +50%. [Delirium]: High chance of significantly increasing Stress at the start of the round. Guaranteed to trigger Sudden Disaster. Severely obstructed Vision. Shard of Shadow gain +200%. Enemy Control Resistance +100%. Deployed characters get a decrease in Focus Chance. After completing an exploration, you will receive Shards of Shadow. These shards can be used to unlock new Catalyst incantations, Instinct buffs, or reset the cooldowns of certain Instinct buffs. If the Indulgence value is at 0, the Suite of the Moon will become inactive and no effects from Indulgence will impact you. You will also no longer be able to obtain Shards of Shadow. As the difficulty bracket of the Suite of the Moon increases, you'll be able to activate "Instinct" effects. By tapping on the broken mirror shards surrounding the image of the moon, a variety of Instincts can be chosen. The higher the difficulty bracket, the more Instincts can be activated, and the stronger their effects will be. After activating Instincts and clearing the second area, some of the Instincts will go into cooldown. Each time you clear the second area, or each area after that, these cooldowns are reduced by one round. Alternatively, you can use Shards of Shadow to instantly refresh the cooldowns. Stress in Battle After loading up the expansion, your characters will display a Stress meter while exploring. Actions taken during exploration will affect their Stress levels, which in turn will affect their behavior on the battlefield. When a character's Stress is low, they have a chance to trigger Vigilant Behavior based on their Afflatus. When a character's Stress is high, they have a chance to trigger Disorder Behavior based on their Afflatus. When a character's Stress reaches 50, they have either a low chance of triggering Focus Behavior, or a high chance of triggering Meltdown Behavior. Enemies also have Stress levels. The higher an enemy's stress, the more dangerous they become, forcing you to stay vigilant at all times. Core Content The core content is also updated—load up the new expansion to experience the following: New Catalysts: Two new Catalysts are added—the Silver Compass and the Rationality Loupe. New Path Nodes: Four new path nodes are added—Misty Domain, Into the Unknown, Perilous Encounter, and Treasure Trove. New Catalyst Incantations: Each Catalyst now has a new Catalyst incantation that can be unlocked by using Shards of Shadow. Some of these incantations can be cast by consuming Stimulus after completing certain path nodes. New Artefacts: Exciting new artefacts are added to the game. For more details, you will need to play through the new content yourself.

"Fugue of Reflections" is the latest expansion for "A Series of Dusks." This expansion adds a new ending to the base game and introduces character-exclusive artefacts known as [Acoustica]. More characters will rise to prominence in the pre-Storm Vienna. New Ending You don't need to have the expansion loaded up to experience the new ending, but you do need to have completed the [A Wish Granted] ending. Explore Vienna to see how to unlock the new conclusion. [Acoustica] Artefacts With the expansion loaded up, you can acquire [Acoustica] artefacts during exploration. These artefacts represent exclusive power ups for certain characters, and require the character to be in specific party positions to activate their effects. You can enhance Acoustica artefacts by meeting certain conditions. By meeting all enhancement requirements, an Acoustica artefact becomes [Fully Enhanced]. Based on how many fully enhanced artefacts are in your layout, additional [Harmonia] buff effects can be triggered, further strengthening your team. Completing the final path node of the Ring Road and defeating the [Impending Crisis] battle guarantees you one [Acoustica] artefact, prioritizing those exclusive to your current companion. You may also find Acoustica artefacts during exploration. [Current Characters with Acoustica Artefacts]: A Knight, Eagle, Voyager, Spathodea, Sonetto, Ms. NewBabel, Lilya, Lorelei, An-an Lee, Lucy, Jiu Niangzi, Anjo Nala, Lopera, Willow, Flutterpage, Barcarola, Charlie, Regulus, Druvis III, Matilda, 37, J, TTT, Semmelweis, Eternity, Medicine Pocket, Centurion, Sotheby, Melania, and Pickles. Tougher Battles With the expansion loaded up, enemy stats are increased. During an [Impending Crisis] and the final battle, you will also gain three powerful special incantations. Once used up, however, the enemies will become significantly stronger. Base Content The base content has also been updated with the following: New Path Node: The [Tuning Hall] path node has been added. New Combat Mechanics: Some battles can now include extra detrimental incantations that are added to your hand during combat. New Artefacts: [Acoustica] artefacts and [Fabled] quality artefacts have been added. More content awaits your discovery.

"The Effervescent Silence" is the final expansion of A Series of Dusks. The Effervescent Silence builds upon the base game mode by introducing new endings alongside the "Decisions" and "Tolls" mechanics, which require Timekeepers to make meaningful choices when selecting an area. Additionally, a new type of artifact, "Counteractive," has been added to counterbalance the effects of Tolls. New Ending Accessing the new ending does not require installing the expansion, but players must complete the ending "Wish Granted" first. The method to unlock it is left for Timekeepers to discover. Craftmaster's Favors With the update, Craftmaster's Favors will be introduced and do not require the expansion to be installed. At the end of an exploration, depending on the number of cleared areas (1/2/3/4/5), 2/3/4/6/8 Craftmaster's Favors will be automatically consumed, granting the same number of Keepsakes. "Decisions" and "Tolls" With the expansion installed, area selection will show Decision Effects and Toll artifacts. Each Decision Effect applies only to its respective area and disappears once you leave. Upon entering an area, Timekeepers must select and obtain one of three pre-revealed Toll artefacts and bear its Toll. Upon leaving the area, one of the remaining two Toll artefacts must also be chosen and obtained. Multiple Toll effects will continue to accumulate, even if they are the same effect. By toggling the Toll display option in the top right, Timekeepers can switch between viewing an artefact's base effects and the details of the Tolls. When making a Decision selection, Timekeepers may refresh once to reroll the available Decision effect and the Toll artefacts. While selecting a Toll artefact, refresh attempts can be used to change the artefact's Toll effect—but not the artefact itself. Fewer Path Nodes When the expansion is installed, certain areas will feature fewer path nodes, reducing the number of battle encounters. New Artefacts The expansion introduces Counteractive artefacts, which can be obtained during a playthrough. Additionally, more characters will receive their own Acoustica artefacts. For more information related to Acoustica artefacts, install the Fugue of Reflections expansion to explore their full potential. A set of sharp instruments, neatly wrapped in pristine white cloth. They pierce skulls, carve thoughts, and elevate the craft into an art form.
A lone chess piece among many, existing within the realm of imagination. While others drift and linger, this one leaps from its story, eager to charge into the next era.

Compact, convenient, and reliable—ever since its invention, these have been the hallmarks of its design. Arcanum managed to reach the finish line before human technology even took off. If only every user could control electricity, things would be much easier.
A well-worn clapperboard. With each retake, the title and scene numbers grow more scribbled, yet the sturdy wooden board remains dutiful and unchanged—Clap!
An invitation to a psychology salon from a spirited young scholar. A trembling quill seeks kindred minds, and the envelope carries her boundless insight and enthusiasm.
A humble set of painting tools. The colors are limited—perfect for children, or rather, for the future stars in the art world.
A handcrafted pendulum— a small echo of a budding artistic movement. A skilled user can sense its energy: fluid and unbound, like new branches stretching with life and potential.
A tool for straightening teeth—delicate, precise, and unyielding. With gentle force, it guides enamel and bone into perfect alignment over time.
A theater ticket to an enchanting performance of Tosca. The theater depends on its actors, and the actors on their craft—but no matter what, her portrayal of Tosca remains unmatched.
A clean, delicate, and immaculate headscarf. At this point, its symbolic value surpasses its practical use. Put it on—after all, who would suspect a maid?
Ice crystals, honeycombs, aromatic hydrocarbons—within finite geometry lies infinite meaning. Symmetry and balance are virtues, worthy of admiration and preservation.

A finely calibrated instrument designed to measure solar azimuth, first motion, and magnetic flux density—all to vectorize and analyze the fluctuations of a specific target's arcane fluctuations. Or, in simpler terms, it's a handy tool for gauging "ley energy."
A wooden model canoe, a crafted souvenir from across the ocean. Poets let their thoughts drift upon it—some glimpse rustic simplicity, others sense a deep yearning for home.
A peacock feather, one of the hundred eyes gifted by Hera. Handle it with care, for a tool of keen insight can just as easily become a blinding curse.

The gates stand open, the clock has stopped, and the tower's guardian is gone. And so, this journal becomes the object of greatest intrigue—clues within may reconstruct the truth, or weave an entirely new tale.
A simple, hand-stitched doll, found in street stalls and nestled by children's pillows. It has slowly learned to blink, to speak, to live—within the imagination of a child.
A practical reference book—sourced from mushrooms, shaped like mushrooms, and all about mushrooms. Warning: be mindful of hidden toxins while reading.
An instrument, a collectible. Priceless yet not for sale; ancient yet unverifiable; melodious yet now silent.

An instrument from an ancient civilization across the globe, yet favored by naturalist enthusiasts on Vienna's streets. A gentle tap lets it harmonize with birdsong and rustling leaves, composing a symphony of the wild.
The starry sky—the meeting place of reason and emotion. Amid endless revolutions, humans and arcanists converse, science and arcane skill complementing one another. She believes in it wholeheartedly.
Following the North Atlantic Drift, it merged into the waves of the river. The bottle's journey may rival the tale contained within.
A black veil, concealing grief and long-held wishes. In solemn silence, even tears become unnecessary.
A common flower—an unassuming yet passionate soul. In this era, silence and caution are virtues, but for a small bloom, such concerns are distant.
So much spinning, colliding, interlocking—given how busy they all are, does it even matter whether the result is tea or coffee?
It always aspired to be a solid, elegant shield, but alas, it was born too small and delicate. If the moment is right, perhaps it can bravely block a bullet aimed at your heart.
The street magician insists he never broke his promise—a king on a card is still a king. He suggests the Carbuncle seek out the rest of the deck to gather his own subjects.
A folded note, a piece of evidence, or a dose of poison? Choose freely what secret you wish to entrust—an ornate exterior always makes the best disguise.

It often tells the other pieces in the box about its origins—a suit of tiny armor with a soft body, its enamel glistening under the ocean's waves. If given another chance, it would still choose to be a shield.
