Thank you for the data, Vertin. Ahem, let's start the update right away. Now, about our new friend ... —X Ezio Auditore was born in 1459. In a diary entry from 1474, Maria Auditore, one of the greatest Florentine chroniclers and Ezio's mother, describes her son as "competitive, stubborn and loud mouthed, but so passionate that it is impossible to fault him for anything." His official records completely disappeared in 1476, as if he had never existed. In the same year, Uberto Alberti, Florence's Gonfaloniere, accused the Auditore family of treason against the city and sentenced them to death. Ezio's father and brothers, Giovanni Auditore, Federico Auditore, and Petruccio Auditore were thus executed in public at Piazza della Signoria.

1476 Ezio's family were arrested when he was out on an errand. In an attempt to stop their execution upon his return, he screamed that Uberto Alberti was a liar—the Gonfaloniere possessed the documents that could prove the Auditores' innocence, yet he denied any knowledge of such evidence. Ezio's vain attempt exposed himself; he barely escaped with the help of Giovanni's friend. Afterwards, he started to learn the skills required for being an Assassin. To fix the Hidden Blade which he inherited from Giovanni, Ezio was directed to Leonardo da Vinci, starting a friendship that would endure for the rest of their lives. With his Hidden Blade repaired, Ezio conducted the first assassination in his life: he sneaked into the courtyard of the Basilica di Santa Croce and stabbed Uberto Alberti through his chest. "The Auditore are not dead! I'm still here! Me! Ezio! Ezio Auditore!"

1476 After Uberto's assassination, Ezio became the most wanted man in Florence. He left the city with his mother and sister and found shelter at his uncle Mario's villa in Monteriggioni. Mario informed Ezio of the Assassins' existence, yet the young man refused to embrace his heritage. His top priority was to protect the family he had left and seek vengeance. 1478 During his hunt after the Pazzi family, Ezio gained information on a conspiracy against the Medici. He protected Lorenzo de' Medici from the public assassination at the Florence Cathedral. As the Pazzi's and Medici's troops battled in the streets, Ezio chased down and slew Francesco de' Pazzi at the Palazzo Vecchio. At Francesco's last moment, Ezio mourned for his enemy. "Meglio essere felici in questa vita che aspirare a esserlo nella prossima. (Better to be content in this life, than aspire to it in the next). Requiescat in Pace. (Rest in peace)."

1485 Ezio had already travelled through the entire Italian peninsula. In 1481, he went to Venice with Leonardo and formed an alliance with the Thieves' Guild. Later, he learned that Rodrigo Borgia, Pope Alexander VI, and Carlo Grimaldi were plotting to poison Giovanni Mocenigo, Doge of Venice. To stop them, Ezio flew across the sky of Venice using the aircraft made by Leonardo, but he was too late to save the Doge. Moments later, Ezio penetrated Carlo's chest with his Hidden Blade. After Giovanni Mocenigo's death, the Templars made Dante Moro the new Doge, who was, however, assassinated by Ezio at the Carnival of Venice months later. I know you all want to try that flying machine in the atrium. I wouldn't recommend that. —X

1488 On the next day after his 29th birthday, Ezio learned that the Templars were escorting a relic called "The Apple," aka "Piece of Eden," to their leader Rodrigo. They had their first fight, after which Rodrigo ran away. On the same night, Ezio was formally initiated into the Brotherhood by his uncle and friends and performed the ceremonial Leap of Faith. Shortly after that, Ezio gave the Apple to Leonardo for examination. The inventor believed that it was made of an unprecedented material and that its design was highly advanced despite its age. Many questions about this unique device remain unanswered even to this day. I added a note to this page, as your friend required: DO NOT SEARCH FOR IT. —X

1498 In 1494, Monk Girolamo Savonarola seized control of the City of Florence using the Apple which he took from Ezio during the Battle of Forlì. He started a movement named "Bonfire of the Vanities," which required the people to burn "the Devil's tools," including books and art. In 1497, Ezio returned to Florence and worked with Niccolò Machiavelli in an attempt to recover the Piece of Eden and free the city from Girolamo's tyranny. After Ezio assassinated all nine lieutenants of his, Girolamo was brought to the Piazza della Signoria to be burned at the stake by the resentful populace. With the decision that no one deserved to die in such agony, Ezio finished him with his Hidden Blade, putting him out of his misery. "We don't need anyone to tell us what to do. Not Savonarola, not the Medici. We are free to follow our own path." "It is our ability to choose—whatever you think is true that makes us human ... There is no book or teacher to give you the answers, to show you the path. Choose your own way! Do not follow me. Or anyone else."

Arnolfo di Cambio designed the Palazzo della Signoria (also known as the Palazzo Vecchio) in 1299, for the rulers of Florence, the Signoria. The Signoria was made up of nine members (or Priori) selected by the city's guilds and a Gonfaloniere of Justice. Interesting fact: The tower in front is off-center because it was incorporated into the Palazzo from an earlier structure. It contains two small cells, one of which was used to imprison Cosimo de' Medici. Besides, the Piazza della Signoria in front of the Palazzo Vecchio used to be an execution ground. A Knight: An execution ground right next to the center of power ... Someone believes some of those who sat on the throne were merely cowards.

One of Italy's largest churches and the largest landmark in Florence, Santa Maria del Fiore is considered by many to be the first masterpiece of Renaissance architecture. Although the church was designed by Arnolfo di Cambio in 1296, the dome was not started until the 15th Century. None of the architects at that time had any idea how to construct such an enormous structure, since the use of buttresses was forbidden in Florence and mortar took several days to set. But all was not lost. In an amazing comeback story, Filippo Brunelleschi, an architect who had been defeated in an earlier bid to design the Baptistery doors, won the competition to build the dome. He beat out Lorenzo Ghiberti, the same artist he had lost to before. Brunelleschi invented machines to hoist the bricks needed for the dome up to the workers and was able to construct the entire dome without using centring. X: Respect to Brunelleschi and his inventions! I think I'm inspired by his story. Since we already have machines that lift things up, why not invent something completely different? For example, a machine that drops things down.

Completed in 1473, the Palazzo Auditore is notable for its rusticated stonework and Roman pilasters. Giovanni Auditore designed the palazzo himself, based on initial sketches by Leone Battista Alberti. Once built, the palazzo became a fixture of the Santa Maria Novella district. Lorenzo de'Medici mentioned in a letter addressed to Giovanni, dated 1474, that he admired the façade's lack of "ostentation." An-an Lee: So cool, so fancy! If I could set a branch here ... think about the fortune I'd make!

Leonardo da Vinci opened his own studio after completing his apprenticeship to Verrocchio, one of the most successful Florentine artists of the day. Between 1476 and 1481, Leonardo probably continued to collaborate with Verrocchio, although no one is quite sure what he was working on. In 1481, he was given his first commission by the monks of San Donate a Scopeto, to paint The Adoration of the Magi. In true da Vinci style, he began the painting, but never finished it. Regulus: Hey, I must defend him on this one. "Unfinished paintings are more admired than the finished ..." No! That doesn't apply to the 27 club!

Constructed over an existing church in 1258, Santa Trinita (Holy Trinity) is known for its Sassetti chapel, which is decorated with frescos of the life of Saint Francis by Domenico Ghirlandaio, a painter most famous for his brief role as one of Michelangelo's teachers. Santa Trinita was the mother church of the Vallumbrosan order of monks, a very serious group that strictly enforced both poverty and silence, for life. 37: I don't think they knew anything about their numbers, but they still remind me of my friends on the island ...

Designed by Filippo Brunelleschi and opened in 1445, the Ospedale degli Innocenti (Hospital of the Innocents) was an orphanage for unwanted babies. Babies were typically abandoned in a basin in the front, although later transactions were facilitated by the introduction of a rotating horizontal wheel which moved infants into the building without the parent being seen. Many a mother abandoned her baby in order to be hired by the Ospedale as a wet nurse, so she could be paid to feed her own child. X: Life was a bit boring growing up in the orphanage. Fortunately, I had a lot of old components to play with. This makes me wonder what these children did for fun. Maybe catching animals, climbing trees, or ... studying alchemy?

The Church in which all the Medici went to die, San Lorenzo claims to be the oldest in Florence. It was consecrated in 393, while still outside the city walls. Michelangelo designed the inner façade, while Filippo Brunelleschi, the creator of Santa Maria del Fiore's dome, designed the layout. He died before the church was finished and several of his designs were subsequently modified. Containing nearly fifty tombs, the Medici crypt was intended to house the Holy Sepulchre containing the body of Christ at its centre. However, attempts to buy it and, then, to steal it from Jerusalem failed. Necrologist: These stone coffins speak with the utmost courtesy. People's habits are indeed hidden within their souls.

The Palazzo Ducale was constructed from 1309-1424, in the Gothic style, as the residence for the Doge. The Doge was the highest ranking elder in Venice and served in his position for life. In 1172, the selection of the Doge became entrusted to a committee of 40 (the Forty), whose members were chosen by the Venetian Great Council. Venice liked to think of itself as a Republic, meaning that the people could participate in the government. When the Doge took office he was introduced to the people with the words: "This is the Doge, if it please you." In fact, members of the Great Council were appointed by the forty, which in turn chose the Forty. Candidates for the Great Council were selected from a small pool containing only noble families and although the Doge could nominate anyone to the Council, the Forty and the Council itself had to approve the nomination. Druvis III: They built a club which they claimed to be open for everyone, yet left a barking dog to guard the door.

The Scuola Grande di San Marco was one of the six large charitable organizations founded in Venice to help citizens afford food, dowries, processions, marriages, burials and anything else they might need. Notably, membership was open to any citizen of Venice, not just the elite. Citizenship status was conferred on third generation Venetians or those who had paid taxes for fifteen years. The façade of the building, which was built in 1260, was destroyed in a 1485 fire, causing it to be rebuilt in its current, opulent Byzantine form. Desert Flannel: Strewth! Free food and supplies? If only they had a branch in Melbourne! Think about the money I could've saved!

This famous bridge spans the Arno at it narrowest point. The original version was presumably constructed by the Romans, but the first written records only appear in 996. Two previous incarnations of the bridge were swept away in floods before the present structure was built in 1345. A tower was built at the southeast corner to defend it. The bridge consists of three segmental arches. It has always had shops lining the central passageway, a feature which seems extraordinary now, but was common during the Renaissance. In 1549, the Medici family purchased the Palazzo Pitti and rebuilt the bridge. The new design included a secret tunnel through which the Medicis could travel between the Palazzo Pitti and the Palazzo della Signoria without being spotted. Lilya: Secret tunnel? Hah. They'd better pray no one intercepts them in the middle. Not everyone's as merciful as I was.

First built as a naval depot for private ships, the Arsenal was rebuilt and enlarged in 1320. From that point on, it was used by the Venetian state to construct and maintain its ships. Famously, at the peak of production, shipbuilders were able to produce an entire ship in a day. The impressive front gate (the Porta Magna) went up in 1460, in the Classical revivalist style. Fogwalker: Produce an entire ship in a day? That workload could've taken much more time. Would the workers be allowed to rest in the next few days?

Constructed in the late 15th century as a display of Venice's wealth, the Torre dell'Orologio displays the time of the day, the current phase of the moon, and the dominant sign of the Zodiac. According to legend, the designers of the clock face were blinded once their work was complete, so they could never duplicate it elsewhere. The designers lived inside the clock tower for the rest of their lives to maintain it. The Torre dell'Orologio ended up serving one very important practical purpose; it was used by sailors in the nearby harbor to time their departures with the tide. Ms. Radio: The bell ringing was the only "broadcast channel" they had at that time. Whatever era it is, people always need broadcast to bring their hearts together.

The illegitimate son of a notary and a peasant woman, Leonardo da Vinci was raised in Tuscany. At age 14, he was apprenticed to a Florentine painter, Verrocchio, who taught him chemistry, drafting, painting, sculpting and modelling. When he was 20, Leonardo established his own workshop, and then travelled across Italy, eventually painting his masterpieces "The Last Supper" in 1498 and "The Mona Lisa" in 1503-1507. During his travels, Leonardo studied the world with unquenchable curiosity. He created designs for a helicopter, tank, solar power and a calculator, among others. Despite this epic list of accomplishments, Leonardo was hounded by his patrons for his chronic procrastination. Pieces frequently took years longer than he anticipated and many were never finished at all. APPLe: There's no doubt he's a nice friend! But artistic talent always comes with a loose concept of time. This APPLe learned that long ago from the Captain ...

The world-famous Carnival of Venice began in 1296, as a public holiday on the day before Lent. It soon became a time for masquerades, parties, theatrical performances, parades, street dances, egg throwing, flirtation, and general hijinks. Regulus: I'm going to be there sooner or later! A carnival where people enjoy freedom and chaos, haha! I'm sure they can use the Pirate Radio to lighten the mood! APPLe said Mr. Assassin, in every sense of the word, had had a wonderful time on this carnival. I guess he wouldn't mind taking me there ...

Diagrams of the human body and the printing press influenced Renaissance medicine greatly, which had in turn been influenced by Arabic medicine during the Middle Ages. By the 15th Century, science had already begun its slow climb toward becoming more relevant than spirituality in the field of healthcare. However, many people clung to old ways, visiting local mystics instead of doctors. After the plague ravaged Europe in 1350, many doctors dressed in special plague gear to treat patients. To prevent contamination, they wore a cape coated in wax, and a primitive gas mask in the shape of a beak. Mesmer Jr.: Every Mesmer knows that history and how it developed into the standard precautions. I didn't wash my hands for no reason.

Every Renaissance community needed a blacksmith. Swords, locks, pans, knives, nails and armor were all made from metal and all needed to be shaped. In addition, architectural ironwork flourished during the Renaissance as blacksmiths began to apply their practical craft towards making art. A skillful Assassin can't do without a skillful blacksmith. J: Our new friend's from Italy? Then I gotta let him try the Haight Street gear and the Hawaiian pizza ... No? Especially not the latter?

The countryside during the Renaissance was filled with bandits, causing most travellers to move in armed groups called caravans. Anxious voyagers usually sewed valuables and gold into the soles of their shoes or the lining of their jackets. Guides called Vetturini were sometimes hired to help plot the route of the caravans and book rooms at local inns, but those carriers were often working with the bandits. Name Day: Whatever era it is, travelling is not an easy thing, don't you think?

With the advent of double-entry bookkeeping, which allowed bankers to keep track of their clients' deposits and withdrawals, and the proliferation of many different types of Italian currency into the pool of circulation, banks became an essential part of everyday Renaissance life. Sotheby: Mr. Karson and Ms. Moissan said bookkeeping was a must-learn for every lady, but I didn't know it was also a necessary skill for Assassins! I guess Mr. Auditore learned it from his sister, who he said was a great accountant. I wish I could meet her in person.

The shops of Renaissance artists were usually small, and dealt mainly in religious decorations for churches or homes. Artists were treated as craftsmen, just like carpenters and blacksmiths. The production of art was usually cooperative. The head of the shop was the master, who received commissions and oversaw the assembly of the painting. He was expected to be a businessman and turn a profit, usually creating copies of whatever religious paintings were in vogue at the time. Melania: Painters became merchants in the end ... I guess that's just what life is like. I'd prefer a path with more possibilities though.

The dome of Santa Maria del Fiore was designed by the famous architect, Filippo Brunelleschi, yet built by a group of ordinary workers whom no one remembers. During the construction, they were required to bring their lunch to the site and finish it where they worked, since it was dangerous to descend and climb the scaffoldings. In 1426, Brunelleschi opened taverns within the dome with kitchens and wine, allowing the workers to eat without leaving their work—even though the project they were working on was bound to go down in history, they cared more about the food on the table and the money in their pockets. X: Let's take a break. I'll see you at the canteen.

The Parthenon is one of the most well-known buildings in the world, and an enduring symbol of Ancient Greek civilization. While it is located on the Akropolis, the building is not a traditional temple. It was built by the sculptor Phidias and the architects Kallikrates and Iktinos as a great monument to the glory of the city of Athens. That glory is evident in its many carvings. One of the most carved monuments in Greek architecture, the Parthenon's decorations depict several mythological scenes. These include the birth of Athena, her fight against Poseidon for the patronage of Athens, the gods' battle with the giants and the procession of the Great Panathenaia. Cristallo: The book says it was "the cradle of a civilization." I told that to the nurse ... then she brought me a pinch of soil the next day. I put it under my pillow and fell asleep. That night, I dreamed of myself having fun among a parade ...

The Athenian assembly was known as the ekklesia. It met at the Pnyx forty times a year to discuss various civic matters, and each session usually lasted a few hours. The word pnyx is believed to mean something close to "packed together." This was probably a reference to the fact that during meetings of the ekklesia, the location would be filled to its capacity, with citizens packed in practically shoulder-to-shoulder. All male citizens were allowed to directly participate in the democratic process. Those over twenty years old had the right to speak and vote, while those over thirty could be elected to the higher position of magistrate. In total, there were approximately 30,000 citizens in Athens in the classical period. To draft and adopt decrees, 6,000 of them had to attend the meeting. Poltergeist: "Packed together"?! Th-That's horrible! It's like the crowded beach torture all over again ... I was lying on the sand, covered under my white sheet, but no one noticed me ... They just stepped on my body as if no one was there ... *crying*

Next to the Naxian Sphinx stood a simple structure to display offerings from the Athenians, most of which were spoils of war. In particular, these offerings—called "ex-votos"—were prows of sunken Persian ships. The Athenians built the portico after their naval victory over the Persians in 478 BCE. This building showcases Athens's dominance as a naval power. Its location suggests that the Athenians attributed their victories to divine favor. Archaeological findings also reveal that each ship's prow underwent a ritual purification before it was permitted to be displayed as a war trophy. Jessica: "Ex-votos"? I get it. It's like a token of memory, right? My friends who ran away from the forest had left me many "ex-votos." Like iron boxes with food in them, a little button that makes fire ... and a lot of glasses of water that can make critters dizzy.

The theater of Delphi was situated above the Temple of Apollo. It offered an expansive view of sanctuary and the valley below, and could accommodate around 5,000 spectators in its seats. The theater hosted different artistic contests, especially during competitions like the Pythian Games. These contests included plays, poetry readings, and musical performances, and were held not only for the audience, but also for Apollo, the god of arts—among other things. Diggers: It melts my heart! Who designed this art piece? They must be a genius! If we had a theater like this in London, everyone would understand the truth of love and peace!

At last we arrive at the Temple of Apollo, where the Oracle relayed her prophecies. The temple was the final destination of those seeking an audience with the Pythia, and its appearance matched the majesty of its purpose. Atop its imposing columns, the structure's pediments displayed famous mythological scenes sculpted by the renowned Greek artist Antenor. But as grand as the temple looked from the outside, it paled in comparison with what happened within. Ms. Moissan: Although buildings stay silent most of the time, I always told my students that history—the "truth" of what happened in the past—could be found in the corners, but you must be careful enough to notice them.

According to Pausanias, the two most important Spartan temples were the temple of Artemis Orthia, and the temple of Athena Chalkioikos. Pausanias describes the building of the sanctuary of Athena Chalkioikos in great detail. It was located on the Akropolis of Sparta, west of the agora. Its construction was started by the mythical king of Sparta, Tyndareos, but was completed by the Spartan sculptor Gitiadas in the 6th century BCE. The epithet Chalkioikos (house from bronze) was attached to this temple due to the bronze and copper decorations on its walls. These embossed sheets depicted mythological scenes like Herakles's labors, achievements of the sons of Tyndareos, the legend of Perseus and Medusa, and the birth of Athena. The bronze decorations and the bronze statue of Athena were the works of Gitiadas, who also composed a hymn to the goddess. Sweetheart: You have to admit that distance makes the heart grow fonder—people are crazy about legendary goddesses and stars on TV ... I keep my distance well. That's how I maintain my charms.

The Akropolis of Sparta consisted of several buildings that date from different chronological periods – from the Archaic to the Byzantine era. At the top of the Akropolis was the sanctuary of Athena Chalkioikos, dated to the 6th century BCE. It was originally a sanctuary of Pitane, as confirmed by archaeological discoveries dating as early as the Mycenaean period. Near the sanctuary of Athena was the ancient theater of Sparta. It is based on a structure dated to the Roman period. The theater probably had a wooden stage; a fact supported by several inscriptions from the 2nd century CE. Excavations next to the theater also revealed connected shops. The Akropolis of Sparta also held visible traces of the Skias, the semi-circular building of the archaic-classical periods—but with visible repairs from the Roman period. Pickles: Woof ... Woof? Woof.

The Olympic Games were dedicated to Zeus, and all the ceremonies and events were hosted in his honor. It's no surprise that the largest temple in the sanctuary was the Temple of Zeus. While most temples were restricted to priests, the Temple of Zeus welcomed all who visited Olympia. This openness was most likely meant to show off the gold and ivory statue of Zeus that stood within the temple's walls. The building also featured art depicting both versions of the Olympic festival's founding myth. The eastern pediment showed a scene from the legendary race between Pelops and Oinomaos. The temple's metopes, meanwhile, showed the twelve labors of Herakles, the other mythical founder of the games. Spathodea: If only we could hold the Uluru Games there one day ... perhaps both humans and arcanists would forget about all their conflicts and simply immerse themselves in sports.

The Heraion was a temple dedicated to Hera. It is one of the oldest temples in the sanctuary, dating back to approximately 590 BCE. The structure included columns painted with images of women who won the Heraia, an athletic competition made up of running events. Every four years, sixteen women were chosen to make a veil dedicated to Hera. These women also organized the competition, though they did not compete in it. The Heraia was unique for its focus on female athletes, in contrast to the male-exclusive Olympic Games. Ulu: Despite their races, colors, and backgrounds, all athletes deserve the right to enjoy sports and pursue after victory!

This workshop was built for the renowned sculptor Phidias after his work on the Akropolis of Athens. In 435 BCE, Phidias came to Olympia to begin working on the great chryselephantine statue of Zeus. He died five years later, shortly after completing his masterpiece. This grand statue would become one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. Phidias's workshop was located right next to the Temple of Zeus. Its structure has been well preserved, mostly owing to its conversion to a church in the 5th century CE. Archaeologists have also discovered lots of ancient materials in the surrounding area, such as casting molds and sculpting tools. The most famous artifact, however, is a cup bearing an inscription that aggressively states: "I belong to Phidias!" Hissabeth: I should label my sandwich before putting it in the fridge. "I belong to Hissabeth!" ... No, Pointer won't even have to worry about stealing the wrong sandwich if I do so.

The Theater of Dionysos as it exists today dates back to the 4th century BCE, when the statesman Lykourgos reorganized the sanctuary. lt features a circular orchestra, with a stone skene—or stage—in front of it. However, archaeologists believe that the original shape of the orchestra was a square. In the Hellenistic period, 67 marble thrones reserved for city officials were added around the orchestra. At the center of this row was a seat meant for the priest of Dionysos. During the Roman period, a new stage was built in honor of both the god and the emperor Nero, and extra seats of honor were added around the edge of the orchestra. Mercuria: Since ancient times, especially when life was hard, people have sought relaxation in music and dance—it is the call of our souls.

Located in Ithaka, Odysseus' Palace is said to be the personal residence of Odysseus, the hero in Homer's epic poem Odyssey. He was the most illustrious of all Greek heroes and one of the chiefs who set out for Troy. He returned to lthaka and reclaimed his palace twenty years later. In 431 BCE, Kassandra sneaked into the palace to retrieve the Shroud of Penelope. During her operation, she came across Odessa, a descendant of Odysseus, and freed her from the cage. The two of them explored the ruins together before they left. Lilya: The only way to retrieve the respect one has lost is to fight, and that's true for both men and kingdoms.

Oh, this profile must belong to the other new friend of ours. It says she made herself a nationwide legend as she travelled around the ancient Greece ... —X 431 BCE Kassandra and Herodotus arrived in Athens, where she met Perikles and Kleon for the first time. The politician and the general were exchanging debates at the Pnyx, fighting for the citizens' support. Herodotus told Kassandra to attend Perikles's symposium to tell him about the Cult of Kosmos. She showed up there and met Socrates, Aristophanes, Alcibiades, and Aspasia, Perikles' lover. Eventually, Kassandra managed to speak to Perikles, starting the search for her parents.

451 BCE On a stormy night, Kassandra as a child tried to save her brother from being sacrificed but was thus condemned as a traitor to Sparta. Her father was forced to drop her off the cliff, yet Kassandra luckily survived and escaped to the open sea on a boat. The raging storm, however, turned her boat overboard and eventually brought her to the beaches of Kephallonia. There, she was found by a local merchant Markos, who offered her a piece of bread in exchange for her help in the future. Kassandra accepted, marking a new beginning of her life. "Don't see fishes like you everyday, eh?" —Markos

431 BCE After killing Elpenor, Kassandra used his outfit to disguise herself and infiltrated the Sanctuary of Delphi. In there, she saw a group of masked people in black robes surrounding a glowing pyramid. While she was eavesdropping on the Cultists, Deimos, the weapon of the Cult, entered the chamber with Elpenor's head in his hand, claiming that a traitor lurked in their midst. To find the traitor, Deimos used the pyramid to examine the members' memories. When it was Kassandra's turn, the artifact showed them memories of their childhood. Kassandra realized that Deimos was her lost brother Alexios, while the latter was disturbed and confused. In the end, to cover up their relation, Deimos let go of Kassandra and executed a scape goat with the pyramid. Mind reading technology, sounds dangerous ... both mentally and physically. —X

429-426 BCE Kassandra returned to Sparta with her mother Myrrine, hoping to free their homeland from the Cult's control. She suppressed a helot revolt to win Pausanias's recognition, which granted her an audience to the kings. Archidamos, the other king, however, didn't like them for what had happened on Mount Taygetos. To prove her loyalty, she had to leave Sparta to complete the kings' tasks, during which she ended the Cult's control over Arkadia and found Pausanias's true identity—a Cultist. Returning to Sparta, Kassandra exposed Pausanias as a Cultist, causing him to be dethroned and exiled. As he ran away, Kassandra tracked him down and killed him, achieving the goal of her return. "These traitors are willing to kill hundreds to rule thousands." —Kassandra

451 BCE Myrrine, the daughter of King Leonidas, and General Nikolaos met and got married after Kassandra's father left them. Seven years later, they had a son together named Alexios. They had lived a happy life until one rainy night. A prophecy said that Alexios would bring about the fall of Sparta, which could only be stopped through his sacrifice. The priest of Sparta was about to drop Alexios off Mount Taygetos when Kassandra attempted to save her brother. Unfortunately, she pushed the priest and Alexios to their apparent deaths. But the tragedy was not over: Nikolaos, adherent to Spartan law, was forced to drop Kassandra off the mountain as a punishment. That night, the wail of a mother echoed around the entire Sparta. Our world is good at making orphans, and you never know how. —X

428 BCE Kassandra escorted Testikles to Kyllene for the Olympic Games on Pausanias's order. When the latter wanted to harass Kassandra, who dodged his hug swiftly, he fell into the sea and was eaten by a shark. Suggested by her ally Alkibiades, Kassandra took Testikles's place and competed in the pankration for Sparta. Defeating two opponents in the qualifier, she advanced to the final, but then she was told that Alkibiades had been poisoned, so she subsequently went to Fort Koroibos to find an antidote before continuing with the game. During the final, Kassandra fought the champion Dorieus and won the competition. Later, she found that Kallias, the judge of the game, was a Cultist and the one who poisoned Alkibiades, so she killed him, securing the safety of the Games. "Players usually applied olive oil on their bodies to avoid being grasped" ... I should keep this document from Ulu and Spathodea. —X

Behind the Propylaea was the giant bronze statue of Athena Promachos, or "Athena who fights on the front lines." That name was reflected in the spear and shield the statue held in its hands. It was erected in the mid 5th century BCE by the artist Phidias. According to an inscription, it took nine years to make, and cost almost half a million drachmae. At approximately ten meters tall, the statue was apparently so large that Pausanias claimed its helmet and spear tip could be seen from the sea near Cape Sounion, sixty kilometers away. The ornamentation on the statue's shield was engraved by the metalsmith Mys. Diggers: Look at the spear and shield in her hands ... They are the origin of avant-garde art from 2,000 years ago! They signify the spirit to fight!

The Great Dionysia was supervised by the head magistrate known as the archon, who was assisted by twelve other magistrates. Among his duties, the archon picked choregoi—rich Athenian citizens responsible for providing the budget for rehearsals and performances. Two days before the Dionysia, a ceremony called the proagon took place where playwrights introduced their work. The Dionysia finally began in earnest with a procession to the god's temple, followed by sacrifices and a symposium. The next two days centered on dithyramb contests, while the final four days were dedicated to drama competitions. The contests' outcomes were decided by ten judges, who were appointed at random by the archon. The judges placed their votes in an urn, and five of the votes were randomly picked to determine the winner. The Fool: The most important part of a tragedy is the curtain call—the king who just shed blood opens his eyes again, the princess who committed suicide rises once more ... Their bows towards the supreme leader make the tragedies complete!

The sirens were beautiful but deadly creatures that lived on a rocky island. Their song was so enchanting, sailors who heard their singing fell to the rocks. Sirens were half-women, half-birds—or at least, that was how they were represented in Greek art. They were usually depicted played musical instruments, such as harps. In "The Odyssey," Odysseus was very curious to listen to them, so Circe the witch told him how he could enjoy their song without danger. Odysseus had his sailors plug their ears with beeswax and tie him to the pole of his ship. When they passed near the sirens, Odysseus was mesmerized by the song. He begged his sailors to release him, but they couldn't hear him. This trick saved his life and the lives of his companions. Lorelei: The sirens ... They were expecting listeners who understood them, don't you think? But the side effect of their voices is too strong ... Hmm, maybe they should just sing to the conchs.

Prophecies were given in the most restricted part of the temple, the adyton, by a chaste woman known as the Pythia. Before delivering prophecies, she first purified herself with water, then burned laurel leaves and barley flour to begin the ritual. Finally, while seated on a tripod surrounded by offerings, the Pythia delivered Apollo's messages. Her words were often strange and indecipherable, and required further interpretation by the temple's priests. Despite much research, the exact causes of the Oracle's behavior while prophesying are debated to this day. Mercuria: Burning laurel leaves ... Its smell remains the same after thousands of years, and it will never change, like the laws of the universe.

Sparta's political system differed from most of Greece's. One of its most distinctive features was that it was ruled by two kings. These kings belonged to two separate dynasties: the Eurypontids and the Agiads, both of which were said to be descended from Herakles. Both kings shared equal powers, and disputes between them required the intervention of special magistrates known as ephors. However, if one of the kings were more charismatic or experienced, they could influence the weaker king's choices. Isolde: Heh-heh ... One kingdom with two kings. How curious, just like one body with two heads. If either of them had a knife ...

The pentathlon took place at the stadium on the second day. As its name implies, it was made up of five events: discus throwing, javelin throwing, jumping, racing, and wrestling. There are several differences between the ancient version of events and their contemporary counterparts. For example, ancient long jumpers held weights in their hands to give them momentum to launch, since there was no run-up before the jump. Similarly, if an athlete won the first three events, they were immediately declared the winner, instead of being judged by their overall performance in all five events. Running events worked the same as they do today—with the notable exception of all the athletes being nude. As for wrestling, competitors were not divided by weight class as they are today, but instead by age. The winner was the first to throw his opponent to the ground three times. X: Update suspended. It's time for some eye, finger, and hip exercises!

In the field of cryptography, the scytale is a device used for transposition ciphers. It involves wrapping a strip of parchment around a cylindrical rod, with the message written across the surface. This method was reportedly employed by the ancient Greeks—especially the Spartans—for secure communication during military operations. This device can carry secret information stably at a low cost, yet its disadvantage is also obvious: anyone can decrypt as long as they have heard of this encryption method. X: This is inspiring ... I wonder if it's possible to invent a new kind of scytale which only those who have never heard of it can decrypt ...

"Lysimachus, where are you? For the love of Athena, I told you not to provoke those dangerous men ..." The anxious priestess looked around, her eyes pleading for help.
"Eagle Bearer, Lysimachus has gone missing for two days. Find her I beg you, and bring her back safely."

Lysimachus's house looks ordinary and quiet.
Perhaps a little too quiet—an uneasy feeling lingers in the air.

The back door was wide open, and the interior was in disarray.
The intruders didn't seem to loot the place; the floor was marked with signs of struggle and dragging.
In the corner by the doorframe, a few dark snake scales lay scattered.

"Stop your rituals. Your fake god deserves no offerings. Stop now, or you will lose more."
The handwriting is barely legible, and at the end of the letter, a poorly-done snake pattern is drawn.

"No warrior can say no to a finely forged sword, and there's one that cuts through iron like butter—a sword perfect for you."
The bard tries to pique Kassandra's interest.
"Do you know the sword's origin? The gods used it to uphold justice. It was once hidden in Athenian ruins but has since gone missing. If you want to find the sword, search the bandit camp on the city outskirts ..."

"When he tantalizes our hearts, *hic* it's through ... getting drunk! He shows me the art of ... dancing!"
A heavily drunk man staggers through the street, leaving chaos wherever he goes.
"Someone help stop him; the Dionysia hasn't even started yet! Hey, put that jar down! Stop smashing things!"

"O mighty Zeus, barbaric bandits are terrorizing our village, please grant us a worthy warrior to wipe out these thugs at their hideout in the Melissani Cave!"
Did Zeus hear our plea?  Does he care about us? No one knows. Either way, fate has brought you here.

"More and more wolves have been appearing on the mountain lately, and people are too afraid to go mine iron."
The old blacksmith speaks with worry, sighing and pounding his hands nonstop.
"What use is a blacksmith without iron ore? I beg you—please deal with those wolves on Mount Ainos."

A merchant caravan is in an uproar; Kassandra decides to see what is going on.
"I shouldn't have put my faith in your petty vineyard. If the goods don't arrive soon, we're leaving!"
"Listen, the transport team is supposed to arrive this morning. I worry they might've run into trouble on the road."
Kassandra asks about the transport route and departure time, her expression growing serious. "I'm afraid things aren't looking good."
Following the trade route, Kassandra reaches a clifftop where the hoofprints and wheel tracks are in complete disarray.

Looking down the cliff, Kassandra notices that the wagon has shattered into pieces, and all the cargo was stolen.
"With so many heavy crates, the bandits couldn't have gone far."
Kassandra spots the bodies of several merchants. It appears they had tried to hide from the bandits but were shot down by arrows.

The bandits tried to cover their tracks, but with so many people involved, plenty of clues remained.
The scattered footprints appear again to the west, and Kassandra heads in that direction.

The temple healer tends to the wounded soldiers. Stone statues stand solemnly around them, and the injured dare not groan too loudly.
"You see, there are many wounded here, and we've gone through the antler powder far too quickly. If you're familiar with Mount Parnassos, could you help me find some deer antlers?"

"Misthios, the sapphire worshiped in the temple has been stolen! The gods will surely take out their anger on us!"
The priest's anger flares up, eager to personally thrash the thief.
"I heard thieves like to hide in caves, and there are some abandoned caves west of the temple. Maybe you can find them there."
Just as she was about to leave, the statue at the end of the cave caught Kassandra's attention. An inconspicuous hexagonal groove is hidden beneath the statue's chest.
Upon inserting the sapphire, the statue slowly moves aside, showing a narrow tunnel behind.

At the end of the tunnel, Kassandra discovers the long-forgotten treasure. Could it be that the sapphire's original purpose was to open the secret chamber? Then who was the first person to place the treasure here ...
The town's bulletin board displays the latest bounty: a wild boar is injuring people, and sharp spears can't penetrate its hide. Brave warriors are needed to take it down—quickly!

"Demaratos hasn't reported yet, which is unusual—Spartan soldiers never forget their assembly time."
The sergeant's face is stern. He clearly trusts his men deeply and is now greatly worried.
"Something must have happened ... but I can't leave the camp now. Could you help me find Demaratos?"

Tracing the road from the assembly point, Kassandra arrives at the path Demaratos might have taken.
It is a secluded area, overgrown with trees and bushes—an ideal spot for an ambush.
Sure enough, in the bushes, Kassandra discovers a broken spear. She senses the presence of a fight.

Following the trail of bloodstains and footprints, Kassandra reaches a hilltop, where a makeshift bandit camp comes into view.
The bandits are scrambling to try on the stolen Spartan armor, while the poor young victim lies tossed aside.

"I know you're an excellent athlete, and if I'm not mistaken, you're quite skilled with a javelin too?"
Kassandra nods, as this is nothing unfamiliar to a seasoned warrior.
"Then please take a look. I suspect the opponent's javelin is rigged. And cheating is not allowed in Olympia."

The suspected athlete appears calm, but Kassandra notices something off—the javelin, though well disguised, has a different weight distribution and is made of non-standard materials.
In other words, it's a custom-made javelin designed for cheating in competition.

"The athlete suddenly fell ill?" The judge, upon hearing the news, scans the surroundings and locks eyes with Kassandra.
"You look fit and agile—if you step into the arena, the crowd is bound to give you the warmest of welcomes. Care to give it a try?"

While admiring the Heraion, Kassandra discovers a string of unfamiliar symbols on a hidden pedestal slab.
"Maybe the scytale can be used here too?"

"Olive tree ... southeast ... Olympia ..."
Does this point to the location of some treasure? Or perhaps a trap set to catch those sniffing for sensitive information?
There seems to be something hidden among the roots of the stunted olive tree.
Built to the glory of Athens's protector, the Parthenon housed the gold and ivory statue of Athena made by Phidias. Made of Pentelic marble, the structure held the city's and Delian League's riches.
Situated on a hill, this was where Athenians gathered for assemblies. Decrees were ratified, budgets voted on, and administration members appointed. It was where citizens could have a voice.
This building was constructed against the polygonal wall that supported the terrace of the temple of Apollo and was used for setting up ex-votos, mostly spoils of war.
The theater of Delphi was situated above the Temple of Apollo. It offered an expansive view of sanctuary and the valley below, and could accommodate around 5,000 spectators in its seats.
This was built inside the god's sanctuary and introduced Greek theater to the heart of the city. The great works of Euripides, Aischylos, Sophokles, and Aristophanes were performed there.
Behind the Propylaea was the giant bronze statue of Athena Promachos, or "Athena who fights on the front lines."

The Dionysia began in earnest with a procession to the god's temple, followed by sacrifices and a symposium. The next two days centered on dithyramb contests, while the final four days were dedicated to drama competitions.
Spartans used a cipher to communicate during military operations. They wrote on leather strips, which were wrapped around a wooden stick.
431 BCE, Kassandra and Herodotus arrived in Athens. Herodotus told Kassandra to attend Perikles's symposium to tell him about the Cult of Kosmos.
The sirens were beautiful but deadly creatures that lived on a rocky island. Their song was so enchanting, sailors who heard their singing fell to the rocks.
Odysseus, the most illustrious of all Greek heroes, was among the chiefs who set out for Troy. He returned to Ithaka and reclaimed his palace twenty years later.

451 BCE, Kassandra was brought to the beaches of Kephallonia by a raging storm. There, she was found by a local merchant Markos, who offered her a piece of bread in exchange for her help in the future.
431 BCE, Kassandra disguised herself as a cult member and infiltrated the Sanctuary of Delphi. In there, she realized that Deimos was her lost brother Alexios.
Prophecies were given in the most restricted part of the temple, the adyton, by a chaste woman known as the Pythia.
The Panhellenic Sanctuary of Delphi was renowned for the Oracle of Apollo, and considered the center of the world in ancient Greece.
429-426 BCE, Kassandra publicly unveiled Pausanias the cultist King, forcing him to be ousted.
451 BCE, the priest of Sparta was about to drop Alexios off Mount Taygetos when Kassandra attempted to save her brother. Unfortunately, she pushed the priest and Alexios to their apparent deaths.
Sparta's political system differed from most of Greece's. One of its most distinctive features was that it was ruled by two kings.
The temple of Athena on the akropolis was one of Sparta's most important monuments. The bronze sheets that decorated its interior gave birth to the name Chalkioikos.
The Akropolis of Sparta consisted of several buildings that date from different chronological periods – from the Archaic to the Byzantine era.
428 BCE, Kassandra competed in the pankration final, fought the champion Dorieus and won the competition for Sparta.
"Pentathlon" is held on the second day of the Olympic Games.
The temple housed one of the seven wonders of the ancient world: Phidias's statue of Zeus. To close the Olympic games, a procession led to the temple where victorious athletes were crowned.
The Heraia were games for women organized in honor of Hera. Every four years, the sixteen Elis women in charge of organizing the Heraia wove a new veil for the goddess and placed it in her temple.

Phidias was the greatest Greek sculptor. He created many masterpieces, including the Olympic sanctuary's gold and ivory statue of Zeus, which was considered one of the seven wonders of the ancient world.
I'll do everything in my power.
How strange, a siren calling for help.
Athens doesn't usually have people as ... straightforward as you.
A mercenary asking another mercenary for help?
Do you need me to fight your enemy?
Does this mean I will be working with a Gorgon?
I can't think of any feasible way to do that.
She seems to be an irrational number like you said.
She couldn't give me any proper response.
I don't think theatergoers would casually talk about the Cult.
I'm surprised I can actually understand some of this.
Maybe I'm witnessing an oracle being revealed.
Why? In fact, I'm just the right person for you: I'm a misthios—I solve problems for a living.
It's okay. Your secrets are safe with me.
A siren is calling out by the roadside, but all passersby cover their ears to avoid her.
Please! Hear my words! I am looking for a warrior who is brave enough to challenge the stormy sea!
At last, a kind and brave woman. People here tend to see Rusalki as sea monsters. It's hard to find someone who'll listen.
Long story short, a sea monster—your people seem to call it Skylla—has come to this coastline. Someone must drive it away, or the harbor will be flooded.
If you're willing to help, go find Ms. Lorelei by the shore. She's holding Skylla back and waiting for a brave soul like you.
At last, a curious woman. People here tend to see Rusalki as sea monsters. It's hard to find someone who'll listen.
Skylla, Skylla, go back to your strait. Your friend Charybdis isn't here; there's no one to play your whirlpool games with.
A siren by the shore is singing toward a whirlpool just a stone's throw away, unaware that she herself has become a threat to passing ships—fortunately, none are nearby.
No need to keep singing. I'm here to help.
Oh, you've come, just as the little seashell's message foretold.

Skylla has been waiting a long time too. She's particularly playful and quite mischievous, trying to keep six friends all to herself ... But her selfishness will only make her friends sad, and that's not good.
This place is too big, and my song can't reach her. Could you go tell her that for the sake of her health, she really shouldn't eat too much?
You did it! The people here don't have to fear the flooding anymore.
Beating Skylla with a siren's help—that's a first for me.
Our unity gave us great strength! My dear friend, I'll tell my comrades of your brave deed!
Hey, you look like a fellow mercenary to me—and not a bad one. Got a job for you, interested?

Yeah well, maybe Athenians are polite and all, but what's that to me? I'm not from Athens. And Athenian gangs are dumber than my pal Andrea—it took me quite some time to teach them what a fun gang is like.
But some people just don't appreciate my effort, especially that "Indigen"—what a lousy code name!
The job I've got for you is to take him out.
Hiring a merc costs money. But no one's hiring me right now, and this job doesn't suit my tastes.
So I need someone else to go take out this 'Indigen' guy. Thinks his cult name can protect him. But he's really pissed me off.
Looks like you've got a score to settle with those fanatics as well. Then I'll take it as a yes. Follow me.
He's just an buffoon. I'm not paying much for a buffoon. This fake bead pulled from a goat's backside is the best I can offer. If you're in, come with me.
Good job. Now, take your payment, and don't come looking for me again.
First I was dragged around in a suitcase, and now I've reached the end of Odysseus's epic adventure.
We help shape this story from afar without realizing it, and in turn, it shapes us.
Hard to guess what comes next, isn't it, heroine?
A misthios with a mysterious past, a lost brother turned rival, and enemies lurking in the shadows ... Maybe once you meet your wise mentor, you'll finally see where this adventure leads.
But it's too soon to talk about endings. Let's start with the beginning—how about taking out some bandits?
These savage thugs have taken over Odysseus's palace. You can tell the author had no intention of bringing them back again—perfect for highlighting the protagonist's courage early in the story.
Oh, I'm no philosopher—I'm a writer. I live for storytelling, and I always hunger for inspiration.
Odysseus's palace must be a wellspring of inspiration. I'm curious what I could create there, but a gang of bandits has taken it over. It's now harder to get in than a prison.
Maybe you could help me deal with them? I think this is the natural course of our meeting here.

Look at this one—after you took him down, a letter fell from his body. The letter shows that he was part of some dark, secret cult. Your story is connected to a grander one, naturally and yet with surprising coincidence.
Your poems sound strange to me, but for a bard, you're awfully good with a sword.
My pen is my sword. As long as I keep writing, my blade stays sharp.
It's okay if you don't understand my story now. But once you see my swordplay, you'll understand my literature someday.
An eagle bearer ... you must be the helpful mercenary Vila spoke of, says a foreigner exuding the aura of an Athenian philosopher, clutching a strange device in her hand.
Vila ...? Am I supposed to know her?
Of course. You've met her—a Rusalka—er, I mean a mermaid, or a siren. Not exactly common around here, I imagine.
I thought all her friends would be sirens too.

Well, true friendship transcends race, but let's not dwell on that. Do you have a moment? Like Vila, I'm in need of some ... martial support. It's a matter of great importance—my academic research depends on it.
I guess you could say that. My research is being hindered by a creature born of ley energy. If you can eliminate it, I'll share the minerals I've gathered during my studies.
Really? I knew it—the study of ley lines is bound to find its audience, somewhere, sometime.
But this isn't the moment for academic lectures—we're on the clock.
My colleague is monitoring the creature on-site. She'll explain everything to you. Though I should warn you, her appearance isn't ... well received in these parts. Try not to be alarmed.
A Gorgon speaks to you casually, with a cheerful smile—her "hair" even adds commentary.
So you're the helper Windsong found?
Will she attack us like the other hunters?
That foreigner might be a witch.
Or perhaps a goddess to guide you on your journey. Your local myths are full of such things, aren't they?
Unless I'm some kind of a demigod.
Why not? I know you folks think Gorgons are dangerous creatures, but I have at least forty-seven ways to prove I'm friendly—and technically, I'm only distantly related to Gorgons ...
The energetic Gorgon certainly makes a case for her amicable nature.
The Gorgon raises both hands high.
Easy, easy ... See? We can talk, right? I'm not some rampaging monster. Let's work this out peacefully, okay?
Honestly, to me, Gorgon's just a distant classification. We may look alike, but—anyway, let's talk about the job.

Thank the Aegean for its pleasant climate—I've got so much energy to burn when it comes to research. But a terrifying legendary creature—one of the Gigantes—has taken root near my ley energy research field.
My petrification arcane skill isn't effective against creatures made of ley energy. So I need someone who can fight it. Though it's powerful, I have faith in your capabilities.
I'm not sure I can live up to Herakles' legacy, but I'll take the job.
Thank you! Here's your reward. Say—got time to grab a bite after this? I'd love to try some Athenian food. You must have recommendations!
Don't bother. The entire city's vendors would turn their backs on you ...
Huh? Why can't I go in? Isn't this a place for seeking truth?
If that Pythia only accepts oracles blindly without proper verification and discussion, how can she be sure her theories are correct?
Oh hello, dear integer, you look like a marvelous number—do you know how to get into this temple?
Integer? Umm ... what does that mean?
Everyone has their own soul number. Yours is clearly an integer, with lots of 3s and 2s as factors.
So, do you have a way to get into the temple?
Sneaking in? That's a great idea. It's not my strong suit, but it shouldn't violate the Scripture in any way.
Oh, I have an idea—you can go in and debate the Pythia on my behalf. I'll write a letter for you; the Pythia will definitely understand it, unless she's a terribly irrational number.
Hmm ... looks like I'll have to try other methods. Maybe I can find some flaws in the temple's spatial geometry.
You can then go verify the flaws I find—if you're interested, that is. Don't forget to take the letter.
You sneak into the Temple and leave the Mathematician's letter on Pythian's desk. You also confirm that she's a Cultist after reading the other letters on the desk.
Wow, you came back so quickly—has the Pythia given you an answer?
What? Oh ... then I should look for someone else to discuss with. Thank you for your help.
Hmm ... looks like she couldn't solve the problem. I should go check elsewhere. Thank you for your help.
Excuse me, are you Kassandra the Eagle Bearer?
To think my reputation has reached the theatre of Delphi.
It would seem so. I haven't been here long, but many guests mentioned a mercenary traveling with an eagle.
There are also occasional rumors that you're searching for a secret organization called the Cult of Kosmos.
Haha, you're probably right, but when you first show people your sincerity, they can't wait to return it ...
The chatter after plays can last quite long; sometimes it even spills shocking news. I've long since learned how to get used to it.

A guest claiming to be a Cultist invited me to join. He spoke of the Cult's 'great cause' and grumbled about your interference. Out of courtesy, I took his address—you might be interested in meeting that chatty guest?
I just want to make sure I get to further enjoy my peaceful holiday here, Ms. Kassandra. Besides, his behavior reminded me of the despicable paparazzi back home.
Thank you so much, Ms. Kassandra. I'll spread word of your deeds among the guests—I'm sure that'll help keep other Cultists away.
Hey, we meet again. Are you also traveling the phenomenal world in search of the truth?
I guess you could say that. I've gathered a lot of clues along the way, but I haven't found the final answer yet.
Have you tried setting the clues up as a system? The phenomenal world can be very deceptive—formulas can help us see the truth more clearly.
I always thought math was just for counting chickens or something like that.
Nah-uh. Everything is numbers, and everything can be solved. Let me show you—give me a look at your clues.
See, if you express these unknowns algebraically, and then use the known conditions to ...
I solved it! That was easy—you can go to this location to verify the result.
You find two cultists at the exact location that the Mathematician gave you.
Umm ... how much longer do I have to stay like this?
Help me! Can anyone help me?
I'm modeling for a sculpture. The sculptor was called away just now. Before he left, he told me to hold this pose and not move.
But I've been holding this pose for hours. I'm so hungry ... If you see the sculptor, could you tell him I'm still here posing?
You find the sculptor not far from the road and see him being harassed by two Cultists for refusing to create a sculpture for them.
The situation looks dire. To save the sculptor and his starving model, you must act immediately.
Ms. Kassandra, I'm lucky to run into you here.
Vertin? What brings you to Olympia? Are you visiting the Temple of Zeus? Or joining the games?
I'm recording memories of this era—of this moment in time. You could call it a professional habit of mine.
But while traveling, I stumbled upon a monster that shouldn't exist here. I can't ignore it. I hope you'll help me take it down.
My blades will be at your service.
This creature seems to be some kind of evil consciousness given form. Its origin may not be what I expected, but its danger is beyond doubt. Please be careful.
Thank you for your help, Ms. Kassandra. Without you, this would've been a brutal fight for me.
What do I do, what do I do ...

Should I go to the guards? But some of them might be working with them secretly ... Announce it in public? No, it won't work ... Ask the Timekeeper for help? But she's on vacation—it'd be rude to burden her with work at a time like this. Who can I even talk to ...
All your worries ... you just said it out loud.
Wh-What?! I'm sorry, I didn't mean to! Could you pretend you didn't hear that ...?
A misthios ... maybe I could hire you with the money I've saved? No, I haven't even explained the request, you couldn't possibly give a price ...
Really? Then can I ask for your opinion? But you really mustn't tell anyone else. This could be dangerous ...

So here it is ... I discovered that a seemingly ordinary citizen is actually a member of the evil cult that secretly manipulates the entire Greece. He's planning to use the sports games to carry out their plot. My arcane skill doesn't lie, but I have no solid proof ...
Tell me who that citizen is—I'll stop him.
And ... you really can tell who's with the cult?
Yes, thanks to my arcane skill—I can read many things from a person, and that helps me determine their identity ...
I wish I had met you sooner.
The Harpist is right. A suspicious citizen and a Cultist are talking about their scheme for the next Olymipic Games.

Following the trail, Kassandra sneaks onto the roof of a dilapidated house.
Through the broken boards, she sees a woman in priestly robes tied up in a corner.
Thankfully the woman's unconscious, as the room is filled with ominous hissing—the sound of venomous snakes raised by bandits.

"Sharp indeed." Kassandra effortlessly finds the dagger in the camp's warehouse.
Just then, the bandits arrive, ready to gear up for their raid.
"Well then, looks like it's time for a trial run." Kassandra wipes the blade clean.
Calming a drunk citizen isn't an easy job—especially at a festival. Best not let anyone get hurt, hopefully.

Deep in the cave, Kassandra finds a group of hidden bandits arguing over how to divide their loot.
"If you can't figure it out, why not return it to the villagers?"

Wolf tracks are everywhere, with livestock carcasses scattered on both sides of the road.
It's time to drive these beasts back to the mountains.

The bandits haven't gone far—clearly, moving the loot by hand isn't efficient.
"Well then, are you ready to pay for your crimes?"

Following a mountain stream, Kassandra quickly finds the herd of deer drinking water.
Taking one life to save another—Artemis will understand this hunt.

Glimmers of light dance across the cave wall—someone is holding a torch up to the gems.
Clearly, the thief has no intention of surrendering, blinded by the glitter of firelight.

Kassandra has just set her trap when a roar erupts from behind.
"Hey, I don't remember this being Mount Erymanthos!"

The bandits clearly know what happens when you anger a Spartan. They hesitate over what to do with the soldier.
Kassandra is already close to the camp—just waiting for a moment's distraction to make her move.

The exposed athlete flies into a rage. "You've got no right to ruin this for me!"
He shoves the judge aside and charges in with fists raised.

The gladiators are itching to fight—everyone wants to beat up the "amateur" to secure an easy win.
Well ... good luck to them.

[Route]: On the Streets cards are STRONGER than Fortification cards.

There are chances for special weapons to be available in a round.
O brave sailors, though the waves rise—hoist the sails and set forth to meet them! For over the horizon lies glory to claim and treasure to be taken.
Select a destination, assemble your fleet, roll the dice and roll high to win.

New [Destinations] will be generated every day. Roll high to to explore the [Destination].

After selecting a [Destination], select from three ships (repeated ships allowed) to build your [Fleet]. Each ship has an independent dice array.

After you have chosen your fleet, the system will roll the dice arrays 3 times according to your selection. You succeed if the sum of your dice rolls meet or exceed the required points.
Simulation Failed. You've drawn too much attention. But don't give up hope; prepare yourself and try again.
You blade may not have found its mark this day, but your efforts have laid the foundation for next time.
A Successful Assassination. Though you were spotted, justice was served.
A Successful Assassination. You have escaped without a trace and the message of freedom spreads further in your wake.
The water's surface is as still as solid glass and as peaceful as a dream. Schools of fish teem below, tempting hungry sailors.
"They're not far beyond the harbor—a worthy sight to see, but don't venture too close. Out there, if the reefs don't sink you, the pirates will."
Like the Charybdis, this swirling maw has claimed many an unprepared crew. If you pass this way, pay homage to their memory.
A rusted sword, rotting wood, and bones picked clean. Treasures too. Take them, if you dare—along with what's left of the dreams of its crew.
No trace of wind, nor light from the stars, pierces this haunting veil. The oarsmen will see you through, but first you must choose your heading.
An unexplored stretch of sea, how many unlucky voyages have been lost beneath this nameless water?
More suitable for a leisurely cruise than an adventurer. Why even leave port when you can sit back and enjoy another sip?
A safe and simple choice. Show the world that you fear neither tide nor swelling waves.
"Nothing in excess." The old masters say. Not too wild nor too plain. Sailing under the golden mean should balance you even in the roughest seas.
The ambition of her crew is fit to take you beyond even the Pillars of Herakles.
Those that set out under these sails will either return laden with treasure and glories or else never return at all.
An enigmatic choice that may prove an inspiration when navigating uncharted waters.
Fit for the stone-hearted. Those that cling to the old ways, stubborn to change, find comfort under her gaze.
They say only fools would choose a challenge over an easy victory. Others say that overcoming failure is the mark of a true hero. What do you think?
[On the Streets] type, strong against large buildings. An assassin moves across these rooftops with the silent grace of a cat.
[On the Streets] type, strong against large buildings. Yes it smells, but at least they can't see us down here.
[On the Streets] type, strong against large buildings. Who knows how many eyes might peer out from the darkness?
[Marketplace] type, strong against narrow spaces. Nothing is more effective—and aromatic, than a spice bomb to your pursuers' faces.
[Marketplace] type, strong against narrow spaces. Its elegant grace and the sound of flowing water offer a useful distraction.
[Marketplace] type, strong against narrow spaces. Familiar layers of poking straw offer both a cushion for falls and temporary refuge.

[Fortifications] type, strong against public gathering places. An open square will give the enemy more room to deploy their forces—but it also gives you the freedom to wield your sword without restraint.
[Fortifications] type, strong against public gathering places. From here your enemies can see many things with archers at the ready—you know what to do.
[Fortifications] type, strong against public gathering places. A heavily fortified place. Well built to keep people out.
[Medium Sword] type. There is more to be appreciated in this blade than just its elegant guard.
[Medium Sword] type. A sturdy blade balanced for both speed and grace.
[Blunt Weapon] type. The answer to many questions can be found in the appropriate application of force.
[Blunt Weapon] type. One strike, many wounds.
[Short Blade] type. Made for cutting flesh. It does its job brutally and well.
Special weapon: victory guaranteed. A memory from the eyrie recalled to your hand.
Special weapon: 50% chance to win A volley of arrows ready to fly from the shadows; yours to command with just a whistle.
Special weapon: victory guaranteed. Make the enemy's power your own.

"According to X, the messengers have orders to carry out the Borgia's conspiracy—and 1503 Florins in total! Catch one, and we'll crush their scheme and have enough to buy ourselves a brand-new APPLe III! Get ready, mate; let's chase them down with our rolling souls!"
"Aye, Captain ... Though I really wonder which one we are really after."
Select your chase method for the day (rewards may vary).
Keep your eyes on your target, and attack from the perfect angle—simple.
When you feel you've lost your way, remember to look up. The birds will show you the way.

Elegant and swift, they inevitably find their way to your enemy, often shortly before you do.
With a bit of luck, you can take down two birds with a single shot.

Section 1 of Sled Dogs Behind-The-Paw Training Manual: Make friends with them first.
