The Danube Dawn, operated by Vienna-Pannonian Railways, departing from Istanbul, passing through Belgrade and Budapest before finally arriving in Vienna. Throughout the journey, breakfast, lunch, and dinner are served, allowing passengers to enjoy freshly prepared dishes from various regions while taking in the ever-changing scenery from the dining car.
If it wasn't the year 1913, it truly would be a wonderful journey.

Semmelweis, one of the companions on this journey, was born in Szeged, Csongrád County, Hungary. At the age of 14, she joined the Foundation as an investigator. Her arcane skills are weak, but she is calm, precise, and dependable.
Those who have worked with Semmelweis share the same opinion about her: an arcanist as rational as human, if only there were more arcanists like her.

They hate sunlight and garlic, drink human blood, can turn into mist and control small animals such as rats and bats ... People ambushed by vampires often become infected and die immediately.
Local testimonies are close to expectations, but the parts the Foundation refuses to share are well-protected. It's very difficult to confirm if the rumors are true.

Video equipment, camping gear, snacks, and some games to help pass the time.
Everything's been prepared, even the contraband has been stowed away. The catch? Weight. I let my eagerness of going on a Foundation-sponsored trip get to my head.
Might as well share some of the snacks with the others.

The extra luggage slowed us down, forcing us to travel through the night to make up for lost time. Based on my calculations, we will have to travel for a total of 22 hours today.
The others have expressed concerns about traveling at night, but their fears are clearly unnecessary. According to my research, this area is so deserted that even wild beasts don't bother to pass through. We are the only ones using this route. It should be perfectly safe.

A non-real entity appearing in hotels, along highways, inside abandoned hospitals, and in urban rumors. It is everywhere, able to seep into any space. "It lurks beneath beds, deep within keyholes, behind curtains that flutter without reason, in the teary eyes of crying children, and even ... within your dreams." When logic fails, fear takes hold.
"It is slowly merging with my heart. We are becoming one, and it feels warm and safe. I have never experienced such intense happiness before." Who can say this is not a different kind of blessing?
"I yearn to see it again. Does this make me insane? No—no! If the world calls this insanity, then I will embrace it completely." It offers more than just pleasure and chills—so much more.

She lifts the baton to her chest—not out of pride, but out of duty. She knows well that, within this graduation ceremony, she is not the one being honored. She is an ornament of achievement, a living testament to the Foundation's triumph—its discipline and design shaping a new generation.
The music swells. White doves scatter into the open sky. In perfect rhythm, she steps into the solemn, gleaming hall of white. This is her threshold—the moment she leaves the academy behind. She looks up; the sky stretches endlessly above, the sunlight sharp against her eyes.
Everything feels bright yet unfamiliar. And deep within the heart engraved with "loyalty", something faint begins to stir.

Mission Number: XXX-1912-XX-13 Location: The "Danube Dawn" Security Level: Top Secret Intelligence Summary: Key Report 1: Multiple investigation records indicate that during the past three operation cycles (exact dates in encrypted attachment), abnormal arcanum energy traces were consistently detected inside the "Danube Dawn," the international train running between Istanbul and Vienna. These energy patterns closely match the activity signature of a known Beyond entity—the vampire (see encrypted attachment for detailed characteristics). Key Report 2: Meanwhile, a series of unexplained deaths and disappearances have occurred along the train's route. Preliminary examinations show that the victims suffered blunt-force trauma and displayed tissue mutations of unidentified form, differing from the pattern of known vampire "Infected." The upper division suspects direct contact with a new strain of vampire. Threat level has been classified as severe. All evidence suggests the presence of an anomalous vampire aboard the "Danube Dawn"—either active on a periodic cycle or as a vampire "Infected" with atypical traits. Squad members are to prioritize personal safety during the operation. Mission Objectives: Based on prior performance, Level Four Investigator Semmelweis is hereby assigned to the "Danube Dawn" investigation team. Objectives include: 1. Board the "Danube Dawn," confirm the authenticity and number of vampire entities, observe their activity pattern, and assess passenger threat level. 2. Investigate whether vampire activity correlates with newly observed vampire "Infected" incidents along the train's route. They will supply all mission-critical resources and equipment. St. Pavlov Foundation November 2, 1912

The "Danube Dawn" was once the Versailles Palace on rails, gliding along the banks of the Danube River. From Istanbul to Vienna, silverware clinked a harmonious tune, vase violets glistened with dew, and even the stokers carried themselves with the poise of Habsburg courtiers—at least, that is what they believed.

But the glory days didn't last. Once the roar of cannons had grown louder than the whistle, it was abandoned—forgotten in a warehouse.

Later, Vienna-Pannonian Railways pulled the train from the warehouse and refurbished it, stripping away the last threads of velvet and cramming in seats hard enough to turn your back straight. The silver tableware disappeared, French cuisine vanished from the menu, and flavorless beef stew took its place. The train now resembles an aging gentleman in an ill-fitting tuxedo, clinging to the last shreds of his dignity.

And then, there was the missing conductor, Mr. Hermann. With a pale face, hollow eyes, and a drooping mouth, his very presence reeked of morbid neuroticism. His dress, however, was pristine in every aspect: from his uniform to his pocket watch chain aligned perfectly with his buttons, to the gloves which never left his hands—not even while eating. None ever saw him sleep. Like a ghost, by midnight, he would wander the train, inspecting every carriage. The "Danube Dawn" was his home. He knew every passenger's quirks, every worn cushion, every stain on the windows. Or so the passengers claimed—that is, those who remembered him.

One night, three years ago, while passing through a fog-drenched stop near Budapest, the conductor vanished—swallowed by the mist, gone without a trace.

Yet a story still circulates among the passengers: the vampire on the train took him. His body was hidden in one of the cars, and his eyeballs embalmed and nailed to the ceilings of cars one and ten so that even in death, he may keep watch over his beloved train.

Forevermore ...

— UTTU Editor: Verity
Excerpt from the Vampire Beyond Entity File

File No.: XXX-1912-B (The Beyond - Vampire)

Clearance Level: Top Secret

The vampire is an extremely rare Beyond being bearing a strong resemblance to humans, yet with several defining traits: its skin is notably pale, its irises typically crimson—varying in depth with its tolerance for blood intake. Anatomical studies confirm that blood functions as one of its key energy sources. Vampires exhibit a compulsive craving for blood, particularly that of highly active animals.

Key Traits:

1. Bloodthirst

A vampire's obsession with blood often triggers bouts of extreme aggression and heightened tracking ability (showing acute sensitivity to the scent of blood). However, certain reports suggest blood is not their sole means of sustenance. A rare few can resist Bloodthirst altogether or survive on alternative food sources without dependence on blood.

2. Photophobia

Vampires exhibit a marked physiological aversion to sunlight. Prolonged exposure to strong daylight causes irreversible tissue damage. These entities cast no visible shadows or reflections—whether upon water, glass, mirrors, or polished metal surfaces.

3. Vulnerabilities

Ordinary physical attacks are largely ineffective. Only bullets forged from metals refined through specific alchemical techniques (most notably pure silver) can inflict permanent injury upon them.

4. Vampire Infected

When a vampire bites or exchanges bodily fluids with an individual possessing innate arcanum affinity, there is a high probability of "conversion."
The infected undergo █–█ hours of violent physiological and psychological mutation, with a 93% mortality rate and over 96% incidence of mental instability among survivors. Those who endure the process ultimately become "the Infected," gradually gaining the creature's biological traits and mastering its arcane skills.

Note: Intelligence suggests "Manus Vindictae" is conducting ongoing experiments to convert ordinary humans directly into vampires. The success rate and stability of such transformations remain unknown.

Both vampires and their infected derivatives are officially classified by the Foundation as "the Beyond," distinct from both humans and arcanists.

Outside, it's as dark as if someone had spilled a whole bottle of ink. The glass window reflects me and little William sitting opposite each other. I bet he's not really asleep! The kerosene lamp on the table casts our shadows on the wall. I stare at them, hold my breath, and clutch my teddy bear tight.

The train clatters along the rails, like someone's chasing after us, chasing us away from Istanbul, away from Uncle's house. When Ms. Dorothy was packing our clothes, her hands were shaking so much she couldn't even fasten the buttons on my shirt. Her face was pale as paper, lips pressed tight, as if the moment she opened her mouth, all the awful words trapped in her throat would come flying out like crows. She just said, "Children, hurry! Come with me." Everything happened too fast. I didn't even have time to pack all my dolls—Jenny, Jack, Nina ... I'm sorry, I couldn't bring you with me!

Where is this train taking us? Budapest ... Father's home. Will there be a warm fireplace there? Sweet Dobos cake? The smell of roses? I've already forgotten what Father looks like ... but he must be tall ... tall enough to protect us! Like the heroes in bedtime stories ... the powerful, brave, amazing vampires who only appear at night and vanquish everything in their path!

If only ... if only a vampire would really come! They'd drain the blood of all the bad people and protect good children who behave. So they'd surely scare away whatever's hiding in the dark, whatever it is that makes Ms. Dorothy's face go pale.

I keep praying silently, again and again. I believe the great vampire will come to save us!
Notice of the "Danube Dawn" Resumed Service - Vienna-Pannonian Railways

Vienna-Pannonian Railways announced yesterday that after a full year of maintenance, the "Danube Dawn" will officially resume service next Wednesday. The new train is said to drastically reduce travel time between Istanbul and Vienna, strengthening connections throughout the Danube region. Rumors, of course, soon followed. An engineer—who wished to remain anonymous—claimed that the train's remarkable performance might not be entirely due to human work. He reported glimpsing peculiar, Critter-like entities near the engine room and wheel bearings, somewhere between a beetle and a firefly in size, dark brown in color, with two slender antennae that glowed faintly red. The workers nicknamed them "Scarlet Nightmares." "They seem... very fond of staying close to the engines," he said. "When the machinery runs smoothly, they're lively; when it doesn't, they bunch together and start ... glowing, bright red." Vienna-Pannonian Railways declined to comment. However, several arcanobiology enthusiasts have suggested that these beings are far from ordinary Critters. They might, in fact, be familiars of vampires—social, volatile creatures said to feed on the blood of laborers. "This isn't a metaphor," they insisted. "It's real." "People have long said the disappearance of the 'Danube Dawn''s former conductor was connected to a vampire. Now these Critters show up, and somehow it's the same story again ... maybe the train itself is a familiar of the vampires ..." "Hah! If tickets weren't sold out, I'd get on board myself, maybe even catch a few to show everyone!" "Don't joke about that ..." ... Whether the so-called "vampire familiar theory" holds any truth or not, the "Danube Dawn" will depart on schedule. Will it truly reshape the Danube region's transport network as promised by Vienna-Pannonian Railways? Has it truly been touched by supernatural power? Only time will tell.

... Sonya, 60 years old A noblewoman, sharp-tongued and fussy, seemingly fleeing from the war. Sixty years of pride might have made it hard for her to face reality. She was supposed to travel with her butler, but tickets for the "Danube Dawn" were nearly impossible to get. It seems war treats nobles and commoners alike, or perhaps her family's status isn't quite as lofty as she makes it seem. After ten minutes of complaining about having to travel alone, with no butler to set her table or press the creases from her skirt, she finally boarded by herself. Do people really spend their whole lives learning to place their cutlery at a perfect forty-five-degree angle? In any case, she's the archetype of a noblewoman straight out of an oil painting, gown in hand. Let's hope that on her road of escape, she learns what the world is really like. ...... ... Arbuthnot, 45 years old Middle class. A decent, respectable gentleman. Nothing remarkable about his demeanor—just an ordinary man who fits neatly into his social standing. A businessman with investments in Eastern European railways and oil. Vital infrastructure and strategic resources. He's well-connected and has an eye for opportunity. The war cost him dearly, and he worries for his future. Special times demand special measures. What troubles him isn't death or hunger—it's the thought of losing a life of luxury forever. ...... ...

Passengers from Car No. 3 often come to me with their troubles—not over the tasteless stew or the unbearably chilly nights, but a sound: a crying that seeps through the partitions and burrows straight into the brain. It feels as if the train itself has come alive, endlessly recounting all the pain its body has endured through the years. And so, tonight at 11:51 p.m., I went to Car No. 3, sat by the window, and quietly waited for the "cry" to come. When the hour and minute hands aligned, I heard it—that delicate, indescribable rhythm. The tone rose and fell, turning in on itself, resonating at a frequency barely perceptible. To me, it was more like a ... song, one that no throat could ever produce—something primal, pure, flowing unconsciously from the soul. Once the word "song" took shape in my mind, it stirred a memory. Along the Danube, there is an old legend of "the Song of the Spirit." They say it is the most beautiful melody ever imagined by humankind, able to pass through any physical barrier and reach the listener's innermost consciousness. Could what I heard be that very song? Or was it the faint cry for help from the frail former conductor, Hermann, his decayed vocal cords vibrating through some supernatural force? Then, without the slightest warning, the singing stopped. The carriage sank into an absolute, suffocating silence ... as though the "Danube Dawn" itself, along with every living and dead thing within its belly, was holding its breath ... waiting for an unseen baton to fall again, or for whatever the song had briefly subdued ... to reawaken. — UTTU Editor: Verity

Today's tale doesn't start with "once upon a time." It begins in "a quiet, ordinary village." In that village lived an equally ordinary little girl whose father was a vampire. But unlike him, she didn't live apart from humans. She felt a natural fondness toward both humans and arcanists. Perhaps because she was a hybrid—an "impure" half-vampire? In any case, for a long while, the girl lived peacefully with her parents.

Until a shell fell.

Yes, war. Again.

War brings death, and death spreads. Her family didn't escape it; one by one, they died. Only she and her uncle survived, wandering endlessly. But shells don't discriminate. Human, arcanist, vampire, or half-breed—none are spared. The girl was wounded. How badly? No one knows. Severe enough that she nearly died. Her uncle wanted to save her—his only remaining family. Even if it meant making a deal with the devil, he would.

He carried her to an old castle. Its mistress, as all stories go, was powerful and mysterious. She healed the dying hybrid girl. The price—if it could even be called that—was an overactive regenerative power that let her recover from any wound with ease.

Since then, the girl's body has always been wrapped in bandages.

Dear colleagues,

Regarding Corvus, the conductress of the "Danube Dawn." As you all know, she was once one of us and my most trusted partner. Thus, for personal reasons as well as curiosity, I have attempted to glimpse traces of the partner I once knew. I must admit, she's changed. There is barely a trace of the person I remember. The glimmer in her eyes remains, yes, but where that gaze now falls ... no longer has anything to do with me.

Still, in a way, our destinations aren't all too different. For that reason, I still cherish this brief journey we now share.

As for Ms. Pandora Wilson, it's been some time since she vanished. Since then, I've found it difficult to sense her through the wind. It's as if some unseen force quietly erased every trace of her. Yet lately, I've faintly detected something ... an echo which mimics the wind. I have tried many times to reestablish contact, but I've received no response. Even so, I still believe she is out there somewhere.

Despite this, UTTU continues to publish articles in her name and tone. I understand why. Losing her would mean losing the very spirit of UTTU—something none of us could bear. That is why I took it upon myself to handle external correspondence under her name. Yet, the unease lingers: we are all trying to imitate her—her style, her rhythm, the way she thought, the words she might have written ... but none of us truly understand the meaning behind them. For me, this imitation is like calling out a name in the dark, over and over again, knowing it will never answer back.

As for the strange happenings aboard the "Danube Dawn" and the many details pertaining to vampires ... I will explain everything in full once I have alighted.

Verity, UTTU Editor

"Hey, Fleck family! Package for you!" A hurried young man shouts from in front of the building.
He glances at the doorplate: [Fleck Tombstone Museum]. Before anyone can answer, he drops a heavy [Black Sack] at the doorstep and bolts, as if fleeing death itself.
"A new commission." The heavy, silent doors creak open as the mistress of the museum lifts the sack.
The broken stone stirs within, shaking off the flecks and dust gathered from its journey.
A new tombstone, one ready to join the museum's ever-growing collection.
"Necrologists" are known for their ability to let families hear the last words of their departed.
Use an arcane skill to awaken the tombstone.
And the voice that dwells within it can at last be heard.
"Friend, we have more important things to do—first, turn on the light."
"I don't like to be in the dark. It brings up terrible memories."
"Those nights were filled with roars. But now the silence is more deafening."
The stone shard sent to the Tombstone Museum is but a small fragment of the monument that it came from.
Yet, the shard bears the name of its owner: Mueller.
The tombstone trembles rhythmically. Perhaps it's a nod? "Kind lady ... may I ask—where is this?"
"This is the Fleck Tombstone Museum, sir. Though many also know it as the House of Spirits."
"People come here bearing the fragments of restless souls, hoping that we might help find them peace."
The room is quiet, yet crowded.
It's attended by tombstones in every nook and corner. Some polished white, some mossy and gray, others so old and worn that their markings have faded—erased by time.
"My apologies ... the Tombstone Museum ... what exactly is this place?"
"You've traveled far to reach this place. This is Liechtenstein."
"..." The tombstone falls into long silence.
And for a tombstone that has already known death, it borne more than enough bad news for one lifetime.
"Damn it, where on earth did those brats bury me?!"
"I've been banished to this forsaken place while they returned home in glory ... "
"They betrayed me?!—Betrayal! Blatant betrayal!" The tombstone shakes violently, its anger clear.
"Too much trembling will worsen your cracks. That will make it harder for you to rest ..."
The mistress of the museum knows well how to handle such things. "In fact, the regret you fear may not be beyond repair."
"What, you plan to go rough them up for me, Ms. Stranger?"
"Hatred leads away from peace. It cannot soothe the dead."
"You can trust me ... at the very least trust the other 31 tombstones that rest patiently here."
"They were once like you, burdened with regrets that could never be resolved."
Necrologist's softened voice calms the reactions within the sack.
"Very well ... You can pick me up now. Place me in the glass case you're holding."
The tombstone doesn't forget to add, "But only for now."
Beneath Mueller's tombstone, Necrologist spots another broken stone.
This tombstone drips with collected moisture.
It is weathered, ruined, and steeped in sorrow.
A weaker, more timid voice finally speaks.
"N-no ... I'm not part of that loud fellow ..."
Beads of water drip from the stone, like unceasing tears.
"I—I'm not him. My name is Smith ..."
Whatever age the "Storm" may hurl her museum into, the commissions never stop coming.
A [Commission Letter] arrives together with the [Two Strange Tombstones].
Necrologist, entrusted with managing the belongings of the dead, does not deal in worldly gold or silver. She tends to other rarer things.
A lonely ghost that refuses rest, or a chatty storybook in an attic—it is those things that she gives new value.
For now, the task is to understand what these two gentlemen of stone desire.

"Mm ... Given Mr. Smith's current state, I think we'd better return to your commission for now, Mr. Mueller."

"I had a zeal beyond words. Designs of impossible grandeur."

"Gunpowder? You mean you can smell the smoke?" He presses incredulously, shaking off flecks of grit with something like envy.
It seems every tombstone holds a [Lingering Ghost] with its own peculiar traces. "Only an atmosphere this thick can forge strong soldiers. Of course, the weak-willed may not stand for it."
Smith doesn't respond to Mueller's words, but his stone trembles silently.
"In fact, Mr. Smith, you really ought to learn to be a proper soldier. "
"Right here, just like us—we followed orders, bled for the Great War, brothers to the end."
"Berlin will give you faith, or at least cure you of this nonsensical aversion to smoke."
"Mr. Mueller, not everyone is meant to be a soldier. And not everyone wants to be."
The proud stone threatens to ramble on. Necrologist cuts him off cleanly.
"It is time for us to leave."
Upon taking a step, Smith was struck by a strong sensation. Mueller felt it as well.
Maybe this is the perfect opportunity to discover the wishes the dead once had.
"So this is the street you're so proud of, Mr. Mueller?"
"Yes. This street boasts Germany's finest tailor shop.
"Nobles and dignitaries came from all over, and it was the pride of the entire city." Of course, including him, when he was alive.
"Opera singers claimed they would wear their gowns to perform at the Moulin Rouge, in Rome, in Milan, in Warsaw ... every hall of victory.
"It was the calling card of Berlin."
"Turn that corner and you'll see it, the most elegant of them all."
Just as Mueller said, the finest tailor shop stands at the corner.
But its doors are shut tight, and its golden sign lies beneath a delicate film of dust.
"Hello ... is anyone there?" She raps gently at the door.
The hurried footsteps outside pass by. The locked door stays silent.
At last, a neighbor takes notice. "Don't bother knocking. They've been gone a long time."
"No, impossible. They'd never leave." He denies it desperately.
"Sometime after this war started, that's all I know. One day, soldiers came to the shop, drove out everyone inside, except for the couple who owned it ..."
"Then they were dragged away; no idea what became of them."
"Sir, do you know where they were taken?"
"They were our pride, Berlin's pride. How could they have been arrested?!" But his frantic words reach only Necrologist's ears.
"Who knows ... maybe, like the others, they were packed onto trains, trucks, or ships, sent off to some godforsaken place."
The tailor's neighbor waves a hand and slams the door shut.
Necrologist and her two tombstone companions head toward Mueller's second destination: a city far to the east.
Smith tentatively nudges the other stone.
Ever since leaving home, and even now on the truck to St. Petersburg, he speaks far less than before.
"What's this? Pitying me?" Mueller snaps back at the gesture of comfort.
"This diversion is only temporary; when I finally figure out what is going on, I will return to rest in my homeland."
"Or did you think all of that was enough to shake a soldier's iron will?"
"And you, Mr. Smith, are you ready to face the outside world?"
"Real soldiers are already marching toward St. Petersburg."
"Ms. Necrologist, you said it's 1920? Then most likely they've already reached it."
"Mr. Mueller. Perhaps St. Petersburg won't hold the answers you expect. I hope you're prepared ..."
Necrologist looks out the window. The storm of war has ravaged the land. Ruins and scars cover every town and village they pass.
The suffering etched on faces is not hers alone to witness.
"... For final victory, sacrifice is necessary."
"Once we triumph, we'll return to the proper path, to the heart of a better Europe."
"We'll have warm rye bread on Red Square, fresh caviar ... and of course, vodka."
"Those things sound pleasant ... but the price seems far too high."
"No, no, Ms. Necrologist. When you reach St. Petersburg, you'll see. You'll change your mind ..."
The sound of a passing train interrupts him.
On the far tracks, a steam engine howls as it passes, drowning every voice, reverberating between stone and skull.
But it's clear the reason has nothing to do with Mueller's grand vision.
"Ah ... the monster, the monster's scent ... it's getting stronger ..."
"I-I remember now! That sound! That was it!"
"A massive, gray beast ... this sound always accompanied it."
"...! These whistles come from trains, factories, ships. And for your harbor, Mr. Smith ..."
"So the great gray monster wasn't some arcane creature after all, but ..."
"A ship." The other stone interrupts. "Hah! That makes it simple."
"Let me guess: a harbor, a ship, ignorance of the outside world ... confidential work, perhaps?"
"You must be an English sailor too cowardly to face the truth ..."
"London or St. Petersburg, our end is the same."
"Mr. Smith will see that soon enough."
Perhaps putting these two in the same box was a mistake from the start.
A blaring horn halts their quarrel, followed by the screech of brakes.
St. Petersburg's noise rivals Berlin, but the winds here are far sharper.
This is where the New World clashes with the Old Order, with no middle ground.
Though the city bustles with activity, none of it is what Mueller had expected.
Following the flow of the crowd, Necrologist eventually finds herself near a factory.
Though it seems there isn't any work going on, instead crowds of people stand together engaged in a heated discussion.
At the arrival of Necrologist, their faces change. Some look at her with fear and others anger.
"What are you doing here, young lady?"
"I didn't mean to disturb you." She holds up the tombstone box in her hand and offers a brief explanation.
"Ah, I see. You are here for the dead ..."
"Unfortunately, this is no time to be visiting Petrograd."
"Our strike is about to begin. For your safety, I suggest you leave quickly ... or join us."
"A strike ... then the war is over?"
"Not yet, but it's only a matter of time. If the Germans signed the [Agreement], we should have ended this damned war! We're all waiting ... and that moment will be worth the finest bottle of vodka."
"But right now, none of that matters more than the march. A new age is coming ..." His eyes gleam with longing.
Necrologist stops a hurried, wary-looking man.
"Hello, excuse me. Is this ... St. Petersburg?"
"Of course, this is St. Petersburg! But I can see you must not be from around here."
"You should not have come; there is supposed to be a strike throughout the city. For your safety, I suggest you leave quickly."
From inside the box comes a dull, heavy thud, again and again.
The stone smashes itself against the glass until the pane shatters.
"Did we lose?!" he cries in disbelief. "How could we lose?! How could we possibly lose ..."
"My comrades, their sacrifice, their blood—did it mean nothing?"
"Why doesn't it all lead to victory?"
"Mr. Mueller, the war is ending. That is a good thing."
The tombstone slumps against the edge of the box, his cracks spreading wider, moss creeping deep inside.
He calls out to Smith, but his voice is like a spent shell, hollow and powerless.
"We lost, and you are the victor. Now you can mock me all you want! For yourself, for your country!"
"I ... I'm no victor ..." The other tombstone trembles in reply.
Now Necrologist understands ... why this soldier with such unshakable will could never find rest.
Perhaps the tragedy was decided from the very start of the war.
"You're no longer a soldier, Mr. Mueller. Your duty is already done."
The journey from St. Petersburg to the English Coast is no short voyage.
Passengers sway with the swelling waves.
"Mr. Smith, you seem down. Haven't you found your 'gray monster' here?"
Countless ships patrol the waters, steel beasts embodying the pride of the Royal Navy, the hopes of the people, the work of thousands of hands.
"The gray monster ... it was the greatest ship of them all."
"I tightened its bolts, painted its hull, checked its instruments ... every day, every night." His broken stone fills with surging memory, his voice fevered, like a shot of adrenaline.
"Not a farewell ritual, a chance to meet old friends ... I would have thought this meant much more to you."
"Hah ... that's for the great men to arrange."
"A ship that size won't stop for a single loose rivet. It has bigger missions."
It gestures faintly toward Mueller's silent stone. But the soldier is already at rest.
"... We were just ordinary men. Now we're just ordinary tombstones. No different from stones on the roadside."
"Even as tombstones, I can tell you apart."
"The aura you carry, the uneven edges, the size of your cracks ... they all bear your mark."
"Thank you, Ms. Necrologist ... but it doesn't matter anymore."
"If you can, place me in the lighthouse closest to the harbor."
"One day I'll see it again, setting out or returning ..." His tone brims with hope, "[The Dreadnought]."
He waits, forever waits, for the ship in his memory.
In silence, he sinks into eternal peace.
"I think I know what I must do."
For the first time, she breaks a promise to the dead.
Behind her, the bookseller eyes her with suspicion.
"You've examined every newspaper that mentions the Dreadnought ... Miss, what exactly are you looking for?"
"You're not some enemy spy, are you?!"
"No need, sir. I've already found it."
"The Dreadnought was struck by torpedoes on the starboard side and tragically sank."
In the crew list, she finds Smith's name.
She gently wraps his tombstone in the old newspaper, not placing him in any lighthouse, as he had wished.
"Stripped of their grand words, the steadfast soldier finally raised his hands in surrender."
"The ordinary sailor never escaped the shadow of a sinking ship, even after memory failed him."
"In war, everyone becomes a number. A forever-silent tombstone."
In front of the Fleck Tombstone Museum.
"Honestly, I don't even want to know what's inside these packages."
"... But didn't you announce you were closing down?"
"These tombstones, these lingering souls ... I once treated them as vessels for the regrets of the dead, as ghosts tainted with strangeness and impurity ..." But perhaps the truth is not so simple.
"Y-You don't mean those tombstones, do you?!"
"You mean I've been carrying those things all this time ...?!"
Before the mistress can reply, the postman bolts, fleeing this uncanny place without another word.

Echoes Pour from the Heavens to the Earth Below

It's more than just her birthday. From the moment she first met the sunlight, Rubuska became "her" shadow—gone only when she slips into the darkness, or raises her flute to play. Where there is light, there "she" is. Rubuska will never be alone.|"The rightful heir to Castle Arges, the dreaded 'vampire' Duchess, the illustrious Rubuska the First, celebrates her two hundredth ... and-something birthday today—probably!" Rubuska lifts her flute, and her spectral procession performs for the children a birthday dance they will never forget.|On the night before her birthday, Rubuska walks alone to the graveyard. Among the thorn-choked tombstones, she lays out her once-splendid silverware, quietly murmuring tales of the Impaler beneath the sullen sky until the moon sinks and the sun rises. She spends this day in remembrance of her homeland, her family, and the strange mercy that still allows her to linger between life and death.
A masked wanderer, a piper whose melodies command the shadows, and one of your most vampire-savvy friends.

When told a date of birth is required, Corvus exhales softly and rolls the end of her pen between her fingers. On the back of the form, she converts a certain date and writes it down. "I suppose this will do for my birthday," she murmurs. " I can't think of a better date for now."|Time never breaks its promise, just as the "Danube Dawn," once under her command, was never late. Today, she boards it again as an ordinary passenger, retracing sights and steps she has seen a thousand times before. Once, everywhere was home; now, nowhere is.|The day, like a cuckoo emerging from its clock, reminds her that the days of war have long since passed. Her old friends and companions have each gone their own way, leaving her to walk this road alone—though Aima's cake still manages to break the spell of memory and gently returns her to the present.
The conductress of the "Danube Dawn," the fierce raptor overlooking the Thracian skies, and one of your most dependable friends.

A weathered red cloak, pocked with scorch marks and frayed edges, flares behind him. The interviewee loves it for the thunderous roar it makes when it catches the wind.
"Is this fast enough for you? Watch this! The dial's about to explode!"
With a snap of fabric, the interviewee accelerates towards the horizon in a blur.

Vampires: Horrific Legend or Romantic Fantasy?

"Either light it on fire or bury it in the ground!"
"Chop off the head and drive a stake through its heart!"
"Bring garlic, and silver, and some holy water!"
See, people have devised so many ways to deal with those fabled, blood-drinking monsters, though some are little more than the ramblings of fools, or superstitions handed down through time.

Today, the vampire has moved from the realm of Balkan-Slavic folklore to the circles of Danubian literary salons, marking its transformation from folk horror myth to a fashionable theme in urban literature. Works such as Carmine the Blood-Feaster and Drac the Impaler found instant acclaim upon release. Soon, the fervor spread—readers donned fangs and velvet, some even stepping into the limelight to become the very monsters they adored ...

"Perhaps the vampire need not always be a monster. We could paint them as melancholic—perhaps even beautiful beings,"
remarked a literary critic from the Red Wool Apartment overlooking the Danube, complexion pale, eyes crimson, and a smile betraying oddly sharp fangs.

The Surviving Passenger "Yes. A little girl with red eyes. That means she might've been a monster, the kind that knocks on your door at night and drains you of every last drop of blood ..." "But then again, how could she have had the nerve to sit there, calmly drinking soup with a silver spoon?" Station Quarantine Officer "She had no shadow—none! I swear on my mother's grave! That Rubuska didn't cast a shadow under the light, and her reflection didn't show in the window either! Damn it, this train's looking more like a sideshow by the day ..." "Still, I'm only here to check for diseases, not vampires. She's clear. Next!" "New" Attendant "An interview? Can you keep my name out of it? Alright—hello, I'm one of the train attendants and I just got this job recently ... Rubuska? Of course I know her! She's a vampire—and what a vampire— she's easily the most popular attendant on our train!" "She's a smart one. She knows she's small, sure, but that tiny frame can cast a shadow big enough to scare anyone. Whether folks see it or not, they're scared either way!"

Pandora Wilson: The revered and terrifying vampire Duchess, heir to Castle Arges, last descendant of the Impaler, the twilight shadow, the nightmare of the Danube—Her Excellency Rubuska I ...
Pandora Wilson: My apologies, Ms. Rubuska, our interview time is limited. Would it be alright if we dove right into your story?
Rubuska: Oh? Then you like vampires too, huh? Alright ... but where does mine begin? Well, just look at me—I've got red eyes, fangs, and no shadow at all. I look the part, don't you think?
Pandora Wilson: I'm inclined to believe you, though your tone suggests I should reserve judgment.
Rubuska: In truth, I'm a real fake vampire, or a fake real vampire, if you like—or even a fake fake vampire!
Rubuska: I mean, I've got all the makings of a vampire—don't I? So tell me, why shouldn't I be one?
Rubuska: People take one look at my red eyes and start to wonder. Then they notice there's no shadow behind me ... and that's when they start to believe—and start to fear.
Pandora Wilson: That's quite clever of you, Ms. Rubuska. In chaotic times like these, fear is our greatest shield.
Rubuska: Well? What do you think, Ma'am? Am I real, or just pretending?

Lady Corvus's fingers traced down from the brim of the hat, along the "lines" of her own face, before she cut herself short.

A notebook recording various details and trivial matters from the train's journeys. The full text remains unknown (perhaps classified).
The interviewee ended the topic with a reminder: "We guarantee absolute safety during each journey, and that the train will never be late ... but we make no promises that the train won't be haunted.

When the whistle was mentioned, a rare smile crossed the interviewee's lips.
This whistle followed her from the mountains of Oreinósia to the beautiful yet war-torn banks of the Danube, where she commanded a steam train as it thundered along the rails.
However, considering the interviewee's past experiences, this whistle may have been put to use in more places than the train car itself.

Railways reshaped the world. During the flourishing nineteenth century, as this new mode of transport spread across Europe, it changed how people journeyed. Luxury itself found a place aboard the train, turning travel into an elegant pastime.

From Vienna to Constantinople, from Berlin to Baghdad, and even farther than the distant East, the railway made the world smaller and smaller. The new magnates of industry rose with the era's current, seeking comforts worthy of their fortunes. They rode eastward to distant lands, gliding through the peaks and rivers of the Balkans, their dreams steeped in velvet and caviar, turning what had once been a year-long journey into mere days.

When war descended, every seat represented a hope to escape the shadow of battle and fire. By the winter of 1912, the war had reached the peak of brutality. Victory appeared certain, yet to ordinary civilians, their lives were worth little more than cattle unless they could secure a ticket out of the crossfire, or somehow slip aboard the train to the safety of Habsburg territory.

Tickets were scarce for the "Danube Dawn," whether in wartime or in peace.

"Looking for a ticket, friend? Genuine, of course! The "Danube Dawn," first-class all the way! No fakes, I swear it!"

Dearest Sister, I'm writing this letter at Sirkeci Station. It's now 3:22 in the afternoon. Snow is falling over the Golden Horn, and there's still a while before the "Danube Dawn" departs. This winter is bitterly cold, and snow is falling over Istanbul. The conductress promised to carry this letter safely to Nica Station, where you'll take the train to Uncle's home in Vienna and wait out the war and the cold. I've already paid for your ticket and meals for the rest of the trip. Stay safe, and may your journey go smoothly. To My Dear Alice, I will come to Budapest to see you. When the snow melts in the old city next spring, we'll meet beneath the bridge, at the spot where I first took your hand. We lost the battle at Edirne, but I made it out alive. Thank God. I only hope the war ends soon, and that I can see you again before long. Few trains yet run these days, but through my Oreinósian connections, I came upon Lady Corvus. I am a soldier of the Empire, and she naturally holds no fondness for me. Even so, she agreed to carry this letter to Budapest. Yours with love, Lieutenant Maris December ■, 1912 Train Cleanup Report: The conductress recovered only two remaining letters from the blood-soaked carriages.

Pandora Wilson: Good afternoon, Ms. Corvus ... or, if I might presume some familiarity, may I call you Iglika?
Corvus: If that is your wish, then of course.
Pandora Wilson: We've learned that you once served in an armed organization known as the "Thracian Liberation Front." Forgive me if this sounds intrusive—but what made you leave home and take up arms against the rule of the Sublime Porte?
Corvus: Some people saved me, so I joined them.
Pandora Wilson: Hmm, that must have been quite an ... extraordinary experience. I'm curious if your group discriminated among your comrades—whether they differentiated between human and arcanist, for example.
Corvus: We had all sorts among us—bandits, herdsmen, killers ... even a vampire or two. When you're fighting side by side, things like that do not matter.
Corvus: We don't concern ourselves with such things. Prejudice and fear of the unknown only lead to hostility. On the "Danube Dawn," too, I do what I can to stop that from happening.
Corvus: There has been too much hatred and killing born from differences. All I wish is to save the innocent from the conflict. To bring them a new dawn.

A classic Victorian-style soft hat from the venerable Swedish atelier LINNR A. Only ten are made each year.
The front of the crown is adorned with delicate handmade lace, while the body is wrapped in moss silk. Its matte texture absorbs all harsh light, protecting the delicate young lady who wears it.
"I saw a black cat, a crow, and a blood-red moon. Was it a dream? Oh, how I'd love to dance among them."
The interviewer observed that, as she spoke of this, her eyes shone like panes of stained glass catching the light.

"I've been here far too long—so long that I've lost all sense of time. The chronic pain kept me from moving until my doctor improved things," the interviewee recounted gently stroking the medical device that never leaves her side. "Now, for a few days each month, I can be like a bird let out of its cage, flying free, out of here, past the little window that has kept me prisoner for so long!"

It was once as fragile as the interviewee herself, its petals curled, its color faded, unable even to withstand a single gentle touch.
Later, through carefully measured dehydration and desiccation, it was permanently fixed at the moment before its withering.
"This was a gift from my mother," the interviewee recalled. "She told me, 'One day, you too will be able to walk against the wind, strong and healthy.'"

A hat with an unusually wide brim, meant to conceal the interviewee's fair hair and let it blend into the night.
Within its ruby ornament lies a drop of vampire blood, its scent a quiet guarantee to the castle's master that the midnight banquet shall proceed as planned, with no uninvited guests in attendance.

A rifled flintlock. Each bullet has been cleansed with holy water and consecrated through arcane ritual. The patterned grooves set into the gun's stock derive from recent advances in ley line studies—it is said that they can guide bullets. The interviewee described the principle with enthusiasm, but we declined her offer to demonstrate it on the spot.

A mithril candelabrum enchanted to filter light and heat to blend with the moonlight, causing its flames to glow a pale, lustrous blue.
"This little flame marks the last line between sanity and madness. As long as the candle keeps burning, one remains connected to the civilized world."

"What you see is a dream within a dream," the interviewee(s) stated. "We are swathed in moonlight—the masque never ends. I donned this cloak and took on the role of another. From then on, the living could no longer discern my identity, and I too merged into that dream, becoming one of its many disassociated images."

During the interview, the interviewer noticed the subject(s) fiddling with their mask several times. After a brief exchange, they at last offered a response.
"On the back of the mirror, in a seam moonlight cannot reach, if I angle my gaze so it slips through the mask's crack and back into the world, I can again perceive eternity. A millimeter of error, though, and it all goes wrong—like the rose watered from the Fountain of Immortality, which only lost its first petal when a thousand and one days had passed."

A suit ornament shaped like bones, dotted with blood-red gems.
It was the interviewee(s)' most lavish ornament, and the one they knew best.
"I kept my eyes on it, pondering on its meaning without pause. I saw death fall upon it. Every image I made was an ode to it—'nevermore,' 'nothing more.' In the end I followed it, and over a time that felt almost eternal, I returned to quiet."

Only moss and vines could calmly keep company with this knight. For centuries they have grown, climbed, and swayed, continually blooming anew.
The knight forgave the sinner waiting at the road's end, just as the moss and vines forgave a century of solitude.

An arm guard braided from tenacious vines, with silvery metal forming the knight's finger bones. The interior is hollow, but the interviewee remarked that only the most noble and valiant would dare to peer within.
"As for what counts as noble and valiant ... Someone recalls an ancient wager regarding an axe—would you be willing to prove your mettle?"

A long sword forged from fine steel, shaped like a bleached bone. An emerald is set into the crossguard, rumored to see right into the heart of anyone brought before it.
The knight rides out at summer's end, declaring who will soon be reduced to bones and who will be reborn with the coming spring.

A New Knock's Aftershock: Greetings from Laplace!
Before I could comprehend the flood completely, it already knew me. Now, I exist within its ebb and flow—together with countless eras.
Before the flood could consume me completely, I had already remembered it. Now, I once more return to its ebb and flow, seeking the forgotten visions deeper within.
Upgrade Ashen Beast to Lv.10 and clear Manifest Analysis 3.
Upgrade Primitive Urge to Lv.10 and clear Manifest Analysis 3.
Tap, tap—each step falls as relentless as a ticking clock.
Beneath that icy gaze beats a fiery heart.
Tremble before the great vampire Rubuska the First!
In the long shadow of sunrise, she sits alone, savoring the scent of a fading dream.
No need to pray before taking the shot; she has already calculated the bullet's trajectory.

A true vampire hunter needs a keen sense of smell and eyes that can pierce through lies. Fortunately, she has both.

Two things drew her here: a generous bounty—one sufficient to sustain her studies in ley lines, and an ornate and yet abstruse invitation.

Danger? She's faced the furious outburst of wild ley energy before.

Excitement? Perhaps, since she has never walked the halls of such a bizarre mansion.

Dark emerald shadows dance in silence. The twisted pendulum sways to and fro. A black cat perches on the clock, its golden eyes fixed upon her. Blood-red moonlight pours down, a cold shroud upon her skin.

A phantom masquerade, eerie yet beautiful. She alone stands out, like an uninvited guest. Yes, every dance must come to an end—a curtain call requires a moment of subtle transition with the power to feed the imagination.

And so, she slowly raises the gun in her hand—her sights fixed on that single flash of red amid the shades.
The dead, the dying, the manic, the deranged ... All are his creations.

He wakes in the cacophony, in the midst of a masquerade. All around him, figures in crimson masks dance wildly, their movements contorted by frenzy yet brimming with joy.

He quickly realizes who they are—his own creations come to life: the neurotic elder brother, the sister buried alive, the lover consumed by obsession, the Red Death behind his mask, the black cat, and the raven that refused to be silent.

They gather around him, drawing him into their dance, pulling him back into the pages of his book. The mirror reflects his fractured figure. In a whisper, he asks himself, "Who am I?"

—He is their author, their friend, their beloved, and also their captive.

Moonlight cascades like a stream. The visions he once penned still frolic, and the raven keeps singing—

"Only this and nothing more."
Green overtakes the tombstone, marking another victory of life over the weight of destiny.

Once upon a time, a desperate outlaw fell to the ground in exhaustion during his flight. There in the fog, he met a knight in green, whose sword bore an emerald on its guard—an emerald that reflected the outlaw's own fear.

The fugitive shook uncontrollably, believing judgment awaited him. Yet the knight did not raise his sword. He simply stood there in silence, as though waiting for something.

So he spoke, his voice unsteady, confessing a life steeped in sin, and of the remorse he had never dared admit. The mist consumed him, and only his voice lingered, echoing deep within the forest.

Patiently, the Green Knight listened, following the story to its final word. From behind the tombstones came the sighs of lingering souls, and only then did the jewel on his sword grow dim.

The knight turned and vanished into the endless fog. He passes no judgment, but listens. He does not raise his blade, but allows the tormented to find peace in confessing their guilt to him. His sword, together with his ancient legend, waits silently for the next soul willing to lay bare its sins.
She wakes under the full moon, embracing the life the story has brought her.

Long, long ago, when time existed only as a thought and the moon rose as it always has, a girl crossed paths with a writer. He was dead, but could not rest, bound by obsessions that still consumed him.

The girl's body was fragile. She yearned for freedom, for a glimpse of the world beyond. Upon learning of his identity, she began to ask him question after question, each more difficult than the last.

Can a writer's stories ever be forgotten? Will his creations live on forever in the minds of those who read them? When a story ends, do the people within its pages live on until the end of time?

The writer answered swiftly, his answers flawless, but perfection was not what she sought. So the girl asked him to tell her a story.

He granted the girl's request, weaving story after story. The girl lifted her eyes, clear as glass, listening in silence as she pondered each word, until, within those stories, she found "life" again. And in the writer's eyes, her silhouette slowly fused with a vision once born from his pen ...

Is there something I can help you with?
Hello. This is the Zeno army. The road ahead is dangerous. Stay safe.
Don't get carried away when moving on ice, or you'll end up like this ...
A cage holding a Critter has been left behind here. Though its workings are unclear, the toybox's glass-headed Prime Minister once carried cages like this into battle to boost his strength.
In your current situation, you can't afford to turn down any potential advantage, even if it's radiating with strange arcanum. You reach for the cage.
The cage is broken. This little Critter, eager to win its freedom, dug a hole through the bottom. It gives you a nip, then seizes the chance to dart away.

From what you've seen, there may be free lunches in the world, but rarely free items. Your colleagues usually have to fight, answer questions, lend a hand, or run back and forth across regions to get their hands on one ...
Looking closely, you notice the Critter left behind a pile of dust inside the cage. These dust-eaters aren't known for saving food.
A hole, likely dug by its previous occupant. You can almost picture it working at night, gnawing through the cage's floor and into the soil while humans slept, waiting for its chance to escape ...
Some Critters are never meant to be caged. Every strand of their fur shines brighter in the light of freedom. Or could it be that all those trapped in Critter cages feel the same?
You shake your hand hard, flinging the Critter off you ... along with a few other things.
The grave marker looks hastily erected. You reach out but recoil as you feel it crackle with electricity. The burst of energy momentarily throws your fishbowl-faced companion into disarray.

Whether a bug in the system or merely a quirk. There doesn't seem to be a connection between electricity and the grave. Though another explanation springs to mind—of a rumored exorcist, who claimed spirits could generate electricity.

You examine the gravestone. The carved date tells a story of a boy that had just come of age, yet fell after only a week on this battlefield. Trading his life just to destroy a cannon. The disabled gun looms nearby—covered in flowers. Ironic.
You pluck a flower and set it down by the gravestone. No death on the battlefield should ever be forgotten.
He shows no surprise at seeing a Laplace employee step out of an office building. Instead, he poses a philosophical question ... how deep can the spirit go?
100m? 200m? 450m? 500m? In the world we know, the Mariana Trench reaches a depth of 10,994m. Could our spirits reach such depths too?
You may never know. But maybe one day you'll see it—that chasm of spirit, an abyss overflowing with grief and torment.
Looks like it's heading off with its friend to join a faction. In this box, unless they have a special purpose and go alone, most arcanists will join a faction that suits them.
You tell it that on one floor there's a free kingdom, ruled by a Critter well-versed in strategy that always finds ways to quell unrest. A perfect fit.
You tell him the Foundation has many employees fond of philosophical debate. Joining them might lead them to some interesting new ideas.

Laplace—the haven of great researchers, a dueling ground where ideas and technology collide. Join Laplace, join progress! Oh, one condition: you'll need a basic understanding of math, enough to give yourself a code number. I don't get it, but that's what they do.
Inside, it's far more spacious than you imagined. The stands are almost full, everyone waiting for something.
You barely open your mouth before being shoved onto the stage. "We've got a volunteer!"
The host praises your courage. Looks like you're about to stick your head into Olitiau's mouth.
This is no more dangerous than being stuck in your average Laplace lab. You pull it off flawlessly.
Suddenly, a circus worker bursts onto the stage, "The yeti is missing!"
There's no one behind you now—except the yeti.
The circus thanks you for helping retrieve their yeti.
Oh, sorry, did we disturb you? I was about to watch the show, but my siblings insisted on sorting out the seating order first.
Three are hibernating, leaving five to argue in a mess. Maybe you'd like to offer some objective advice?

I'm Two. Four wants to sit right next to One, on his left. Six refuses to sit beside Five. Three doesn't want to be next to Six and insists on sitting the furthest to the right. 
Now One wants to know who else is sitting next to him besides Four.
I knew it would be Five. Thanks. Looks like I've got an extra ticket, why don't you come too? The show's sure to be lots of fun.
Really? Forget it; what's done is done. Let's eat first. Do you want to see the show? I could sell you my ticket for this one.
Sit right below them. They like to watch the show from on top of my head for the best view. So, do you know the answer?
Want to see the show? I could sell you my ticket for this one.
Amid a chorus of boos, you step down from the stage. It almost makes you wonder if you made the wrong choice.
Last night I died countless times in my dream, all to the same grotesque, giant, coconut-shelled Critter. And all I had was a crowbar, but I swung at it with everything I had.
I must have died a thousand different ways. I'd swing too slow, stumble over a rock, or that critter would hit me with a sudden attack I'd never seen before.
Death, rebirth ... every time I shut my eyes, the cycle starts again, until I open them once more ...
No. What I need is a way to beat that Critter.
What's important is the moment I blocked its shell with my crowbar! I reckon I can stop every strike until I wear it down.
Thank you! Someday we can figure out how to beat that Critter together. I've already written down my notes, here ...
You know about it? Hey, that's part of our latest research! It lets you live out a completely different life.

Of course, would you help me try it out? This one—Soul of the Coconut Shell. Sounds like some strange scenario where you wake up next to a campfire. By now you're so used to dealing with the upper ranks, your first instinct is probably to ask whether this research has safety clearance.
Of course it does! Of course! But ... uhm, best not to mention it to anyone. It's top secret!

He doesn't really, so what you need to do now is shut down this dangerous operation and report it properly up the chain. Supervisor to supervisor until it reaches someone who can actually deal with it. Damn it, this calls for special handling.
He's gone—dragging half his instruments with him. You're responsible for returning the other half to the research center, but before that, you can salvage what he left behind.
With the coconut shell, you've turned into a dopey-looking Critter with a weapon in hand. Not far away, you spot a strange glass-headed figure digging in the sand.
It feels so familiar, but your memory is foggy. Ahead stands a short fence and a shabby, broken gate.
You can't get over it. You've already jumped higher than the fence itself, but it seems like an invisible wall blocks your way.
The gate seems locked in place, not budging an inch. You try again. Until the fishbowl blurts out: "The gate can't be opened from this side!"
You exhaust the Carbuncle language trying to get someone's attention.
You're not sure if it's just hysteria setting in, but your vision blurs. Dizzy and nauseous, you try desperately to exit this experiment.

You ask a person dressed like a knight. He tells you they're preparing to escort a young lord home to inherit his family estate. A rich man in the suitcase—it only reminds you of your ferrofluid colleague's tragic scam. You hold your tongue and move on.
You go back to find the knight. He apologizes and returns your belongings. He admits with a helpless look that his peculiar compulsion has tormented him for years. It's completely beyond his control.
As an apology, he invites you to join them on a guard mission. Alongside him is a thief skilled with muskets and daggers. A knight and a thief ... what is this, a fantasy role-playing game?
The knight looks embarrassed but adds that you'll get your share for this mission.
The strange sights along the way and the eerie bandits leave you uneasy. On this ruined road, anything and everything feels like a trap waiting to spring.
You reach the destination safely. True to his word, the young lord pays you fairly.

This shabby little town clings to a moss-covered castle—strange, helpless, and unbearably dreary. The people whisper among themselves as you approach. Their clothes are all different, like each one carries a story of their own.

The young lord's ancestral home has a few problems of its own. Inside are strange creatures and unspeakable horrors. To clear them out, the knight and the thief are putting together an expedition ... and you've been invited.
Good. You decide to split up and make preparations, then rendezvous in front of the castle.
Your makeshift expedition gathers before the castle, determined to see this mission through.
The shadowed halls reek of decay, your torches burning ever dimmer. Just when you feel on the edge of madness, a shriek cuts through the dank air. Another Critter lunges out from the dark.

Endless battles plague you as you continue your journey. Grotesque paintings and a castle as dim as a prison. You feel your mind being worn thin. Suddenly, your head starts to ring. Is this unseen pressure set to drag you further into despair, or will it pull you back from the brink?

Maybe this is nothing more than a hollow simulation, yet in this moment you still feel that surge of defiance, welling up from within and flooding through your body—yes, we suffer, but in suffering we rise.

Why must you endure such torment even here? It feels as though the world has always been unjust to you, whether inside this box or outside ... right now you only want to leave, to escape this cursed place.
But your struggle wasn't wasted. You cut your way through and reach the exit. Your courage lifts your companions' spirits, and they gladly share part of the spoils with you.
You stumble out in a rush, your Laplace comrades staring at you in confusion.

Then something strange happens ... your fear vanishes. When you turn back, the once towering castle has become nothing but ruins. In fact, the townspeople insist that it has been a ruin for as long as anyone can remember.
Meeting again brings no joy. Instead, you sense they've sunk deep into despair. When you ask what happened, they tell you they are on the edge of going mad.

But that's fine. You're an Arcanist. You've seen an apple on the run, a pirate without her ship, an Awakened with a fishbowl for his head—in fact, that fishbowl is even watching you right now. You don't think anything can scare you.
Courage is always rare. You suddenly feel a bit like Ulrich, back when you offered him a kind word—and that memory stirs a faint urge to refuse for refusal's sake.
But in the end, you choose to help them. Leaving something so strange, so terrifying, locked in this box can't be right ... or at least, that's what you tell yourself.
From their muddled words you gather no clear clue, only that the root of it all lies in that castle.

You arrive at the castle. The gate looms high before you. Push it open? Of course. Maybe procedure demands the owner's invitation. But don't worry, you're not a vampire. Formalities won't keep you out.
You throw your weight against the door. Adler, it's time to face your fears. In that instant, visions flood your eyes. The damned simulation even shows you the faces of those long gone.

You grit your teeth and scream until your voice breaks, but you hold on. Back home there's a saying: "Fortune favors the brave." Right now, you've earned a little luck. When everything finally settles, you're already at the exit, fresh air tearing at your lungs ... what a feeling.

You pull back. Sometimes curiosity brings no answers, and you've taught your colleagues the same. You know well the safety and stability that caution brings. You also know that with the unknown comes equal peril. Leave now. Never come back.
A familiar unease pushes you to check your pack. As expected, your Research Notes are gone.
You ease a door open. A dog lies there, old, as if it's been waiting here all this time. You step closer. It doesn't even raise its head to bark.
On the table rests a notebook, likely left by its master. It may very well contain something interesting.
It's a diary. The first entry was eleven years ago; the last one, ten. A year's worth of life—master and dog, side by side. Staring at the sky together, pondering the universe beyond.
Though you know there is no true universe out there to ponder. Only the whir of Laplace's endless projects and endless accidents.
You close the diary and glance at the dog beside you. Then, as if on cue, it rises and runs to the door, ready to greet someone—its master, perhaps?
Time passes. But the master never arrives. The dog returns to its spot, curling down again. You set food in its bowl. Still ... the place is tidy, as if someone comes to clean it often.
You let your guard down, only for doubt to creep back—just pieces on a board. Yet each of them does, in their way, "live."
You crouch, reaching to pat it, then stop short. Not out of fear. Just because that touch should be left for its master.
You can almost picture it; that massive fish breaking the surface before the fisherman, and the fisherman brimming with excitement, convinced the catch was already his.

But now he's fallen silent—yes, he bested the storm, he conquered the great fish, but he couldn't defeat the sharks drawn by the scent of blood. They tore into the fisherman's hard-won prize, stripping it bite by bite, until they drank down the last trace of blood and swam away satisfied. All that remained was him, sailing back with nothing but bones to show for his work.

An unpleasant memory returns to your mind—the day you burst into your "leader's" office, shouting in rage. You railed at those "sharks," perched high above, devouring the hard-won bounty. But she said nothing, save that her mission was over and it was now your turn to be the fisherman.
Only now do you realize—the true prize isn't the tender meat, but the bones. The bones tell every fisherman waging war with the deep sea that they still have something to give this world.
You sit down beside him, lost in thought. Musae III appears to have not programmed in any response; the old man remains silent beside you.
This isn't an hourglass. It's a Klein bottle.
I'll say it again—this isn't an hourglass. It's a Klein bottle.
One last time! Not an hourglass, A KLEIN BOTTLE!
Why can't you understand the precision of the term? A complex name like this gives the object its uniqueness. Call it an hourglass, and it becomes something ordinary, something utterly forgettable!
He flares up as though insulted, ranting nonsense, deeply offended.

As his impotent rage falls into reluctant compromise, you catch a trace of complaint in his tone. "You people drinking coffee from mixed blends—how could you ever know the splendor of a true, well-sourced bean?"

Your concession seems to please him. He starts talking at length—about only drinking coffee from pure beans from secret groves, about Darjeeling tea picked in March and April. Every word drips with status. You start to lose patience.
You flip him over. His eyes stay shut, one arm raised awkwardly, pointing toward a plate.
You call into his ear. No reaction, but his finger holds its aim towards the plate.
You shake him hard. Still no response, still pointing.
You slap him across the face. He bolts upright, furious, and drives you out of his sight.
On the plate, some unknown substance spells something: Ca ... ?
Cart? Carbuncle? Whatever it means, it's the only clue to why he collapsed. The substance gives off an atrocious smell, yet one that somehow makes you hungry.
He remains still on the ground.
He wakes again, but the moment he sees the rations, he faints once more. Maybe Laplace really should rethink its catering, both inside and outside the suitcase.
The smell wakes him, and he begins gobbling up the food presented to him. The thought occurs once more: Laplace really does need to review its catering, whether inside or outside the toybox.
That's how my radio got fixed. Can you fix cars?
Thanks, just in time. I still have more rations to deliver.

Yes, "a daily ration." Don't look at me like that, I know you're fed up with having the same tasteless food day after day. Apparently some folks have even started refusing to eat. But every department is fighting for funding ... where is logistics supposed to find the money?
Even so, I'll deliver them. But those hunger strikers are determined ... I saw someone faint at their post earlier.
If you're headed somewhere else, maybe you could bring him something different to eat ... something better than these rations.
Clearly, the Critters want nothing to do with it. Still, he keeps circling and watching.
The place is a mess from the fighting—cans are knocked over, a Carbuncle stomps right over them. No one wants food covered in mud.

Critters have their own habits, their own social order. They have no need for any condescending "enlightenment." And if eating canned food counts as enlightenment, then his wits are lower than that blundering overlord the ferrofluid Awakened once ran into.
My inspiration is gone! My muse has left me. Help!
Of course you can help! He immediately showers you with praise—a "melancholy drifter's gaze" and "wild, romantic hairstyle" ... Seems like he wants you to be his new model.
People sometimes fall into these frenzied, irrational states. Laplace's usual solution is a good punch. Once again, it works.
Hearing you're willing to track down his old model, he's overjoyed and gives you a portrait of the "muse" as a reference. A black curly-haired horse with mournful eyes.

The stable master greets you warmly and leads you through the stables. But the horses here are all different kinds of strange. You pass one wearing sunglasses and a beret, swaying to records ... a shaggy one scratching patterns into the dirt ... a scarecrow horse with birds perched on it ... and one draped in blue cloth pinned up with horseshoes, though it's not clear if there is even a horse beneath it.
The stable master doesn't know the Timekeeper, but he does recognize the horse in the portrait. He points you to his old stables. That misfit horse often runs off there, locking itself inside.
"Want to paint it? Fine by me—if you can drag her out." He shrugs. "But I suggest you don't bother. That horse is stubborn."

The weeds are waist-high, and the old stable has half collapsed. In the dim ruins, you hear the black horse snorting in agitation. Somehow, you understand ... she knows her world has been abandoned, left in ruins, and she refuses to move on. She's exiled herself to a corner of the broken past.

The times must always move forward, never back. That's the principle you've always held to. There's no right or wrong in it—whether for this strange horse, the world around it, or even the stable master himself.
You try to speak, but no words come. There's no bedding here anymore, no clover for it to eat or rest on. At last, wearing an even sadder look, the horse steps out.
Do you think she never tried? That she never once bent, even a little? She endured the torment of reason, lived among monsters, and bore the stares of suspicion and self-interest!
The more she held on, the more she lost. Cynical, bitter—but nothing more. Then she too, walked away.
That sentimental painter is still waiting for his muse.

Yes! This melancholy that rejects life itself has somehow stirred the young man's urge to create! Clearly he sees in this horse some deep philosophical truth shared by all living things. But you can't keep looking into her eyes, nor can you bear to stay here any longer.

The horse looks nothing like the one in the portrait. Her gloom and melancholy are gone, and now she paces with a restless mockery and defiance towards everything around her. The painter seems to revel in this change, murmuring words like "fate and challenge" and "release and awakening," but you've already grown too impatient to listen.
Now the only one who still comes here is that horse ... along with the Critters blocking your way.
A ragged researcher grabs you and starts explaining his grand theory: the world is a box, a toy chest shaped by the hands of God.
But who doesn't live in a box? The real question is how you define the box. After some debate, he leaves you a gift and walks away, content.
You don't bother with his outdated fantasies and turn to leave.
But something is missing—the soup hasn't turned red. The Critters lift their wet, shining eyes toward you. Who taught them to do this?
The Critters end up with a pot of red soup just as they imagined, and they share a bowl with you in thanks.
In the end, the Critters get a pot of bright red, sweet-and-sour soup. They love the taste and offer you a bowl as well.
But when you add the one red ingredient every Laplace employee knows, the whole pot turns into thick smoke.
Furious at losing their lunch, the Critters decide to throw you into the pot instead!
Chattering wildly, the Critters scatter, leaving a complete mess behind them.

According to him, both humans and arcanists trace back to a legendary continent that once connected the whole world, now long vanished. That, he says, explains why similar myths are found across all cultures.
You find it impossible not to argue the point with him, but you can't exactly drag him to the bottom of the Pacific to see for himself, so the matter ends without a resolution.
Still, he's delighted to have found a kindred spirit and gives you a necklace said to come from that lost continent.
But when you catch him slacking on the job, you report him and confiscate the occult society pamphlet he had hidden under his desk.
The sign beside the apple reads: "I am taking part in a clinical trial. The potion is right here, but please do not cure me." A brightly colored vial sits next to it.
What have you done?! Back in human form, he cries out in despair.
I finally found a job where I could lie down and still get paid. What have you done?! No! I won't go back! Nurse! Nurse!
He bolts upright from the bed and charges screaming into the hallway.
For some reason, you suddenly feel like throwing the apple at him.
Hit and hurt, he scrambles to slam the red button by the bed with every pair of limbs he possesses. A nurse rushes in and drags you out.
Before you go, the creature pats you on the shoulder, dips its headless stump, and presses an apple into your hand.
As you turn to leave, the bug points one limb at the trash can, telling you to take out the garbage. It reminds you of how you once recklessly squandered your own holidays.
But just as even the most precise machine has its margin of error, Musae III seems to have slipped a faint trace of hope for Laplace's future into its calculations.
You see a man built of muscle—Laplace's uniform draped over his shoulders, a sleeveless shirt beneath, veins bulging from his rock-like frame.
He spots you and greets you warmly, clapping you on the back. At once your insides shudder, as if they might burst out through your ribs.

You don't even have time to think before one healthy, muscle-bound body after another steps out from the gym doors. To you, their very presence in a budget meeting already radiates authority and unquestionable power.
Yes, at a budget meeting, only one department can stand tall.
Then a man dressed like a coach approaches, looks over your thin frame, and eagerly pulls out a training plan. He asks if you're interested in working out.

With equal enthusiasm he explains: when the "Storm" comes, Laplace can rush in ahead of everyone else to save vital instruments. During the last "Storm," he personally carried off every single Game of Life machine.
You click your tongue, face twisting. He almost convinces you! But no—you're not ready to pour your passion into these iron torture devices.
Still, the coach won't give up. He presses some supplements into your hand and urges you to try them.
He leans closer and reveals both palms, each with a pill. Quick! Make your choice!
You swallow the red pill. Nothing happens. The world doesn't change, nor do you wake in a capsule surrounded by tubes. But there is a hint of strawberry.
You swallow the blue pill. Nothing happens. No glitches, no cracks in the air, just a lingering taste of artificial blueberry sweetener.
Good. The researcher pulls out a notebook and checks a box dutifully. Looks like most people prefer the strawberry flavor.
Good. The researcher pulls out a notebook and makes a checkmark. One more for blueberry.

Oh yes, we've developed plenty of other flavors too. He fishes out a handful of brightly colored pills, proud to show them off. Thank you for supporting the project. Per our regulations, I also owe you some pay for volunteering.
Hey! Wizard! You look like a clever one!
Clever men are almost always wizards, and wizards must therefore be clever. You look like both—clever and a wizard!
Actually, I'm king of a nation. But my people don't believe me. Do you know how I can prove my claim?
Once I'm recognized, I swear to name you my court magician!
The old legends offer a solution; you tell him to seek a sword from the Lady of the Lake. That should be proof enough to crown him king.
You leave the rambling man behind and return to your task.
Ah! Lady of the Lake! Grant me the proof of my kingship!
But no matter how he shouts, the water stays still as glass. Then he notices you.
Oh, wizard! You've revealed yourself again. You must have foreseen this! Grant me wisdom. What must be done to win the Lady's favor?
Who did this? Aren't you satisfied tossing just old coins in?!
Just as expected, you and the young man end up cleaning trash out of the lake to make up for tossing a sword into it.
You feel insulted all over again. His mind is barely sharper than a Critter's!
Maybe the Lady of the Lake had never seen someone hurled straight at her before. Outraged, she lunges at you, dragging that foolish young man along with her.
The fight ends. Everything falls quiet again ... except for the foolish youth, who fainted before and is now murmuring beside you.
Someone begins a mime act right in front of you. His skill is remarkable—every wall, every teacup in his hands feels real. He even sits down on a chair built entirely of imagination!
He stares wide-eyed as you walk straight past. In his world, there may really be a wall there ... but you rudely chose to break this illusion and his performance by strolling straight through.
Suddenly, the mime rushes at you with an invisible knife.
"You ruined my world!" he cries. Yes, you tore through his act, and with it, his dream. Yet to the very end, he still uses his performance to show his fury. His dedication is admirable, in a way.
It's just a charade, isn't it?
Out of respect for his craft, you decide to take another path so as not to disturb his act. Look, he even leans out of his nonexistent window to wave at you.
You step inside, edging closer to a pile of shining trinkets—then your eyes adjust to the dark. They aren't trinkets, but nameless dog tags.
