They're the ellipses in frontline reports, the smallest unit of a gravestone, the final full stop of fate. Countless people have given their names to them, for the things they believed in and for a future they would never see.
Signatures matter. They ensure that when bodies scatter, we don't lose each other. Like the numbers marked on puzzle pieces, like the tearful cries of mothers who've lost their children.

You hope there are other things left ... substitutes, time, choices, bullets, daydreams, or maybe a favorite chocolate shared with someone you love. Call it greedy, but there's nothing wrong with idealism.
You sit, lifting the rusty stack of tags into the sunlight. Their glints scatter across your face, across an empty corner of the wall ... peace.
With a deep breath, you put them back.
You stride closer, but someone inside must have sensed you. The lights go dark, the sounds fade, until all that's left are your steps and the sound of your breath.
You pull back the curtain. There's nothing behind it but a quiet static-filled TV and popcorn scattered over a table. Such strange silence. You almost wish the place were loud again.
You step in, only to spot a shadow creeping up behind you. You lunge for the lantern—only to have someone dive at you too.
A girl draped in a bedsheet apologizes, begging forgiveness for her blunder before darting off.
Meanwhile, her friends leap out of the corners, marveling at how well the horror movie trick worked. They chatter excitedly about their experiment, ignoring you, the victim.

While they're distracted, you snatch the cursed discs from beneath the TV, grabbing the stack from the table too. Without a backward glance, you march out of the tent, leaving behind only their wailing voices.
He lowers his bloodied fist and turns toward you. That's when you notice the Uluru Games tag hanging from his neck—not gold, not bronze, not even a "participation award." It says enough.

He fixes you with a stare and begins recounting his long, arduous journey through the competition. However dramatic the twists and turns, he was still just one of thousands of nameless athletes. Little talent, no coaching, not even a sturdy punching bag—and no one to listen. Until now.

He talks without pause, telling you how he scraped together travel money from tips, leftovers, and even hitching a ride on a truck hauling chickens and ducks. In the very first match, he lost a front tooth, but he laughs: "That bloke's punch was nothing compared to my old man's."
He takes a swig of beer and keeps going. He breezed through his opening round, only to face the reigning champion next. As expected, he was pounded into the dirt without landing a single point.

"No, no, no," he waves away your sympathy, proudly showing the scar it left him, like a general displaying medals. "I've been hit by my father, by punks, by cops ... but believe me, that punch was the best I ever took in my life."
He stops, swaying his bottle, staring at the ragged sandbag. After a long silence, he mutters: "Maybe I really don't have the right stuff. What do you think?"
He locks eyes with you, no barrier between you. Then his shoulders slacken, and with them, his spirit. The fight goes out of him.
He lets out a dry laugh. "Well, looks like you've thrown a solid punch in your time too."
Alcohol dulls his nerve. His words trail off into fragments, then gibberish. You can see he's about to drift off, so you just sit and listen until he begins snoring through his crooked nose.
The bottle rolls to the ground, the fire still burning. As you turn to go, you catch a strange phrase he murmurs in his sleep: "Throw the eggs at the high wall."
One cat, two cats ... thirteen cats. You're surrounded. This terrifying species tamed humanity thousands of years ago, and not even the "Storm" could shake their feline grip.
You take out your thin stack of Research Notes, the only belongings you brought into this box. All provided by Ulrich.
Now you have cats, and you have currency. By all accounts, you already hold what's needed to rule this box.
You stare at the cats before you, then at the Research Notes in your hands. You start imagining a perfect state—stable, prosperous, without tyranny, where all work together against the "Storm."
Until Marcus politely reminds you: cats don't take orders, and those papers will only buy you a few Picrasma Candies.
Pieces come together, forming a complete letter draft. No sender, no recipient, just a discarded message.
In it, a man calling himself General P writes to a soldier's family with raw, honest regret. He admits he started a "mistaken" war, one that resulted in thousands of unnecessary deaths.
"It was born of my own selfishness. In a clash of wills, I shot him. And to cover my crime, I committed another unforgivable sin ... I started a war."

"Afterward, I walked away unscathed. And the man I shot was honored for 'giving his life in the pursuit of glory.' When I realized I had the power to bury the truth so easily, I felt a chill. Yes, if I wanted, with the right excuse, I could start a war that stripped away all humanity ..."
The tone feels clumsy, unpolished. It's more like an unfinished story than a real letter. Because you know one simple truth ...

Obviously, gray-checkered suits and silver heads are not the same. And the checkered ones tend to be harder to fool than Laplace. No, sir, this is the Foundation, and if you're not staff, you follow the rules.
He rattles off procedure fast, mixing in code names only insiders use, synonyms that point who-knows-where, and acronyms that mean nothing to you.
Luckily, you've learned how to fish for key details from the Foundation staff. In short, you need to file an entry application, get it approved, collect a temporary pass, and then register with him.
But with the ongoing crisis, they've locked down the building. Every staff member has been confined inside, and no one is allowed in or out.
In other words, to go inside, you must apply, and to apply, you must go inside. Any good rulemaker knows—some procedures aren't made to be followed but to stop you from following them.
Still, the staffer bows politely, apologizes for the inconvenience, and says you're welcome to return once you have a pass.
Laplace employees, of course, know how to cut corners and find clever solutions. You take his badge, cover his shift in the building for a while, and even collect his paycheck.
Great. Once the "Storm" sends you back, I'll be able to track you with it. Oh, and here's your payment. Keep it.
Don't worry, I'll find you after the "Storm." This capsule holds enough radioactive isotopes—ten years, ten whole years. No matter where you are on Earth, I'll track you down.
Safe? Of course it's safe. By my calculations, any side effects from exposure won't show up for at least thirty years—gentler than most chronic illnesses ... wait, where are you going?
Fine, looks like I'll just have to test it on myself. Maybe lower the requirements, find someone else to handle the data collection ...
Hey—hey, 3751671! There you are. Didn't we agree to meet in front of the office? Never mind, here's what you wanted. Catch.
No need to thank me. Your last reply was hilarious.
... You're not 3751671? Then who are you? Where is 3751671?
You don't know? Damn it, tell me where the nearest computer is; I need to contact him.
Hello, I'm waiting for my colleague 3751670 to bring me my things. Have you seen him?
Thanks so much. Sorry to trouble you. Go ahead and keep these.
Damn it, I'm at a critical stage of this experiment. Where is 3751670 with my things?
Researcher 3751670 or 3751671? Doesn't matter. Looks like they've run into each other ... and now it's time for a shouting match.
The one who lost storms off, leaving a few things behind.
Ah, a fellow colleague! I'm collecting signatures to change the textbooks! Please support me! The theoretical evidence is clear: the brain is nothing but a snot generator!
Impossible? Think carefully! Ghosts ... Awakened ... The Beyond ... the world is full of beings with no brain at all!
If the brain isn't just a snot generator but the seat of consciousness and memory, then how do you explain the sapience of our nonhuman colleagues?
Join me! Join us! Long live the Brain Useless Theory!
He empties his brain for the sake of his theory. You can't reach him anymore.
Congratulations—from today, you're a supporter of the Useless Brain Theory! Here's your reward.
Here the world is frozen, barren, with no supplies, no people, not even Critters. But it's in times like these that assumptions are broken. Inside this greenhouse, crops are growing ... corn?

It's a farm, but no one's here. You get out of your vehicle and step inside. The whole place is empty, nothing like the haystacks and harvests you'd expect. Of course not ... how could corn even grow in this frozen wasteland?

As you rest, you hear a door open. Following the sound, you see a farmer walk in with bushels of corn in his arms. He spots you and assures you that all is fine. Though he's glad to offer a traveler a place to rest.

You're puzzled equally by his corn and his welcome, but he just smiles and says he bought it from an upper-level store. In a few days, they will come inspect his "cornfields," so he bought a cartload to pile into the granary.
You don't understand the point of it, but you respect his efforts. After all, such things aren't terribly uncommon in your own world.
Before you leave, he gives you some supplies and invites you to come back someday to taste their homegrown potatoes.
But unlike last time, there's no corn in the fields. You head over anyway and, by chance, run into the farmer again.
He's in the fields now, busy digging up the freshly grown potatoes.
He's glad they finally realized corn couldn't survive here. At last, they gave up on that fantasy.
Just as he's about to cook you a stew of potatoes and meat, a squad of ragged soldiers arrives with the newest orders: now he will have to plant sugarcane.
You can sense the farmer's helplessness, but he still forces a smile and agrees.
More worn down and exhausted than you, he looks as if he's been sent off on some impossible hunt.
Oh, I was designing a private exhibition hall for my investors. They promised me a massive budget and total freedom with time ...
But then the budget was cut in half, and the deadline shortened to just two weeks, and then came all the extra little demands ...
And just today they remembered to tell me: "Oh, by the way, the greenhouse needs a five-meter Roman-style statue of Abraxas in it."
Now the design is shapeless, the requirements endless, the goals hopelessly tangled. Everything's been ruined ... it's going to be a total failure.
Take these blueprints, my weeks of work. Use them as a table wedge or firewood ... they're worthless to me now.
Enduring both a strangling budget and unbearable collaborators, you're certain he'd make prime material for Laplace.

You know? Oh, you must be the architect they brought in to take over. Perfect timing, we need to talk things through. For example, this staircase—we want it angled toward the left hallway, leading straight into the right hall.
Yes, yes. We'd like a bit more sense of ascent, but without changing the current style. Cultural expression must come before beauty.
And of course, as the main link between floors, it must embody the concept of "connection." Oh, and it should wrap around the Abraxas statue ...
Yes, exactly, don't you understand? Facing the left hall, leading to the right, something that conveys our openness to visitors ...
Your head finally shakes off their chatter. They scatter, leaving you buried under the materials and diagrams of their "concepts."

The handwriting is crooked. You stare at it for a long time before realizing it's a name. Someone has carved this name into everything ... everything but the sky and the winds and rivers that no hand could ever carve.
"I'm not a robber, not a thief, and certainly not your king!" A figure bursts out of the grass, loudly protesting your judgment.
"You've mistaken me. I don't know the first thing about art." Another figure springs out of the brush, dismissing the claims with a wave of his hand.
He stares at you, seeming to question your intention. After a pause, he answers, "I am me. A keeper of memories. I keep track of everything I say and do, so when death comes, I can prove that I was."

"Present, you say? If no one in the future remembers, then the 'present' can't really be said to exist at all!" He gestures to the leftovers. "I carved my name and the time on the spoon and bones, so people will know I had lunch at this very moment."
Hearing your challenge, he steps back quickly as if avoiding a punch. After a moment of silence, he finally speaks. "Then they'll know it was me who ate this, not you or anyone else."
"This confirms my independent existence." He nods in agreement. "I always plan ahead."
"Go away! Your footprints are overlapping mine. It will confuse people in the future. Now I need to walk the same path again!" He becomes even more determined in his work as he pushes you aside.
He looks up but remains silent.
"I find myself in excellent health, though I appreciate your concern." He gives a slight nod with a benign smile.
"Words must be chosen with care; actions demand thoughtful consideration, my dear friend." He responds with a courteous tone.

He waves, a gentle attempt to convince you to leave. "Let not my presence alter the path your heart has chosen, nor linger in your memory. Keep moving forward. In both life and death, I should not disturb the natural flow of things."
You can feel that this person is entirely different from the "keeper" you encountered earlier. They carry different energies and ... even scents.
He observes your confusion but offers nothing else.
He remains quiet and refuses to make eye contact.
You realize you've uncovered another universal truth: when the "gods" first bestowed the ability to speak, they did not distribute it fairly.

Something's wrong. Why does this place still have ancient Eastern architecture? This stupid box seems built on compounding errors, radiating hostility toward its players. Just as you're about to rant about this simulation again for the thousandth time, a loud explosion goes off to your left.
The blast settles, and the people around you continue their routines like nothing happened. Soon, a man emerges from the site, covered in dust.
He notices your clothes and excitedly asks where you're from. When you mention Laplace, he doesn't recognize the name. He doesn't know Laplace, much less the Foundation or Zeno.

He introduces himself as an inventor and delights in hearing you're something of a scientist yourself. He leads you to his workshop, where you're stunned by the sheer number of bizarre inventions he's concocted.
With great enthusiasm, he shows you his design. Is that a rocket? A manned rocket, no less? A person is sitting in a chair equipped with multiple rockets while wearing a set of bird wings.​
He asks for your help in gathering materials. You hesitate. This new invention feels a little too dangerous. You try to warn him, but there's nothing you can say to deter him.
Humans have always looked to the sky, longing for flight. You're at a loss for words but decide to help him gather what he needs.
So? Did you get the materials?
His eyes widen as he sees the materials. Though still hesitant, you agree when he asks you to bring some alcohol next time to help work up his courage.
When you arrive, everything appears ready. There are no safety measures or volunteers—just him, sitting on a chair surrounded by rockets with leather wings on his back.
You pour him a cup of liquor and take a small drink for yourself. The strong taste hits your head in an instant. He looks uneasy about drinking but finishes it in one go anyway.
"You're the only one who has supported me, my friend. If all this should fail, please take my belongings," he says.

He shakes his head and prepares himself. Finally gripping a bamboo stick with a glowing ember inside to light the fuse. Soon, the rockets fire, lifting him into the sky. His face glows red; whether from the alcohol or excitement, it's hard to tell.
He's finally living his dream. You hold a guide rope ready to direct his landing, but sadly and perhaps not at all unsurprisingly, an explosion soon rips through the air.
You stay silent. He was just a program, you tell yourself, yet you feel compelled to reconsider the true meaning of this box.
You sense someone following you, but every time you turn around, all you see is darkness.
Just when you feel puzzled, a faint light flickers, then another, and soon there are several flames scattered through the darkness.
A bunch of soldiers, huh? Without these flames, you might never have noticed them!

It's a Zeno squad, carrying out orders from their lieutenant to keep an eye on the Supreme Warlord's Critter Kingdom. You may think the goofy Carbunclists aren't worth the attention, but you still give them the respect they deserve.
Struggling with aphasia, the soldiers find communication nearly impossible. Yet you notice their determined efforts—tying knots, using hand signs, drawing in the dirt—all to complete their mission.
Maybe you could help. Your skills in deciphering messages and creating translators might be helpful. You have most of the materials, but there are still a few things you need to find.
You gather the materials and put together a translator. You even add a splash of color to it.
"Grand opening offer! Get the complete package for only 199! The latest propulsor with a full set of maintenance gear!"

You feel tempted because the propulsor would definitely improve your efficiency, but you don't need the other items. Your coworkers at Headquarters are already skilled at keeping their equipment running well.
"The propulsor alone costs 198, and maintenance service is worth 99! But as a set, they're just 199!"
This takes you back to your time in Germany—where a Dunkelbier cost 35, but you could add a sausage for just 40. Usually, you only wanted the beer, but they always offered the combo first.
And once again, you fall for the trap of consumerism, spending 199 for the propulsor even though, like that old sausage, you'll likely never use the maintenance service.
Careful! Resources are precious. Don't waste money on unnecessary things.
"How about our finest engine accelerator? Only 299, and it's all yours!"
A quiet urge stirs inside you. Once it starts, it's easy to find a thousand reasons to justify your purchase.
Your rational side tells you not to go for it, but you can't help imagining how much faster your team could move with this upgrade. But then again, you convinced yourself of the same thing last time.
In the end, you buy the add-on, which will probably offer little real improvement. The merchant walks away, completely satisfied.
The merchant notices your hesitation and enthusiastically describes the advantages of this component, even adding that he'll offer it on a sensible payment plan.
He presents a pile of contracts and explains that with some collateral, they can offer you emergency funding with no interest as long as it's repaid on time ...
In the end, you offer some collateral and buy the add-on, which will probably offer little real improvement. The merchant walks away, carrying your supplies, completely satisfied.
Damn it! That was a close one. You nearly fell for it. This whole lending scheme might be new, but it only makes you feel furious.
When the merchant sees your angry expression, he sheepishly backs away.
"Grand opening offer! Get the complete package for only ..."
It seems like he has too many borrowers to keep track of, as it takes him a moment to recognize you.
"Ah, it's you, sir!" he says, flipping open a notebook and crossing your name off the list.

"Your ... collateral?" He pulls out a pile of contracts again and indicates a term. "Look, since you missed the repayment deadline, we've already disposed of your collateral. What you're paying now is just the interest."
The contract does make this clear. The "repay on time" condition he promised before was only verbal.
By physical means, you teach the salesman a lesson about integrity. He runs away in a hurry, leaving several items behind on the ground.
It seems a disagreement has arisen, with the pirate feeling embarrassed about having to pay for something since she's, well, a pirate.
The young diviner, clearly upset, turns red as she argues in her native tongue, French.
She struggles to keep up with the rockin' pirate's sharp wit and, in frustration, announces that she will ask her maman to help sort things out.
"So, you have a mother too?" You hear the pirate's words. It makes the young diviner's face turn an even deeper shade of red.
As soon as you speak, both of them turn to face you. You notice the young diviner's hopeful expression; it's apparent that she expects you to help her out of this mess.
The rockin' pirate, on the other hand, just laughs. She makes it clear in no uncertain terms that paying full price is just not groovy.
"Oh no! Chief mate, we've got to run!" She shouts and quickly disappears.
The young diviner thanks you sincerely for your assistance and offers you some gifts.

It's truly remarkable how people welcome you with such joy. With plastic flowers in hand, they watch each step you take on the tiles. You're just an ordinary researcher who spends their day toiling away in a dim laboratory. When have you ever experienced such an extravagant and oddly horrifying welcome?
The host greets you with enthusiasm and begins explaining all the free services available: free housing, free land, free food, and free healthcare.
You are blown away by the benefits. All of this, for free? No one needs to work since robots take care of everything. It feels almost like a dream, yet everything seems perfectly normal.
Then the host asks for your help in retrieving supplies that were taken by Critters. In return, he promises to offer support for your team.
Traps can often seem too good to resist, much like the promises of those masked jerks. You realize it's time to leave this place, and the sooner, the better.
You arrive at the Critters' camp. These Critters have been remarkably peaceful since establishing their "Great Carbuncle Kingdom," making their sudden theft of supplies odd.
You decide to focus on getting the stolen goods back, without spending time questioning their motives.

The Critters put up a strong resistance, but you manage to retrieve the supplies. As you're about to leave, a small Critter clamps down on your trouser leg and won't let go, no matter how hard you try to shake it off.
It's just one Critter, so it doesn't pose much danger. After quite a bit of effort, you finally free yourself from its grip and set it down by the side of the road before continuing on your way.
Marcus, however, handles the Critter with more concern. She doesn't try to yank it off but instead delicately places it on the ground. The Critter begins to hop around as if trying to say something.
You return to the town and hand over the supplies. As they open the container to inspect the contents, you catch sight of a few items you've never seen before.
A motley of strange materials without a doubt, but after all the bizarre things you've come across, you choose not to dwell on it. You accept their payment and leave without a second glance.
You try to talk with the Critter, and it seems to understand. It leads you to a strange place with chests that look to be stuffed full of stolen goods.
When you give the Critter a confused look, it acts out a simple scene—one even a Critter could understand—showing that these things always belonged to them.

The situation suddenly clicks into place. How can a town like that enjoy endless resources without working for them? Where do all those free supplies come from? It seems there can be only one explanation: by taking them from someone else.
Without any particular reason, you return the chests to the Critters, call it a whim or a flight of fancy, but it feels right.
The Critters begin chattering excitedly; surprised and grateful for your act of kindness, they offer you a share of their meager supplies.

The "Storm" has flooded the outer towns, forcing residents to seek shelter here. However, it seems only a select few people, those least changed have been allowed entry, leaving others abandoned outside.
With the "Storm" approaching, you must suppress your sympathy; they are only lines of code. Still, the stark inhumanity present here seems to have a reality of its own.
Those outside notice your neat appearance and mistake you for a local. They plead for your help to enter. The "Storm" has left them homeless. You could share your resources or simply ignore them.
You remind yourself not to get too bothered; this is just a simulation and you're not Ulrich.

You decide to distribute some supplies. It's not like you can take them back to Laplace anyway, so letting them have it won't hurt. You tell yourself that. But the crowd pushes forward, desperate, and it takes you a while to break free. Maybe it's time to head into the city.
As you try to ignore the chaos, the packed crowd blocks the way completely, making it impossible to enter the city for now.

A demonstration is taking place in the town where residents protest the local administration's refusal to accept refugees. You are surprised to spot a familiar face from your previous visit, now marching among the protesters.

When you ask about his involvement, he advocates for compassion and the acceptance of refugees while growing angry as he criticizes the town leaders for their inaction and lack of humanity. "They're total jerks!" he says, and you end up adding several words to your vocabulary, all of them vulgar and pointedly rude.
You ask if he would be willing to temporarily host a refugee himself. He immediately agrees, saying that it is everyone's responsibility to do all they can for their fellow humans.
Yet when you mention having just such a refugee friend seeking shelter, his attitude shifts. Sputtering out excuses that his home is under renovation and the room wouldn't be suitable.
You ask if there are any other places to stay in town. Predictably, his answer is sadly predictable. It seems as if his entire neighborhood is suddenly under construction. How convenient.

It wasn't the "Storm" that turned this town into ruins, allowed Critters to settle here, caused refugee riots and looting, or made those "compassionate elites" flee in panic, though the last point might be debatable.
Dust covers the ground. See this, Ulrich? The compassion you seek is nothing more than a house of cards.
The host smiles at you warmly as he waits for you to retrieve the supplies taken by the Critters.

You spot an animal that looks like a squirrel. In fact, it IS a squirrel. He seems to be working on something, but when he notices you approaching, he hurries toward you. The two of you lock eyes through the glass, and then, unexpectedly, he begins using tactical hand ... paw signals.
"Me, trap, help." The message is clear, but then this is a zoo; aren't all the animals "trapped" here?

"Me, Zeno, sergeant, capture, enemy, here." A Zeno squirrel? Imprisoned in a zoo? Laplace is no stranger to strange situations, but this one ... okay, it makes sense when you recall that this toybox was a gift from Musae III.
"Laplace, help me, escape, save, squad." He's not alone. He's leading a squad! This zoo somehow managed to contain an entire Zeno squad. Impressive.

You decide to help the unfortunate squirrel. Following the Laplace Captivity Escape Manual, the first step suggests focusing on physical health and waiting calmly for rescue. All these manuals are based on experience. Should you trust this conventional wisdom?
The squirrel decides to trust you. He puts a nut in his mouth, closes his eyes, and lies down, waiting for the rescue you mentioned.
"Me, prepare, then, back." You know waiting around like this isn't going to work, so you trust your own gut instead. You need to prepare for the rescue.
The squirrel trusts you. He will keep waiting for you.
When you return to find him, he looks noticeably rounder. Still, he's happy to see you, though his mood shifts to sadness. Using paw signals, he communicates: "Rescue, no. Zeno, forget, us."
Comfortable living conditions haven't weakened his determination. He still wants to escape with his squad. You open the manual to the second page.
"If no rescue comes after a prolonged period, you must find the tools to escape on your own." When you try to turn the page, you find that the rest of the manual is blank. Screw this garbage!
You search through your belongings for something useful but only find a small spoon. Forcing a calm expression to hide your guilt, you pass it through the feeding hole.
The squirrel accepts the spoon. Thankfully, Laplace often tests new materials, and this spoon proves surprisingly sturdy. He tests it and signs back to you: "Meet, outside, pal."

He looks pleased as he explains how he used the spoon to dig through the ground and escape via a tunnel. The idea of having dug so far with only a spoon beggars belief, but there's no sense complaining about that.

He accepts your praise and proudly states that this is exactly what every Zeno soldier should be capable of. Then he asks if you'd be willing to help rescue the rest of his squad, still trapped in the zoo.
You agree without hesitation, simply because he asked you. How could you refuse a comrade in arms ... paws?

The squirrel leads you through the zoo, where you meet his squad members. First a squirrel, now penguins. This feels like something out of a cartoon. You discreetly check your surroundings but find no cameras.

You two no longer need to use sign language and talk directly. Growing more and more excited as he discusses his elaborate escape plans for the penguins. That is until he realizes that a zookeeper has been standing behind you both, listening with alarm to each and every scheme.
You manage to send the employee away and create an elaborate distraction by teasing an elephant with a carrot before throwing it to a giraffe. Turns out an angry elephant can be quite obnoxious.
The elephant lets out a loud trumpeting noise, catching the attention of the zoo staff. Now you have to come up with another distraction to buy yourself more time.
You use this opportunity to let the penguins out of their enclosure. Now the squad is fully assembled. The squirrel and penguins give you a textbook salute before running away together.
You move closer to the zookeeper and listen in on his conversation. It seems the animals are about to be sold. A squirrel goes for thirteen research notes, while a Ziro Lizard goes for twenty.
Time seems to be working against you.
You manage to "borrow" the key to the zoo's main gate secretly; pickpocketing hadn't been a part of your skillset before, but it's never too late to learn.
You take the key from the zookeeper, who has now fallen unconscious.
With the staff distracted, you quietly unlock the main gate and meet up again with the squirrel.

You could have simply rescued the squirrel and left, but he refuses to go alone. He can't stand the thought of the other animals being treated unfairly and asks you to help them all escape together. He insists you need to rescue the Lindwurms, Divination Sprites, polar bears, elephants, hippos, Tripoderos, and even another squad of penguins.

Since this squirrel can speak with tactical paw signals, maybe communicating with animals isn't as impossible as you thought. Perhaps you misunderstood Ulrich's serious talks concerning arcane creatures earlier. The squirrel leads you to the broadcast room, where you now have a chance to demonstrate your public speaking skills.

You become increasingly passionate as you speak, using animated gestures while discussing the importance of freedom and solidarity among all living things. Although Marcus's face shows no expression, you catch a subtle look in her eyes—half disbelief, half amusement.
Your words seem to inspire the animals. They charge at fences, barriers, and the glass domes. Alarms blare, and staff rush to control the situation.
When you lead the animal horde to the penguin area, you notice that the penguins also salute you. Now you finally understand who the squirrel meant by "squad members."

You watch the squirrel lead various arcane creatures out of their enclosures and run far down the road, leaving you in unexpected solitude. You walk behind them along the same path, abandoning the bedlam that was once a zoo.
However, the squirrel remembers you and returns with his penguin squad. He offers to present you to Zeno HQ, saying someone with your abilities deserves at least a general's rank.
You humbly decline the offer. You still have unfinished business.

Coming back to this place makes you feel uneasy. Since the box arrived at Laplace, accidents have been happening nonstop, and nothing good has come of it. All you want now is to quickly wrap things up and return to your room. But then you notice your overwhelmed colleague nearby, and it's clear something's gone wrong.

Countless Critters are jumping around on the equipment they left behind earlier. The glory of the Carbuncle shines over the sanctuary like sunlight at this moment, but this situation is doing your team no favors. You immediately beckon your colleagues to restore order.
At Laplace, handling Critters has become part of everyday life. Your team jumps into action, showing off what has come to be called "Laplace efficiency."

The Critters are removed from the sanctuary swiftly and with great care for procedure. Their stay was brief, less than a day inside the box. The splendor of the Carbuncle disappears like a sunset fading into the horizon.
With order restored, you begin planning your next steps. That's when your colleague, Ulrich, has a flash of inspiration.

It seems like there are no other options left. A colleague mentions that the girl who predicted the "Storm" in the box might be at Laplace. She had previously said she would stay at the Foundation to help with the problems.
With no other leads to follow, you decide to give it a shot.

Earlier, the box fell into panic due to aphasia. Language barriers caused different groups to act on their own. Although the translator had helped for a while, the root issue still continues to create confusion.

This time, the Foundation staff arrive with people from Zeno. You don't think highly of Zeno—they drink too much, speak recklessly, and rarely follow procedure. All the same, the girl supports your plan and urges you to speak directly with the group leaders.

Unfortunately, both the Foundation and Zeno express doubts. The Foundation insists they must protect those in the box. While Zeno is too busy fighting against the Carbuncle Kingdom. Yes, the Critters again.

You're frustrated. Building this tower alone would be a gargantuan task for your small team. Thankfully, the Laplace crew in the box maintains their enthusiasm. They take away the blueprints and start analyzing without asking what they're for.

The calculator soon yields its results. The tower will be a monumental task to build and will require a massive amount of labor and material. For better or worse, you do not possess an endless army of slaves, just a small and increasingly tired team of researchers.
The tower will cost a huge number of Research Notes. You might be the only one in the box who can provide them.
You deliver everything on time. In return, the Laplace crew promises to handle the tower's construction. If you can deal with the other two groups, they'll be ready to support you.
As you try to reach the Foundation members here, you spot two familiar figures. They are an investigation team preparing to head down to the lowest level to assess the situation.
They're finishing their last preparations before leaving. You approach and greet them. After explaining your plan, they introduce you to the people in charge here.

You head upstairs, slowing as you hear an intense argument from a nearby room. A woman holding a mug of tea looks frazzled as she tries to mediate, but neither side will give in. Taking notice of your arrival, she sets her mug down and makes her way to you.

They had already heard about your plan before you arrived. Their current argument is about whether to support you. You don't understand why there's any doubt over a plan that clearly benefits everyone.

The Foundation faces many challenges—calming the public, organizing investigation teams, distributing supplies, and evacuating civilians. Now, they must also provide large amounts of materials to build some strange tower.

All on the word of one person, you. While they don't fully trust your opinion, they can't deny the threat of the spreading aphasia. The woman asks you to convince the other two and agrees to accept whatever decision comes from the discussion.

You talk to the first person, who sticks to her view. She believes that evacuating civilians is the top priority and that investing heavily in your tower project will divert vital resources from that task. Her main focus is public safety.
You tell her the sanctuary will provide housing and help with evacuation.

She takes time to debate her answer, openly fearing the Laplace team may use the evacuation to test some bizarre contraption or invention. However, with no better alternatives, she reluctantly agrees.

You talk to the second person. While he concedes that evacuating civilians should be their top priority, he also believes that supporting your efforts to build the tower is a worthy cause. With one stipulation: the Foundation must have full ownership of the tower afterwards.

Utterly typical of the Foundation's politicking, you expected them to make such a demand. He justifies it first as maintaining order in the future, and then as a matter of security given the current chaos. Either way, it's clear he intends for the Foundation to stay firmly in control.

You accept his demand, though you don't see it as giving in. Your mind shifts to the investigation team, who have probably already left, heading down to the lowest level, where language itself ceases to exist.
How did it go? Did both of them agree to your plan?
It seems you have convinced them. The Foundation leaders are pleased that you reached a consensus. They are now sending people out as planned to assist in delivering supplies and building the tower.

You arrive at Zeno's command post just as they finish fighting off an assault. Soldiers are cleaning up the area and tending to the wounded. You make your way to the commander, who recognizes you right away. He brings up a past joint mission against the Crates Gang with a "fishbowl" from the sanctuary.
You assume this means solving things with Zeno will be easy. After all, you and the commander are "acquaintances." But to your surprise, he turns you down.

The commander doesn't seem to have any deeper motives. His refusal is one of pure practicality. They are overwhelmed with their ongoing conflict against these Critters. Because of the "Storm," the Most Supreme Warlord's Critter army has spiraled out of control. He points to the scene of battle, saying that this had been the fourth attack today.

You offer assistance in fighting the Critters, but deep down, you know they'll just keep coming. Alchemy or potions might be useful, but your team consists primarily of language specialists, not alchemists. Lacking a clear military edge, you'll have to start thinking of another solution.
As you leave the tent, you spot two suspicious boxes slipping through the camp. They're hardly inconspicuous, yet the soldiers seem to ignore them. Odd.
You follow the boxes behind the tents and in a flash of movement throw them open. To your surprise you recognize their occupants—a rockin' pirate and a young potion maker.

The potion maker lights up as she realizes who you are and immediately launches into an explanation. It seems they intended to journey to the critter's kingdom via hot air balloon, with the hope of calming the critters with music. But anti-aircraft guns shot them down over this camp, and now they've been locked up as potential spies.
Wait. Does she really think that a hot air balloon concert will have any chance to calm these Critters?

She insists that a proper young lady would never lie; she also suggests her potions could help repel the Critters for now. But without the balloon, their concert plan can't move forward. She suggests you help them, and that perhaps Zeno would be grateful for their support.
Everyone in the camp is busy with their own tasks, and no one has time to speak with you.
You head back and explain the situation to the commander. He's glad that he has received help again and gives a medal to the potion maker, but declines to offer any apology to the rockin' pirate.
Still, this counts as a win. Zeno is now preparing to work on the tower and has agreed to support your plan.
You get ready to quietly retrieve the hot air balloon. If you were caught, you wouldn't be able to wash the mud off your hands.
Though you're careful to avoid detection, the camp guards still spot you, and worse, somehow mistake you for a Critter.

The mission succeeds! With loud rock music blasting, the rockin' pirate and the potion maker help you lift off in the balloon. As the sound fills the sky, you can't help but wonder if they were ever really arrested for spying at all.
The potions are released over the ground, and the Critters react like they've just tasted the most sour lemons ever. In short order they scatter into the distance.

You look around. Aphasia has completely taken language away from this land. The people left here have become incapable of communicating. They stare at you with blank eyes, their eyes no longer showing emotion.
To be honest, you still don't understand Ulrich's "compassion" at all. Even after all you've been through, you can't truly shake the realization that these are only pieces of data in a simulation.
Maybe you should try talking with them.
You watch as they enter the area, evidently frustrated.

Good news arrives confirming that Laplace, Zeno, and the Foundation have all completed their part of the tower construction. Only the top level remains unfinished. Now, Ulrich has given up his observer role and has entered the box.
He stands beside you, going into meticulous detail about plans and preparations. You have convinced Marcus to ask the three groups for technical support, so you two are now alone.

You glance at him, then at the pale land ahead. Stepping closer, you pull off his glass head, causing his body to collapse immediately. His mouth keeps moving, shifting from confusion to anger and finally to a string of loud insults.
Normally, you'd argue back but this time you hold back, because you're heading somewhere where language can't reach. You decide to listen while you still have the chance.

You set his head aside and walk in alone. Maybe the investigation team was right. Whether last time or next time, you take the same action. You need to install translators at three points to protect yourself from aphasia at the tower sites.

As you move toward your destination language starts to break down around you. You try to hold on by mentally repeat, repeat ... repeating every word you remember; the effort feels like fighting against sleep.
Your mouth soon loses the ability to form clear words, until each word you repeat comes out as infantile babbling.
Soon, you can't even babble anymore. Only one syllable seems possible. Like a baby's first "Mama," but when the person it's meant for is gone, that last emotional connection fades too.
You reach a point where your thoughts themselves no longer form coherent words; you cannot hear them, cannot see them. You think now in abstract concepts, as someone blind and deaf from birth might.

A sound breaks your distracted silence. You spot "Lucy" in the sky, though it looks like a replica because of its strange coloring. A temporary translator falls to the ground along with two Laplace employees.
The Laplace duo is happy to help you and excited about finishing the tower. Their mere presence alleviates some of your aphasia symptoms.
You keep moving toward your goal, feeling completely drained, fighting against the urge to stop.

When your backup battery fizzles out, the aphasia comes rushing back in like a tidal wave. You're soon overwhelmed by a blur of garbled code, passwords, encrypted text, and barcodes. The layers of translation and endless encoding pile up.

Luckily, physical actions stay separated from language confusion. Your focus lands on a small Foundation tent made from a familiar material. You remember seeing it before near the stairs on this level, where you once talked with its owner, so you push forward.

There's no one inside, but you find two translators, a battery, and a notebook with coordinates and notes on aphasia under different conditions. You imagine the researchers camped here, watching and recording data. You realize the difficult choice they must have made when they were down to just this final battery.
Rather than evacuate, they stayed to document the advanced symptoms, gathering every glimmer of critical information—trusting that you would come.
You slot the battery into your translator and grab the notebook. It feels too soon to accept this colorless world as your aphasia starts to ease.
Alone, you move through the pure white surroundings towards your destination.

With language itself erased from this pure whiteness, who can even mourn its loss? Along the way, you've communicated with various pieces—whether kind or ill-intentioned, joyful or angry, all of those emotions were once conveyed through words. But here, language is gone, leaving their sentiments to scatter like dust in the wind. Your translator begins to sputter and slow.

You forget how to speak. The irony is sickening—language has always been your greatest strength; you were able to debate Ulrich on equal footing, yet now you can't even make a simple sound. Even the idea of language is nearly lost to you.
"Researcher Adler, explain why you abandoned me by the roadside and stepped on my body." An annoying voice reaches you from above, accompanied by loud music.
Looking up, you see a hot air balloon coming down. Marcus holds the glass head, accompanied by the potion maker and the lunatic of a rockin' pirate.

Maybe you should've thrown his glass head a bit further away. The musings in your head form into coherent thought again as the balloon lands. They hand you a new translator and help set up the base station.

Zeno can't offer direct help, except to provide the fuel needed for the pirate's hot air balloon. Your worried companions can use it to find you wherever you roam, but they believe in the strength of teamwork over individual effort. As your aphasia declines, you're able to at last speak the words "thank you."
The supplies have arrived. You just need to wait a short while longer.

This toybox continues to amaze you. You once wondered how three groups managed to build such a tall tower so quickly. Watching the process now, it seems the construction has been sped up a hundred times, completed in no time.
Once the final block is placed, language becomes unified throughout the entire box. While people celebrate, you're left with mixed feelings, though you can finally relax.
Somewhere hidden from view, a crow flies deeper into the unknown.
​​All translators have been set up. It's time to build the last Language Tower.​
The language translation is complete. Will you leave with the research materials?
Those inside the box affected by the "Storm" become intensely aggressive, relentlessly tracking and attacking anyone who invades their territory.

This new game is a more modern challenge, quite different from the earlier board game. Your Critters represent you on the game board, and your strategic choices determine whether you overcome opponents.
The "Critter Crash" game concept surprises you, as your gaming experience is mostly limited to Conway's Game of Life. You think about joining in but caution yourself not to get too absorbed.
After some careful analysis, you come up with what seems to be the perfect team composition. You feel confident in your choices and yourself.
You failed miserably, Adler. Despite your careful planning, your Critter warriors were thoroughly defeated.

Something doesn't add up. Your strategy seemed flawless, yet the opponent seemed to predict your every move. You have a sudden realization and look under the table, where you find a hidden transmitter. Marcus quickly figures out its purpose: it's blocking you from getting the Critter warriors you need.
You rip off the transmitter, storm across the game board, and grab your opponent by the collar. Winning no longer matters as much as confronting this utterly disgusting and unfair cheat.

Your Critters may have lost the game, but you came out with the real victory. The other Critters fled in fear without hesitation, leaving only your warrior behind. It has witnessed the entire fight. You look into its big, innocent eyes and decide to let it go. As for the cheater—let him have a rest on the ground.
You recognize this small Critter, the one that had faced defeats under your command before. And the person it's chasing? It's the same cheater from earlier.
This mess is your own doing. You allowed a dangerous Critter to attack a defenseless person.
As you watch the Critter overpower the cheater, you think for a moment, then make up your mind. You and the Critter are in sync, and together you give the cheater another beating.
You reach down and pick up the small Critter. It squirms, trying to break free, but ultimately fails.
The cheater runs off in panic, his earlier arrogance gone.
The paper looks ancient. Its signs of oxidation suggest it's over a century old. It is covered in dense writing, in a script you don't recognize.

That's odd. This writing is unlike any language you know. You can't identify its vocabulary or make sense of its structure. It appears as continuous strings of primitive charms without any punctuation or breaks, making you wonder if it even holds any meaning.
Eventually, you find some familiar symbols in the margin. Arabic letters. At least this confirms the document comes from human civilization.
You keep the page for future study, hoping to decode it when possible.
This page is over two centuries old. Though the text is still unreadable, you're certain this script is different from others you've encountered.
As expected, a familiar number appears in the usual place. It looks ordinary, but its meaning remains unclear.
You add this page to your collection, now holding two mysterious documents.
The third page is over three centuries old. This time, you ignore the content and focus on the page number—you've already recognized the pattern.
Even if something seems to serve no purpose, it wouldn't have appeared out of nowhere. You now have enough keys, but what are they meant to unlock?
Very well, now you need a "lock."
Every page in this book uses a different writing system. You quickly look at the usual spot, hoping the page numbers will give you a clue.

But the numbering follows no recognizable pattern, leaving you further confused. The numbers seem to emit a strange rhythmic sound. You return to the pages, finding the page numbers act like their incantation names. You recall the number from the first page ...
The page merges into the book like a drop of water dissolving into the sea. You realize you'll never find it again. Now, onto the two-century-old page.
This page, too, merges into the book, like a leaf drifting into a forest. You say goodbye as if parting with a fellow traveler. Only the last page remains, with its number, its name ...

The final page vanishes, like a grain of sand falling into the desert. You flip through the pages of the book, watching as it expands with every flip. It seems to be a collection of all the languages of all civilizations and writing systems that have ever been. You're unsure whether those three pages were the "keys" to this "lock" or if the book itself is just a "key" to yet another lock.

The page is rejected by the book. You flip through the pages of the book, watching as it expands with every flip. It seems to be a collection of all the languages of all civilizations and writing systems that have ever been. If one element is missing, does infinity still remain infinite? It feels like you've disrupted something fundamental. Now, the book is useless to you.
Paper! Paper! Want a paper, mister?
And I have some information if you're interested ...
You are standing in my way. Do you mind?
Stay calm. You can reach me in case of an emergency.
Comrade, how can I help you?
In these challenging times, we must support one another.
Watch out; there could be some unknown risks ahead.
Don't worry, Zeno will protect you.
Hello, I'm on a mission here.
What's the mission? Sorry, I can't share the details.
Lost again. Great, the captain's going to chew me out.
Maybe you'd like to talk about the recent policy changes?
Could there be a mistake in the calculations? The margin of error looks way too big ...
Just in time. Can you take a look at this formula?
Would you be interested in hearing about Laplace's benefit programs?
Come on, sit and have a proper chat with me!
Hi! Do you ever have dreams?
Having dreams is important, but it's fine if you don't have them too.

It seems the box system doesn't recognize you or properly assign you to the Laplace group. But that much is fine. Laplace's distinctive style likely only appeals to its own members, so your colleague doesn't raise any questions about your presence. Through his explanations, you begin to understand the current situation within the box.
Inside the box, the civilians, Laplace, the Foundation, and Zeno can't cooperate due to language barriers. Over time, this has led to hostility between the groups.
Each of the four factions controls its own territory. Even the Critters, once abandoned, now act like rulers. In fact, they've even taken to calling themselves a kingdom.

The Most Supreme Warlord, a troublemaker from LSCC, has created a faction called the "Glorious Carbuncle Kingdom" in the lower area of the box with his other Critter followers. They have been relentlessly attacking Zeno's position in hopes of taking it from them.
To solve the problem, it seems you'll need to address them first. Prioritizing their communication issues first, of course.
He turns to you with a surprised look and immediately draws his weapon. What's going on? Has the Foundation teamed up with the Critters? Why is he attacking us?

The restrained Foundation member still shows defiance, muttering angrily in a language you can't understand. Remembering the language issues outside, you pull out your translator. Once it's working, you realize he's spent the last fifteen minutes trying to insult you, though at least they've been relatively polite insults. But this certainly isn't the time to bother with taking offense.
As you're about to leave, a colleague calls out. You stop, and he approaches to greet you. The language barrier no longer matters, thanks to the translator.
Oddly, he's dropped the polite tone he had outside the box. Now, he's speaking loudly, almost a little manic. Despite his efforts to appear composed, his behavior is chaotic.

He mentions the "Storm" before moving on to the strange language issues at hand. Suddenly, it hits you that Ulrich's less expressive but direct communication style might make interaction with this crow easier.
As you're lost in thought, he produces something quite bizarre—a rooster.
The sight of a crow holding a rooster is strange enough, but then the rooster crows twice and changes into a hissing snake right before your eyes.

Ludwig seems pleased by your startled expression. He explains he found this object in a box on the beach and believes it holds the key to his dream: a perfect, eternal language with no misunderstandings. You ignore his lofty vision, your mind focused on a few key phrases he just mentioned.
Getting that object will fix everything! No more language decryption, no more stupid Wanderer's Guide, no more babbling chaos! Hey! Ludwig, stay right there! Don't move! No! Stop!
But Ludwig does something beyond your capability. He flies off with the treasure. You stand frozen below him, utterly defeated, while your colleagues laugh at you without mercy.
Our world is drowning in trash! It's everyone's job to help protect the environment. That's why I've decided to gather all the rubbish around here and make sure it's disposed of properly.
Well done! Thank you for your brave efforts in environmental protection. Please accept these rewards.
Let's hear what he has to say.
Want to recruit me? You'd better show some sincerity. Like giving me 100 Research Notes.
Want to recruit me? You'd better show some sincerity. Like giving me 200 Research Notes.
Want to recruit me? You'd better show some sincerity. Like giving me items worth over 300.
Sparkling unclaimed treasures, waiting to be discovered.​
A shipping container. Might hold some materials inside.
He flares up as though insulted, ranting nonsense, deeply offended.
This Foundation member clearly didn't expect you to act so rashly.
The rockin' pirate, however, just laughs mockingly. Clearly, she will not accept something as humiliating as paying properly.
The Carbuncle, enraged by your sudden strike, bares its fangs at you.
You can't stand these people's nonsense any longer.
Ulrich, I'm starting to understand you.#Retreat
The young artist is clearly offended by your behavior.
A shabby camp, once inhabited but now overrun by Critters.
Your sudden appearance startles the worker.
Your words seem to stir the animals. They charge at fences, barriers, and the glass domes. Alarms blare as staff rush to regain control.

You two no longer need to use sign language. He grows more excited as he loudly discusses escape plans for the penguins, until he discovers a zoo employee has been standing behind you both, overhearing the whole scheme.
Even though you're careful, the guards still spot you and somehow mistake you for Critters.
A bot with corrupted code—it explodes on contact, causing massive Resistance loss.
A bot with corrupted code—it explodes on contact, greatly reducing Resistance.
A box-dweller warped by cognitive contamination, now violently aggressive. It relentlessly pursues and attacks, causing massive Resistance loss on contact.
The makeshift Translation Institute. Here you can translate and gain Translation Progress.
You find a campfire long extinguished. The owner seems to have left.
Before you lies a battlefield, both sides locked in combat. You turn to leave but notice a gravestone.
A Foundation member stands lost in thought. Lonely, contemplative.
Guess they're lost in thought again.#Better not disturb
It's a small, thoughtful dog. You recognize it. It once met your chatty colleague in this box, and now, it's your turn.
Three Thousand Six Hundred Fifty Days of Waiting
An astronomical tower. You recall your prime minister friend encountered one too.
A fisherman stands alone at the harbor, a giant fishbone behind him. His sunburnt skin and calloused hands are a testament to countless battles with the sea. The fishbone is his medal of honor.
You approach a tent. Inside, someone is carefully wiping every speck of dust off an hourglass.
Hey, listen to me, maybe we're all living inside a box!
A group of Critters crowd around a pot, seemingly recreating an old Eastern European soup.
A zoologist discusses the origins of intelligence with you.
You're not just seeing things ... a massive beetle lies in a hospital bed, using two forelegs to flip through old magazines, eating apple slices with the others, humming a pop song.
A gym inside Laplace in the box. You almost laugh—it exists solely to showcase Laplace's "passion" for work through cold detachment.
No one in Laplace ever goes there anyway.#Leave
A researcher looks secretive—seems to be working on something.
A street performer is miming in silence.
A dusty corner filled with rat droppings—a perfect hideout even seasoned veterans wouldn't find. You're about to leave, but something glints in the dark ...
A moonless night, even the earth is swallowed by darkness. From the tent comes screams, the roar of chainsaws—and yawns.

He stands there, battered and bruised, blood streaked across his brow. Anyone watching would wince in sympathy. Yet he keeps swinging—at sandbags, tree roots, walls—anything ... As if the world itself were his sparring partner.
Approach him, ask with concern#None of my business
A strange statue that seems to be worshipping some kind of feline creature.
Torn scraps of paper lie quietly on the ground.
Pick them up and piece them together#Leave
A grand building. Places like this never lack translation materials or talent. Unfortunately, the Foundation staff at the door refuses to grasp the importance of letting you in, insisting on an ID.
Isn't my reflective uniform obvious enough?#Leave
My research is focused on finding the whereabouts of those who have been rewound by time. A rare opportunity has come up, and I'm looking for volunteers. Interested?
A researcher calls out to you. You don't recognize him.
A researcher looks like he's waiting for someone.
A researcher looks ecstatic, ready to launch into a rousing speech.
Walls, floors, cups, fishbones ... everything that could be carved is covered in writing. Every object seems desperate to prove its existence.
What does it say?#I'm not interested in lunatics
The "sculptor" from before now sits on a rock. A bird perches on his shoulder, pecking at his ear, but he stays motionless, far quieter than before.
You arrive at a silent, empty camp.
A rock pirate is yelling at a divination arcanist's booth.
A colorful tent. Music and laughter spill from inside.
A gorgon argues with the snakes on her own head.
A Zeno soldier paces back and forth, mumbling to himself.
A researcher adjusts his equipment. He looks like a hamster caught stealing cheese.
A guard lies face down on the ground.
A rhythmic "clank-clank" comes from nearby—someone's trying to fix their car with their foot.
A group of Carbuncles gather by the road as a passerby offers them food.
You meet a young man wearing a crown—his voice deep and resonant.
The crowned youth prays to the lake in that same deep voice.
Another card table. The last winner, although faceless, somehow still gives you that smug grin—you do see a smug grin on no face.
From afar, you see a Critter pummeling a man relentlessly.
What's going on?#None of my business
It's freezing, your steps heavy. In the distance, you spot a greenhouse.
You're here again. The weather's good today, and you can see that farm from afar.
An architect stands there, exhausted and desperate.
Like me right now?#Working hours? Figures.
Several people crowd around a hopeless-looking private gallery design, pointing and debating.
A Far Eastern-style building. It looks lively inside.
You bring along the wine that Ulrich last brewed in the toybox and find that Inventor from the East.
A salesman appears to be hawking his goods.
You arrive at a dark camp. Three people rest inside, hands near their weapons, eyes on you. The tension is thick in the air, adrenaline rising.
A strange, helpless, tasteless building stands here.
You meet the light-fingered knight again. He looks cheerful and claims to have repented sincerely for his crimes.
Let's hope you don't reach into my pockets again.#Pray, huh
You're not completely sure you saw it clearly, but it looks like the knight and thief seem to be here again.
Say hello#Bad luck, better stay away
A young man stands before his painting.
A private stable in such a chaotic place is surprising. Small, but the horses look beautiful.
A sheet of paper lies on the ground.
You're not even surprised to find yet another lone page.
Finally, as if destined, you find a book just the right size to hold your stray pages ... Or perhaps it found you, demanding its chapters back.
You reach a community. Grand landmarks, tall buildings ... None of this belongs here.
You return to the community. Outside, a group of refugees seems to have gathered.
This is likely your last visit. The place looks destroyed.
A zoo filled with all sorts of animals in cages.
A zookeeper appears to be on a call with someone.​
The same zoo again ... Some kind of traveling exhibit?
"Hey! Buddy!" A shout interrupts your train of thought. You turn ... the squirrel from before, excitedly running toward you.
Looks like you made it out of that jar.#Leave
Where's this strange flower trying to take me?
Using the translator, you finally reach Laplace and meet the girl from before, learning her name at last. You propose building the tower.
The group frets over the massive cost of the tower's construction.
You reach the Foundation, but chaos reigns. People are fleeing, and the town is in disarray. Aphasia seems on the verge of spreading.
One of the Foundation's directors. To get your plan approved, you'll need a rock-solid argument.
At the Zeno camp, the aftermath of battle is clear. Soldiers clear debris and treat the wounded.
A hot-air balloon belonging to the rock pirate, now confiscated by Zeno.
You spot someone ahead. She's from the Foundation's investigation team, preparing to safely enter the "Storm" Zone.
This is the target translator setup point. You can start anytime.
With the base station built, you reach the tower's center.
A raven—you've seen him before. Outside, he's better known as Ludwig. As you spot him, he also spots you and flies over to greet you.
A Foundation member. You're glad to find an ally so soon. You greet him warmly.
A man dragging a huge burlap sack, gathering something as he goes.
Movement duration +50%. Has a chance to drop [Junk] in this terrain.
Periodically erupts with flames. Being inside reduces Resistance.
Movement duration -50%. Has a chance to slip in this terrain.
Movement duration +50%. Random waterspouts appear in this terrain.

Defeat the invading monster <color=#ff0000>[Brotherhood Big Shot]</color> on Day 7.
Enigma returns to the Silver Sanctuary, now plunged into chaos. To fix the box-world, Ulrich suggests heading to [Laplace] to find the girl who once predicted the "Storm."

One tower isn't enough to resolve the chaos. Enigma heads to the [Safe Haven], argues with the Foundation officials, and gets the Language Tower project approved.

Either stores or releases misfortune. Shake well before use.
A fire burns in my heart, though passersby see only smoke.
Said to deform more under awkward situations.
They say the mix of sweet and savory is addictive.
Strength and beauty are said to originate here, though the priests disagree.
The edible part has already been removed.
More effective when worn by someone with a bad cold.
Ensure what once happened will happen again.
A word of advice: don't toss it into storage and forget about it.
The power flowing within could topple a dynasty.
Just as the fruit ripens on the branch, ribs are entwined with venomous snakes.
Swallow it whole to understand the language of love and beauty.
The congealed blood of the earth.
A coiled tape, winding through the stars.
A circle that blocks and repels the darkness. Handle with care.
It's hard to tell from such agonized strokes that the entire poem is written only with the letter "P."
True forms melt like wax in its glow.
It calls upon dusk, midnight, and dawn.
Unlike the sword in the lake that grants endless strength, this one offers about five tons' worth.
Read it in darkness, lest moonlight poison your shadow.
A small, thoughtful dog. You recognize it. It once met your chatty colleague in this box, and now, it's your turn.
An astronomical tower. You recall your prime minister friend encountered one too.
A mad philosopher who believes everyone's living inside a box!
A researcher studying the fate of those who went back in time. He hopes you'll volunteer.
A researcher stops you. You don't know him. He slips you some experiment data. Maybe someone needs it ...
A familiar "sculptor" sits on a rock. A bird perches on his shoulder, pecking at his ear, but he stays motionless, far quieter than before.
A little dog whimpers softly. Where is it taking you?
A guard lies face down, seemingly on a hunger strike.
You meet a crowned youth, his words tinged with a thick accent.
Another card table. The last duped researcher now grins at you with that faceless but still unmistakably smug appearance.
A greenhouse in the freezing cold, tasked with growing crops impossible for this season.
A dark camp. Three people rest inside, hands near their weapons, eyes on you. Tension is thick in the air, adrenaline is rising.
A young man stands before his painting, seemingly searching for his missing model.
A sheet of paper lies on the ground. Collecting them all might trigger something special.
A zoo filled with all sorts of animals in cages. There, you meet a strange squirrel and decide to help it free all the animals.
A zoo filled with all sorts of animals in cages. There, you meet a strange squirrel and decide to help it and its companions escape.
The plan failed, but that's fine. There's always next time. Just promise me, no more rowing on land, alright?
A staircase now connects the floors. At least we no longer need to worry about Medicine Pocket trying to act polite.
You've crossed every inch of this boxed world, searching for a true solution. Well done, you've found it.

The whistle fades into silence. The wind cuts across the snow, carrying everything toward the unknown.
Where the rails meet, steam roars. The living and the dead share the same end of the line.

Along old rails, through graveyards, against the snow—we ride till time itself falls behind us.

Welcome to the City of Light! Excellent taste, this shop you've stopped by is none other than the Cabala Parlor of Crystals, the proud gem of Paris.
What defines classical style? What embodies aristocratic grace? Cabala was personally appointed by Louis XV, and they've been crafting fine crystal and glassware for nobles for over 170 years. Ever since its debut at the World Expo, its creations have been nearly impossible to obtain. 
But those days of exclusivity are long gone. Now, if you're willing to pay, there's little you can't take home. Crystalware is all the rage these days, and many new shops have popped up in Paris. Some fakes are so good you'd hardly tell the difference. If you happen to need a guide with a sharp eye, look no further. A friendly Parisian driver at your service!

Today's stop—Notre-Dame Cathedral! 
Ever since The Hunchback of Notre-Dame was published, countless visitors come each year to admire this centuries-old monument.
You've come at the right time, because some of the walls and statues have started to crumble. A few more years and it may close for repairs. Half of Parisians want it restored exactly as before, while the younger Dadaists are calling for modern design elements.
Let them argue! The people of the present always hear the bells of the present, even if the sound comes from a bell forged a hundred years ago.

The Louvre houses three women who haunt the dreams of the entire world. Do you know who they are?
Of course—Venus, the Winged Victory, and Mona Lisa. Finding them isn't easy, especially now with tourists crowding every hall and cars filling the royal courtyard—yes, the very spot where you just got dropped off.
The curators are considering renovating the plaza, though no plan's been set. Maybe one day a glass pyramid will rise here, who knows? But if we're talking architecture, keep an eye on the upcoming World Expo. Knowing us French, I doubt they've even started construction yet!
Paris in the Scale of the Dead

If you ask me, Père Lachaise Cemetery is Paris's second Pantheon.
Founded by Napoleon I, it now holds a host of historical greats—many reinterred here from elsewhere. Not just generals and statesmen, but artists and thinkers alike: Molière, La Fontaine, Balzac, Proust, Wilde, Chopin, Bizet, Comte, Fourier ... the list goes on.
The Communards' Wall also stands here. See? It's workers' march season, and every day mourners come to lay flowers ... so many that they seem to bloom right from the stone.
Still, I'd advise against joining the crowd. It's quite the sight, but not without risk.

If you're a lover of books, you must stop by Shakespeare and Company!
This is the birthplace of Ulysses—a novel I can't make heads or tails of, but it certainly shook the literary world. From 12 Rue de l'Odéon, its fame spread across the globe. Rumor has it that Hemingway himself used to smuggle a copy in his coat pocket, and now some shady fellows at customs seem to be imitating him.
Sadly, the shop's struggling these days. Monsieur Gide is hosting readings and fundraisers to keep it alive. If you'd like, you could help support the cause for the love of books and the art of publishing.

451 BCE Myrrine, the daughter of King Leonidas, and General Nikolaos met and got married after Kassandra's father left them. Seven years later, they had a son together named Alexios. They had lived a happy life until one rainy night. A prophecy said that Alexios would bring about the fall of Sparta, which could only be stopped through his sacrifice. The priest of Sparta was about to drop Alexios off Mount Taygetos when Kassandra attempted to save her brother. Unfortunately, she pushed the priest and Alexios to their apparent deaths. But the tragedy was not over: Nikolaos, adherent to Spartan law, was forced to drop Kassandra off the mountain as a punishment. That night, the wail of a mother echoed around the entire Sparta. Our world is good at making orphans, and you never know how. —X

Rumor has it this bell was once worn by a famous actress in one of her most iconic films.
But our interviewee seemed more interested in its practical use:
"It can summon those who have strayed too far from home—whether they're living, dead, or just a little Critter lost on a snowy night."

This unusual decal tattoo was designed by the interviewee herself: mysterious, dark, and dangerous—the thorny vines climb toward the heavens as the star and moon gracefully descend.
"This night is brimming with calm and peace, much like the energy surrounding you right now," the interviewee said softly with her usual smile.

An exquisitely designed earring with a round ruby at its center. When the interviewee stood to hang ornaments on the Christmas tree, the snowflake-shaped drop swayed gently, emitting a delicate, shivering chime.
"Red—the color of fire. It suits the warmth of the hearth, don't you think?" the interviewee explained. "Just perfect for the holiday season."
Yet the interviewer couldn't help but feel that the interviewee herself embodied the spirit of the holidays more than any ornament could.

Might as well include a pair of earplugs for a certain someone who, regrettably, can't appreciate disco music.

Isn't every day an interrogation comes with so much ceremony—you've got the latest in lie detector technology and the big guys out to see the results. Now, let's confirm your statement for the third time.
Laurent Roseau, a member of Manus Vindictae, deceived his students, including your friend Célia.
You were forced to partake in Manus Vindictae's activities. They took control of you.
Yes. They dispelled my consciousness from my own body.
And Beryl helped you regain control of your body and led you out of the overflowing Depths of Myth.
And throughout the whole incident, you never saw Beryl Bouanich acting alongside Manus Vindictae.
And to this day, you haven't seen any evidence that Beryl Bouanich is in contact with Manus Vindictae in any capacity.
Your fate ... It takes an ambiguous form.
Wait a moment—it's about to take shape.
Fate's fragments drift like scattered lights.
Their true radiance only forms when they finally meet.
For fragments too faint for the eye, turn the gaze inward.
All it takes is a flash of clarity ...
The "Storm" threw everything out of order—names and destinies reshaped and reformed.
I cannot help but wonder, my dear daughter … if it changed yours too?
I have seen your story play out countless times. A flawless gem hides nothing.
And yet, I still have hope that the "Storm" has brought you something new, something unseen.
How curious. Even the gem I know best has turned cloudy and unclear.
But perhaps this is for the best. After all, it is uncertainty which excites me most of all ...
There is no amount of effort which will make the future any clearer.
Perhaps we ought to stop here. Whether joy or sorrow awaits, what matters most is the experience she is soon to live through.
I only hope that one day, she can tell me herself about that which I have yet to see ...
