It was two years ago, or sixteen years hence, depending on which chronicle you follow.
To me, it was as vivid as yesterday. But to young minds like yours, it seemed a kind of chaos unheard of.
We should start from the beginning.
With the war coming to an end, France faced countless possibilities. Its people, weary yet filled with hope, longed for lasting peace.
The economy flourished for a time, and people from all walks of life came to France.

Still, the impacts of war inevitably surfaced. As the wartime factories closed, people struggled to survive. Their hardships gave rise to new demands, and before long, Paris became a swirl of competing ideas.
And just how is this connected to your story?#A story about this taxi driver, I presume.
That very much depends on your perspective. If your only interest is in the story itself—not the context—you might think it irrelevant.
But I believe context matters. It keeps you from being thrown off by the details.
That said, neither the economy nor society is our chief concern today. What I share with you now is a story, hearsay really—
You presume correctly. A taxi driver caught up in the whirlpool of ideas that spun within Paris.
A heroine born tied to a fate that promises adventure at the cost of her life, who only ever desired a quiet life in the city she loved.
But fate does not ask for permission.
And when this journey comes to a close, regret will be all that remains.
Sounds like this story doesn't have the happiest of endings.
It ends, as all stories must—whether that end is a happy one. You will soon find out.
I was running a crystal parlor in Paris back then.
People came for all sorts of products—from ordinary crystal ornaments to the enchanted ones—I had them all. I recognized a few of my customers in your Suitcase.
But many came seeking something I never put on the shelf—prophecy.
I can imagine. Who wouldn't want to know their future?#So you sold prophecies too, then.
But our path through fate's garden is already set. No prophecy can change where it leads.
And I dislike putting a price on things that have no use.
So I made myself a promise: that only those I trusted would get a glimpse of what lies ahead of them—a gift, nothing more.
I am afraid that was never an option for me. I could never put a price on it. Whether one knows about the future or not, their fate remains unchanged.
A prophecy to fate is like a title to a book, and no bookseller should charge for the title alone.
So, I only offered the gift of prophecy to those who did not come seeking it.
To my surprise, it did something unexpected for my business. Word spread, and I recovered my investment soon enough.
Nor was I. Few things in life have ever surprised me, and this was much the same.
I saw doubt on Mademoiselle Brume's face. As a diviner, you encounter that look more often than people think.
Some have called me a schemer, a fraud, as the Vigiles Bureau did. Perhaps they are watching me even now, listening in to our very conversation.
Some were frightened by what I could see but kept coming back to sate their own curiosity.
Some showed nothing but disdain—not for me, but for the very idea of a predetermined future. I admired their courage.
Brume was not any of these. She was a fourth kind—one who tries to ignore the prophecy but, in doing so, only finds herself carried further into its stream.
The Vigiles Bureau?#What kind am I, then?
Oops. Have I let it slip?
Well, I suppose there is no use pretending now. There was a disagreement about my decision to take a certain handful of arcane objects without consulting their rightful owners.
In the end, I paid all their penalties, among other not-so-charming consequences.
Not that it has done anything to prevent them from hounding me at every turn. To them, it seems I am only a fear-mongering schemer who knows secrets best left unknown.
Someone who walks between eras and through the "Storms," what is your view on fate?
Few people can imagine the nature of your position. No more than three, I would wager. And I wish I could say I was one of them.
Alas, I am but a puppet dangling at the end of fate's thread. My limited vision cages my imagination.
Though I may still see a little more than most people, I cannot do as I was meant to.
Your hands are tied—is that what you're saying?
I have lived long enough to know better than to act against fate.
Though, in fact, what I would have done differs very little from what I was meant to do.
What do you think? Is it perhaps fate that determined my personality, or my personality determining my fate?
And there she was, glowering at the empty passenger seat, yelling as if quite alarmed by someone inside.
I believe she called her ... Félicie? No ... Félicienne.
Yes. That was her name. Indeed, I once knew a Félicienne as well.
Do you believe it's the same person?#Isn't this Félicienne rather important?
Well, it is far from a common name; that much is certain.
But then such a coincidence would border on ... theatrical, no?
I should like to think that fate has more elegant ways of crossing my path with Brume's. Though, of course, it is possible that fate favors the comedy of the absurd.
Heh heh, you do know how to make me laugh.
But Félicienne is no Napoleon. She never became a household name.
Perhaps her demeanor and her air of self-assurance gave you that idea, but I advise you to look a little bit closer.
That said, the Félicienne I knew would not take well to being mistaken for just any Félicienne.
Before the Second Industrial Revolution, the blood in her veins was more prized than liquid gold.
She's of noble birth, isn't she?#She's a powerful arcanist, isn't she?
Indeed. Her family was once renowned for their command over thunder and lightning. Though their influence faded when humans learned to harness electricity for themselves.
Even so, the fortune her ancestors gathered would keep the family running for another two centuries. More than enough for our Félicienne to live a truly opulent lifestyle.
The Barons were known as fighters, heroes, Priests and Priestesses of Lightning. That legacy was passed down through generations.
Even a century after the last aluminum furnace bearing their name went cold, she still remembers the heat of fame, of success, of envy.
So she comes from a time before the "Storm."
Precisely. When she was born, the "Storm" had not yet begun.
Not that it matters much, you see. In times like these, those born before the "Storm" often still cross paths with those of another era. Just like you and your friends, and myself and Brume.
Yes. The Félicienne I knew disappeared long ago.
Absent a miracle, I doubt anyone will ever see her again.
It is true; I have held back many important details.
Concerning matters like the nature of Félicienne and Brume's relationship, and Professor Roseau's true intentions.
But I believe it is not my place to disclose such things. People deserve to discover these things on their own.
You've fooled everyone.#I need an explanation.#I'm more interested in the part involving Matilda.
And you have placed far too much importance on prophecy. The course of fate remains the same, whether I speak about it or not.
In this kind of business, one must remain neutral—all of my clientele understand that.
I take no sides, only payments.

The "Storm" has affected many things, including the Depths of Myth. One day, Laurent Roseau stumbled upon a rift that caused it to spill over, and his mind has been captured in its maelstrom ever since.
As for Felicienne—she was a soul lost within the Depths of Myth. Thus, their streams of fate inevitably crossed.
With the villains in their proper places, Brume's story had truly begun.
Ah, of course—and why not? My Matilda ... such a lovely, radiant girl. She has inherited my strength and added to it a vitality of her own. Those who speak with her often leave smiling.
As for her future, I cannot share it with you here.
But I can assure you: her path is one worth looking forward to.
So far, the story has followed along a classic direction—Brume walked "the Hero's Journey."
But just as it seemed that it might end with triumph, down came the "Storm."
This is the fifth joke fate has played on me.
I have no love for the "Storm" either.#Well. I admit I saw it coming.
I must be honest with you. There is something in it that I like.
As dreadful as it may be to stand before a future I cannot foresee, I feel something else. Perhaps you might call it hope.
For someone born with my abilities, there is a strange beauty in moments like these, to know how it feels to know nothing.
Of course you did. You know the "Storm" better than most anyone.
I suspect you knew how it would end the moment I told you how it began.
Yet I cannot see beyond the "Storm," so it always takes me by surprise.
Are you hoping that the "Storm" will break fate's course?
Yes, though I understand it may come at a great price.
Ah! Perhaps that is why the Vigiles Bureau and the Foundation have kept such a keen eye on me.
Perhaps they think me one of those "Storm" advocates.
But why would I advocate for it? I have never asked for it. All I have done is try to understand it.
It was then that I decided to help Brume one last time.
There was risk in my choice. I could not see what the consequences would be.
Still, I succeeded, and the rewards were most generous. Many suspected that I had planned it from the start—a common accusation made of diviners, of course.
You chose to let the villain live.#How's your vision?
Do you think I did not punish her enough?
She lives, true, but sealed inside a false diamond. I doubt that was the life she had intended.
Besides, Brume has the right to decide her fate. It was not my place to choose whether she lives or dies.
Thank you for your concern; I am doing well, though the future now comes to me through an ever-thickening haze.
Though, I should say, I find myself welcoming the lack of clarity.
I am now able to watch my daughter grow, to observe her, and feel true surprise in every step she takes.
If there is anything to take away from Brume's story, I would suggest this:
Sometimes, good can come from being blind to fate's path.
How exciting it must be to arrive in this world knowing nothing and, after a long, beautiful journey, realize just how much there is still to discover.

In a recent report, Paris was named the most preferred city for arcanists seeking residence. Respondents note that living in a metropolis dominated by humans is no easy feat—arcane skills, whether deliberate or incidental, often disrupt established social norms, inevitably creating confusion and conflict. Yet Paris, long known for its inclusivity toward people of many diverse backgrounds and traditions, stands apart. Parisian salons have come to regard arcane skills as a kind of marvelous and romantic art, and arcanists are frequently welcomed as guests of honor. To humans, Paris is a cradle of art; to arcanists, a haven of creativity. Reports indicate that several renowned arcane product entrepreneurs have opened new branches in Paris this year, their trust in the city drawing increased attention. The historic capital continues to attract arcanum talent and resources from across Europe. While human concerns about the spread of arcanum persist, many believe that more cities will soon follow in Paris's footsteps. —Arcanist Observer Journal

Hello. Yes, I ... I need to report a missing person.
My Aunt Mary. She's the youngest among the elders in our family ... She's a quiet person. She's always reading poetry we don't really get ... She doesn't drink, and she bakes the best cakes for the kids ... But now she's disappeared. We can't find her anywhere! All her belongings are gone too—her clothes, her books, her baking supplies. Who would take all that with them ...
What does she look like? Oh, sure, she's small and thin, with neat, short brown hair. Ah, and she has a birthmark on her right arm ... No, no, we don't have a photo of her. Yes, we checked every album. I think it's strange too, but there isn't a single picture of her anywhere. She's part of our family, so I don't know why she's not in any of our group photos ...
Wait, what do you mean you can't help? Too many missing people with no proof they exist? What does that even mean?

During Louis XIV's reign, life for most nobles of the sword was tough. They had to live at Versailles and follow elaborate etiquette to show their loyalty to the king. Earning even a small amount of royal favor meant extra rewards and yearly salaries, which helped them manage their debts.
However, some families refused to exchange their swords for robes. Old aristocratic families with arcane bloodlines continued to flaunt their "unique" arcane skills. The Baron family was one of them. Once commanders of thunder and lightning on the battlefield, the Barons now performed parlor tricks at banquets to gain social status.
As time passed, their wealth dwindled. After the Napoleonic era, these noble families found themselves deeply in debt, often selling off their possessions to survive. Investing in business became more common and was no longer seen as disgraceful. Fortunately, the rise of aluminum gave Monsieur Baron the chance to apply his arcane skills to this new industry, bringing his family a steady income.
But their success didn't last. As new weapons and a new social order emerged, human technological progress made low-output arcane skills obsolete once more. Electric lights and wiring became commonplace, and the Hall-Héroult process made aluminum cheap, wiping out the Baron family's last viable business.
What a pathetic glory of the past, what pitiful noble souls. These nobles desperately needed an opportunity, some support, a chance to change times and restore the arcanists' prestige ...

The girl twirls across the black-and-white tiles, showing off her coat embroidered with the same pattern. It hangs a little loose on her, but the joy in her movement makes such a detail irrelevant.
Beryl brushes the fringe from her daughter's forehead and nods with a gentle smile.
"Of course, Maman! I'm all grown up now."
Matilda hops over to her desk and grabs a letter.
She carefully unfolds it, as if afraid it might tear.
"In recognition of special investigator Matilda Bouanich's outstanding performance, the Committee has decided to promote her to official investigator level three."

"This appointment is effective immediately. Identity and clearance levels will be updated shortly.
—St. Pavlov Foundation, Investigator Management Center"
"Finally! I've waited so very, very long for this. Aha! Finally!"
"Now you can't make any more excuses, Maman!"
She puffs her cheeks and shoots her mother a playful glare.
Some time ago, her mother had vanished without a trace. Even the Foundation couldn't find her. Matilda had spent many nights tossing and turning over it.
Then, a few days ago, Beryl reappeared, safe and calm as ever. Rumor had it she had returned to meet with Madam Z and Matilda's old classmate, the one who became the "Timekeeper."
But no matter how Matilda pressed for answers, her mother only smiled and said—
"You must uncover the truth yourself. I have already taught you everything you need to know."

Just as she is now.
That's how her mother has always been. Matilda has learned to accept it.
"Alright. The only thing left is to hand over my duties as monitor assistant. They said they have already found someone, and I must meet her today."

"While I'm away, the newcomer will take over disciplinary duties at the school. So, today is my great foray into tutorship! Lucky for me, it's [Field Trip Day], so there won't be any students around."
She confidently puffs her chest, then tilts her head, a slight frown growing on her face.
"Still, ever since I woke up this morning, I've had this uneasy feeling. Like something bad is going to happen ..."
"I tried divination with my orbuculum, but the reading was unclear."
Matilda glances at her mother, already knowing what kind of answer to expect.
"I have taught you more than just divination."
"It's that awful woman—the monitor director. She doesn't like me. Hmph, well, I don't like her either."
It was not long after Matilda's graduation, on one of her many visits to St. Pavlov Foundation, that she caught sight of a familiar figure in the hall.
There was no way she'd let this opportunity slip by.
"I submitted my application to become an investigator, but I still haven't heard back."
"All my classmates have been assigned except me! Do you know why? Hm? Do you?"
She paused for a moment, then gave a faint smile.
"I'm not sure about the details, but if I remember correctly, you're younger than most of your classmates, aren't you?"
This wasn't the answer she was hoping for, and not something that could be fixed through determination alone.
"I know you did well in school. I'm sure you'll make an excellent investigator one day."
"But this is a dangerous line of work. Perhaps for now, you could start as a monitor assistant—build some experience. What do you say?"
An exclamation of disbelief from a voice Matilda had hoped she'd never hear again. The monitor director stormed over, her face dark with outrage.
"Madam Z, I know I asked for help in finding a candidate, but ... her? Please tell me you're joking."
The director shot Matilda a glare, her expression a mix of shock and fury.
"She's got to be one of the least disciplined students we've ever had!"
Two girls, one after the other, walk down the shaded path that follows the school building.
One is chattering nonstop, the other quietly following behind.
"Here we are! This is the path all students take to class every day."
"The class monitor reports to us on attendance and whether anyone is feeling unwell. If someone is ill, it is our responsibility to check on them."
"We just use the same old method: take a drop of blood, drip it into a glass of water, and if the fern inside changes color, there is a problem."
"But sometimes this method isn't so sensitive. So, if a student looks really awful, I just ..."
The girl's eyes briefly flick up from behind her glasses, then drop right back to the notebook in her hands.
Matilda can't help but recall the moment the monitor director introduced this new monitor assistant: [The Successor].
The usually stone-faced director looked at the bespectacled girl with visible pride and satisfaction, the kind that left no room for doubt.
By comparison, her opinion of Matilda was likely the complete opposite.
Since she started as a monitor assistant, the two have clashed more than once—Matilda giving in more often than not. But there is no question that those exchanges were unpleasant for both sides.
Matilda snaps back to attention, noticing the steady scratch of a pen across paper.
"What are you writing? Did I really talk that much?"
The eyes behind the lenses drift back to the [Notebook], the pen never stopping.
A cloud of suspicion builds in Matilda until a thought takes shape.
The uneasy feeling that's been hanging over her since morning washes over her once more.
If something were to go wrong with her promotion, there's only one person who could be behind it: the monitor director.
It may not even be out of malice. The woman has been in her post for decades. She's a relic.
It's not as if Matilda ever means to defy the rules; it's just that the whole system is hopelessly outdated.
A good arcanist needs broad knowledge, an open mind, deep understanding of arcanum, and quick judgment in crisis.
But at the SPDM, whoever obeys the dusty Student Handbook best is considered "excellent." The more like a puppet, the better.
Becoming a monitor assistant was never her plan, but once appointed, she tried to bring something new and better to the school. Sadly, to the director, that was an unforgivable misdemeanor.
In Front of the School Building, SPDM
"No. It's more like she's always believed that deep down."

For Beryl, birthdays are anything but meaningless. Every year, she picks out a gift for Matilda, tucks it away, and mails it on the exact day. Each present fits perfectly with the last—like a gear locking into place.|Revealing one's birthday as a famed diviner is unwise. As such, few know Beryl's, and she's never spoken of it. People say she hides her birth date so no second-rate fortune-teller can pry into her fate. But the truth is simpler: no one ever asks, except for the Foundation's record clerk.|While on assignment in France, Matilda mailed Beryl a mousse cake and some macarons. Beryl shared them with the children inside the Suitcase, immediately winning their praises. From that day on, they treated her with utmost respect, enough to catch the Tooth Fairy's attention.
A diviner who peers into things yet to come, tracing the ripples—and the stillness—of fate. One of your closest friends in the art of divination.

That day, Brume received a heartfelt letter and a bouquet of dew-dropped irises. It reminded her of the birthday cards her parents used to send from afar—never on time, but that didn't stop her from always wishing for one more.|On her birthday, Bunny Bunny surprised her with a French mousse cake. A flawless crystal, born with an unmatched gift for capturing hidden light.
A slight shift in angle sends rainbows dancing across its surface, though its own true color is impossible to define.
Every beam that passes through it bends away, and no one can say if the crystal itself has changed in the process.

One of the workshop's finest creations—a new vessel for a fragile being, now unafraid of the passage of time.
When it spreads its wings and lifts into the air, the shimmer it casts can hold any gaze.
Interviewees didn't deny its remarkable effect in advertising.
What Was Meant to Be Small

A young girl, careful but unskilled, finished her very first piece of polishing and strung it with her favorite ribbon to give to her mother. Crude beside the woman's other fine jewelry, perhaps—but from the wear on its edges, she clearly wore it for years.

The shop on Rue de la Paix changed hands. The buyer—a young woman. The property agent, puzzled by the high price, asked why she chose it.
"Bouanich's atelier will open here," she said.

Within months, that name had spread throughout Paris, drifting through every salon, waltzing through every ball, and lingering on the lips of every aspiring fashionista. Exquisite crystal pieces that captured every eye, and the rumored "special card" sometimes tucked inside, drove the curious and the vain alike to obsession.

Some customers, of course, balked at the prices. As the decade opened with an unprecedented financial crisis, the self-sufficient France had held on longer than most—but the French economy could not outrun the Great Depression forever. Recovery was slow. Spring came and went, yet wounds still remained.

Even in such times, the lady of the crystal workshop always smiled with understanding.

"We offer something different for everyone, but look ...
"People are fighting to protect peace, to turn the tide of despair. These beautiful crystals are just like their beautiful wishes. You have to hold on to something tangible before you can face the unknown, even if it seems foolish.
"This has remained true throughout the ages."

In the months after their daughter was born, the Bouanich family lived in constant worry.

She never stopped crying; no matter what they did to soothe her, those round, tear-filled eyes always seemed to drift off toward something unseen. As an infant she babbled as if trying to speak, but the older she grew, the quieter she became ...

Clairine took her to every sort of reputable doctors, yet none of them found a cause. In the end she had no choice but to seek out a diviner she had hoped to never meet again—a brilliant practitioner, but unbearably arrogant.

To her surprise, the diviner's expression changed the moment the reading ended.

"Your daughter isn't ill. But ... she carries a frightening gift."

What should've been an incomprehensible skill to master came effortlessly to the child. It was as if she were blessed by some higher power—even without performing any rites, her vision contained signs and prophecies ... People seeking guidance flocked to them, and the Bouanich crystal business flourished.

But Clairine never forgot the diviner's face that day, caught between speaking the truth and biting her tongue.

"Clairine ... you should understand. This gift may not be a blessing."

Pandora Wilson: We all know you're a successful businesswoman; the crystal pieces from the Bouanich Workshop have turned heads for years. But more than that, you're a powerful diviner. Pandora Wilson: In fact, I've heard your divinations have never proved false. Is that true? Beryl: If you mean to speak of the words written on the cards I slip into my merchandise boxes ... As far as I am aware, yes. Pandora Wilson: That's astonishing. Even the authoritative Applied Arcanum: Modern Divination Theory and Methods says in its introduction that "every diviner is prone to error" ... Pandora Wilson: How have you managed such a feat? Could you share something about your gift with our readers? Beryl: Heh ... My apologies, but it is something of a trade secret. Pandora Wilson: So those little inserts are part of the marketing strategy, then? I also heard you once posted a challenge—anyone who could disprove one of your predictions would receive a generous payout. Pandora Wilson: Is that offer still valid? Beryl: Always. Pandora Wilson: I'm sure some readers will be thrilled to hear that. Unfortunately, your products seem in short supply at the moment. Beryl: An issue we are endeavoring to solve. Beryl: ... Since your magazine has such an impressive readership, I wonder if I might interest you in a collaboration? Pandora Wilson: Let me guess—this has something to do with the crate delivered to our editorial office this morning? Beryl: It does. Pandora Wilson: Then you must have foreseen my answer already.

A proud little dragon, its scales gleam like gemstones, its flame is hot enough to burn through any disguise—
it's just a shame its compact size makes it far less intimidating than it thinks it is.
Active and friendly by nature, it never refuses a curious pat or whatever treats it's offered.

This lightweight metal pauldron is the favorite perch of the interviewee's tiny partner.
The stall owner at the Saint-Ouen flea market swore its original owner was a brave dragon-rider from the late 16th century—
but changed his story the moment he learned what the interviewee's arcanum can do. In the end, they settled on a price both sides found agreeable.

The interviewee wears an unusual bracelet; its largest crystal shines with a deep, quiet blue.
Despite its outward beauty during the interview, we noticed she doesn't seem to like this piece at all.
She avoids talking about where it came from, and when asked what it means to her, a rare sadness flickers across her face.

Their ancestors served as revered paladins under Charlemagne and, centuries later, as jewel hunters entrusted by the Sun King himself.
One recovered the royal treasures of Napoleon III lost overseas during the Revolution, and their parents supplied curiosities for the Exposition Universelle ... For reasons no one can quite explain, the calling to roam the world for the glory of France has been etched into the Tavernier bloodline.
At the end of any journey, there should be a waiting prize—
and few prizes shine brighter than gemstones. Where people's love for these radiant minerals comes from is hard to say: identity, status, power, wealth, or some blessing ... or curse. These glittering, silent witnesses have carried too many meanings.
Mounted on swords, crowns, reliquaries—they saw Charlemagne's empire thunder across Europe, then fracture into three, watched kingdoms rise and fall, and finally saw the light of enlightenment sweep away the dark as liberty and democracy took hold ...

But for those who chase these jewels, none of that truly matters.

"Diamonds, emeralds, and a bit of onyx—that's what Mom and Dad brought back this time.
They said they'll add some fine pearls and make a bracelet to take to a fair in America.

"Look, isn't it pretty?"

(A city map of Paris distributed by a taxi company. Many landmarks are circled with notes scribbled beside them.) Louvre Museum If asked about famous pieces: Venus de Milo (ancient Greek sculpture), Mona Lisa (stolen once twenty-plus years ago—thief was a museum employee). Nearby are Tuileries Garden (nice for a walk, no entry fee) and Place de la Concorde (old execution square, but no guillotine now—just the Egyptian obelisk). Eiffel Tower Built for the 1889 Exposition Universelle. Once the tallest structure in the world, until the Americans started building skyscrapers (no need to bring up). Crowded by day, better at night. (Find Marcel—discounted tickets plus 60/40 split.) Champs-Élysées Quick drive from one end to the other, but most prefer walking—make sure to allow enough time. Ends at Arc de Triomphe. Viewing deck overlooks the whole avenue. If guests don't like walking, bring straight here—can admire carvings and the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. ...

Pandora Wilson: By now, you've lived through six "Storms," haven't you?
Brume: Now that you mention it ... I suppose I have.
Pandora Wilson: You haven't kept count?
Brume: Well, it doesn't get any easier, I'll tell you that much.
Pandora Wilson: Have you experienced any trouble over the past years?
Brume: ... Nothing worth complaining about. Ms. Bouanich is a straightforward employer. Even if this job wasn't part of my original plan, traveling everywhere, seeing different places—it's been rather fun, in its own way.
Brume: Laugh if you want, but ever since I was young, I've longed to see the world someday ... In that sense, I suppose I've achieved my childhood dream—just not in the way I'd expected.
Pandora Wilson: So you haven't had a fixed place to live for years, right?
Brume: I have my Peugeot 201. Wherever I go, that's home.
Brume: Though, since you bring it up, I suppose it does come with its difficulties. The old girl's been with me for years—which comes with plenty of quirks, of course. It can all be quite nightmarish when I need a repair on the road.
Brume: The mechanics either tell me, "We don't have parts for antique cars," or they open the hood and freeze, saying, "I've never seen anything built this way" ...
Brume: That's why I've started carrying around the backup parts Laplace provided me with.
I'd say my repair skills are getting rather good too. If I ever lose this job, perhaps I might make a living as a mechanic.

A collar woven from gold and rubies, its design embodies what some might call "the web of desire."
The interviewee denies any association with bondage or restraint, but we still advise readers to treat any chain offered by a demon with caution—contracts and deals included.

A golden-threaded floral face ornament—nothing suits a young girl's features better than a pair of flowers.
For a succubus, charm flows as naturally as a flower's scent. She seems unaware of her own blooming allure. Such innocent life.

A speaking-staff studded with ripe fruit, capable of sending out hints of sweetness, beauty, or any number of tempting sounds and smells.
We have no idea how it actually assists her singing—perhaps interviewing another talking apple would help?

A gold collar, as exquisite as it is unnerving, with bone-shaped clasps that tighten around the throat when worn.
Just looking at it seems to conjure the weight of suffocation, though she claims it causes no pain. Given her almost permanently fixed smile, the writer chooses not to believe her.

A dark-glimmering headpiece shaped like hollow butterfly wings, its curve disturbingly precise.
We must warn readers: perfect fit often comes from stripping away will and freedom.

A butterfly specimen that no longer beats its wings yet "flies," fixed into its eternal pose by the lance of a cruel pin.
Such pins are meant for things that cannot feel pain—perhaps numbness itself is just another kind of death.

Painted stars along the arm radiate a strange arcane aura.
She claims the body-warding designs come from old Vedic techniques, but we must state that inscribing arrays onto the body is dangerous—especially one that looks like it could summon an eclipse.

A sheer robe woven with stars and eclipsed suns, as soft as nightfall, and far from a traditional design.
She generously offers to explain the imagery: a prophecy of a future where the sun is extinguished and a new blue star ascends to take its place. The writer doesn't believe in prophecy, but her calm expression as she describes it is nonetheless unsettling.

Earrings symbolizing sunlight, their connecting chains illustrating the process of eclipse.
She shared the legend of Rahu, the Asura who chases and devours sun and moon. Modern astronomy dismisses invisible star-beings affecting celestial bodies—but the world often answers in unexpected ways.

A copper hand mirror with a noticeably blurry reflection. She gently insists that essence matters more than outward appearance—
perhaps clarifying one's inner reflection is simply part of her profession.

A slim chain of tools—a salve tin, scissors, keys, probes—arranged to avoid jingling while she walks.
Contrary to expectations, the tools were all quite mundane. After enough interviews, we've learned the greatest healers rely on nothing more than relentless resolve.

A rare symbol: Asclepius's serpent curled around a frameless window.
No one can truly step inside another's heart; doctors can only guide people toward a door that they must open themselves. Her answer came with unmistakable sadness and resignation.

A weighty gilded cane perfectly suited to its owner's refusal to ever appear ordinary.
Besides supporting her gait, it also chases off anyone who offends her sense of style. Most of our team were deemed suitable—our disheveled editor wasn't so lucky.

A brooch clinging to a floral eye, its lines flowing like molten gold.
A suit is a person's cover; the brooch is their signature. "Don't become the kind of book you see everywhere," she advised.

A tie inspired by measuring tape and tailor's shears—simple materials, unforgettable design.
He says it captures his philosophy: classic, traditional, yet sharp and fashionable. Out of respect for his confidence, we did not ask how long it will be before cheap copies flood the market.

One night during a festival, a weary wanderer came by a tavern that kept its doors open long past midnight. Drawn in by the sweet aroma of wine, he sat down to rest and drank cup after cup. As his vision blurred, he noticed a mural on the wall of a fairy, with a silk-flower lantern balanced on her shoulder, smiling gently. With a flick of her pale wrist, a wine jug shimmered into view, and she looked straight at him as if beckoning him to enter.
His heart stirred, and the wanderer staggered forward and fell straight into the painting. When he opened his eyes again, he had arrived in a paradise. There was sweet wine to melt away all bitterness, breathtaking sights to soothe the soul, and immortal fairies who laughed and drank with him. Shedding the troubles of the mortal world, the man wished only to remain in this enchanted valley forever.
But after three cups, dawn had broken. He roused from his slumber, lying atop an empty jar. Everything from the night before had been nothing but a dream.
He looked up. The mural still showed the peach-blossom paradise, but the Blossom Spring Fairy was nowhere to be found. Only the tavern girl's voice remained beside him: "Shall I open another jar for you?"

An elderly woman in Yongfeng Town often claimed she once encountered a spirit in her youth. She said that as a child she dug up an enormous ginseng root in the mountains, but before she could tie a red string around it, it burrowed back into the earth and vanished. The old woman believed it had transformed into an immortal spirit. Though her neighbors dismissed it as nonsense.
Her son worked the fields for a living. One day, after finishing his chores, he returned home to find a young girl playing by the doorway, twirling a red string between her fingers. A faint glow shimmered around her, though her face was oddly blurred and indistinct. Confused, he approached to ask who she was. The girl seemed to sense him and slipped away into the grass, leaving only a piece of red string behind.
He brought the string home to show his mother. The old woman clapped her hands in excitement. "It's her! She's the ginseng spirit I saw all those years ago!"

A young scholar set off for the capital to take the imperial examinations. Fearing misfortune on the long journey, he hired an elderly servant to accompany him.
While passing through a remote mountain range, lightning split the sky, heralding the approach of a violent storm. Fearing the ravages of the elements, the young scholar spotted an abandoned temple in the distance and wished to take shelter.
His servant tried desperately to stop him, for the temple was rumored to be haunted. Locals called it the Shrine of the Jade Bottle Lady, whose statue held a sacred vessel and was said to delight in tormenting travelers. Those who entered to escape the rain were often frightened out of their wits, and some lost their very souls.
The scholar scoffed at the warnings and stepped inside.
At dawn the next morning, the servant searched the temple. The scholar's belongings lay scattered across the floor, but the man himself had vanished without a trace.

"When my grandfather was on his deathbed, he asked us for a dish called Jade-Shard Rice. When I asked him why, he told me this story."
"He said that in his youth, he once encountered a wandering ascetic. The stranger's robes were white as snow, his manner pure and serene. He claimed to be an attendant from the Celestial Palace. The man opened his bundle and took out a bowl filled with rice that shone like jade in the moonlight. He invited my grandfather to eat with him ,and the meal was unlike any other he had ever tasted."
"I followed Grandfather's instructions and traveled far away to the place he had met the ascetic. I searched every village and field, but no one had ever heard of the dish, nor had they seen the man. Knowing my grandfather had little time left, I returned home with a heavy heart."
"The moon was already high when I returned. At first, I was dismayed to find that Grandfather had already passed. I feared I had failed him in his last request. But then I spied it, an empty bowl beside his pillow, containing the last glowing fragments of miraculous jade-like rice."

During every festival season, a shadow-puppetry troupe would visit the town. Their craft was extraordinary—every puppet danced as if alive. Crowds swarmed the streets, blocking the roads; every show met with thundering applause and laughter that filled the air.
Over the years, villagers grew curious about the troupe master's origins. Despite many inquiries, no answers surfaced. One day, a mischievous child quietly lifted the master's sleeve and found his body was thin as a shadow puppet.
Suddenly, a great wind swept across the land. Every shadow puppet flew off its frame and rose into the air, clashing and spinning with metallic chimes. As the crowd watched in awe, a booming laugh echoed from above—the troupe master cast a long rope skyward. It soared into the clouds. He climbed it with ease, and both he and the rope vanished into thin air.
It can be hazy, uncertain, fickle—and, most of all, beautiful.
From the driver's seat, the afternoon sun presents an invitation for fun and freedom.
A hero may pass you by, but a taxi driver never will.
Men judge the fruit for a sin of their own making.

A bright red, juicy apple hangs in the center of the Elysium.
Ignorant of its meaning, the starving take notice of it. Growing just low enough to reach. Its color vivid, its scent sweet.
A whisper curls through their ears, saying: "Take it." Because it hangs so tantalizingly close, because it draws every eye, the fruit is guilty of its own brilliance.
There is no reason not to reach out.
When the sweet juice blooms across their tongues, they feel the world lighten for the first time. The flavor enthralls them, and they hurry to taste more until a new thought takes root in their minds.
"This fruit will belong to me forever. This world has hidden delights that I am owed."
Even as they drown in their blissful dream, they never realize that the urging voice came not from the outside, but from within.

In the end, the fruit finds a branch where it can finally rest. At least here, no one will judge it for its sins.
Don't tremble, don't fight it—you'll only ruin the pattern on your wings.

Spring in Paris isn't so different from Vienna.
This is where the elite gather, discussing the latest fashions in clothing, jewelry, and perfumes, wearing smiles dressed with elegant disdain, as etiquette demands—she knows this world well.
A gentleman displays his butterfly specimens, a rare collection. The delicate creatures are pinned to black velvet, gossamer wings shimmering with a beauty only captured through death.
At the center of the Palais Garnier, the orchestra rises on cue, and she steps into the spotlight beneath a thousand expectant eyes.
A butterfly's life is only a breath against the void. Why should it linger? Why not hurry toward that eternal beauty? The voices of the dead whisper in her mind, sketching out a vision of a glorious tomb.
Her soul aches to rest—beneath the specimen glass, within a coffin like a crystal jar. Death would be the perfect escape.
Volatile as the moon, ephemeral as the day.

Rahu has swallowed the sun, yet the burning sphere still scorches His throat.
She returns to Jantar Mantar, a place haunted with many stories. The stars can free a wandering soul, but they cannot heal an earthly wound. Nothing changes; the sky remains eternal, and so too does pain.
The short-sighted cannot see the star she describes. If that star were to replace the sun itself, what expressions would they wear?
This eclipse arrives without warning, as though a god hidden in dark matter shifts the heavens themselves. No instrument sensed its coming. A massive celestial body hangs overhead, its crimson halo washing the land in fire.
While every lens and every eye burns under the glow of its red light, she sits on the huge black palm atop the observatory, watching the star as it settles into her gaze.
Her hand stretched out to rescue but grasped only air.

When was the tower built? By whom?
As she climbs the steps, she has no time to ponder over these questions. She did receive omens of failure, but in this moment she sees only the fire at the summit and the wailing spread across the land. This era has been sick for far too long; it needs a surgeon's blade to cut away its rot.
So she climbs higher, step by step, seeing farther, seeing more souls crying out to be saved. Beneath the flesh lies thought, and within thought lies the subconscious. Every strand of thinking is a path leading into the dim unknown. She follows the path forward, forward ... forward. Until she forgets how one is supposed to turn back.
When no path remains, she finally remembers the omens. To try to save others is always an act of arrogance. The cost of shepherding an entire age is something she must have understood.
But she accepted that price long ago, even if it means leaping from the tower's peak.
That which changes your look may alter your soul.

"A long coat with a V-neck sweater—that's the current trend. It brings out a gentleman's presence, and it suits you well."
The customer studies his reflection. A Daedalus deep navy flannel suit with a pale yellow cashmere V-neck. Clean lines, perfect tailoring. Even the harshest critic would find nothing to fault, so the customer gives a small nod.
"Wrap it up for me."
The Pioneer watches him melt back into the rippling stream of crowds outside. Cloth is by its nature pliable—it shapes around the body while quietly molding the soul. He never minds spending a little extra time sculpting the perfect silhouette. Fashion is a fleeting lie that reflects a very real desire. People step into the shop to change and step out wearing a lie on their bodies but carrying the seeds of truth in their minds.
There in the beating heart of Parisian fashion, as a designer on the bleeding edge of the avant-garde, this is simply another ordinary day.

You stumble into your comrades' ritual, their cold eyes hidden beneath black robes. Normally, you'd leave quietly, but one of them stops you:
"Coppélia, didn't you help with rituals when you were in the orchestra? We're short-handed. Let's see what you can do."
You would often do this in the orchestra.

The lords and ladies in black robes watch your left arm's vibrations, then instruct you to check how far the arcane fluctuation caused by the ritual reaches.
They have now given you more specific directives.
After the ritual begins, walk away until the vibrations stop completely. When it does, you stop. Understood? Now go. Remember, this ritual will bring glory to all who participate.
You start setting things up as you once did for the orchestra, but they stop you.
Do you only know the orchestra's way? Our needs are different. We will use this ritual as a powerful weapon.

We've reached one percent of its full potential.
Use this ritual in your future battles. We need to test its stability.
You've always been good at following orders, but the robed lords and ladies don't look pleased.

Why are you standing around? We're dedicating this ritual to the Guiding One. Its power will win her favor.
If you can't help, then do better or leave!

You walk down a long, dark passage seemingly without end. As you go, you tap a stone on the wall and hear a recognizable hollow sound behind it.
You remember hiding things behind stones like these before, so you continue tapping, listening for that tell-tale clear note ...

Follow the furry one, and you'll enter a magical underground world ...
You're not sure where you heard the story, but now you've proven it's real.
You look at the tangle of wide pipes and the bridge over the river, then take a deep breath.

You stumble upon an unexpected "Wordless Workshop." Like others, you know it has no refreshments and needs no invitation.
You can join whenever you like, if you'd like.

You recognize the fragrance. It’s the same one from the notes she left for you. You listen carefully but don't hear her voice.
Her voice also carries a fragrance. When you smell it, you often avoid punishment, get candy, or hear things you don't fully understand.

You follow the strongest scent, hoping to find her.
The scent seems to form her shape. Her lips move, but no sound escapes: Coppélia, you must think—is there anything you want to do besides following orders?
Returning to your childhood dreams, are you willing to embrace growing up?
Choose to embrace the influence of the overflowing Depths of Myth and gain its distorted boon. How will you change yourself? (italicized)
You shut the world out behind a blue door. After a distant metallic clang ripples into a chain of notes, you look around. The colors in the room seem to shift.

Cotton candy twirls before your eyes, speckled bluebird eggs sway, a tower of blocks shivers, and rows of doors hum with blueberry-like waves.
You press your trembling left hand, trying to trace the source of resonance. Were it not for the snoring coming from the corner, you might have joined the chorus already.

You stroll through a courtyard on the Île de la Cité.
All around you, nature's melodies fill the air.
You catch a strange voice among the tunes.
At the source of the sound, you see a strange bird—identical to the one engraved on a coin.

A group of children shove you toward a row of sweet-smelling barrels, begging you to open them.
They keep shouting "Diabolo" and "lemonade." It seems that these barrels contain both lemon soda and ... devils.
The barrels' owner pays no attention to the commotion. You look at the children hesitantly.
You aren't quite sure whether they mean that devils make good lemon soda or that a devil waits for you inside.

You weave through upright easels and scattered jars, so focused that you nearly bump into someone swinging a paintbrush.
He doesn't scold you but insists you share your thoughts on his painting.

You take your time looking around the dazzling shop, forgetting all else.
Someone half-buried beneath piles of merchandise speaks up as you pass by: What exactly are you looking for? 
You hadn't even noticed him before. His question makes it clear—you should trade some of your Goldfinch Coins for what you want.
You arrive at a noisy street and find a peculiar pocket watch. Its proud hands march forward—though you can't tell whether they're moving clockwise or backwards.

You walk through the fog slowly, the rooftops vanish, and you find yourself in a forest.
Tents, grass, sticky mud ... you're lost, that is until you hear a voice.

You accidentally wander through an open door into a glittering room.
The sprites inside lead you to a cabinet.
Atop the cabinet sit a few crystals and a note.
The note reads: "The owner is away. Take what you need."

A group of people stands before a fountain. They close their eyes, toss shimmering coins, murmur something, then turn and leave.
It seems to be some kind of simple ritual.
The black-robed lords and ladies study the tremor in your left arm, then swiftly issue precise orders.
Go out. Strike your left hand in different places. Remember, you must wait for the previous vibration to fade before the next strike.
Our ritual isn't like Lyra's. This is a weapon—looks like you can't be of use here.
Fine, then go fight someone. Testing the weapon's power over and over is part of the job too.

Gain 3 Strength on the next floor.
Success: Strength +3, Failure: Strength -3.
Perform a Strength Check. Obtain a Harmonic of variable rarity.
The shopkeeper starts recommending items to you, and you realize the mask is stuck to your face. Looks like you're not getting out of here without buying something.
Perform a Strength Check. Gain 1 to 3 Strength.
Obtain a variable amount of Goldfinch Coins.

Devote yourself fully to Manus Vindictae.

Perform a Dexterity Check to determine what happens.
You notice an unusual tapping. You knock around the special stone slab, and suddenly a strange, brightly colored creature pushes the stone aside, hisses at you, and darts away.
You look into the hole it left behind. It's larger than you expected—large enough for you to crawl into.
You're happy not just to find something hidden, but also to find that people in this place, your "hometown," still hide things behind these stones like you used to.

You get so caught up in the tapping game that you forget to watch your step.
You trip over some loose debris, fall, and hit your head on the wet sand.

Dizzy and spitting out sand, you feel something buried beneath you.
It seems the last person who fell here left a present for the next unlucky wanderer.

The foreboding darkness of the cave gives you a quiet warning to stop tapping on the stones.
You trust your instincts, turn around, and walk away.
You hear rustling from the cave—that animal seems to have friends.
Crawling on your hands and knees is difficult, but you imitate the animal's low posture and go inside.
As you crawl, you find something, but the tunnel gets tighter and the growls closer.
You feel something sharp poke your knee, and as you shift, you realize that "rock" might actually be useful.
You get into a good rhythm, moving your hands and feet together. It feels like you've just learned something new.
Your reckless movements startle the creatures in the cave, blocking their only exit.
You collect the tiny thing that poked you earlier. It looks shiny.
You've gotten the rhythm right. Your hands and feet are in sync now.

You listen to the sounds of the caves beyond. The low guttural growls sound anything but friendly.
Time to leave.

You're even more certain those growls aren't friendly.
Time to leave.
You tap a large rock deep in the cave, and the sound is thick and dull, with no hollow space behind it. The tapping game ends here.

As you chase the furry one, you feel the bridge beneath you begin to shake; it feels like it could break at any second.
You're two steps away, one step, then jump and ... grab it!
The furry one slips into a smaller pipe with a clink. Something falls from its fur.

As you chase the furry one, you feel the bridge under you begin to shake; it feels like it could break at any second.
You almost lose your balance, and when you look up, your quarry is gone.
You cross the bridge carefully, attempting to maintain balance on the unstable surface.

As you chase the furry one, you feel the bridge under you begin to shake; it feels as if it could break at any second.
When the furry one jumps up, you lose balance and fall in the river.
You sit up, soaked in mud, and notice something shiny deep in the water.

Later, you recall the rest of the story. Your friend got a harsh scolding over it, and you learned from those warnings.
This story leads to pain. Maybe it's best to walk away.
The paint on the wall is peeling, and you sense a pattern.

Some marks are only dirt, but others appear to be intentional markings.
You recognize a line of faded arrows. You're good at following those.

You've seen rivers, but never one inside a house. You find a ladder, climb down, and walk into the middle of the river.
Mud covers your toes and some shiny things. You hold the dirty Goldfinch Coins in your hands and whisper a "thank you" to the river.

You've lost sight of the furry one, so you leave the story behind and head back outside.
Which way now?
The bridge you crossed is still shaky and falling apart, but you notice another path in the darkness.

You can't find another way and cross back over the bridge.
It gives way under you, and with a loud crack, you fall into the river below.
The lid clicks open. The arrows continue ahead, and you follow them out of the magical pipe world, along with all the little things in the suitcase.
The lid clicks open. You take the pipe world's final gift and leave.
The box stays closed, staring back at you. You crouch there for a while, then bid your quiet friend goodbye for now.
Maybe you'll find some small trinkets.
You find an [Unclaimed Key] and a legendary artefact from the very bottom.
You smash the lock and climb to the second floor.
You unlock the door with the key and head to the second floor.
You pick up Curio X and choose your path forward.
You recall that the master key might work on this door too.
I want to return to childhood.
I want to grow up fast.
You break the seal on the chest and obtain a Resonator.
The chest only opens a small crack and you obtain an artefact.
You break the seal on the chest and discover an extra incantation you recognize inside.
Obtain a Resonator and an artefact.

A vehicle with four wheels pulls up beside you. Relying on your limited memories, you recall this thing is called a "car."
A little red dragon sparkling with fire pokes its head out the window, and a hand waves a friendly hello.

Hey, are you alright there? You look lost. Need help?
... Félicienne, look at the poor thing's arm. You mustn't say such things.
The driver argues with someone you can't see. Though she continues to invite you in, a strange, heavy melody is holding you back.
There you are. Thank you very much for your kindness, Félicienne. Generous indeed.
The driver dramatically ends her one-sided argument and opens the back door for you.
So, mademoiselle, where might I take you?
ㄚ-I can't tell a ㄙㄊ-stranger ... the place.
That's no worry! I'll just drive you about Paris until you want to get off. How's that sound?

You enjoy a tour through the city, then hop out where you like.
Seeing so much lovely scenery makes you feel less likely to get lost later.
She's only a lost child, Félicienne. What's got you so stubborn?
The one-sided argument grows more intense, and the weight of the heavy melody becomes too great. You leave before it crushes you.
You mustn't mention Manus Vindictae to strangers, so you refuse the driver and continue to wander alone.

Amid the heavy melody, you hear a single, pure note from a lady. She's sitting in the passenger seat! Perhaps she can take you back to base?
You slide into the back seat and sit up straight. The small car suddenly feels as safe as the room painted in Klein Blue.
So, mademoiselle, where might I take you?
No need to answer the driver. You quietly await orders from the unseen lady in the passenger seat.

... Do you know the mademoiselle, Félicienne? Why is she staring at you like that?
... She's still a customer. I can't give orders to a customer. Perhaps you should talk to her.
... Fine, if you insist.
After a long exchange between the driver and the unseen lady, the driver hands you a small, round biscuit.
My apologies, you know Félicienne, n'est-ce pas? She's not up to seeing visitors today. She says to take this and leave.
The orders of lords and ladies are to be obeyed. You get out of the car. The driver gives a soft, sad smile and waves goodbye. You watch until the car disappears around a corner.

Simply put, you're lost. The streets in this city wind unpredictably. Even knowing where your comrades are, the walls keep blocking your path.
You could try going around them, but that might take you farther from your goal.

It's hard to convey the feel of arcanum through language, but you manage to tell a passerby where you need to go, and they describe the route to you.
All there is to do is remember their complicated instructions and follow them closely.

You mustn't mention Manus Vindictae to strangers, so you attempt to use a variety of other sounds to explain instead, but no one understands.
They resolve to take you to the police, which you know will end badly, so you run off.

You need a better view, so your instincts tell you to find a higher place.
With the power of your left arm, you pull yourself up onto a rooftop.

Your view isn't as clear as you thought. It seems most buildings in this city share the same height limit.
You figure their height must be a sacred number with some significant meaning.
Still, without walls to block you, you quickly find a shortcut.
Even under the open sky, you still feel as though a shadow hangs above you.

You need a better view, so your instincts tell you to find a higher place.
You try to jump a ledge and miss, and some great force drags you down hard.
It hurts. Maybe climbing wasn't a good idea.

You let your intuition and sense of direction guide you.
Though the streets and buildings all look the same to you, the melodies of your comrades grow closer and closer.

You let your intuition and sense of direction guide you.
However, the identical streets and buildings confuse you. The melodies of your comrades fade farther away.

Familiar but chaotic sounds drift to your ears again.
You recognize their source. She appears now and then, though you've never seen her face—and her words are always opaque.

Amid the chaos, you catch some regular vibrations. It feels like she's showing affection, or perhaps offering a blessing?
Something inside you shifts a little.

You catch every sound but still can't make sense of them.
The voice's owner doesn't seem to care. Just as suddenly as she appeared, she is gone.

The sounds irritate you, so you block your ears. While it doesn't silence them completely, it helps you endure.
Before long, the sounds disappear as suddenly as they appeared.

The tough lady stands ahead, looking as angry as ever. Every comrade who passes her gets scolded for reasons you don't understand. Three of them are being lectured right now for how they walk while wearing masks.

The scolded mask-wearers emanate misery.
You slip into the shadows and escape before it reaches you.

The scolded mask-wearers emanate misery.
You try to escape it, but the lady calls you back and launches into another lecture.
You stand there until your head feels heavy. Only then are you finally allowed to go.

You ought to greet her! You've been ordered to do so!
The lady looks surprised.
Hmph ... How unusually forthcoming of you. I only hope such enthusiasm extends to your faith.
Your greeting seems to have softened her mood. While you receive a much lighter lecture, the others quietly slip away, extending hushed thank-yous as they go.

A huge puppet stands in front of you. The lord inside gives you a wave.
Fear swells in your chest, but you're not sure why. Maybe the puppet's appearance is frightening, or maybe it's something this lord did to you. He stays silent. You can't tell if you've done something wrong or if he's expecting you to do something.

You try to concentrate on controlling your feelings.
Suddenly, it feels as though something has been thrown out of your mind, and the fear subsides.
Didn't you like ... the gift I put there?
He scratches the back of his head, tears off a patch, and pulls out some stuffing.
How about this? Hope you like it better.

You try to concentrate on controlling your feelings.
But your legs won't stop shaking. You stumble back, almost falling as you run away.
Hmm ... Then, we'll play together next time?
Orders are orders, and you know you have to greet politely.
Oh? You say hello when you're scared?
Or ... are you not scared at all? But I already put the fear inside your head ...
In his confusion, the lord starts frantically scratching the back of the puppet's head. It topples off, revealing a boy's face inside.
Oh no! The head came off! Don't look!
Grabbing the puppet head, he hurries off. He moves much faster than you'd thought possible in such a large costume.

You try to concentrate and greet him as ordered.
But your throat tightens and your mouth won't open.
You stumble back, almost falling as you run away.

You run into a lamp-lit lady deep in a dark cave. In her right hand rests a skull.
She doesn't look at you, but she poses you a question.

Bones ... the soul's prison, or a place to rest?
If thrown into the fire ... do we lose our passage to the afterlife, or do we cross to the other side?
I see. One wouldn't wish to burn their own home.
But is the body kept as the resting place of the soul, or so that it might one day walk the earth again?
She turns away, and the cave falls silent.

You're practical. Or perhaps that's as far as your understanding goes.
This may be too much for you. Let us speak again when you've learned the true meaning of death.
A faint light flickers in a corner.
You may leave through there. Don't lose yourself in the catacombs.
A greeting? Here? At this time?
Someone gave you orders to act human? How fascinating.
Take this. Save that greeting for the one who gave you the order.

A lady who loves to sing is practicing in the distance, her voice fading into the wind.
Maybe she's sending a message on it, or waiting for the wind to bring something back.
You follow the little lady's melody, and your left arm moves in rhythm with the wind's vibrations.

You follow in gentle harmony until you catch a wrong note. It reminds you of the old mistakes made in the choir.
Before you get too nostalgic, you quickly adjust, bringing the melody back in harmony.
When the performance ends, the little singing lady looks at you, holding something that wasn't there before.
Not perfect yet. Your passion slumbers still ...
I hope to one day hear the voice from within your heart, those tremors yet untouched by rationality and worldly concern.
She places the object in your right hand.
I've no need of this any longer. It's yours now.

You follow along in gentle harmony, but when the song ends, she looks at her empty hands and shakes her head.
You know this gesture means your efforts fell short, and that it usually leads to disciplinary measures.
This time, though, she only smiles as usual and quietly waits for you to leave.
You close your eyes, letting the wind and melody carry your thoughts. Then you lose consciousness.
When you awake from your dreamless sleep, the little lady is gone. You're alone.
The song stops, your greeting breaking its tempo like a rest on a sheet of music. The short lady turns her smile toward you.
Yes, Coppélia? Is there something you need?
This is an ㄛ-order. I should ㄍㄖ-greet you.

From the one who sent you here? I'll be sure to greet her later.
Don't you have any other orders to carry out at the moment?
Her smile remains unchanged, but you feel the beats in the air grow sharp as if to say, "If you're done here, move along."

You hear a soft whimper coming from the wall nearby. Looking up, you realize it's coming from the talking painting.
You've seen it before. It's the one depicting a woman with three eyes. She usually looks sad, always carrying out the same orders from the lords and ladies: "Take this."
But now, she's pleading with you to take something away.

Both of you are just following orders, so she's your comrade too. The thought makes you feel a little closer to her.
Carrying her things doesn't break any rules, so you take it from her.
She thanks you excitedly. You feel her vibrations become lighter and happier.
When she pulls out a body wrapped tightly in bandages, you accept it, but your knees give way and you collapse to the ground.
I'm ever so sorry ... there's simply so much in here that I didn't notice what I'd pulled out. Haha, silly me. Allow me ...

She quickly busies herself with stuffing the body back inside. She no longer has time to talk to you.
The waves in the air feel as heavy as the body. You quietly step back—as experience with the lords and ladies tells you, it's time to leave.

The person in front of you is transforming into a beast, writhing and squirming like an earthworm caught in the sun.
This reminds you of something you've seen before, when someone put on a mask and experienced the same agony.
He moaned and cried and whispered, begging you to end the pain.
You remember that, back then, you didn't hesitate with your choice.

Back then, you hit him over the head, and he became your comrade.
Now, this beast is only angry at you for striking him.

Back then, the crying was too heartbreaking to hear, so you tried to comfort him.
In the end, he calmed down and closed his eyes peacefully.
Now, this beast seems grateful for your brief moment of care and gives you some things he no longer has need of.

You enter an eerily quiet place called a "café."
Beasts and humans sit here side by side, not speaking or even looking at each other. Everyone just drinks brown liquid and eats in silence.
You take a seat. The scent of the brown cake on the plate in front of you fills the air.
It all feels strangely familiar—the closed space, the food set before you, the silence ...

Back in the blue room, you assumed pain was normal.
Most of the time, it came from your modified arm, but sometimes you'd feel another ache somewhere inside.
When that happened, you'd do your best not to think about it, hoping time would move faster.

You sit in the café, unsure of how long you've been zoned out. The beasts and people are all gone.

Back in the blue room, you thought shouting was the only way to communicate.

Your steps feel light, but the sky above seems to grow heavy. You sway and fall onto a soft blanket.
Toys surround you. You see a doll slowly spinning above you and reach out to touch it.

The room is softly lit, its walls painted pink, cream, and azure—nothing like the deep blue in your memories.
You spot a nearby shadow humming a soothing lullaby. It makes you feel safe and cozy, as if you've heard it before ...

The moment you say the word, you jolt awake—you're on a park bench. It was all just a strange dream.

She is the most honored lady, the one you must never call by the wrong name. You remember her well, even though you've never seen her before.

You suddenly awake amid ruins, feeling as though something inside you has changed.

The crab-faced lord nods, but the big hats seem less pleased. Did you say something wrong?

You're confused, but you're glad to see them happy.

A purely thoughtless answer! The perfect executor indeed!

No one's ever asked you such a question before. You tilt your head, lost in confusion.

You tap your left hand lightly, and a short melody bounces between the layers of paint.
You describe what you feel honestly. The colors seem a bit chaotic.

You see the second hand follow the minute hand, and the minute hand follow the hour hand. The monotone rhythm against your fingertips resonates with your strings.
But before you can react, the hands all stop at once, becoming lifeless and inert.

You mimic the others and toss in your coin.

You mimic the others and toss in your coin.

Your instructions lead to chaos. Boxes fall, supplies spill, and the crab-faced lord scratches his head with a claw.

Go bother Hypothetik or Lyra. I will handle this.

In the dimly lit hall, you notice a lady glowing with flames, casting a blue light across the room.

You notice someone with an armband weaving through the crowd, asking people questions.

So, he's telling us to be on the lookout for something nobody has ever seen. Pft. We aren't scared of that! We aren't scared of anything!
The city's melody starts to shake, pulling the crowd into its rhythm. You see them getting more excited. No amount of shouting seems to tire them.

Right! It's true people have been disappearing, but that is exactly why we need to stick together! No Beasts will break our line or our resolve!
This brightly colored animal used to be part of the crowd, but now it only roars. Its friends don't seem surprised by this, as if it were always this way.
Using your usual way of communicating with your comrades, you figure out what it wants.

What you really need is a safe place to stay. Sticking close to your comrades might be the best way to do that right now. Everything else can wait.

Strange feelings well up inside you, making your heart beat faster and harder.
But the various buildings, the leaf-like patterned decorations, and the gentle wind help calm your pulse.
Perhaps a little time in the city air isn't so bad. Your comrades can wait.

With no one to talk to and no orders to follow, you have no idea what to do.
So, like always, you simply wander, waiting for someone to give you orders.

Familiar roars echo in your ears, mingled with the voices of the lords and ladies in the distance. The banquet hall before you is the city residence of your roaring blue comrades.
You've been taken to places like this before, but only at the command of the lords and ladies. Coming here on your own feels new.
It's comfortable talking like this, familiar as ever. Chatting with your comrades passes some meaningless time here.
I saw Lyra too. Exactly how many are coming to this gathering?
Laurent Roseau invited just about everyone he knows—even Animus.
Animus? She loathes any gathering without the Guiding One present. I doubt she'll show her face.
She's already here. Laurent was quite boastful in his message ... Not that I care for his bragging—he asked something of me.

You listen to the two talk and realize you have stumbled upon a grand banquet, with even those who rarely show their faces in attendance. Not that it matters much, anyone taller than you is a lord or lady, right?
You know what grand banquets mean—a chorus of voices and more food than you could possibly eat.

Everyone looks busy preparing for the banquet, the cacophony of sounds creating an air of excitement.
You ignore them and walk between the tables and chairs in the hall.
Something forgotten in a corner becomes your reward for exploring.

You wander between your busy comrades, not sure what to do—like a moving bump in the road.
They shoo you off to a corner as if you were a fly.

Even when you move among your comrades, you feel like an outsider. Whether you stand still or move about, you're always wrapped in a judging gaze.
Now, surrounded, you face their close inspection.
Everyone here has a mission of some sort, and even an unexpected helper mustn't stay idle: "What can you do?"
Hm. That is the one thing you're any good at—sensing vibrations.
Go and find some new musicians in Paris for our orchestra, as you did before.

The little lady's words are encouraging. Her clear order sweeps away your confusion for now—you need only to obey, as you always do. You nod over and over, swinging your arms in a clear sign of acceptance.
You have been offered such grace, yet only wish to serve as the believer farthest from her, hm?
Fine, do as you will. But even in these trivial tasks, at least do not bring her shame. I know there are none who can truly serve her but me.
The tough lady's harsh, suffocating tone leaves you bewildered.

He grabs you and carries you out of the banquet hall. And just like that, you escape their watchful eyes.
An angry mob approaches, chanting words you can't understand. Their anger seems to intermingle with the anger of the city, almost pulling you into their fervor.

They respond with loud shouts, mentioning strange phrases like "eight-hour workdays," "time off," and "benefits."
After listening carefully, you realize that they're rejecting orders simply because they dislike them. Unfathomable.

Though they're clearly speaking words, they sound more like the roars of your comrades.
You hear them, but can't make sense of what they're saying.

Whether out of curiosity or simply because you're caught up in the mood, you walk with them through the city, circling again and again. Except for the occasional stop in open squares, they never seem to tire.
After some time, and some decent exercise, you realize they aren't just wandering aimlessly like you. They're marching with a purpose—to protest the orders they've been given.

Whether out of curiosity or simply because you're caught up in the mood, you join them as they walk and shout. But, much like you, their movements seem to be aimless. Except for the occasional stop in open squares, they never seem to tire.
Your energy is no match for humans. In the end, you fail to keep up with their endless angry march.
An orchestra? Sure! Music will carry our voices farther than shouting ever could. Let's beat the drums and shake those hoity-toities off their pedestals!
Your left arm's performance connects with some members of the crowd, and they become your friends.

You manage to win over part of the marching crowd, and they become your friends.
Out of the way! Don't even think you'll buy me off! I'll never be a scab, and I won't betray the union!
They shout words you can't understand, push you aside, and keep marching on.
With the few words you know, you manage to convince some of the strikers to follow you without question.
They simply laugh and keep marching on.
Since the orders they're protesting have nothing to do with you, you decide to leave.
You show your power to the crowd, and most of them run away in fear. For some, however, that same fear drives them to follow you.
Your display of power can't convince them, and you can't understand their anger.
You can't convince them, nor understand their anger.

The absurd melody continues to spread, its roar infecting all around. Your left arm vibrates violently, as if it's channeling the thoughts of the entire city.

Playing brings back memories of a loud, wordless past, as though those carefree days have returned to the city.

Chaos causes wounds, and wounds bring pain. To protect people from harm, you decide to try something different from your comrades.
