Inside, you feel the cold, narrow stone walls. You wrestle a fuzzy thing with sharp little teeth.
You punch the fuzzball—it screeches and stops biting.
Victorious and undisturbed, you're free to take everything from the Critter's stone den.

Inside, you feel the cold, narrow stone walls. You wrestle a fuzzy thing with sharp little teeth.
It bites your hand hard. You yell and pull back.
Now you have traded 150 Goldfinch Coins for a hurt hand. Not worth it! You leave, sulking.

The closer you draw to the room, the more the joyous and somber melodies intertwine. The dancers' arms cut through the air, leaving a blur of shadows. Outside the window, time seems to warp—one moment it is day, the next, moonlight glows. The scene feels familiar enough to draw you near, yet strange enough to make you want to run away.
You enter the room. Your arm begins to hum with the instruments in the corner, and your surroundings change like the shifting light outside the window. Your legs start to sway along with the crowd.
You feel both happy and miserable as you stumble toward a spot to unwind.

You understand instruments more than anything else, so you decide to sit by the musicians. You recognize the guitar, violins, and double bass. Their warm quintet blends with your own vibrations.
A strange feeling hits you. Suddenly, the crowd in the room vanishes.

You look outside and see streets you've just walked through. The sight reminds you of where you are, but you then spot a similar building in the sky that disappears quickly.
A strange feeling hits you. Suddenly, the crowd in the room vanishes.

They welcome you warmly. Talking excitedly about the tune—mentioning "Gibsie" and "sy-jazz."
Ten hands reach for you, ten pairs of eyes watch you closely.
A strange feeling hits you. Suddenly, the crowd in the room vanishes.

You shake your head, trying to focus, and notice unusual vibrations in the fur-covered dancers.
You shake their shoulders, shouting, but the dance wave pushes you back.
Dizzied, you look up, and the strange crowd in the room is gone.

You're not sure what happened, but it was confusing, like many things today.
You decide to leave, thinking it might be best to forget what you just experienced.

A comrade once told you that remembering too much can drive a person mad.
"Mad" sounds scary, so you decide to stop thinking about it altogether.

The one who left you notes told you that memory is like the sweet wine of life.
"Sweet wine" sounds good, so you decide not to forget anything easily.

You wander into a room where someone is pacing, just like you do when you're bored and alone.
He sees you and smiles.
"Finally, someone! What can you do?"
He spreads out a stack of papers covered in writing, seemingly waiting for you to pick one.

You hear a sound nearby, different from the usual singing of your comrades. Its sound is a confused and lonely solo.
Following the sound, you find a triangular comrade walking in circles.
The banquet hall is inside a massive building, leading you to wander through its endless hallways and rooms. You enjoy opening doors, but this time, you attract the attention of a tough lady.

A talking stone lion stops you and claims to be an ATM for Mane's Bank. It offers loans, withdrawals, high-interest savings, and more.
After it explains several times, you understand it's like the talking painting in the banquet hall. You can leave Goldfinch Coins you don't want to carry and retrieve more later.
You encounter the talking stone lion once again.

A beautiful melody lures you to the door of a spacious room. People are dancing in pairs, spinning and twirling, their coats and skirts fluttering as they move. Some of them are covered in shimmering fur.

You follow a horde of people into the house.
They sit in small groups with books, newspapers, canes, or teacups in hand, talking quietly among themselves.
Someone carrying a tray walks up and politely asks what you'd like.
You're exhausted from your journey, and you make a beeline for the couch in the corner.

Safe, soft, perfect for resting.
You slowly sink into the cushions, your head lowering more and more until it brushes the fabric, and you fall asleep.
After an uninterrupted nap, you wake up feeling like you could walk the length of the city twice over.

You ignore the server and head toward the small groups, curious what they're talking about.
But the moment you step closer, the conversations stop, and someone waves the server over.
A moment later, another smiling staff member walks up, slips a few coins into your hand, and, together with the server, gently ushers you out the door.

You figure that "holding something" must be some rule everyone in this room follows, so you take the tray of food.
Sure enough, no one ushers you out. You wander around with the tray in hand and overhear all sorts of conversations, half of which you only vaguely understand, but all of which sound interesting.

You pat your pocket, fish out a key you found on the road, and hand it to the server.
He seems to recognize it and respectfully leads you upstairs to a nicer room filled with curious decorations, completely devoid of people.

They seem to be letting you rest here. You flip through a book of incantations on the desk, take sips from strange bottled liquids on the shelf, and fiddle with a metal device puffing out strange little clouds.
Eventually, you curl up on the silk-covered bed and take a nap, slipping out the window after you wake.

A beast bursts out from its lair, opening a new space for you.
The room is a wreck—fallen picture frames, blankets, cramped cabinets, wax frozen on the floor ... clearly not an ideal place to rest, but no reason to rush off either.

The fire lights up the room, and something shiny in the corner catches the glow, reflecting vivid colors.
The beast won't mind if you take it.

These are portraits. Their expressions hook your curiosity—some smiling, some unhappy, some looking even scarier than the lords and ladies.
You lose yourself in the paint and the strokes, as if you're talking to the portraits without saying anything.
A strange, pleasant feeling washes over you, sticking around in your subconscious.

Doing what you've seen friends do most often when scavenging, you start opening drawers.
Everything inside is intact. When you pick it up, you remember what the kind lady once told you: people always hide their treasures somewhere sturdy.
The beast no longer cares about it, but you can take it and look after it.
Beneath the carpet is a trapdoor. You lift it and crack it open just enough to peek inside—then a surge of force blasts through the gap, sending a puff of brilliant beast fur into the air.

The hairs rub against each other, ringing like a hundred instruments at once, the room echoing with countless overlapping sounds ... and when it all fades, some of the melodies still linger in your ears.

Rather than you locking an enraged beast outside, it feels more like you've locked yourself in.
The door is sturdy enough to save you from claws and teeth, but you'll need to find a way out eventually.

Maybe there's another way out at the end of this path.
With that hope in mind, you head deeper—only to run into a group of Critters before you find the exit.

You decide to sit and rest before making a plan.
Time slips away quickly when you're lost in thought.
Before you can figure out anything useful, the scraping of claws against the door stops—it seems like the danger wandered off on its own.
The Critters scatter toward the depths. Maybe they know where the exit is.

The light dims, and you're left relying on sound and touch to guide you forward.
Then, beneath your footsteps and the distant dripping of water, you hear a low, ominous growl.
Time passes as you retrace your steps. When you return to the door, everything outside is silent. Looks like the danger left on its own.

You defeat the creature.
As it collapses, it crashes into something. Stone crumbles, debris falls, and a faint light appears in the distance.

Looks like this is the second exit you were hoping to find. Unfortunately, it's not just an exit, it's someone's nest.
And judging from how it reacts to the tremors, it's very clear your presence is the last thing it wants.

A Chance Encounter on the Champs-Élysées

You lose your way in a salty fog and find yourself in a forest. A cave appears through the canopy.
Thick grass, clear water, moist air—your feet sink into the mud, but for a temporary "auberge," it's surprisingly cozy.

Your ears ring with frenzied shouts ...
"Long live Blum! Long live the People's Front!"
"For bread, peace, and freedom! Fight!"
Uncontrolled chaos inevitably breeds violence and blood.
You see some people sprout tails and sharp fangs.
They're all tangled together, and you can't tell who's a civilian and who's a beast. But you sense that everyone here is in danger—including you.

A street band hums a soft tune. You dance to the lilting tune. The melody flows through your left arm, and you notice something hidden within the notes—
"Bread, freedom, ideals, and the future of Paris."
"Just hoping for an ordinary day. Even one would do."
An elegant salon filled with maestros. You can quietly recruit them, or you can stop the music and show your own talent, though doing so might upset someone.

A beautiful melody lures you to the door of a spacious room.
People are dancing in pairs, spinning and twirling, their sleeves and skirts fluttering as they move. Some of them are growing shimmering fur.
The closer you draw to the room, the more the joyous and somber melodies intertwine. The dancers' arms cut through the air, leaving a blur of shadows. Outside the window, time seems to warp—one moment it’s day, the next, you see moonlight. The scene feels familiar enough to draw you near, yet strange enough to make you want to flee.

You recognize the fragrance. It's like the notes she left for you. You listen carefully, but you never hear her voice.
That voice carries a fragrance. Whenever you smell it, you avoid punishment, get candy, or hear things you don't fully understand.

A memento from the Mystery Box Carnival—a crown made by your loyal friends. It holds no official power, yet it crowns only one.
On the inside of the cardboard crown are a few small doodles. You know who drew them. And you know they'll always be with you.
Breaking free from rules, we need only become the selves we dream of.
Night flower blooms, no clouds, no moonlight in the hall.
Clear moon and few stars, clouds drifting and rolling—the perfect time to read by lamplight. You befriend ancient scrolls, I wander with the breeze.
To seek the secrets of revival and revenge, from one wretched era to the next.

From high above, all that has faded and all that returns lie beneath your gaze.
At the far end of memory and the near edge of reality, our lives walk between the two.
Through these brick walls, history refracts its brilliance once more.
The memories of countless people shine on.
A city flows on; in its murmurs drift the dreams of craftsmen, scholars, and artists.
Beneath the descending reflection, her citizens sing, blazing with passion, every note a spark burned in homage to the City of Light.
Matilda once told me about the Suitcase's ever-shifting terrain.
But seeing it myself, I must admit—it is far more intriguing than any words could capture.
A place of unpredictable change: mountain slopes today, running water tomorrow ...
Vertin, how many mysteries lie hidden in this place?
Oh, but I do not. I have had some truly ... new experiences.
Yesterday, I got lost for the very first time.
And for the very first time, I asked someone for directions. I asked several people. Everyone had a different guess.
I mean no complaint; it was a very engaging half hour indeed.
Of course, not everyone appreciates the concept of "getting lost."
Adèle once planned to return to her old craft here in the Suitcase.
But with all these changes, it will not be easy to achieve.
I found this by a pond.
Do you recognize it? There was a group of Critters chirping around it at the time.
So it really is a dragon?!
Feufeu's been eager to breathe fire on it.
It seems he doesn't quite believe his kin would leave behind nothing but bones.
Do you say that because you're confident it's real, or because you're also unsure? Allow me to hazard a guess ...
Hmmm, non. I can't tell from your face at all ...
Alright then. Let's see whether it turns to ash, or—
Ohh, Vertin! You've got the real thing.
Can you believe it? An authentic dragon bone, just lying beside a pool of water! Bon sang, any adventurer would be giddy over this place.
Heh ... These days, the children have been querying me over the winner of the coming matches.
It is this "Critter Crash" game they play.
They tell me you are quite a formidable opponent, Vertin. Many place their bets on you.
Then you, too, wish for an early answer. I am afraid ...
I must refuse to foresee it.
The answer would spoil the fun—for players and watchers alike.
Allow me this small enjoyment of the unknown, will you? I have already booked my seat for the finals.
Is that so? Then her determination to win is little wonder.
Whenever the children come to me about it, Matilda finds a reason to slip away.
A mother knows her daughter. I do not believe she would divine such a thing.
Matilda is a determined young woman. She will doggedly chase her goals, no matter the answers given.
Not even the unpredictable "Storm" has changed that about her.
Vertin! Here, I prepared an invitation for you.
Do you have a moment to take a look?
Ever since you first told me to step into this Suitcase, I've been thinking.
The invitation was intriguing, but what I found inside the Suitcase was astounding.
Preparing a gift to match it was ... troublesome, to say the least.
So I've prepared a little surprise in the trunk of my car. It somewhat resembles "stepping into a suitcase," n'est-ce pas? How about it? Want to try?
Let me think ... left foot first?
Hahaha, no, no. Just go ahead and open it.
Before I'd stepped into your Suitcase, I couldn't have possibly imagined it being so vast inside—my trunk isn't nearly so magical.
Promise me you won't be disappointed by what's inside because of that—oh! Did I just spoil it?
No need to exaggerate for my sake
Could Matilda divine the results too?

Do you really believe you can escape this? Escape me?
My dear, foolish Adèle ... You are but a grain of sand before the tides of fate.
What good could possibly come from fighting me?
The rift is widening. We have to stop her.
Those monsters ... they're forming some sort of shield. We need to break through ...
If the Depths of Myth is nothing more than a sea of collective unconscious, then the creatures born from it must be ...
Is that feeble little flame supposed to scare me?
Open your eyes and look around—can you not see what these miserable people want?
I am Félicienne, she who defies death—the one true existence among you short-lived creatures!
Who are you to think you can stop me?
I'm nobody. Just a tour guide from Paris who can handle a car—and tell truth from lies!
By fire, what is false is purged!
You're no master of this city. You're not even the master of yourself.
Vive L'Empereur! The free men of Paris will never be defeated by the likes of you!
Hey! I'm a free woman of Paris too—I'm on your side!
Lies! You're nothing but a lapdog of the aristocracy! A blight on our society! A parasite to all of France!
I think you need to calm down, monsieur!
Professor Roseau ... what have you done?!
I had wanted this to be a surprise, Célia. Our research has entered a new phase.
A new phase? All I saw was Vincent turning into a monster!
Hush ... no need to get so worked up. All he has done is assume the form his subconscious most desired. Isn't that right, Vincent?
Please, Célia, let us resolve this misunderstanding civilly.
Don't you see—Vincent gained a body far superior to the one he'd had before. And let's be honest, he wasn't my most exceptional student.
But you—you have the potential to be so much better. Through the Depths of Myth, you can be freed from this flawed mortal shell!
Come, Célia. It's time you took the step that will change the world.
Stay away from me, you lunatic!
What a pity, Célia. You had such promise.
You truly are my finest pupil. Must I treat you as I did Vincent to make you see?
This will be a tragic loss ... for my academic legacy.
Must you crash the party in such a barbaric fashion, Adèle?
What happened to my body? What did you do to me?!
Enough questions. This body is mine now.
It comes with some amusingly useless arcane skills, but I suppose I could do worse.
From this day forward, this body will serve only my noble soul. You ought to feel honored.
This was a shameful display, Laurence Roseau.
The outcome was far from unexpected. Taira, now lower that weapon. I'm still observing this fascinating turn of events.
Señor Roseau's research wasn't all roses either ... Hmm, where did Animus go?
She left in a great huff, something about "blasphemy."
Apparently, she had no patience left for "this farce."
How utterly stubborn can you be?!
This false era is ending. If you intend to continue to exist in the one to come, you must surrender your body to me!
I'm done listening to you order me around. You may think it "amusingly useless," but let's see how you handle my fire.
Tut! How much longer do you intend to play around with that cursed flame?!
Not long, just until you leave my body—for good.
You did well! Hit it again! Hit it again!
At last, we'll have a complete life ... hm?
You still have a chance to back out. Don't throw your life away.
You listened to those headless ramblings and want to chase death too?

Each drop of water a ripple of fate,
Melting beneath her bright, fragile gaze.
One thousand ripples, one thousand creases,
Yet one remains, unmelting, ceaseless.
—A drop of fallen blood.

Born to be free, we are fish in water,
Born to drift, we are boats on a river,
Torn by the tempest, our vessels we'll shed,
Naked we'll drown—
Or we'll leap the riverbed.

It rests in my pupils, runs in my veins,
Crying, laughing, whispering my name.
It beats in my heart and wanders my mind,
An unspeakable bond—what's yours and what's mine.
For we share one shadow—one body, two souls,
An inseparable bond: two people, one whole.

Reflections capture every embrace, 
but they cannot recount the fullness of the moment. 
The warmth of arms, the lift of brows, the quiet breaths—
we exist here, as the truth beyond the reflection.

Forged from high-carbon steel, a double-edged blade and handle shaped from a single billet. Nearly twenty inches in length, yet it weighs only one pound and seven ounces—light in the hand, deadly in use.
You would not want to see an enemy pull out a blade like this from twenty paces away. The fine engravings and ornamentation are charming, but all of that is nothing compared to its honed edge.
It has served for many years, tended with meticulous care, and it has earned its place as a trusted companion—a gift given with ceremony upon adulthood.

May misfortune pass you by, and may enemy bullets and blades never reach you. May you skim the plains like an eagle, and then soar toward the horizon, not losing even a single feather. May your courage bring victory, for we will pray to the gods on your behalf. For ages unending, the sun and moon watch over the land and guard your health and your peace. And one day, as you depart now, so too shall you return to us.

The crescent once worn on his left ear is now a keepsake, a memento. And the moment his kin see it, they will understand.
A people that values families, they believe bravery runs in their blood, and that the shashka grants them unstoppable strength. But not everyone possesses such physical might. Incantations and spells can rarely stop bullets. His proud steed fell under a single slash, and his life was no match for a bullet to the brow. Yet neither he nor his people would ever regret riding into battle with shashkas drawn, chasing death head-on.
The last crescent moon waits to return home, to cross the vast steppe with his kin, to taste freedom again on the wind, and finally knock on his family's door, coming home to where his bloodline began.

Your mother's last letter held her longing and blessings for you, and I feel the same, so I will keep this short. You know I am not good at writing letters. A few years ago, I was like you, always on the road.
Your mother worked hard to make this felt mat. It is soft, elegant, and should match the saddle I crafted for you before you left. I taught you to ride, so you know well enough how important the saddle is. Whatever fine steed you ride now, take care of it. Do not let its back chafe raw and bleed.
Next time, you should receive felt boots and a short coat. I saw your mother measuring—or, more precisely, imagining—your current height. To spare her some worry, send your measurements in your next letter—yes, I am telling you to write home. Do not forget.

I know no one wants to hear babbles, and I do not enjoy writing babbles either, so I will be direct: the wheat is growing great this year. Planting season has only just ended, yet the fields are already turning gold. Give it a little longer and we will surely have a fine harvest.
When you return, you will be eating the best bread, I promise ... though it reminds me of old Anton. He said the wheat is growing too fast—eighty years of life and he had never seen anything like it. Grisha joked it was because he hadn't lived long enough, and earned himself a whipping. Anton may be old, but his temper is as sharp as ever, and he can still swing a shashka well enough to silence any teasing. That said, he claimed it was some kind of omen and insisted we send the kolduny in the village to take a look.
All right, I have babbled, after all. If you read this far, thank you. Truth be told, I'm already waiting for that bread myself. You truly—truly have nothing to worry about at home.

"It exists, I swear it does! Look, right here—inside my flesh, inside my organs." The offering-bearer raised his shredded hands high, still smiling. Yes, even without eyes, he was still smiling. For he longs to become a part of it.
"Countless moths, nameless moths—they drowned the sun and moon in darkness. They drowned themselves as well." Until the cocoon is complete, do not expect anything from what rests inside.
"Truth. I saw the truth—so pure, so beautiful. Look, look, everything I sought now has an answer!" At last, here and there, they shed "chaos" and became part of "order."

In an old bookstore on Rue Saint-Honoré, a faded book draws your attention. Its contents are exactly what you want to understand. You brush your fingers once more across the gold-stamped title.
Yes. A book that helps you blend into society.
Yes. A book that awakens the wild.
Yes. A book that lights two souls at once.
Yes. A book that questions the nature of the world.
A masquerade ball is taking place in Montmartre. It lacks a clear theme, but a mask is required for entry. So you pick up:
A polished silver mask with a polite smile
A rough wooden mask carved with totem motifs
An enamel mask adorned with multicolored feathers
A lifelike paper mask painted to match your face
Pretend, for now, that you are still yourself.
Chants from marches and protests echo through the streets. You begin thinking about the roots of this era's unrest. Those surges of fear, anxiety, and anger—perhaps they come from:
The collapse of morals and the decay of the human heart.
Vile people with no sense of virtue.
A crisis of civilization and primal aggression.
A breakdown of connection and distance between people.
No one truly understands anyone else.
A world out of order and a universe out of balance.
Maybe the gods have lost their minds.
A kind friend sends you a fortune-telling postcard, saying the pattern on the back reveals your fate for the week. You flip it over and see:
Still a square, as you can tell.
The most complete, most flawless pattern.

You're just about to enjoy your Mont Blanc and a rich cup of coffee when the argument at the next table gets louder. They're bothering you, sure, but one person's view does strike you as the more reasonable one:
"Those who withdraw from society are running from their responsibilities."
"There is no evil, only good that society has yet to recognize."
"A lover is the part of yourself that got lost among humankind."
"One must realize they were whole from the very beginning."
So what are we even chasing.
Before a shop window on the Champs-Élysées, you stop for a long time, so long you don't notice the sky changing. What you're staring at is:
A Klein-blue gown flowing with black liquid.
You have to admit, it's impeccable taste.
A restored illustration of ancient Critters.
A smoking pipe cut clean in half.
Makes you wonder where the other half is shown.
An astronomical clock with its hands reversed.
There must be a deeper metaphor.

The entire history of humankind lives inside the human mind—what we call "racial memory." Over time, these shared memories condense into four "archetypes." Through their imagery and expression comes the "collective unconscious."

According to your assessment, your inner core resonates most strongly with the Persona.

You adapt to every era.
Decorum and social instinct are your tools; only the citadel of order can hold back the collapse of chaos, can't it? Even though relying on crumbling structures is risky, there is always another social role waiting to take you in for a while. Layer upon layer of masks—you don't mind being the hero or the clown, the sage or the fool. You are you, and you are the multitude.
Remember: a masked person gains an identity but loses their own face.

You believe truth lies beyond reason—found in dreams, madness, and primal impulse. A decaying age suits this tendency well; after the necessary destruction, everything will be reborn. It's dangerous, but worth it. You feel summoned by something older and greater. You are you, and you are the world's inverse.
Remember: the undercurrent is the source of motion, and also the abyss that devours.

You complete every era.
Conflict comes from divided souls—how could they not struggle? The damaged, the incomplete, are always calling out for what they lack. Something must be missing, so you search for the other part of yourself among humankind. Somewhere out there, a perfectly whole ideal waits to be confirmed. You are you, and you are your missing half.
Remember: projection creates imagination, and imagination always leads to disappointment.

According to your assessment, your inner core resonates most deeply with the Self.

You are every era.
To pursue the center and totality of the personality is to pursue the Self. No matter how turbulent the world becomes, you yearn for a higher-dimensional, more primordial, more eternal order. Inner harmony and cosmic harmony are, in truth, the same thing. To reach that place, anything may be carried out—or abandoned. You are you, and you are the sum of all ages.
Remember: transcendence in higher dimensions often demands sacrifice in lower ones.

Click shows the battlefield photos he took, and Charon touches them gently, as if he can still smell the sulfur and earth in the pictures.
Sentinel pulls out her last sealed military ration from her pocket. She takes one bite before drinking four or five mouthfuls of water.
At dusk, Fatutu meets 37 on the beach. After talking, they decide to take a walk on the beach together. When they make a pinky promise, both remember many things about the beach.
Loggerhead forgets to set the oven timer, which causes thick smoke to fill the kitchen. Bunny Bunny then gives her a long-term"kitchen ban."
As Matilda describes the scene, Sentinel slowly rebuilds the image of Place Saint-Michel in her mind and starts to miss the cafés there.
After enjoying dozens of days in the sun, Flutterpage gets a healthy tan and creates a deeper bond with Leilani.
Because of a clock malfunction, Oliver Fog leaves work 2 minutes later than usual. He carefully records the time as evidence for use in future time-off claims.
On this day in 1959, the Antarctic Treaty was signed. "Fluffy Duke," "Scarlet Titan," and "Brother Jake" are always in high spirits on this day.
Charlie played both Napoleon and Napoleon III on stage, her own way of paying homage to the emperors.

In 1910, neon light made its public debut at the Paris Motor Show. From that first rudimentary, red glow would evolve a spectrum of dreamlike hues, destined to illuminate the streets for an entire century.
Windsong could never thank Sotheby enough for her nutrient potion "Lady No. 500," which kept her going through the long winter field survey.
In 1930, All Quiet on the Western Front was released. Many years later, Charon sat alone in Noire's screening room and watched it in stoic silence.
In 1957, Vanguard TV-3 managed a heroic 1.2 meters before falling back and exploding. Sputnik reportedly offered her condolences.
A rare arcane bacterium was identified. Reports suggested that the colder the environment, the faster it feeds on food.
In 1968, the computer mouse was introduced to the public. Before that, X had his own experiment with pointing devices using a bowling ball as the trackball.
In 1957, Illiac Suite, the first score ever composed entirely by computer, was completed. John Titor showed great interest in it, while Barcarola felt it lacked a human touch.
The Statute of Westminster was enacted on this day in 1931, a foundational law for the modern Commonwealth.
On this day in 1901, the first radio signal was successfully transmitted across the Atlantic Ocean. Even today, the thought of this achievement still makes Ms. Radio's heart flutter with excitement.
Nautika joining the field survey significantly reduces travel expenses. A change that greatly pleases Windsong.
On this day in 1773, 342 chests of black tea were hurled into the sea. This also marks the day that the sirens in Boston Harbor were able to sample tea from Wuyi, China.
On the first day of Saturnalia, Druvis III conjures an evergreen tree at the children's request.
Ulrich quickly steps in to prevent some Laplace employees from using 32K memory disks to commemorate the release of the IBM 7090, pointing out how utterly inefficient and impractical the idea is.
Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol was first published on this day in 1843. Oliver Fog knows the story very well.

On this day in 1983, China introduced its first self-designed supercomputer, Yinhe-1 to the world. Madam Z sent a card to a schoolmate who contributed to its development, expressing her happiness for their achievement.
Near the end of Saturnalia, Shamane made small sculptures made of evergreen wood for everyone. Buddy Fairchild was happy to help him gather the raw materials using his front teeth.
Inspired by an ad from another soft drink brand, Regulus persuaded Jessica to pull a sleigh as she gave away cans of Dr. Papper.
The movie The Exorcist was released in theaters in 1973. Blonney strongly disapproved of the director firing guns during takes to get real reactions from the actors.
Flutterpage has been happy to help deliver letters between two pen pals living in the suitcase, even if the trip only takes about 30 seconds.
Pavia immediately gave up his plan to toughen himself for blows when he found out Spathodea would be his practice partner.
On this day in 1924, Edwin Hubble announced the discovery of the Andromeda Galaxy. Sometimes, Voyager can be seen looking at its direction.
With the catchy tune of Love Me Do looping in the background, Vertin had an undisturbed, quiet day.

Hissabeth burns a CD of Voyager's violin performance, hoping that someday it will be launched into space like the Voyager Golden Records.

It turns out Phil, the famous groundhog who predicts the weather on Groundhog Day, is actually a Critter—a purple squirrel, which explains why people think it's been the same groundhog making predictions since 1887.
Jealous of Luna 9's moon landing, Sputnik is secretly saving for a rocket of her own to return to space.

After a Manus Vindictae member botched a high-altitude landing with a "Short-Distance Safety Paraglider," Eternity, the one who had arranged its purchase, promised to provide additional safety training.
Bette finally quit her physically demanding role in a horror movie after several failed attempts. She was tired of contorting her body trying to play a character possessed by a ghost.

A new cookbook series titled "Special Cuisine" has landed on shelves, featuring titles like How to Cook Dirt and How to Cook Shamirs. It was written by an arcanist with the goal of helping people eat during hard times.
Pandora Wilson read an issue of Arcanist's Digest and felt it was too dry. Yet she appreciated its wide range of subjects and fresh marketing, saying UTTU should take notes.
While Cristallo read Little Red Riding Hood to everyone in the Wilderness, Rabies dozed off on a haystack, snoring away.
During a routine checkup, Ulrich chatted excitedly about a new Mersenne prime. Mesmer Jr., however, couldn't have cared less.

Recoleta struggles to keep up with Marcus's unnaturally quick reading speed. She's been forcing herself to write faster to meet "reader demand"—despite Marcus always saying that she needs ample time to digest a page.
Sweetheart got an offer to star in the movie The Grand Age of Entertainment.
Leilani couldn't answer the questions on her history test about her home, Hawaii. The examiner from Zeno had no choice but to fail her.
It's Ms. Radio's special day today. Her companions in the Suitcase surprised her with a gift of blue zinnias.
Necrologist spoke with a couple's tombstones and learned they had died with no regrets. As it turned out, their lack of regrets meant she got an extra day off.
An LSCC researcher presents a hypothesis: Manus Vindictae's enigmatic black substance could be leveraged as a foundational material to engineer autonomous arcane artefacts.
A new vampire film, An Unfinished Dream, has been released. Reportedly, it was made by an arcanist director as a tribute to his old friend and fellow director, Brian Finn.
IDM's "Klein Blue" computer lost its first match against the world chess champion. John Titor declined to comment on the outcome.
When arcane scholars added Pluto to their theoretical system of astrology, one astrologist complained its energy didn't match any known planet's profile. Nobody really listened back then.
Over afternoon tea, Bunny Bunny and Satsuki talked about how to skillfully handle unruly guests and other topics unrelated to ... or perhaps related to their roles as waiters.

SPDM hired contractors to reinforce the school buildings, hoping to prevent "certain incidents" from occurring again. After the work was done, the teacher overseeing the project made sure the crew forgot all about it using a "safe" arcane skill.
Door showed a reflection of a Carolina parakeet in his mirror. He claimed it was the last one on Earth.
Ezra planned to coat either Lisa or Louise's clothes with glowing fungi so he could tell them apart. However, he gave up when he realized his plan required identifying a twin to work.
After ONiON characterized a Teakettler as a "drooly, yappy puppy" in a report about Ms. NewBabel's Critter Rehab Center party, Ms. NewBabel responded by mailing her a book on Critter ecology.
In 1987, a supernova called SN 1987A exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud. After receiving contact from Canadian astronomers, the LSCC assisted in observing and documenting the entire event.
Argus tried Tennant's M1917 revolver and agreed it was fast and lightweight. But at the end of the day, she still prefers her Summers 311A double-barreled shotgun.
During the 1979 total solar eclipse over North America, an American writer wrote, "I pray you will never see anything more awful in the sky." aliEn T said he totally agrees.
After "Giga Girl," Spathodea has discovered new game characters that have her totally hooked: a bipedal lizard with a flammable tail and a crawling frog carrying a mandrake on its back.
Vertin and Lucy played several slow chess games inside the Suitcase. Sonetto suspended the matches when Vertin ran out of energy.
Regulus had a dream where she was broadcasting a radio show from the dark side of the moon.
Pickles admits that Loggerhead is a great listener, but he wishes she could be more than that.
In a 1959 newspaper, Pioneer discovered that the first U.S. spacecraft to escape Earth's gravity shared his name.
The song "Happy Birthday to You" became a huge hit in 1924. This made Voyager wonder what people used to sing at birthday parties before that.
The "Saving the Ozone Layer" Conference was held in 1989. To share its message, Buddy Fairchild held several lectures for his friends in Antarctica.
After Noire showed the movie Zorro in her screening room, eye masks became the latest trend with the kids.

Scientists found rings around Jupiter in 1979. Pioneer joked that they should name the planetary ring system "Jupiteria" after a certain diviner friend of his, but Sputnik buzzed with concern that it would go against celestial naming conventions.
The year 1952 saw the first successful use of a mechanical heart built without any arcane power.
Hans Christian Ørsted, who discovered that electricity could create magnetism, died in 1851. By then, the age of electromagnetism was already well underway.
Fun fact: the more chickens people keep in an area, the less often Ms. Kimberly seems to show up there.

A new lunar edition of the "Special Cuisine" cookbook series has been released, featuring must-reads like How to Bake Moon Dirt and How to Safely Harvest Water from Moon Ice for space agencies everywhere.
Argus tried Sentinel's rifle, "The Nameless," and agreed it was incredibly accurate and deadly. But at the end of the day, she still prefers her Summers 311A double-barreled shotgun.
Recoleta writes so much every day that she suffers from severe semantic satiation.
Beryl predicted that the text printed on today's calendar would be this exact sentence.
Tennant made sure to avoid Brume all throughout World Consumer Rights Day.
The space age officially began in 1926 with the launch of the first liquid-fueled rocket.
Bunny Bunny decided to catch the nightly kitchen raider by using Ezra's glowing fungi.
Inside a simulation chamber, Kiperina practiced the same movements made during humanity's first spacewalk.
Since the inception of patent law in 1474, no arcanist has been granted more invention patents than X.
A group of Critters converted Dust into fuel to propel their hot-air balloon around the world, but it took a big chunk of their food supply to do it.
On the International Day of Forests, Druvis III submitted her survey and protection report about the forests of the Wilderness.
On World Water Day, Vila submitted her survey and protection report about the waters of the Wilderness.
Spathodea looked it up and found there's no World Fire Day. Good thing she's not great at writing those survey and protection reports anyway.
John Titor has found the best way to fix an old computer: call Moldir.
With no adults around, the kids huddle around a jar of fireflies at night and listen to Lopera's stories.
Sonetto had to explain to everyone that there was no siege mission, and Bunny Bunny had only borrowed Marsha's trench raider club to crack open some giant nuts.
Corvus set up a railway in the Wilderness. Most of its passengers are Critters.
Oliver Fog heard there are other big-hat wearers out there who are just as serious about clocking out on time as he is.
After asking Rubuska to shape her shadows into snakes, Kanjira wonders if they can tie themselves in knots. It turns out they can't.
Back in 1971, a coffee shop with a pureblood mermaid logo opened in Seattle. It grew into one of the world's biggest coffee chains.
When the Eiffel Tower was finished in 1889, it wasn't originally meant to shoot electricity.

A Conversation Among the Big Shots

Inside a Foundation office, the sound of a ringing communicator interrupts a briefing.
    Irinei glances at the device—a direct line to Zeno headquarters. He nods, signaling the committee member to wrap up mid-report. Once the door closes, he picks up.
    "Somme here. According to Ivan's report, the cavalry has been harassed by bandits for weeks."
    "Oh? Are these bandits connected to the Manus?"
    "No evidence of that. More like a mix of local warlords and scattered gangs. Though a couple of the rapidly growing factions seem suspicious."
    "Have your people maintain surveillance. Contact the Foundation the moment anything develops—we'll send reinforcements."
    Irinei is rarely this cooperative, but Somme knows he can't stake the entire steppe's fate on so-called "reinforcements."
    "No need. Ivan has enough manpower."
    "Assuming the Cavalry Corps can be fully trusted—I looked into Commander Ivan. He was a trusted subordinate to that former admiral. Plus, I heard they're both from the Don River region ..."
    "I will handle him." Somme firmly cuts off his attempt at political maneuvering.
    "I hope you understand that the Don River region is a critical component of the Foundation's strategy. To ensure downstream stability and the safety of our new recruits, supporting the Cavalry Corps is our top priority." The leader of the Hawks leaves no room for argument.
    "Save it. Since 1999, I've dealt with more politicians like you than I've smoked cigarettes. The Don is just a crack in the dam. What really matters is the line of battle along the Black Sea and the Baltic Sea, right?"
    "Stay in touch, Admiral."
    After the call ends, Irinei straightens in his chair, drumming his fingers against the desk.
    He begins to ponder: could this small "crack" pose a risk of total collapse?
A Poem Written on a Riverside Tree Trunk

Weeping Wheat

Glittering golden plains
A gentle breeze passes, yet no grain dances
The earth is like a misunderstood mother
Again and again
Reaching out her withered hands

I see sunlight fall on the fields
The wheat stands quiet and clean, almost cruel
O weeping wheat!
May you bear silent fruit, enough to sustain.
Even if only enough to fill a child's smile

—Anonymous poet, wandering along the Don

Dear Vertin,
    I hope this letter finds you well.
    I'm sorry I won't able to see you off—things have piled up due to factional disputes within the Foundation. We live in such chaos that even an organization as self-professedly rational as the Foundation cannot avoid being swept into the political whirlpool. I wish you safe travels to the Eastern Front.
    I've enclosed a copy of Commander Ivan Ivanovich Burakov's file. You're about to enter the jurisdiction of the Zeno Cavalry Corps. Ivan and Igor have known each other since childhood. Both come from an old village downstream of the Don, yet fate drove them apart along the same muddy roads. They once commanded two separate units within Zeno, nominally independent but with an unspoken understanding that lingered between them.
    Commander Ivan is difficult to gauge. According to the records, he's plainspoken and awkward in social settings, which has earned him Admiral Somme's high praise as a "loyal and trustworthy" man.
    However, I must caution you: don't place complete trust in him. Hearts rust in wartime, especially those of soldiers who've endured betrayal and hard choices. Moreover, the bond between Ivan and Igor may pose hidden risks. In times like these, you'll have to weigh trust and suspicion for yourself.
    Winter is coming to the Don. The damp cold settles heavily over riverside cities this time of year. Along with the file, I've included several packets of ginger tea. Steep it in hot water and drink—it helps ward off the chill.
    Stay in touch if you can.
    Safe travels.
Zhang Zhizhi
November 25, 1920

Rye Bread Aged flour, wheat husks, potato skins, a little salt. Dry and grind the potato skins, then mix them with the wheat husks into the aged flour. Add warm water and knead it into a dough, then bake beside the stove ashes. The Golden Famine leaves us short on oil and grain, so there's no oil for the bread. The baked loaf comes out hard and bitter, but at least it fills the stomach. Ivan loves smearing chilli paste on top—he says he's eaten it this way since childhood! I've made a note to prepare extra for him next time. Smoked Fish River carp, elm twigs, one old newspaper. Clean the fish, salt it, then smoke it with elm twigs and newspaper until the skin turns black and dry. The smell carries three houses down, but don't be greedy. Save the fish oil—freeze it for soup. Grass Roots Soup Ingredients: Wild grass roots, nettles, half a potato, a pinch of chili. Instructions: Boil the roots until soft, add chili, stove ash, and salted grass seeds to mimic borscht. The recipe came from a young man I met by the riverside wheat field. He claimed to be a nameless wandering poet. *Missing Ingredients: Sour cream, carrots, and onions. Can't make proper borscht. Grass roots have been dug out nearly everywhere. I can only forage along the ditches now. Jam from Neighbor Valia Note: They hid two jars of real apple jam before the famine hit, and gave me one ... I've tucked it on the top shelf of the cupboard, wrapped in old cloth so the rats won't smell it. Her husband lost an entire wheat field's harvest ... May the Mother Earth bless this kind couple. *I've told Ivan to stop bringing food home. The people at the front have it harder than we do. Besides, in the face of disaster, soldiers and civilians must be treated equally! Even with his position, I won't allow our family any special treatment.

The Lost Diary of a Captive

[An old diary with black, viscous stains smeared across its cover. The corners are torn and dog-eared. It seems the owner abandoned it recently.] November 11 Every night since my capture, I've heard terrifying, fragmented whispers coming from outside ... and screams—not just one or two people, but many, shrieking and wailing in pain. I can also smell something burning and rotting. Damn it, are those Manus dogs burning corpses? Or performing some twisted ritual? ... November XX I've lost track of the date. Time and life hold no meaning in this godforsaken place. I once saved lives as a doctor ... now, they've used my medical instruments to brutally murder Boyaryshkin, Artyom, and Malyekhov right in front of me. I don't care anymore. If they're going to come for me eventually, they might as well hurry and end it now. ... November XX I don't know how to write this. I actually survived that nightmare—which feels like a curse in itself. We were herded onto an empty clearing where a koldunya in black robes was chanting a song. I could barely make out the words: "... Inculcator of Arcanum, let me manifest decay anew." She pulled away the shroud covering the corpse. As the black mist dissipated, a broken body lay before us. She handed me my old scalpel: "Dissect it." I looked down at the remains exposed to the air. Male, early twenties. Mottled, wrinkled skin. Ribs collapsed and fractured. I didn't know what I was doing—fear made me forget everything I once believed. Standing beside her, I raised the blade and started cutting. The scraping of bone was monotonous, but I freed that soul from its mortal prison. When I lowered the knife, I realized we were surrounded by a black fog reeking of death. All the other captives had died, their faces twisted in agony. The koldunya seized my filthy hand and laughed: "Thank you, Charon! You helped me unravel death and command it, master Death, and aid its power!" ... November XX Boyaryshkin, Artyom, Malyekhov—they came for me! I didn't mean to! I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry ... [The remaining text is obscured by black, viscous stains.]

Background Picrasma is a deciduous medicinal tree, found in both wild and cultivated settings. Its roots and fruits possess medicinal value, with the primary active extract being a fat-soluble resin. The primary pharmacological agent in Picrasma is Picrasmine, which activates cell populations throughout arcanists' brains and bodies and has shown no observed dependency effects. Valley, Outside the Ancient City of Ai-Khanoum
Along the riverbank, young riders grip their reins as they make their way back toward the village garrison.
At the head of the column rides the [Lieutenant] on her red-brown [Akhal-Teke], and behind her the slanting sun sweeps westward, hanging alone at the edge of the earth.
Snow peaks rise with solemn majesty, catching the late-fall afterglow before casting their shadows downward. The horsemen ride through this ancient dusk, winding their way back toward the garrison.
Their luck has run thin today. Several soldiers lost their way, and the rendezvous has been set an hour late to give them time to rejoin the column.
Out of consideration for her new recruits—young soldiers newly arrived to this unfamiliar land—she holds out just a little longer.
And her fortunes turn. As Lieutenant Moldir prepares to send riders out to search, her stragglers finally appear on the hillside, overdue but unharmed.
"Pick it up. We need to be back before nightfall."
She lifts the reins, and her horse rises before breaking into a few quick strides, circling back along the flank of the column toward the rear.
She counts each rider, making certain each man and mount match. No soldier left behind, and no horse allowed to lose its way home.
"Fyodor, what are you carrying in those side pouches?"
She brings her horse to a halt beside one of the soldiers, turns the mount, and rides in step with the young soldier, pointing to the crude burlap pouches hanging from his saddle.
"Picked up a few fine catches this afternoon. Nothing beats hunting at this time of the year!"
The soldier loosens the pouches and proudly shows his treasures to his commanding officer.
"Be prepared. We could be sent to the front anytime."
The young soldier laughs, glancing back at his comrades.
"We've been waiting for it! This is how all young men should live: on horseback, rifle in hand, carving out glorious legends on the battlefield."
His headstrong words earn a cheer from the others.
"Just watch! We'll pick off the enemy one by one, like hunting rabbits."
"With that rifle? Hmm, seems you're a decent enough shot."
"Naturally! No one brings in more game than I do! Every shot bags a kill with me. I never miss!"
The lieutenant presses into her stirrup, draws close to Fyodor, then snatches the rifle slung over his shoulder.
"We didn't have any shooting drills today. I did not give you permission to fire your weapon."
With that, she changes her tone, confiscates the rifle, and quickly pulls back onto her own mount.
"Order must be maintained, Fyodor. If you don't know when to pull the trigger, you will hand the gun over to me."
"I don't want this to happen again."
She raises her voice, issuing the order to everyone in the line.
"Drop whatever you've hunted. All of you."
With the confiscated rifle in hand, she urges her horse forward, returns to the head of the column, and turns to deliver her command.
"I understand your enthusiasm, but orders come before everything. Discipline above all else."
"Right. Now get rid of anything you weren't carrying when you left camp."
As the last word leaves her mouth, she nudges her boot against her horse's flank. The mount catches the signal at once, its pace quickening until it surges into a gallop.
She grips the reins with both hands and leans forward, rising and falling like a wave in time with the Akhal-Teke's gallop.
Riding at the front, the lieutenant leans into the wind and glances back. The riders who had been idling along the river earlier are now picking up speed to keep pace with her.

Among them are both the so-called "rebels" withdrawn from Antarctica and the young recruits the Admiral has gathered since returning to this era. Few of the former remain, while the latter, like Fyodor, make up the bulk of the column.
Hooves hammer the earth, their numbers causing the earth to tremble around them, holding a tight formation as they approach the garrison.
The lieutenant rides a good seven or eight lengths ahead, watching the line behind her as she scolds herself beneath her breath.
"Give them a little more time. We'll make them soldiers soon enough."
A stray wave of nostalgia rises up in her chest. Old memories drift around her like ghosts. She closes her eyes to empty her thoughts and fall into rhythm with the horse beneath her.
For a girl born deep on the inland steppes of Asia, all of this comes easy. With so much of her time wrapped up in military duties and camp chores, the chance to ride feels like a long-awaited rest.
It's a fleeting and precious rest, letting her soul run free in the rush of the evening wind.
"Last one back to camp is on stable duty with Fyodor."

She calls out the command, and somewhere behind her a loud wail rises, chased by bursts of laughter. The horses keep their pace, the sun falling lower as the group nears the village where they're stationed.
Military Camp, Outside the Ancient City of Ai-Khanoum
Their camp sits in a riverside village beyond the ancient city of Ai-Khanoum, not far from the ruins where her unit has set up camp.
By the time the lieutenant returns with her riders, the sun has only just dipped behind the peak. For the locals, that means night has already fallen.
She is the first to step down from the stirrup, offering a long and reassuring pat to the Akhal-Teke that has carried her all day. After a gentle reminder, she hands the reins to the stable boy.

Soon enough her men dismount and gather around her, chatting idly over the day's training and their detour.
Still talking and laughing, she makes her way toward the fire-lit courtyard.
"Is that so? Go have Doctor Yelena take a look. If you can still walk, jump, and carry things, it probably isn't anything serious."
She lifts the new recruit's sleeve, revealing the mark left from his fall off the horse earlier in the day.
"Nothing serious. At your age, I hit the ground far worse and far more often."
With that, she pats the young man on the shoulder and sends them all off, walking alone toward a courtyard fenced in by earthen walls.
The fire represents the villagers' welcome, a sign of light and good intent. People gather around it, passing tea, dried fruit, and warm smiles.
Here, all is calm and quiet, far from war and turmoil. The lieutenant approaches the village elder, and the aging man meets her with a grin.
"Drink, traveler from afar. May the flame light your path."
The lieutenant takes the bowl of milk wine in both hands and finishes it with a single gulp.
She recognizes the flavor: a taste of her childhood, long before she donned a soldier's uniform. In the safety of her grandmother's home, a life that was simple and carefree.

Now, after leaving the frozen wastes of Antarctica and returning to an unfamiliar age, she has taken on a new assignment: travelling to the far eastern highlands and river valleys to take command of a newly reformed unit, with orders to make them ready for the battles ahead.
"We'll be staying here for a few days, sir. Thank you for taking us in."
She takes a seat beneath the thick trunk of a desert poplar, her eyes lingering on the bonfire burning nearby.

The blaze gives off a faint warmth even at this distance. In the courtyard beyond, troops and the ever-hospitable villagers mingle and joke as they pass around milk wine, salted lamb, and thick, stuffed samsa pastries.
The fire's light creates a tiny patch of life in the still darkness, an island of peace in this age of war.
"We welcome our guests, as we always have. But tell me, what name should I give my people when they ask who you are?"
Your decision changes what is yet to come.
"We've come from further north. My father commands a unit there in the Don River region."
As the elder speaks the title, he raises his pipe and pulls in a deep breath. Firelight spills across his lined, weathered face, tracing every crease and old scar.
"Yes. A Hetman, and a respected one. That's a fair way of putting it."
"I'm an officer from the Zeno Arms Academy."

The lie curdles on her tongue. But then she reminds herself that, though she may not bear the title, her life is nonetheless bound to Zeno through her past, her adoptive father, and the sisters and brothers she grew up with.
There is a touch of doubt in his hoarse voice. The firelight paints his white beard with streaks of burning red.
"It's where soldiers like me are trained."
"My ancestors were fighters too. They came from far away across the western sea and made their home here."
"Yes. I know. That is why I've come here."
She states her purpose plainly: to recruit more soldiers for her father's army and to strengthen their influence in the remote regions along their rear flank.
The old man's eyes narrow, revealing a depth of wisdom behind his gaze.
"And what would you give us in return, officer?"
She names her terms with a steady, unguarded honesty.
Her father stationed her here so she could drum up support for the front lines and so she could win over every force that has not yet chosen to oppose them.
Stone by stone, a citadel rises. Small gains become towering strength. The lieutenant understands this well. If the battle roars in the west, then she rides east to gather allies.
"Our troops in Ai-Khanoum are more than enough to maintain peace in this region."
The old man holds a long silence, opening his shaking right hand as though laying the village before his far-traveled guest.

This particular village has been built around a medieval citadel, which climbs up the mountainside, pressed tight against the slope, overlooking the pass along the river moving east-to-west. It's a perfect chokepoint.

"When my ancestors mounted their horses and drew their curved blades, they were warriors. When they dismounted and donned their robes, they were merchants. From east to west, west to east, this is how we have lived for twenty-odd centuries."
"We are friends to all who meet us."
As he speaks, the old man waves someone over. A girl in her early teens comes at his gesture, her face glowing in the firelight like an unripe little orange.
"This is my last remaining granddaughter. Her brothers answered the call from the north and have gone far from here."
"I'm Lieutenant Moldir; I'm very pleased to meet you."

A Name Etched in the Wall

The children of soldiers who retired in 1945 grew up in the afterglow of the Great Patriotic War. They donned their uniforms, entered the military academy, and became the celebrated "next generation."

As the shadow of the Cold War descended, the academy's progressive education shook these young inheritors—they would no longer fight for hollow concepts like territory, but pursue something far grander: the "Vision of Balance."

A young man named Igor rose above his peers. His name began appearing in military briefings: commanding cross-border operations, quelling rebellions, directly overseeing high-level missions such as containing arcanists ... The years carved scars and wrinkles into his face like knife marks, yet his gaze grew ever colder, like the dark current beneath a frozen river. He had nearly forgotten—both the ideals the Great Patriotic War had etched into his heart and the myth of peace and order.

Until that day, when he studied the "invitation" on his desk—a yellowed, timeworn envelope bearing the seal of Zeno's Tortoise. The Zeno Military Academy, an international institution capable of maintaining peace, a center of order dedicated to the true "Vision of Balance."

He walked alone into that imposing building. Inside the Hall of Merit, countless names—some strange, some familiar—were carved into the towering walls. He recalled the fierce ambition of his youth: to carve the name his father gave him onto those stone walls, to stand alongside history.

Page 1: Special Purpose The commander in chief gifted me a notebook. He hoped I would inherit his habit: recording every challenge from my subordinates. They bring vigilance and wisdom, making the troops more loyal and brave. Page 17: A Record of Failure Captain Chris pleaded with me to order the flank's retreat. The supply line had been cut—sooner or later, they'd all freeze to death in those mountains. I began to waver: "Hold for twelve more hours and reinforcements will arrive ..." He roared: "But twelve hours means hundreds of lives!!" It was a hard call, but I agreed to the retreat. *Note: The flank was lost. Ten times as many soldiers died as a result. Mercy destroyed that battle. Page 38: Reflections on Sacrifice The medical team sent to assist was trapped in the city—an obvious trap. As commander, I could not afford to be foolish. I rejected all objections and pleas, ordering a full-speed retreat and abandoning the rescue. We won the battle, but the logistics chief refused to attend the victory celebration. I realized then that my troops would likely lose considerable medical support going forward. *Note: An overcorrection born of shortsightedness. I still paid the price for my own foolishness. Page 69: Disagreement with the Chief of Staff Clearly, morale was low. We needed a chance to breathe. I refused to execute high command's order to hold our position. Chief of staff Krutov strongly disagreed, protesting with barely concealed sarcasm. I told him: leak word of our retreat, then blanket the withdrawal route with artillery fire. Retreat was seen as "cowardly failure" at the time, but later proved an effective tactic for buying time to prepare our counteroffensive—we successfully lured the enemy deep and struck back. *Note: Preserving morale is vital, but feigning weakness is an even greater skill.

Pandora Wilson: Sorry for the wait, Mr. Igor. Our preparations took longer than usual because we rarely interview someone with a ... delicate identity like yours.
Igor: That is understandable. I take no offense.
Pandora Wilson: First question—and forgive the indelicacy—why did you agree to an unofficial interview from a magazine?
Igor: I did my research on you—independent principles, wide-ranging topics, and no record of manipulating public opinion.
Pandora Wilson: But surely we're not the only publication like that.
Igor: An old friend of mine often submits to you. I have read a few issues of UTTU myself in my spare time.
Pandora Wilson: ... Oh? We're honored. Was there anything in particular that appealed to you?
Igor: I am quite interested in your published records of arcanists and arcane skills. Beyond that, your perspective on history is refreshingly unique.
Pandora Wilson: You have discerning taste. We refuse to be a "mouthpiece for politicians" like traditional media.
Igor: It seems you have answered the first question for me.
Pandora Wilson: *chuckle* You're more talkative than I imagined, and more dominant. This has given us some unexpected material.
Pandora Wilson: Now, let's move to our main topic—your past with the St. Pavlov Foundation ...
Igor: Your scheduled time is running short, and all you'll get are the words of a "mouthpiece for politicians."
Pandora Wilson: ...
Pandora Wilson: You're right. Let's skip that topic.

A cleverly designed portable medical kit. The interviewee demonstrated its quick-access features and explained her unique system for organizing medicines. She added that in emergencies where a full medical case isn't practical, this kit represents the bare minimum for travel.

A pair of knight's gauntlets bestowed upon the interviewee by the Hochland Order. Forged from finely polished wrought iron with classical, restrained lines. Their surface still bears the warmth of careful upkeep and the marks of time. In our view, gauntlets used for rescue and aid embody the truest expression of chivalry.

A solid, heavy trench weapon. Unlike any other melee weapon we've documented, the interviewee has melted away what should have been its most lethal edge. As an "unqualified weapon," its smooth surface conveys a restrained, tranquil beauty.

With the end of the Crusades, Europe's knightly class embarked on a long journey from the classical world toward modernity. By the late 19th century, when the embers of faith still flickered, even the Hochland Order could not remain untouched.

The Order's revival also occurred in that final century before belief faded entirely. A red-haired girl trained in the stone halls of the monastery. She polished her longsword after morning prayer and studied ancient maxims—until war came.

In that catastrophe known as "modern warfare," knights stood numb upon scorched earth. Every ancient creed crumbled under the thunder of artillery. Industrialized war had no room for knightly glory—before roaring guns, creeping poison gas, and endless trench warfare, mercy, protection, and sacrifice all seemed small and laughable.

She saw it all. She saw the Order's members began to accept that the age had turned. They no longer believed themselves saints from legend, but ordinary people holding fast to old oaths. She saw that this long night devouring humanity had never belonged to ancient knights, and had never promised glory to those who kept watch.

It was on that day she laid down her arms.
War Report: The Miracle of the Knight in White

To investigate the rumors, I crossed half of Europe to Montpaix in eastern France. Some call her a miracle; others describe it as some arcane practice of classical medicine. To me, it seems more like hope born from the desperation of the wounded.

Thanks to my profession, I was able to meet the "Knight in White" herself—Marsha Rosenhart. She sat calmly at the edge of a bed in the makeshift tent. Sunlight filtered through canvas onto her shoulders.

"A technician happened to notice my use of painkillers and reported it out of concern," she said evenly. "The Logistics Committee worried I was overworking myself and decided I needed a temporary rest."

"Is it true? Why do you rely on medication?" I asked directly.

"My arcane skill can absorb pain, but not eliminate it. Without painkillers, I'd never sleep through the night." She answered without hesitation.

An unexpected answer—one that also solved the mystery behind her miraculous treatment.

"Why push yourself this far?" I asked, knowing my readers would ask the same question.

"I am a knight," she said, her voice firm. "To be a knight means enduring and protecting. Those are vows I must uphold."

Dear readers, I've always prided myself on objectivity and restraint in my reporting.

Yet beyond the miracles she performs on broken bodies, perhaps there truly is another kind of miracle dwelling within the heart of Marsha Rosenhart.

Pandora Wilson: I imagine many readers will be astonished by your experiences—absorbing pain from so many different people, in so many different degrees. Would you say those experiences made you who you are today?
Marsha: I'm not sure ... The way I see it, pain doesn't make people stronger. It's just that in learning how not to break, you slowly become someone different.
Pandora Wilson: You mean suffering itself has no meaning?
Marsha: I haven't thought that deeply about it. Suffering is just suffering—there's nothing special about it. Like ... someone who's never been through war can still understand how precious life is.
Pandora Wilson: Oh? Excellent. Let me try to distill your point: you believe that pain itself has no inherent value—what matters is the spirit and resilience people show when confronting it. Is that right?
Marsha: ... Hm?
Pandora Wilson: Thank you for sharing. This has been a reflective and inspiring interview.

A folded-brim cavalier hat. Its upturned brim is designed to avoid interfering with the steel winged headpiece the wearer has on her head. The interviewee seems particularly fond of the tall, pointy decorations, wearing them even at the risk of piercing through the hat's crown.

A magnificent, dignified cape—not designed for ambush or combat, yet one that allows the interviewee to move freely through palace halls. "The deep jewel tone is solemn without being dreary. The embroidery balances classical motifs with Art Nouveau styling. The tassels must be short enough, and the fabric needs to be stiff and well-tailored so it won't interfere with shouldering and aiming a rifle." The interviewee clearly possesses considerable expertise in costume design, which deepens our curiosity about her professional background.

A smokeless rifle with finely engraved detailing, meticulously maintained inside and out. The rifling bears not a speck of grime, guaranteeing each bullet departs at peak velocity to pierce cleanly through the skull of any who would shatter the peace. Peace, of course, is forged by weapons—it always has been.

A silver circlet. It remains attached to her no matter how she moves, as if it were a part of her body. The engraved patterns likely originate from the steppe of her homeland. She once mentioned: "When something moves me, it must be connected to a place I've lived."

A set of repair tools. When the writer arrived, the interviewee was polishing them. Judging from their gentle gleam, they must see frequent use.
While demonstrating them for us, her clothing accidentally knocked one tool loose. Clearly, with her military background, she has yet to adapt to such decorative attire.

A handcrafted medal remade into a brooch. The emblem is etched with traces of windblown sand, in stark contrast with the silk ribbon beneath.
When we brought it up, the interviewee's gaze turned firm—"It's just an old thing." The writer understood the subject was closed.

An "unusual" syringe.
Its casing is cast from lightweight alloy. The interviewee prepares the solution—a mixture of mercury, sulfur, and small amounts of purified chemical extracts.
The writer noticed a tube connected to the rear of the syringe. When asked about its purpose, they explained: the formula requires their blood as a base. They have conducted this experiment hundreds of times already.

A gauntlet cast from base metal alloys. Intricate mechanisms are embedded within, capable of responding to heart rate and skin temperature.
This gauntlet once caused an accident—the spare metal on the laboratory bench instantly liquefied.
"Need to adjust the sulfur ratio—more than the mercury, less than the salt. Lower body temperature below normal readings. Then it will be perfect," the interviewee wrote.

Multiple badges pinned to the interviewee's waist and chest, engraved with different arcane symbols representing enlightenment and ...
"No one cares what those things actually mean," the interviewee cut in. "But they've got a nice bite to them. Want to try?"
Since the badges' material remains unverified, the writer strongly advises readers against imitating this peculiar habit ...

A tea set for beverages and desserts. These pieces arrived at the castle across different eras. A century ago, the old master favored the silver teapot, while his great-granddaughter treasured the porcelain teacups. Now they are all lifted gently by a steady hand, producing melodious, layered chimes as they're set down—bringing delicacies and attentive care to every guest.

A brilliant gold medal adorned with rubies and pearls. Not something you'd expect on an ordinary waitress. Is this impressive medal a royal commendation, or a secret gift from someone powerful? The interviewee offered no explanation, and faced with such a bright smile, we found ourselves unable to press further.

A ring of keys and a slumbering teddy bear, guardians of the castle's order and peace around the clock. When young guests fear the shadows that fall at night, the interviewee leaves the bear as a companion. "It's enormously strong and can chase away all the bad people. It has a brave heart, too."

He carries so much—sins, betrayals, and the names of fallen comrades.
The living and the dead charge together beneath an invisible banner.
They walk through fire to wipe away the dust that dims their glory.
She sacrifices herself to fulfill the true meaning of ancient oaths.
The bell's toll echoes, a silent reflection in the mirrored hall, announcing the beginning of a new day.

Now she stands outside a historic venue, dressed in crisp formal attire.
The Palace of Versailles, once the crown jewel of monarchy, drew countless admirers in its time. But now, its beauty goes largely unnoticed. People gather here for one reason only—the possibility of peace at last.
She is neither invited delegate nor palace servant. Drawing on years of battlefield experience, this sniper has infiltrated the magnificent palace. Her mission is clear and unwavering—eliminate any potential threats and ensure this conference, which holds the fate of millions in the balance, proceeds without incident.
Inside the mirrored hall, pens hover over paper, and the treaty awaits signatures—though it is far from fair. Born of competing interests, it inevitably carries traces of hypocrisy and deception. Yet it has halted the war, however briefly, and nudged the world one step closer to something resembling order.
She believes true peace will come eventually. It will live in endless laughter and fill every ordinary moment.
Perhaps this moment of tranquility is what she's been yearning for.

In Provence's summer, lavender blooms into a purple sea.
Not far from the lavender fields stands Gordes Castle. Built in the 11th century, the fortress remains formidable even now, offering shelter to those displaced by war.
Moldir and her siblings have come here. After leaving the battlefield behind, they've finally crossed through the smoke and seen the world as it truly is. The shrieking in the air no longer comes from bombs, but from fireworks bursting overhead.
Yet war's shadow still clings to them. When you've grown accustomed to something, it's hard to simply walk away. Every night, Moldir inspects the castle grounds to ensure it can withstand any attack.
Again and again. Endlessly.
Those creatures who once gently licked our hands have given their lives so that we may make ours eternal.

Inside the dim laboratory, Medicine Pocket records vital signs and physiological data—monitored by the machine, the agony of blood boiling from alchemical practice is converted into measurable data. This agony has value—before long, it will serve a greater purpose.
Intermittent stabs of pain spread through their nerves. In a daze, they see that little kennel again. It was a sunny afternoon. The dogs left their metal cages for the first time, sniffing curiously at the grass before them. Behind their ears, light blue identification codes remained. They were the survivors.
Not far from the lawn, in the backyard, tiny graves dot the ground. Even now, the researcher can still recall how those experimental dogs watched people with their glassy eyes. Those wet licks and soft touches—all of it now sealed inside a single pill.
In 1935, the Monument to the Unknown Dog was erected at the Institute of Experimental Medicine in Leningrad. Every step forward of the human civilization carries the weight of these little lives.
The sun is shining; time to start the day's work.

Bunny Bunny's Schedule 7:00 AM Prepare breakfast—a large serving of bacon and eggs with a cup of butter coffee. Remember to bring the guest in the guest room his meal! He just broke through the blockade yesterday to get here. He's carrying important documents—supposedly vital to the safety of more than 30 big shots ... I need to help him make sure those files don't fall into Manus Vindictae's hands. 11:00 AM Provide lunch for the visitors. These visitors are up to no good—they're looking for someone. I know exactly who! Good thing I hid the guest beforehand ... But they trashed all the rooms I'd just tidied! 2:00 PM Help the butler move today's supplies. Not heavy at all! Apparently these supplies were seized from Manus Vindictae. No wonder the crates feel slimy—how filthy. Don't they practice personal hygiene? 9:00 PM Get ready for bed, but remember to bring the master some late-night snacks. The visitors from this afternoon planted bugs inside the lamp! How sneaky!
