We Sell Méi Blossoms, Not Fish

When readers set out on their travels, do they seek untamed landscapes or traces of human civilization?
In pursuit of spring at its most resplendent, this journey begins in a small fishing village tucked deep within a mountain hollow. White walls and black tiles cover the slopes; when spring arrives, the clustered houses are cradled in drifting clouds of crimson and blush.
Though it is called a fishing village, no fish are sold here—only Méi blossoms in full bloom. The history of Méi blossom cultivation here spans over a thousand years. There is no need to fear the trees have grown too grand: through delicate bonsai, entire mountainsides are folded into shallow pots. Artisans tend them with decades of unbroken patience, binding branches with palm fiber, trimming them inch by inch, until twisted trunks surge like dragons breaking from the sea.
Thus, the art of time and the philosophy of life come to rest—sealed within these living sculptures.
Now tell me—wouldn't you like to journey here and purchase a piece of spring?

Huìpiào
Received Today: xxx, redeemed for forty thousand wén at the big exchange house.
Hereby recorded
Prosperity Commerce Co.
Interest set at thirty wén per string.
...
Issued by Harmony Textiles Co.

This slip of paper is a huìpiào—an exchange note, much like what one might call a teller's check today. Three centuries ago, when local merchants roamed far and wide to trade, such slips traveled along with them, lightening their packs and easing the burden of coin.
With land scarce and people many, these traders ventured across the realm, setting up all manner of businesses and amassing immense fortunes. Bound by shared origins, they stood shoulder to shoulder abroad, even coming to dominate entire trades—yet such unity once stirred public resentment.
So the merchants turned their gaze toward scholars and officials. They funded charities, established academies, and cultivated learning, gradually reshaping their public image—wealthy yet courteous traders who revered letters and propriety. In this way, local enterprise endured, and one legend of great fortune was born after another.

The city is shaped by water. Winding rivers slip through its streets, and along the banks that crisscross the entire waterside town, solitary anglers or small pairs can almost always be found at leisure. Curious about their fortunes, the writer stopped to ask an elderly fisherman about his catch. Inside the basket lay only a single palm-sized fish. Yet the old man spoke with quiet pride, explaining that one of the region's most famous dishes is made from precisely this unassuming creature.
That dish can be found on the menu of a small restaurant along the old riverside street—Smelly Mandarin Fish. The name makes no attempt at diplomacy, and neither does the aroma. Somewhere between fermentation and decay, the scent announces itself the moment the dish arrives. A companion, braver than most, was the first to try it. According to her verdict, the garlic-clove-shaped flesh is surprisingly delicate, deeply flavorful, and pleasantly springy on the bite.
The dish is said to have originated as a practical solution, a way to prevent fish from spoiling during long journeys. Today, it has become a local favorite, lingering in memory long after the meal itself has ended. And if you happen to be a devoted admirer of blue cheese, this peculiar specialty may be exactly the challenge you're looking for!

To the northwest of town rises a mountain range famed for its Daoist heritage. For a thousand years, it has drawn Daoists and recluses into its folds—figures who withdrew from the world in pursuit of transcendence and eternal life. It is little wonder the place inspires a sense of longing.
Unlike Western legends of immortality, which often hinge on innate bloodlines or inborn gifts, the Eastern path to ascension sets no such threshold. It places its faith instead in cultivation and insight—one's capacity to grasp the Way.
The Way, in Eastern philosophy, is the most fundamental order of the world itself. To understand it is said to be to transcend the limits of the flesh and gain freedom of life and spirit. In theory, it sounds almost disarmingly simple—no more daunting than an academic examination.
Yet when the writer finally made the trek into the deep mountains and reached a secluded Daoist temple, the reality was far more austere. What appeared there was a community of arcanists living lives of deliberate simplicity. They keep their distance from the secular world, shedding ordinary emotions and desires as a prerequisite for cultivation.
One Daoist offered a single line of verse in parting: "Look down upon the Five Peaks—human life is but a temporary stay." The writer ended their stay yet to uncover any definitive method of immortality. Still, visitors are warmly encouraged to climb to the summit at dawn or dusk. Standing at the heights, gazing out over a rolling sea of clouds, one may not find eternal life, but the quiet clarity of the moment is often enough to set the mind at ease.

The writer arrived on the eve of Dùshuò Festival, the grandest celebration of the year in the East. Lanterns glowed at every doorstep, and it was the red paper cuttings pasted onto glass windows that captured the eye most completely.
This folk-born decorative art is known as paper-cutting. Unlike French silhouettes, which strive to faithfully reproduce real scenes, or Mexican Day of the Dead papel picado, often full of skulls and ritual imagery, Eastern paper-cutting leans instead toward romance and symbolism.
Carp, bats, magpies—animals whose names echo words of good fortune—carry people's hopes for the days ahead. Alongside them appear countless Yāo, spirits that exist only in legend. In local belief, even the most ordinary creatures stand shoulder to shoulder with divine beasts like dragons, arranged by birth year into a rotating roster of guardian spirits. In this way, the "Yāo" achieve an early and rather charming form of equality across all species.

"How I wish I had a real vampire uncle. Mail from the editor can't make those deadbeat writers hand in their manuscripts, but bloody wings and fangs might." If one desires something strongly enough, will they live to see that dream come true?

Some readers believe the story of The Little Mermaid might have originated from Hans Christian Andersen's possible encounter with the Rusalki.
An arcanist was invited into the Wilderness, but after a scarecrow, a living statue, and a fire spirit all rushed to greet them, they quickly turned around and left.

Diggers writes to Ezra asking if he can create a mushroom-based solvent for use in soapmaking. Ezra is excited to take on the challenge.
Noire is invited to an anniversary event for Tally's Electric Theater, but she's still on the fence about going.
An-an Lee gets a special gig from a science museum. They want to showcase the Ghost Catcher 2021k and other gear from the New Science Exorcism Bureau—and the pay is very generous.

Acey talked Melania out of her perfect plan for The Sundog Painting. Now, Melania's hunting for a new "target."
Barbara really hopes the Loch Ness Monster is real so she can interview it in a dream and write a story for UTTU.

APPLe always follows optical theories like the Theory of Systems of Rays when casting his arcane skill. Regulus just ignores all that complicated stuff.

For those who master the art of music, humanity has no shortage of praise.
One especially exaggerated claim goes as follows: When the most skillful musician performs, even phoenixes will land gracefully upon his shoulder.
Fragments of quiet conversation are swallowed by the darkness.
Fortunately, there is still a single candle.
Under its dim glow, the storyteller's face slowly comes into view.
In every way, he is an ordinary young man, the flickering flames reflected in his eyes.
There are far too many humans like him in this world.
Some grow accustomed to lies; others hold loyalty as their creed. At times they prize their own lives above all else. At others, they sacrifice them for reasons unknown to anyone.
"Once upon a time, there was an incredibly gifted guqin player."
"One spring, he sat alone beneath a parasol tree and played a newly composed piece."
"It was his life's proudest work. Only, it lacked a proper ending."
The listener seems unimpressed. Noticing this, the musician clears his throat and unconsciously drops a hand to his side.
A moment later, as if touching something reassuring, he speaks again.
"When the piece ended, the guqin player looked up and saw a birdlike immortal with a human head standing before him."
"'Why do you stop playing?' He asked."
"The guqin player replied, 'This is as much as I've written. I'm not sure how to continue.'"
"'Then allow me to complete it,' the immortal said, 'and together we shall create an unrivaled score, the likes of which the world has never seen.'"
The candlelight is too dim to reveal the listener's face, but the musician does see a finger idly tracing circles on the tabletop.
Another clichéd story. Another tale of a frustrated human yearning for the unreachable, hoping for the day an immortal might lower their gaze upon them.
Perhaps this time will be different.
He places something from his side onto the table and slowly pushes it into the candlelight. It's a [Guqin].
The musician then slides over a small knife.
The listener accepts it absentmindedly, turning it over in his hand. A rather fine guqin maker's knife, with a plain, sharp blade.
The listener taps the top of the table with the knife handle in response.
The blade pauses on the strings.
A soft gasp leaves his lips as he leans in for a closer look.
The strings are no ordinary black silk. Their hue is a pale blue-gray, with a texture resembling feathers. They shine with a faint silvery light in the candle's glow.

"The immortal and the guqin player became fast friends. Admiring his new companion's talent, the immortal stayed in the human world. Using his arcane skill, he altered the bones of the guqin player, along with his fate. From then on, the guqin player's life flowed as smoothly as a stream, and his name spread far and wide."
Altering one's fate through the changing of bones ... The listener straightens up.
He has heard such outlandish rumors before. Perhaps there is some truth behind them after all.
"Here, before your very eyes, are strings fashioned from the feathers of the immortal."
The listener waves for him to continue. A divine bird descended from a mountain, a gifted human, a reshaping of destiny ... It's a good story.
This musician might just be the one he's been looking for, but is he good enough? Can his talent capture the attention of a divine bird?
Under his audience's curious scrutiny, the musician takes a deep breath. This is not the first time he has told the Legend of the Miemeng, and it will likely not be the last.
"The guqin player in that story was my ancestor."
The rain does not stop until nightfall. The dark clouds disperse, and the moon makes its quiet ascent.
In its light, a single drop of dew slides down a slender leaf, inching its way toward the tip.
The Miemeng draws in his wings and lands in a clearing halfway up the mountain.
Last year's fallen leaves are soaked with dew, the new grass beneath yet to grow in. It is as soft as a blanket.
Cross the path, and the [Shabby Hut] is right ahead.
With a lift of his wings, his bone staff floats lightly into the air and taps at the door.
Above the last pitiful dregs of firewood, the musician sprinkles the crushed tea leaves into water drawn from a mountain stream.
"Even though the water only boiled once ..."
The flame in the small clay stove slowly dims. He sighs and places down a pair of ceramic cups he fished out from some corner.
They're charmingly antique. Not of recent make. He fills them with the tea.
A cup is pushed toward the visitor.
The Miemeng does not drink tea, yet still extends a wing to pull the cup closer. On a chilly spring night, the touch of warm water has a way of settling the heart.
"The aroma of this tea seems different from before."
The musician moves the tea set aside and sits down across from Getian.
"Though you live in the mountains, you seem far more familiar with the lands below than I'd expected."
I take little interest in what goes on down below.#I have indeed heard a thing or two.
Getian takes a cautious sniff of the tea before nudging it away.
"I take little interest in what goes on down below."
"But my kin left behind many records. Thus, I have some small knowledge."
Getian cautiously inhales. Fresh, but with a hint of bitterness. Curious.
Perhaps because everyone brews it to their tastes, he thinks.
"The Miemengs ferry news from below, along with the latest tools and techniques."
"I have never ventured there myself, though. I can hardly claim familiarity."
The Miemeng shakes his head and changes the subject.
Following his gaze, the musician looks to the plain guqin at his side and gently presses a hand against the strings.
"There are no materials in the mountains. It will have to wait."
"A lamentable shame. I had hoped to play something for you."
"Pay it no mind. Your bones have healed well. I dare say your departure from this mountain is approaching."
He stares absently at the wavering candlelight.
In the silence, the lonely wick flickers and crackles.
The faint sound startles the musician, returning him from his momentary stupor. He immediately smiles and turns toward Getian.
"I've imposed for too long. Should I stay any longer, I fear I'd be overstepping."

"The mountains are pleasant, but they are not where I belong. When I arrived, the river was still frozen. But spring has likely arrived in the lands below by now, and the flowers along the Peilin River should be in bloom."
"If I leave now and catch the east wind along the river, I might still make it back before summer. Perhaps even in time to ask a woodcutter for a fine piece of parasol wood."
"And what of your search for that legendary score? Will it continue?"
"This candlelight is far too dim. Would you mind brightening it a little?"
He glances at the candle, quickly looks away, and then smiles once more at the Miemeng.
"The score, ah, yes, that was why I came into the mountains."

"The day you saved me, I watched the sky grow darker and darker, heard the howling of wolves surround me. With a broken leg and my instrument clutched in my hand, all I could do was sit beneath a tree."
"Even then, my thoughts were fixed on that legendary score."
"Even if the wolves came to tear me apart, I hoped they'd spare my hands so that I might at least continue to play."
"Oh, how I wished for an [Immortal] to descend from the heavens at that time, like your kin who once gifted my ancestor that score."
"There is no need to name us as such. Miemengs are no different from humans. We, too, will one day fade away."
"But to me, this truly is the blessing of an immortal!"
In the candlelight, the musician spreads his hands. His fingertips and palms are thick with calluses.
"Though I never found the score, these hands were spared. That alone is thanks to you."
The Miemeng gives an uneasy shake of his feathers.
"But now that I think of it, after searching for so long, the score is probably not in the mountains, or perhaps I am simply not destined to find it. Such things can't be forced."
"Besides, I have already met an immortal on this journey, just as my ancestor once did. When I return and compose a new piece, who knows? It might be even greater than that one!"
The Miemeng thinks in silence, his talons lightly tapping the ground.
"You have made up your mind, so be it, but the path is dangerous at night. Come dawn, I will see you down the mountain."
"However, there is still one place amid these peaks that may hold clues about the score. Since you will leave tomorrow, perhaps you might come tonight and see for yourself."
On this early spring night, in which the ice and snow have already melted but new greenery has yet to grow, it is quiet and lonely.
The musician carries his guqin on his back, following Getian along the mountain path toward the [Temple]. From afar, they look like two sprigs of duckweed, drifting in a boundless sea.

The candlelight is barely bright enough to illuminate the ground beneath their feet. Even with the Miemeng leading the way, the musician looks somewhat ragged, the night dew soaking his sleeves as he pushes through the waist-high grass.
When Getian stops once again to wait, the musician speaks up, apologizing.
"You saved my life, for which I'm already deeply grateful, and now I'm causing you even more trouble. It isn't right of me to put you through so much."
"Saving others is but a simple gesture; I never thought to ask anything of you in return. But you shared something with me I never expected. By that logic, it is I who owe you."
The musician ponders for a moment, then taps his head in realization.
"Oh, your kin who once dealt with my ancestor. After all these years, you still remember him. I suppose you were close?"
"You can't mean you were complete strangers?"
The Miemeng gives a slight nod.
Getian extends a wing, brushing aside a clump of white cogon grass blocking the musician's path.
"I am simply curious why he—or rather, they—descended the mountain."
"I have read every word of every record in the temple, yet found nothing of the answer I seek."
The Miemeng tilts his head toward him.
"You come from the lands below. I'd like to hear your answer."
"After you mentioned it last time, I gave it some more thought. To a Miemeng, centuries may pass in the blink of an eye, while the world down below has changed beyond recognition."
"After so many years of retelling, the details of the story are bound to become unclear. What I've shared is all I've heard. As for any further details, I truly don't know."
"Still, from the perspective of those below, what the story describes does make sense."
He pants as he climbs another stretch of steps.
"Humans may differ in temperament and appearance, but in the end, everyone living in this world wants for something. That never changes."
"Some seek power. Some seek wealth. Some seek generational fame. Others seek everlasting glory."
"And, of course, some seek a peerless score."
He can't help but smile, pointing at himself.
"I risked my life climbing the mountain for it. If your kin truly lingered in the human world for the same reason, that would be understandable."
"Of course, this is just the superficial view of a mere mortal such as myself."
"And you, I mean, immortals—do they also have things they seek?"
This time, the Miemeng does not correct his choice of words.
"Very well. Since you've spoken frankly of your own matters, I shall also be truthful with you about my concerns."
The musician lifts his head to look at him. The moonlight casts its silver glow on the Miemeng's face, lost in thought.
Like humans, Miemengs developed different dispositions over the years ...
The last Miemeng to descend the mountain in memory.#The first Miemeng to descend the mountain in memory.
One had a favorite camphor tree. On moonlit nights, Getian would see him standing silently on the highest branch, wings outstretched.
Getian assumed he likely wouldn't leave.
"And others were excessively curious. I knew one who would bring back all manner of human oddities from the lands below—oddities that would enrapture him day and night."
Passing by his dwelling, Getian had thought to himself: sooner or later.
One would bring back all manner of human oddities from the lands below—oddities that would enrapture him day and night.
"And some Miemengs were mischievous and fond of pranks."
One such bird loved to laugh. Getian can't recall his face, only his cackling when he startled his kin by suddenly flying up from below a cliff.
"Later, they all descended the mountain, never to return."
"All I recovered were their bones. Bones that gave me no answers."
"I read of where they went after leaving the mountain, whom they met, and the places they passed. But ..."
The Miemeng hesitates, his feathers trembling slightly.
"I still do not know why they left."
The musician pushes aside a clump of mugwort and takes a deep breath. He smiles at Getian.
"Life in the mountains may be peaceful, but your kin must have longed for something important deep in their hearts. Important enough to give up their longevity."
"Longevity ... For those below the mountain, it is often a pursuit. But to your kind, it's merely a bargaining chip to be exchanged."
"In the lands below, some work to preserve life through any means, no matter how shameful. Yet there are also those willing to sacrifice themselves for something greater."
The musician thinks it over again and again, then shakes his head.
"Well, I am but a human from below. I can't possibly grasp how the Miemengs in the mountains think."
He adjusts the guqin on his back. The instrument is nearly too heavy for him to carry.
Fortunately, the temple is just up ahead.
"So this is the temple of the Miemengs?"
Seeing the lights kindle before him, the musician pauses.
"It seems this place is not quite what you had in mind."
The musician carefully steps around the layers of paper hung like drapes, almost tripping on the scattered scrolls strewn about the ground.
"Well, I must say, this is nothing like anything I've seen before."
He notices a bone beneath the papers and is unable to hold back his question.
"This is ... the remains of your kin?"
The Miemeng steps further into the temple, not looking back.
"Is this a custom of the mountains? Handling them this way feels somewhat irreverent."
The Miemeng's voice comes from ahead.
"They are gone—but flesh and bone. Why fuss over it?"
His voice pauses, tinged with curiosity.
"Your concern tells me it is different in the lands below. How does your kind treat the dead?"
"Well, we also have temples. In them, we gather the remains of the deceased, assess their deeds in life, and enshrine them."
The musician freezes again, unsure of how to answer.
"How do we assess deeds? By whether they benefited others or whether they served only their own aspirations ..."
"But can anyone but oneself truly know the nature of one's aspirations? How could others possibly judge such a thing?"
On such a night, in such a place, the Miemeng's voice sounds eerily calm, echoing as if both near and far.
"This is precisely what troubles me. By your account, those who descended the mountain must have chosen to pursue their own aspirations."
"But how were they to confirm the purpose of their lives? On what basis?"
"Basis? Now I really don't understand what you mean."
Getian walks back a few steps, gesturing for his companion to look in his direction.
"On the way here, I told you of three of my kin."
There's a scattered pile of bones.
The Miemeng gazes at them in thought.
"Remarkable aspirations indeed. Nothing like those of ordinary mortals."
"Perhaps. But now, that is all but a moment from the past, and they have returned here, silent and still."
"If they had foreseen such an ending, would they still have made the same choice?"
"You said you were willing to die for a score. To me, that notion is no different from that of my kin. I am curious how you came to your choice."
"To give everything for one's purpose in life is indeed a difficult thing to choose. And yet, to have the choice itself may be a blessing."
"In the mortal world, countless people live without freedom of choice."
As he gives this vague reply, his gaze drifts absently out the window. The moon has begun to sink westward, and the sky has shifted from a shade of deep inky black to dark blue.
Dawn is still some time away.
He withdraws his gaze, clears his throat, and changes the subject.
"How are we to find clues about the score among all these scrolls and bones? I can't imagine we'll come up with much of anything."
"There's no need to worry. Just play something."
"Please. Your ancestor bonded with the Miemeng through music. If any clues remain here, they will respond."
A mountain wind blows into the temple, causing the hanging papers to rustle.
The musician reaches out to hold down a scroll that is almost blown away, offering an apologetic smile to his friend.
"I'm afraid the damage my instrument suffered in the mountains hasn't been repaired yet."
The Miemeng thinks for a moment.
"I believe that can be resolved. I do not know what your instrument is made of, but whatever you need ought to be here in the temple."
The gentle smile on his face slowly fades.

The Miemeng lowers his head, studying the musician's eyes. The wind flickers the candlelight, casting the musician's face in shifting shadows.
After a moment, he lowers his head and sighs.
Getian's gaze falls on the musician's guqin.
"Perhaps my arcane skill can be of help."
His lips move, but in the end, he only lets out another sigh.
"I appreciate it, but there's no need. I know how to repair a guqin."
He unfastens the guqin and throws it to the ground. It lands with a heavy thud.
"Please believe me, I have no ill intent."
In the dim light, the musician's hands clench, then loosen.
"I'm not descended from any great master. I am simply the son of a guqin maker. My family made a living this way for generations."
At times, the musician recalls the desolate gate of his hometown, the scent of bamboo leaves and parasol wood, and similar memories that scatter away like wood shavings.
Under the shaded eaves, his father once told him the tale of their ancestor meeting a divine bird.
And so, he said he wished to learn how to play the guqin.
His father laughed, then gently stroked his hair. He did indeed have hands suited for the strings.
Back then, they called him Little Phoenix, and he was doted on like a beloved princeling.
But his father left far too early. All that truly remained for him were a few absurd stories, ambitions with no clear direction, and a parasol guqin missing its strings.
"As you can see, I can't really play the instrument. Not properly."
"I know the materials of the strings and soundboard well enough, but I never had the chance to spend much time learning to use them."
The young fraud took stock of all he owned: the story was well-prepared, and the parasol was a rare piece of fine wood.
"All that was missing was a miracle people could believe in."
The musician found a western merchant who sold arcane materials and discovered that miracles were cheaper than he'd thought: fireproof cloth, the mane of a divine steed, and silk as tough as jade.
And the guqin was complete, one so beautiful it almost looked as if it were really made from a divine bird's tail feathers.
"I left the village like that, with the guqin slung over my shoulder and the maker's knife my father left me strapped to my waist."
The Miemeng is a little surprised but does not interrupt.
There are always people willing to pay a hefty price to glorify their households with stirring legends.
So the story was retold from his lips a thousand times, polished into something extraordinary and complete.
And yet, that instrument has remained forever silent.
An immortal's blessing, a peerless score, a prodigious young musician.
Nights filled with hesitation, a childhood like a drifting tumbleweed, worries tangled and knotted like rope.
A story that charges onward or a real life—the musician can only have one of them.
On many nights, he dreams of the past. When he wakes, phantom strings tremble softly, sadly, beside his pillow. A reminder that they are still waiting.
Perhaps one day, he will finally give in, reach out, and touch those strings that do not truly belong to him.
"Sometimes I think how wonderful it would be if divine birds truly existed. If I really were a man favored by an immortal ..."
Getian lowers his gaze slightly. Birds that can change a person's fate do indeed exist. Yet, for a Miemeng, this is a melody that can only be played and cherished once.
"Then, someone actually believed the story. They forced me to climb the mountain and find a Miemeng for them."
"When I first met you, I saw in your bones that you were hiding something. Now it is clear."
"I don't know. I—I didn't want it to be like this, but I had no other choice."
"I never truly harbored any malicious intent."
The Miemeng lowers his head to meet his gaze. The musician's voice grows quieter.
"I was conflicted. I know not to repay kindness with betrayal, which is why I asked to go down the mountain."
"I was afraid that if I stayed any longer, I'd begin having thoughts I shouldn't have."
"Please, let me go down the mountain. I won't come back, and I won't tell a soul that I ever met you."
At last, the Miemeng calmly looks away.
"In the end, you never truly acted on your falsehood."
"Those below the mountain are all much the same—tossed about, uncertain. There is little that is fixed. I saw how you would choose."
"Besides, what you just spoke of was not entirely fabrication. Although, perhaps, you did not realize it."
He lays his wings over the body of the guqin, falls silent for a moment, and begins another story.
"Long ago, there truly was such a Miemeng ..."
A wisp of pale smoke slowly rises.

In a time long ago, so long that his kin still lived on the frontier, human cities had yet to appear in the central plains, and powerful humans and arcanists still walked the world, not yet reduced to legend.
The Getians—the Miemeng clan—created [The First Song and Dance].
From that point on, countless Miemengs bore the gift of music.
Among them, there was one who was especially intoxicated by rhythm.
"He lost himself in the music, rarely associating with his kin."
"Time in the mountains is long and without seasons. I could not tell when he left."

"For such a lifespan as his, a thousand years and a single moment were nigh on the same."
The thought startles the bird. He turns his head and flutters his feathers a few times, as if to brush it away.

"In any case, that Miemeng's dedication to music was only natural."
"Until one day, convinced he had learned every score the mountain could offer, he ventured down alone to see whether human music held any worth."
A human life spans barely a hundred years. Strip away the days of ignorant youth and helpless old age, and what remains is only a few fleeting decades.
Within that time, one must still endure the difficulties of worldly affairs and endless hardships. A struggle simply to survive.
Time that can truly be devoted to oneself is scarce.
Even if one pours their entire life into music, it can never be compared to the Miemengs with their incredible lifespan.
"That is what life down below is like. As the seasons press on, life only grows harder."
The Miemeng pauses, as if gathering his thoughts.
"He went to many places and saw all manner of people."
Two masters of the age agreed on a musical duel on the city walls with their pipas, drawing a great crowd.
The sound was earth-shattering and sky-rending, indeed. Yet the Miemeng remained bored, believing that something was still missing.
Amid the rush of dignitaries and the drawing of curtains, the tinkling of crystal and pearls filled the air.

On a rooftop not far away, the Miemeng watched with a tilted head. A man in a tall crown rose from his seat, bowed deeply, then lifted his head and played the guqin. Less a song than a soliloquy of grievances.
When the melody properly began, an uproar broke out among the guests. Someone drew a sword. Another turned away with a weary sigh.
Before the turmoil reached him, he turned and left. This was the poise of scholars, not the devotion of a musician.
"... And households where music was passed down through both instrument and song."
The Miemeng recalled a towering courtyard tree, an arm's span thick, much like the one near his mountain dwelling.

The Miemeng heard the owner's faint sigh. What a pity. So brief, after all.
He thought, if heaven had granted her thirty more years, perhaps things would have been different.
"And at first light, he left that verdant courtyard behind."

"You mean, he never altered a human's bones?"
"Of course. Immortals have their own affairs. Why would they concern themselves with the lives of mortals?"

The next morning, beneath a parasol tree, the Miemeng met a young man in passing and heard a short tune he had never heard before.
The melody was free and wild, hardly a proper composition, yet it brought tears to his eyes.
Unable to resist, the Miemeng stepped forward to speak with him. The youth humbly said he had no talent for music and that he simply enjoyed plucking the strings for amusement during idle moments.
"He asked the young man's background and learned that he was just a local guqin maker."
He repeats it twice under his breath, then suddenly stands up.

"Because it was just a simple tune, utterly unremarkable."
Utterly unremarkable—the Miemeng couldn't help but drink in the phrase himself. What moved him was, in fact, something utterly unremarkable.
"There was no earthshaking event that followed. The young man who played the guqin was destined to die young, and so the Miemeng merely wished him a good life."
"And all his desires came true. That was all."

Getian gives no immediate answer. Instead, he lifts a wing slightly, and the broken guqin—once treasured, now tossed away—floats into the air.

The dust is wiped away, and it is turned over, as if by an unseen hand, revealing the instrument's goose feet on the underside. Neither metal nor jade, they are made of some material that gleams with a soft luster in the candlelight.
The Miemeng left his remains to his friend, who fashioned them into a guqin.
In the candlelight, the musician's expression flicks and shifts. After a long moment, he speaks again.
"I understand now. You mean to say there's no need to strive for absolute perfection, so long as our hearts are sincere!"
Getian looks at him quietly, neither confirming nor denying it.
"The truth is clear to me now. The music my ancestor could play, I can play too!"
"If that's the case, then could I stay in the mountains?"
"Life below is noisy, cluttered, and distracting. I know where I went wrong now. I just want to find a quiet place to devote myself to my instrument, as I did when I was young."
"You came from the lands below, and in the end, that is where you belong."
He takes a step back, seemingly in a daze. After a moment, he gathers the courage to speak again.
"But, after I leave the mountain, will fortune ever bring me to you again?"
"As you can see, the path of the Miemengs was cut off centuries ago."
"They left one after another, and now ..."
"I am the last of my kind, and there is nothing down below that draws my interest, perhaps."
"There is nothing down below that draws my interest."
"Yet my kin from the story had no thought of descending the mountain either."
"As time passes, perhaps my thoughts will change."
They look at each other, silent for a time.
Only now does everything finally become clear: there was never any great musician, no score unheard by the world, and no ideal worth dying for.
The young man, who stubbornly chased such ideals to this place, is only a petty fraud, though a harmless one at that.
Dawn is about to break. The extinguished candle gives off a faint trail of bluish smoke.
"It is time for you to go."
A cool drop of dew falls onto the musician's forehead, jolting him awake.

"Could it be that it was all just a dream?"

"I've heard of a place nearby called Pei City, beyond royal authority, where both arcanists and humans live."
"From now on, I'll continue to study this instrument."

He lets out an almost imperceptible sigh. Left with no answer, he uses his imagination instead:
Many, many years ago, on a spring night, a Miemeng quietly descended the mountain, with no word to his kin.
He traversed mountains that seemed endless.
Crossed rivers that zigzagged and intertwined.
Passed human villages, from which came the barks of dogs and the crows of roosters.
Like the divine birds of legend, he flew ninety-nine thousand miles.
Yet he flew higher than the mountains where immortals dwell and farther than the crimson clouds that topped the peaks. Even the heaviest dew could not dampen his wings.
Only when the sky darkened did he stop to rest on an ordinary parasol tree.
The forests, the fields, the mountains and rivers—the entire world was fast asleep.
Getian ponders: What, exactly, tempted him to stay?
"No. Surely not for some mortal joy."
As if answering himself, he immediately denies it again.
"No. Not even for that piece, or the one who played it."

He looks down to the world below the mountain. The morning mist has not yet fully dispersed, but the silken trail of the Peilin River can already be seen glinting in the sunlight as it flows into the distance, toward unfamiliar towns, villages, lakes, and plains.
Separated by a thin veil of mountain mist, life unfolds: some are born, some die; some laugh, some weep.
Like morning dew, with more days gone than to come.
"Perhaps that is precisely why it is worth cherishing."
The thought stirs his heart, beautiful and unforgettable.
After a long while, the Miemeng places the long-silent guqin before him once more.

The musician suddenly springs to his feet and looks toward the mountains.

He clicks his tongue in annoyance and rows hard, steadying the boat.
"You must be hearin' things. The Peilin River's runnin' high today. Can't hear nothin' but the water itself."
The musician does not reply, his gaze fixed on the mountains. A moment later, he suddenly points ahead and shouts excitedly—
"No, sir, someone really is playing a guqin! Look to the bank over there. Even the birds have taken flight!"
The boatman cranes his neck to peer into the distance, then sighs.
"The sun's out, 'course the birds are lookin' for food. What's so strange about that?"
"How loud could one person's playin' be, anyhow? You think it'd reach this far? And only you'd hear it?"
The words slip out of him.
The boatman cannot fathom what strange spell has come over this young fellow he picked up on a whim.
"Ain't no immortals in this world. 'Less you've seen one with yer own eyes?"
He opens his mouth, then sinks back down, defeated. He lowers his gaze to the shimmering surface of the Peilin River.
"It's nothing. I must have imagined it."
The boatman clicks his tongue again.
"All this silly chatter. Just tell me where yer headed."
"I want to go to Pei City."
"Pei City? An' where's that? I've been rowin' for more than thirty years and never heard of the place."
The Miemeng lays his wings over the strings and remains silent for a long time.
Finally, he puts the guqin away.
The Miemeng continues awaiting an answer.
It will be another spring, another winter's night, another utterly ordinary day.
Somewhere else, he will hear another song and stop for it. There, he will find the answer he seeks.
One day, he will encounter it.
And yet, this is no illusion.
A cool breeze brushes past the Miemeng's wings and over the faintly vibrating strings.
It is another very, very ordinary tune, hesitantly played for the first time.

An aged guqin, covered in fine cracks. The lacquer is old, but under the light it holds a shine that can only come from years spent in careful hands.
Its strings tremble faintly, as if an unfinished melody still breathes within them.

A plain, low thatched hut, with a few slabs of bluestone weighing down the ridges of its roof.
It belongs to one of Getian's kin, who descended the mountain before the two ever met, never to return.
Now it has been made the home of a human musician who wandered into the mountain by chance.

To humans, the Miemeng might as well be immortals.
Arcanists with human faces and bird bodies, they dwell deep in mountains no ordinary mortal can reach, blessed with long lives.
Yet what truly awes and tempts is their ability to alter one's bones, and with it, one's fate.

Records of the Miemeng clan's history since their arrival in the central plains are kept in the Temple of Getian.
If an archived copy of the lost score still exists somewhere on the mountain, it may well be there.

The music of the Getian comprises eight songs:
Carry the People, The Swallow, Nourish the Green, Raise the Five Grains, Honor the Way, Exalt the Divine, Trust the Earth's Virtue, and Bring All Things to Fullness.

A white jade sword, broken and no longer holding arcane power, yet still carefully preserved. It once represented a lineage, a sacred duty, a school of Daoists, and a path to immortality. According to the interviewee, its primary function now is cutting various treats.

Vivid, delicate patterns created by folding and cutting red paper. During New Year celebrations in the East, these are used to decorate doors and windows, adding festive cheer. The creator clearly favors Mei blossom designs—likely because their trees grew near her childhood home.

A common porcelain bowl from the old days. Plain and durable, it was made for holding food and water. The interviewee was lucky to keep one. It's not sold as an antique but treasured as a keeper of memories.

One dignitary summoned alchemists one after another to his inner chamber, each excelling in refining cinnabar, mercury, and gold, and possessing unique insights into spirits. Another dignitary dispatched vast fleets across the boundless sea in search of immortals, in hopes of enduring forever like the stone monuments inscribed with great achievements.
Death declared their failure.
The third and fourth dignitaries learned from their predecessors and proceeded with utmost caution, while the fifth fell back into old habits and met a grim end. The sixth conducted everything in secret, and the seventh and eighth now wait in line ... It seems absurd, but if such a thing did exist, who would refuse a perfect elixir? Who wouldn't choose to ascend to immortality?
"So ... we must cultivate ourselves without a single day's rest?"
"As I have said ..."
"... the Method of Longevity does not free one from worldly troubles."
"Indeed."
"On the contrary, it may bring more troubles ... and other burdens."
"They will grow with time."
"Like loneliness."
"Yes, like loneliness."
"I understand ..."
"Are you still willing to study the Practice of Inner Alchemy and take on the duty of subduing the Beast?"
A brief silence.
"I am."
Somewhere, in some quiet corner, someone gave this answer.
The Mei Flowers Blossom as Always

There's a Mei tree on a mountain in Zhu County said to be planted by the White Horse Immortal's own hand. The tree has stood tall for over a hundred years, and thus, as legend dictates, the locals call it the Mei Tree of Longevity. When I studied in Huanzhou as a youth, I often wandered that mountain. That Mei tree was the quiet listener of many of my joys and sorrows. Sixty years later, I retired from office and returned from the capital. It was a clear day in late spring. The rapeseed had just ripened, the wheat was sprouting new shoots, the world had turned quiet. I saw only a young Daoist. Too old and too decrepit to climb the mountain, I asked, "Does the Mei Tree of Longevity still stand?" She replied, "The tree remains as ever. But you've come too late—this year's blossoms have already fallen." I sighed. "The Mei flowers blossom as always, but the people below only fade away." Then I told her my story. The Daoist seemed lost in thought. She said, "I too haven't seen the Mei Tree of Longevity bloom for many years. Perhaps our meeting—or lack thereof—was written in fate. So, since we've met, allow me to show you something." She cut paper into the shape of Mei branches and blew them to the ground. In an instant, the branches sprouted, Mei blossoms covered the sky, and their fragrance filled the air. Seeing their beauty in full bloom, I remembered looking upon the Mei tree, and tears streamed down my face. By the time I had composed myself to thank her, she was gone. Only their sweet smell remained on my hands. —Stories from Huanzhou Volume 7 Casual Note: Now it's called "that Mei tree in the central park!" Who knew they'd build a park there? Carefully Written Note: That's just what people call it on the BBS. You can't assume that's its official name. Casual Note: Fine, you're right. But it's still the same tree.

Pandora Wilson: According to our records, you're traveling to find a way to recover your five senses.
Paper Heron: That's how it started, yes. But I've found that simply wandering the lands is interesting in itself.
Pandora Wilson: Have you found an answer yet?
Paper Heron: Perhaps.
Pandora Wilson: Perhaps?
Paper Heron: The Way has no form. Who can know what my answer looks like or where it will appear?
Paper Heron: Perhaps it's a flower, a leaf, a passing arcanist, or the pastries she just baked.
Paper Heron: Or perhaps ... a piece of paper?
Pandora Wilson: I'd appreciate if you didn't look at my notepad like that, Ms. Paper Heron. I'm well aware of your fondness for paper-cutting.
Paper Heron: Haha. Just joking. Don't worry—we don't use white paper for paper-cutting. Wouldn't want to break tradition, eh?
Pandora Wilson: Good to know. Now, to the next question: Would you consider using modern modes of transportation for your travels?
Paper Heron: Of course! I'm quite curious about them.
Pandora Wilson: But we recently learned from another interviewee that you plan to ride your mule all the way to Antarctica.
Paper Heron: Ahem ... They told me bringing a mule on a plane requires mountains of paperwork ... That's far too complicated.
Paper Heron: And I can't just leave the fellow behind, can I?
Paper Heron: It's not as though we're in a hurry, anyway. I say it's the best method.

A roughly 5.5-foot-long blade with a handle of 1 foot and 6 inches. Weighs in at around 3.3 pounds, but it can be used to dole justice with much greater weight than that. The interviewee inherited it from his father. Thanks to his careful daily maintenance with deerskin and sheep oil, the blade still shines like snow.

Forged from refined steel, the armor resembles goose feathers and can separate piece by piece under the interviewee's arcane skill. When spread, they become weapons; when closed, they provide strong protection. The surface bears many scratches. The interviewee can clearly recount the stories behind the deeper ones.

The interviewee's hometown is famous for inkstones made from locally quarried stone. Each child receives one when they begin their studies. These inkstones are finely made, with smooth surfaces and minute pores. No matter how long they're used, the ink never stains them black.

In Huanzhou, there's an old tradition called the "one-year-old catch." When a baby turns one, the family elders spread objects across a bed: fruits and vegetables, gold and silver trinkets, a bow and a sword, a needle and thread, scales, and a ruler. Then they place the child before these items. This is considered a form of fortune-telling—whatever the baby grabs first reveals their future path. Naturally, the parents each have their hopes. Rich families wish for their child to reach for a silver ingot. Scholarly families hope for the scholar's tools. Of course, the children often surprise them. Cheng Heguang, however, lived up to expectations. The moment he was placed down, he grabbed the sheathed blade—a clear sign he would carry on the family tradition and pursue a military career.

As the child of a military official, Cheng Heguang had a clear and steady path laid out before him. In his youth, he would study classical literature, ethics and morality, archery and horsemanship, and military strategy. Later, he would take the military examination, which in recent years had become an important criterion for promotion among military officials. He would compete in trials of martial skills and write strategic essays. He would pass the exam and be ready to enter the bureaucratic system where, with luck, he might catch the eye of a high-ranking official and rise to the top. Naturally, he would one day inherit his father's position and bring glory to his family name.

His kin, subordinates, neighbors—countless people promised him this bright future. But as he grew older, he began to yearn for a different path: just him and his white horse, traveling wherever the road took them.

At 10:13 a.m. on the 7th, a violent criminal incident occurred on South Road in our city. Two masked criminals armed with knives broke into the Lucky Star convenience store, snatched a customer's handbag, and threatened the storekeeper to hand over the cash from the register. According to reports, a concerned citizen, Mr. Cheng, was perusing the soy sauce on a nearby shelf at the time. Upon seeing the assault, he struck the offenders on the head with several iron eggs. Both criminals immediately collapsed unconscious. Mr. Cheng restrained them with iron wire and handed them over to police who arrived at the scene shortly after. Several customers in the store were left frightened, but fortunately uninjured.

Afterwards, though the storekeeper refused to accept payment, Mr. Cheng insisted on paying for the soy sauce, eggs, wire, and a half-empty bag of noodles. He said, "The eggs will be fine for eating before long. I plan to make braised bass tonight. Stir-fried noodles with eggs will make for an excellent side dish."

Recently, the police and several customers presented Mr. Cheng with a banner inscribed with "Hero in Action, Justice Upheld" in recognition of his bravery. In front of the camera, Mr. Cheng shared some anti-theft tips with our reporter: store grain and money in a cellar; install broken tiles and porcelain shards on top of walls; have neighbors take turns keeping night watch; and keep a gong ready to sound the alarm.

"Of course, you should call the police immediately," he added.

Pandora Wilson: Sorry to keep you waiting. They said you arrived an hour ago. Oh, you're still wearing traditional Eastern clothing.
Cheng Heguang: Yes. I'm more comfortable with the fabrics and cut.
Pandora Wilson: Our records show you were born four hundred years ago. How would someone from that era judge our time? Is this the best of times, or the worst of times?
Cheng Heguang: I am still growing used to things here, so it's hard to say. Everything is so different from Huanzhou.
Cheng Heguang: Suits, skyscrapers, the internet, houses on four wheels, black boxes that capture your image.
Cheng Heguang: There's so much to learn—including an entirely new language.
Pandora Wilson: Your English is very good.
Cheng Heguang: Thank you. There are people from my hometown in the Foundation. We practice English together when time allows.
Pandora Wilson: You've mentioned many ways modern society differs from the past. But I'm curious—after all these centuries, what things remain familiar to you?
Cheng Heguang: Times change, traditions shift, but some things are constant.
Cheng Heguang: On the BBS, there are people from all over the world. While some comments are nasty, many more are genuinely helpful and honest.
Cheng Heguang: Virtue hasn't disappeared. Neither has my commitment to justice.
Cheng Heguang: That is why I live a disciplined life, rising at dawn to sweep the floors and resting at dusk after properly locking the doors.
Cheng Heguang: Some of the others in the Suitcase have heard tell of my routine, which has led to some strange looks ... I'm not certain why.

Afflatus: Writings of a Reed [Plant] Traveling Editor

The notebook cover, woven from reed leaves, was made of materials taken from the interviewee herself. The fallen leaves represent time that has passed. The newly written words represent experiences gained. Together, the interviewee believes, they form the simplest and most direct expression of "life."

The interviewee often carries multiple shoulder bags. The small ones are issued by UTTU, while the larger ones were left behind by a previous Reed. Records show one particular Reed had a deep interest in collecting fashion items, even taking out an advance on next year's salary in order to buy this bag. But every Reed since has agreed: all the bags aside from this one are useless.

One of the office supplies UTTU provides to employees, available for pickup on the first Wednesday of each month with a work ID. The interviewee uses them to organize her notes in a color-coding system. However, since each Reed has different color preferences, the system appears totally random.

In the beginning, people tied knots to record events. Grand events became large knots; small moments, small knots. Memories of all kinds became knots of different colors, materials, and sizes. When elders reached the end of their lives, they could touch the knots along the cord to remember those distant times. As the ages passed, writing emerged. People carved triangular, circular, and square symbols, preserving their stories on clay tablets, wood and stone, bamboo slips, turtle shells, and seashells—tools to fight against what is forgotten in death. Paper appeared much later still. Clever hands pressed papyrus into thin, yellow sheets, and stories began to travel with caravans and ships to distant lands.

In Reed's homeland, the craft of papermaking is equally ancient. People there cut down bamboo and hemp, then soak, pound, and boil them ... Through many processes, the plants are transformed into paper as white as snow. Reed blades can also be made into paper. The first Reed was born surrounded by ink. Her instinct to record drives her to travel, to experience, and to write down stories. Spoken words scatter in the wind, but pages covered in writing only rustle and flutter.

"Once recorded, stories endure."

After hundreds of years of wandering, Reed returned to the homeland she had long left behind. The other passengers on her flight were surprised and somewhat lost. They said everything looked completely different from what they remembered. Reed put away "her" old records and turned to a new page, ready to write a new story.

March 29th Excerpt from a daily newspaper's "Letters from Readers" section: I spent my childhood in the countryside and often visited a mysterious witch who lived north of the manor there. She was a young, elegant lady who lived alone in a small cabin at the center of the forest. She was skilled in arcanum and would give me delicious candies and apple pies. I left to attend middle school, only returning forty years later to find her completely unchanged—not a day older! While I had become an old man. I couldn't help but ask her the secret—curious readers may call the following number: ... Could this be the immortal witch of legend? March 30th I dialed the number and met with a well-dressed guy within 24 hours. He tried to sell me an arcane cream that supposedly preserves youth. But I'm a tuft of reed! I explained this to him, and he quickly lost interest and left. It was all just a creative advertisement! ... May 2nd I met a weird group of people during my fieldwork today. They claimed to possess a method for reviving the dead and invited me to join them in prayer. Revival? Sounds pretty similar to what happens to me—wait! If the previous Reed could be revived, wouldn't that count as immortality? This is totally worth a try! May 3rd A staff member stopped me and explained the situation: it's a psychological support program for survivors. Well, the world's a big place. Somewhere out there, real immortality must exist!

Reed: Ms. Editor-in-Chief! Nice to meet you—well, nice for "this" me to meet you!
Reed: The records say, "New hires must attend a one-hour private meeting with the editor-in-chief to learn about UTTU's operations and job responsibilities."
Pandora Wilson: That's a regulation from long ago. Please relax—this is just a casual chat.
Reed: Oh! Then let me update my notes right away! Ahem ... Obsolete policy ... Already an "old" employee ...
Pandora Wilson: I assume you've absorbed all the previous Reeds' records?
Reed: Oh, those records have massively multiplied in recent years. It'll take me a while to process it all.
Reed: But I already know how to access UTTU's network, how to file expense reports, the previous Reed's favorite outdoor clothing brand, and a super long list of recommended travel destinations!
Reed: And one more thing! My body's way better at drawing nutrients from liquids than any solid food.
Pandora Wilson: Not just for nutrients. Last year you requested a half-month salary advance to purchase sparkling water.
Pandora Wilson: We've placed a case of it in your room, along with some other beverages.
Reed: Ha! I tried them all the second I woke up!
Reed: The sparkling water's a little harsh for my taste. I prefer green tea—it reminds me of the warm morning sunlight.
Reed: 'Cause even though we're born from the same roots, each Reed has her own unique preferences.
Reed: I can't wait to find out what else makes me different!

An item that I still struggle to define. Is it a spool wound with threads of five-colored glass? A secret treasure for raising ice silkworms? The wisp of cold, fragrant smoke it emits only deepens the mystery. Its owner warned the writer to keep her distance—certain Yao are drawn to the scent, but they crave the teeth of the ignorant even more.

The swaying beaded fabric cannot fully conceal the interviewee's figure—such a sparse veil isn't meant to hide her face from others but to ward off those butterfly-like spirits.
Sensing the writer's gaze as she said this, the interviewee smiled behind the veil. "No, not the one on my head. I wove that one myself."

As it flutters and sways, the delicate butterfly form gives an air of harmlessness. Few can see that what glimmers between those pearl-adorned wings are needles sharp enough to kill with a single strike.

A hat given to the interviewee by her master. The brim is woven with small armor plates, while the tassels around the edge are strung with yansheng coins to keep them from obstructing the wearer's view.
"The coins were my master's gift too. It's said they ward off evil and bring good fortune. Whether that's true or not, the blessing offered by my master certainly is."

An ancient silver-and-jade longevity lock pendant with a tiger carved into its surface. It has been with its owner for over a decade. The interviewee says she's stayed healthy and escaped danger countless times thanks to it. Perhaps the writer should consider wearing such a talisman herself.

A standard government-issue ring-pommel saber. As a government-issued blade, it is unremarkable. Yet as a symbol of the highest supervisory authority of its era, it has weathered countless storms.
The sheath is engraved with the names of its seven successive owners.

A silver flute that produces an even clearer, brighter tone than most. Its birdlike notes can pierce through dense forests and carry to the far side of mountains, drawing distant songs in response.
However, when the writer asked if she might sing a few impromptu lines, the interviewee grew noticeably reluctant. Rumor has it that her singing voice was so dreadful it once silenced the crying children of her clan at night.

Ding, ding—the clinking of silver provides the perfect percussion for dance. When dancing around the fire, the interviewee adorns herself with every piece of silver jewelry she owns.
When the writer asked about their weight, their true meaning was unexpectedly revealed: they symbolize her parents' love.

Shadows specially shaped to resemble her clan's brocade patterns. They blend seamlessly into the interviewee's clothing like natural embroidery.
The interviewee proudly demonstrated a series of creative shadow designs: "Clever, isn't it? I can turn plain clothes fancy and old clothes new—something different to wear every day!"

The lamp's glow is faint, barely illuminating the ground beyond two or three meters—dimmer even than a cheap kerosene lamp.
The interviewee often peers into it. When the writer asked what he could see inside, he replied, "Other people's curious expressions."

A walking stick named "Truth." It supports not the body, but the soul. Perhaps "Experience" would be a more fitting name.
On his long spiritual journey, all he can rely upon is experience—his own, his predecessors', and theirs before them.

A sacred cloak that separates its wearer from the secular world.
The interviewee reveals not a trace of skin below the neck. Perhaps this deprivation of touch and physical feeling is also a form of practice.

Inlaid with pearls, adorned with enamel pendants, covered in gold curved into graceful shapes—the theme is unmistakable. Spring arrives, flowers blossom, have the swallows returned?
Beauty always comes at a price, but an experienced dancer carries the weight effortlessly.

The immortal brings flowing ribbons, dotting the spring waters that mirror mountains.
In Eastern dance, ribbons and sleeves often serve as extensions of the dancer's body. A skilled dancer can move the soft fabrics as if they were additional arms. The interviewee had already perfected this art by the age of eleven.

Tender willow branches extend from the dancer's sleeve. Unlike her usual somber style, the sprouting green vibrates with life.
Verdant leaves of yesterday remain, and endless layers grow anew.

A rarely seen wooden wheelchair, born from a thousand years of Mohist craftsmanship. It responds to the faintest movement, as though it were a part of the rider's own body, and is fully equipped with a flying crossbow and silk lantern.
There are rumors that 108 mechanisms are hidden within—enough for one man to become an army and slay his enemies in an instant. Hearing this, the interviewee simply laughed and wheeled away.

Most of the time, the blades stay hidden in her sleeves, others only ever noticing the delicate silver cufflinks. But if someone underestimates her because of her frail appearance, streaks of cold light will show them just how wrong they were.

A common wooden tablet, its back painted with green lacquer and its front inscribed with the ten commandments she has always upheld.
The writer once asked about its value. Her reply was this: "Put it on a scale and it won't weigh much. Put it in your heart, and it's worth a thousand gold pieces."

A horse-face mask, its eyes wide with fury. It is said that the interviewee can borrow the power of the underworld messengers through it to suppress evil spirits. A long strip of cloth hangs from its mouth like a tongue. Some might see it and think of tales about hanged ghosts.
"A tongue?! No, it's just some talisman paper. Here, look—hey, don't go!"

A wooden sword, twisted from absorbing too much malice during a certain incident. From a distance, it looks like a rigid tentacle coiled around the interviewee's arm. The dark stains have seeped deep into the wood.

Bronze bells of all sizes, strung together at random to ward off evil spirits. Around the outside, a loop of hastily written yellow talismans serves to calm the soul during traditional arcane rituals.
"The two aren't contradictory, of course. I need to make sure it doesn't harm me."

When the first omen fell, she received a revelation.
Some distant, indistinct prophecy delivered through the morning sun, on glistening dew, and in a sharp sting between her toes. The dancer must perform an endless dance, never ceasing even should her feet run red with blood—not until the gods answer, not until fate reveals another fortunate omen.
But not every dancer is fortunate enough to receive an answer. She plunged herself into merciless training, imagining herself as a die in the most torturous times, wavering between giving up in one moment and eagerly hoping for a response in the next. She continued, suffering through the temptation of rest, tormented by the space between total triumph and utter failure. And then came a knock.
"Charlotte, are you alright?"
This was the inevitable interruption every immersed player must unfortunately face: concern from loved ones. Fortunately, just as she prepared to abandon the ritual and respond, fate cast a second lucky die her way.

"The great Paladin Erick defeated the red dragon today!"
In the tavern's corner, a dwarf straightens up proudly and begins her story.
"I charged straight into that dragon's lair and fought it for three straight days and nights! The beast even swallowed me whole at one point! But could that stop the great Erick? Oh, no-siree! I hacked away at its guts with my axe until it howled for mercy and spat me out again! Haha! Yet another triumph!"
"Of course, the dragon spent the rest of the day grumbling and rubbing his aching belly. Though I do have to give the brute one thing, it has real taste—especially in mead. I brought a few flagons back. Anyone care for a taste?"
"Making it up? Every word is true, I swear it on my paladin's oath—which is unbreakable, by the way! Huh? Why didn't I bring out any gold, you ask? Well, later, we ran into some ghosts ..."

Even in space, the scarecrow has found work.
He stays at the circus to shoo away the rats that come to steal food—most of them hitchhikers on human spaceships. The rats don't care where the ships take them. They only know there's the delicious scent of cheese coming from the storage room.
At first, the rats were easily spooked, and the scarecrow had no trouble scaring them off. But over time, they grew bold and began raiding the cheese stores without a care—until the trapeze girl spotted their operation.
Soon after, the circus added a new performance: The Rat Pack's Cheese Heist.
She still knows who she is, even after all this time.
Lanterns glow in every home as families gather for the holiday, and all she has is a small boat.
Swift as a sparrow, proud as a swan.
Breaking Free from a Burning Cage
Only with the light from the burning cage could he see the sky beyond.
Recording the distant past in the fleeting present.
Beneath the woven butterflies lies a bloody past and a debt unpaid.

Dusk falls. The loom clicks steadily.
Twilight spills into the room, illuminating the silk on the loom. In an instant, brilliant colors shimmer across the fabric.
"You're here. Why cower in the shadows?" She speaks to the empty room, inviting her guests from the dark.
"Have you heard of the Five-Colored Glazed Cocoon?" She smiles. "The world knows its beauty. People pay fortunes to weave it into embroidery and robes—such a waste. They see only the splendor on the surface, never realizing its true power. Once bloodied and honed, it can cut through anything with ease."
Her fingers twist. The thread snaps taut. Countless black figures plummet from the beams, throats slashed. Silver needles pierce their hearts, killing them in an instant. The thread, now drunk on blood, shines with a glassy gleam.
She lifts the thread again, lost in memory. No matter what it takes, she will use the White Horse School's sword technique manual to sever all threads of resentment. This place will be free of troubles at last.
The moonlight glimmering on her blade, she leaps off the roof, ready to tear through the shadows of the night.

The moon looms over the dueling platform, heavy and round.
A fierce wind pierces through like a knife. Crows shriek past overhead.
Her blade hums within its sheath. Sealed inside is a ferocious beast named Qiangliang, trembling in anticipation of the soon-to-be-deadly battle. She pats the scabbard and climbs the final step. The secret letter from the embroidery house brought her here—to the dueling platform atop this peak. Since the White Horse School's sword technique manual surfaced, the world has erupted into chaos. Even high-ranking court officials have died.
Daring not to delay, she travels under the dark of night, all the while wondering if the embroidery shop owner is safe.
At that moment, black figures emerge from all sides. Their leader stares at her with hungry eyes—the very man mentioned in the letter. A tiger's roar echoes on the wind. Her long blade catches the moonlight. This night will be far from quiet.
Flute notes flutter from the village in the mountain, revealing a dancer among the shadows.

At a crackling campfire by the creek, she blows her silver flute.
It was a gift from her mother, passed down from her grandmother. When she plays it, shadows rise from the firelight and circle her, hand in hand.
They raise their arms and sing soundless ballads, like some ancient, tender call. She knows these shadows by their scent. Before she could speak, they brought her food—something warmer than fire itself. The fragrant meals filled her belly and helped her grow into who she is today.
Grandmother, sister, uncle—she speaks these names aloud, feeling the curve of her tongue and the rumble in her chest. The shadows wave their long arms, smoothing the wrinkles from her clothes and tucking dew-laden flowers into her hair.
Just like her mother did.
In the past reflected on the water, he sings the note of truth.

The river called "Fate" has been written by countless hands.
In the playwright's work, this river runs deep enough to drown Ophelia. Before she could claim her own soul, she became a puppet, lost beneath the shadows of monarchy and patriarchy.
In the poet's verses, this river lies calm as a mirror, reflecting Narcissus. That youth withered away by the water, reaching only for that perfect illusion.
The Hermit wades through the river, neither drifting with the flow nor pausing at the voices that call from below. He maintains his own principles, keeping a measured distance from all.
Solitude becomes his eternity. He is a silent stone in the river, watching the waters divide and flow past.
Wherever the waters may go, the stone remains.
Swallows swoop betwixt the willow, ushering spring to its withered branches.

She hated the rain and sudden shifts in weather. The changing temperature and humidity brought pain to her stump.
She hated spring—the so-called season of renewal, greenery, and new life. She loathed the very symbolism of it. She hated how new sprouts would grow just to mock those that had already withered. She hated it all. To her, every raindrop that struck the eaves and tapped the glass sounded like a heavy sigh.
She spent much of her time leaning against the window frame, watching swallows build new nests. Their graceful movements awakened something buried deep in her heart. She imitated their motions—bending, stretching, practicing. Then one day, when a tender green bud emerged from the old scar on the withered willow, her feelings began to shift. Spring suddenly wasn't so bad.
Its rain still brought dampness and pain, but she started seeing more facets of the world. She couldn't change what had already happened, but at least the future held all sorts of possibilities. Even lost swallows could find a new home beneath the willow.
If only schemes were as easy to see through as traps.

Moonlight glows, illuminating the wooden falcon's eyes. The bird perches silently on the wheelchair, both creations of the Mohist Sect.
Suddenly, wind tears through the bamboo grove—trouble approaches. She steadies her breathing and raises a few fingers. The falcon responds instantly. In a flash, cold gleams slice through the night's sky. When her vision clears, the falcon holds several silver darts in its beak.
"The Mohist Sect apologizes for the poor welcome." She smiles and inclines her head, then claps her hands lightly. Before the sound fades, a chorus of whistling erupts from the bamboo grove. Countless wooden falcons leap from the branches and dive toward a hidden corner deep within.
Moments later, a heavy thud echoes from the forest. One falcon returns to her shoulder, carrying the metallic scent of blood, and nestles its head gently against her cheek.
Dealing with the living by day, roaming among the dead by night.

This is the Daoist's first solo mission, an opportunity he's eagerly awaited.
Before, bound by his master's orders, he had to work alongside his senior sister. She had the strangest methods for dealing with ghosts—like hitting them with candies. Even stranger, her methods actually worked.
He tried her approach once in secret, but nothing happened. Perhaps an exclusive technique.
Now he stands before a dilapidated temple. According to local rumors, a powerful Yao dwells within—so he's come prepared with three peach wood swords and several transportation talismans allowing him to cover miles in a single step.
If all else fails, fleeing is always an option.

Medicine Pocket finds Pemberton's contact info in a cola ad in the Atlanta Journal. They write in hopes of collaborating on a Picrasma-flavored cola, but they've missed one key detail: the newspaper is from 1886.
Reed asks Getian what it's like to be immortal and requests a reading of her fate. But Getian discovers she has no bones.
Most remember the Titanic sinking after hitting an iceberg, but few recall the date of her launch.
Avgust always celebrates this day by carrying a big bunch of sunflowers. He hands them out one by one to kids his age, making plenty of new friends along the way.
Ms. Radio takes a moment to honor Guglielmo Marconi, the man who invented practical wireless telegraphy.
A French volcanologist couple disappeared while investigating strange lava activity and were never found. Some witnesses say a group of Ash Carbuncles saved them back then.
In 1784, Élisabeth Thible flew aboard "La Gustave," becoming the first woman to complete a hot air balloon flight with no arcane help.
Buddy Fairchild calls himself an environmentalist. His proof? A newspaper headline from this day last year: "Hiking Group 'Wiped Out' by Squirrel After Dumping Batteries!"
Tipped off by a report from the Foundation, Zeno Arms Academy secretly heads to the Alaska Peninsula to find out why Manus Vindictae is activating the volcano there, Novarupta.
Several friends inside the Suitcase have complained to Vertin about Regulus blasting Blind Faith all day. The rock music is so loud it can be heard even outside the Suitcase.
Click holds a war photography exhibition inside the Suitcase. The pictures capture fleeing crowds, heavy silences, and the brief pauses just before the shutter clicks.
Lorentz Butterfly accurately predicts today's weather.
Isolde performs the romantic tragedy Tristan und Isolde today to honor Richard Wagner.
aliEn T reveals he once made a "cameo" in the 1982 movie E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial.
On the back page of UTTU, there's a horror story called Child Labor Protest Song, written by Oliver Fog.
Paper Heron teaches X the "Wooden Ox and Gliding Horse" technique and gives him a copy of Notes on Lu Ban's Mechanical Arts.
Though scattered and separated by long distances, Igor's children prepare Father's Day gifts early to make sure he gets them on time.

Darley Clatter points out that over a century ago, Eadweard Muybridge proved with photography that a galloping horse lifts all four hooves off the ground. So it's not surprising that today's horses can "run" on wheels.
On this day, Sputnik made two new friends in space—Awakened communications satellites from Western Europe.
Pioneer quietly collects stylish clothes for everyone, hoping they will be useful someday.
Bunny Bunny prepares a "sustainable" gourmet feast featuring only ingredients from the Wilderness—healthy and eco-friendly.
Recoleta and Зима host a memorial book club session inside the Suitcase, reading The Good Earth together.
In 1982, arcanists and humans held a joint conference on peaceful racial integration, which helped promote harmony among different peoples.
A tech company once again invites Mr. APPLe to an IbOOK launch event. Even though he wouldn't be required to match the logo this time, Mr. APPLe still politely declines.
Kaalaa Baunaa tells Charon that Pluto's moon, which humans discovered in 1978, is also named "Charon." The latter says he will treat the day of its discovery as his second "birthday."
For Ulu, who has centuries of experience tending sacred flames, giving an Olympic memorial speech at the SPDM school sports day is a piece of cake.
A chubby little Critter crowns itself "Henly the Eighth" of the toybox today.
Ms. Ramona says ghosts are often more honest than the living.

On this day in 1997, Harry Potter was first published. At the book club, Horropedia comments that its horror comes from three layers—Gothic style, childhood trauma, and existential crisis, creating a story that is both surprising and deeply meaningful.
On this day in 1967, the UK introduced the world's first ATM.
