A researcher from Weapons R&D stops you and asks for supplies to build a massive weapon capable of taking down large targets. They call it the Ultimate Answer.
Before you stands another of Musae III's contraptions: a message board covered in advice from fellow Laplace personnel. Supposedly, a malfunction has occurred in the area ahead.

You still cannot agree with your colleague's proposal. At the very least, the report should uphold the spirit of Laplace on paper. Forget prioritizing survival through the "Storm"—you and your companions cannot even imagine Laplace employees begging for research funding.

Enigma has chosen his own path, and you have no choice but to intervene. As absurd as it sounds, this is the reality of the situation: even as an Awakened, you have long surpassed this particular human in empathy—but now's not the time to dwell on it. You have to stop this before he commits to being that raven's lackey for good. The Pre-Storm Protocol requires countless revisions, and above all, it must not feel like a prison sentence.

You decide to look for your former "friends" first. They once fought at your side, yet you have not seen them under the raven's rule. Perhaps they are hiding somewhere. Well, it's time to embark on a classic hero's journey to reunite with your estranged allies. Start with [Laplace].

You find the girl you met before. Enigma asked for her name last time, yet you still cannot recall it. Could this be some kind of cognitive bug? You set the question aside for now. There are more urgent matters at hand.

The conversation confirms your suspicions. Thanks to Ludwig's meddling, the toybox has split into polarized extremes—on one side, orderly yet lifeless conformists; on the other, a small number of rebels who continue to fight back.

You express your intent to stand with the resistance and overthrow the raven. The girl is relieved to be able to collaborate with you again. She directs you to the [Graveyard of Dreams] to meet the others.

The girl leads you to the toybox's most contentious location—the former site of the "Glory Carbuncle Kingdom," where Zeno soldiers used to battle that band of Critters. It's abandoned now, the former inhabitants having been relocated to Laplace or exiled.

The toybox may seem small to you, but it is where these pieces live. Following its parameters and calculations, they endure the "Storm" time and again so that you may glean yet another set of observation data.

Perhaps your help merely nudges the toybox's calculations toward another outcome, but for now, showing your gratitude seems appropriate. But don't worry: from the sanctuary to The Edge of the Earth, every piece recognizes you as the famous outsiders.

With the pleasantries over, it is time to act. You need to know what your rival is up to. You could ask your two colleagues to keep an eye on Enigma, they're more than content to just watch the show—stepping onto the stage would be impolite. You will have to handle this yourself.

A potential ally comes to mind, though you have to persuade her first. The unnamed enigmatic girl agrees to help, provided you make the necessary arrangements. Reports indicate the raven will send reconnaissance forces. The people here must be evacuated.

With the evacuation complete, the enigmatic girl chooses to stay. She will help you persuade the shy girl from the Foundation. As for you, your task is to support the impending general strike at the [Darkened City].
By the time you arrive, unrest has already set in. Dissenters flood the streets, confronting the raven's agents. The impact, however, is limited. The onlookers watch with little more than disdain.

Snippets of conversation reveal the crowd's resentment toward those who refuse to work and only cause trouble. Then you spot a familiar face among the raven's clustered followers—no, two of them: Ms. Marcus is here as well.
You decide to greet him. You may be rivals, but it's best to maintain some workplace camaraderie.

Regrettably, the amicable conversation collapses into yet another confrontation over power and survival. Your colleague is clearly enraged. While you are not paying attention, he tears off your head, hurls it into the crowd, and flees. What kind of childish behavior is this? He even leaves his assistant behind.

Thankfully, he still retains some semblance of a conscience. You watch as Enigma slips back out of the alley and takes Marcus with him. You are not truly angry, but when you collect yourself and look around ... Damn it, this has turned into a full-scale riot, and Ludwig shows no restraint in suppressing it.
Thanks to your efforts, the farce comes to an end. It is time to return to the [Graveyard of Dreams] and resume your plan.

True to her word, the girl follows through. Marcus arrives with Enigma at your hideout. It seems he has come to realize just how naïve and terrifying Ludwig's so-called perfect language plan truly is.
You extend an invitation to Enigma, only to be turned down. He claims to have his own approach—one he intends to see through himself.
After seeing Marcus off, you begin discussing the next steps with the girl and the others. In the end, the answer is simple—you must retrace your old path.

You united them once, only to learn the core had been stolen. Now, it's time to do it again. You must head to [The Edge of the Earth] and find them—the Crates Gang, Laplace, the Foundation, Zeno, and even the Critters.
In the meantime, the girl will prepare everything you need at the sanctuary.
It is no surprise that the Crates Gang does not recognize you. Anyone who once did has long been erased by the toybox's cycles. They are willing to help, but at what cost?
After hearing you out, the field investigators agree to help. They have already received approval from the higher-ups—the Foundation supports order, so long as it is the Foundation's order.
Zeno refuses your request. They are already aiding another uprising—sorry, a "righteous revolt." And really, who else could it involve but you?
The Laplace Scientific Computing Center, toybox version. It is completely deserted. Ludwig has likely taken everyone away.
"Keh-keh-keh-keh-keh-keh!" Amid the Most Supreme Warlord's triumphant laughter, you secure a major strategic alliance between the toybox sanctuary faction and the Glory Carbuncle Kingdom.
You have united every force that can be united. All that remains is to find the raven.
You tell Ludwig that a perfect language is one that can be spoken, not one that demands silence.
Find it. Take back the core. The future of the toybox belongs to those inside it—just as Laplace's future belongs to the members of Laplace.

You steel yourself. Yes, too much has already been lost in the rain, and now the toybox is your most reliable shot at finding a solution. It may not be perfect—your noisy colleague and the little scarf-wearing Foundation agent are far from convinced—but at least there will be no more sacrifices.

You need to find that raven and his so-called perfect language system. Fortunately, he's not hard to locate: he's perched atop the roof of this toybox's LSCC, gazing down like an emperor surveying his domain.

He looks unhinged as he rambles to himself like a mad scientist straight out of a novel. He beats his wings, keeping one eye fixed on the sky and the other on the ground, watching the world as its omniscient god. When you try to approach, you are stopped. Overstepping your rank is unacceptable here.
It seems there will be no special treatment. "Build reputation, increase strength, earn rewards"—so the toybox has not forgotten why it was created in the first place.

You have no respect for this peculiar system of rule, yet the work must be done. Soon, you are assigned a "beginner's task." A group of enemies is plotting to undermine this progressive collective. You need to head to the [Graveyard of Dreams] and find out what is happening.

You arrive at an abandoned camp. Ever since the raven took control of the toybox, this place has been deserted for being too close to the Glory Carbuncle Kingdom. Strangely enough, the entire toybox seems powerless against the Carbuncle Kingdom's destructive loyalists.
If it were you, you would've beaten the Most Supreme Warlord senseless already. You do have some combat training, after all. By that logic, are you Laplace's most combative human?
As your thoughts wander, a strange noise suddenly breaks the silence. A Critter—or perhaps your target?

It's quiet all around. Only Marcus is with you, and she's not the type to speak up. As for Hissabeth and Medicine Pocket ... They're only this quiet when they're eagerly waiting for you to embarrass yourself.

You move forward without hesitation. Fear is meaningless compared to the threat of the "Storm." Besides, this is only a toybox—can you really expect a bunch of pawns to build you a Dr. Caligari-style cabinet?
You push the door open only to find a single girl inside. You recognize her, but not her name. Why it still escapes you is unclear, but now is not the time to dwell on it.
She once helped your colleague uncover the mystery of the missing core and aided you in building the tower. Now, she stands against you.

You explain your reasoning, praying she'll understand. But your hopes fall flat, like they always do. She refutes you, point by point, then asks the same question Ulrich once did—what's the point of saving Laplace from the "Storm" if it's going to end up like this?

What's the point? Debating Laplace's usefulness only matters if you can survive the "Storm." Anger rises in your chest. Countless members of Laplace have given everything just to claim a sliver of ground from the rain—and you can name only a fraction of them.

After all, Laplace, Zeno, the Foundation, and those investigators active across the board are already worn thin. There's a solution that allows everyone to catch their breath, but now people are opposing it for subjective, personal reasons.
Language alone cannot convince them. Ludwig's ambition, it appears, falls short of perfection.
As the girl walks away, you feel yourself growing restless.
You don't have the full picture, yet their motivation is clear enough. When you ask your assistant, she appears preoccupied with something else.

You decide to leave her be for now. The immediate issue is that the rebels are organizing spontaneous protests in the [Darkened City], and Ludwig wants you to disperse them. You frown. Things are moving in a direction you do not like.
You reach the plaza, where the protest is in full swing. The onlookers remain indifferent: their only complaint is that the resistance has interrupted their work.
To your disbelief, your colleague is there in the crowd. His glass head impossible to miss. On top of everything he's done in the toybox, now he's ended up leading the rebels.
You are left speechless. Since when did your colleague become so eloquent? Perhaps everything you tried to hide has already been laid bare.
You know the truth already: none of this is really about efficiency, nor is it about silencing interference in order to endure the "Storm." What you fear is reliving the past.
You're a member of Laplace. All you want is to avoid losing more friends and colleagues to the "Storm," denied even the dignity of a proper burial.

Perhaps you can persuade them to leave peacefully. No matter what, you know your approach is the most peaceful way to disperse the crowd. If you fail, Ludwig will deploy armed forces and escalate the situation at the slightest resistance. You have to stop that from happening.

Without warning, you take his head off once more. You cannot explain the impulse—a lingering personal grievance, perhaps, or simply nothing at all. This is just the only way you can think of to draw the crowd's attention.

In full view of the crowd, you throw the "Prime Minister's" head to his supporters. They scramble to catch the "fishbowl," then surge after you in a dark mass, leaving only Ulrich and Marcus behind. Damn it—Marcus is still there. You double back through the alley and retrieve your temporary assistant.
Disheveled and breathless, you prepare to return to [Laplace] to face the raven.

You stand before the raven in silence until he breaks into incoherent cries. His unfocused eyes drift toward you, though it is unclear whether he recognizes your presence. Eventually, he mutters a command to exile them all to the white world beyond.

You have endured this mad bird's erratic commands for a while now. You betrayed the girl who helped you, dispersed the protest, and tore off your colleague's head—all to make things a little safer outside.

This is how you've been justifying it to yourself. But now you see that his madness has long devoured his conscience—does "perfectly" surviving the "Storm" really mean sacrificing everything deemed imperfect? You, for one, are not that far gone!
You walk away, only for Marcus to catch your attention and gesture for you to head to the [Graveyard of Dreams] with her.

She leads you to a small cave. You nearly forgot how powerful this quiet girl's arcane skill is. Perhaps she saw the flaws in Ludwig's so-called perfect plan long ago. If so, why did she not tell you?

It turns out she never meant to hide the truth: she was merely waiting for the right moment. Inside the cave, the girl, Ulrich, and some others are gathered together. There is even a barely articulate Critter among them.
Indeed, your temporary assistant had already defected during your confrontation with the nameless girl. You owe it to her that you escaped the protest unscathed.

She wasn't hiding the fact that Ludwig's so-called perfect language is nothing more than empty words born of absolute ideological uniformity. She was waiting for you to realize it yourself. Damn it—where did she learn such an approach?
The interrogation begins. Under the gaze of your peers, you are forced to admit that the raven's plan is far from perfect. If anything, it is outright inhumane.

You may not care much about these pieces—fine, perhaps only marginally—but if this plan were applied outside the toybox ... forget implementation. Simply submitting it to the Foundation would earn you a swift, well-armed escort under the guise of courtesy.
More importantly, this is not the kind of security you were hoping for.

Marcus offers you an apology, though it barely registers. By Laplace standards, this kind of "opposition" is practically polite. Her restraint rivals that of Madam Lucy and Ms. Simone. Had it been anyone else, you would've been tied up and hauled off to a dark room by now.

That's right: they might not be dependable, and they might never find a perfect solution, but perhaps you could try believing in them.
So where do you go from here?
Ulrich extends an invitation, which you turn down. A decision has formed in your mind. You are going to Zeno. They still owe you a position as a "General."
You arrive at [Serene Bay], where you reunite with the adorable squirrel from before and his many animal companions.

A riot? The word catches them off guard. Call it an "uprising," however, and they are happy to follow you. This is not a snap decision. While you were away, it was these Zeno soldiers who upheld order and enforced the raven's rule within the toybox.

They were forced to appear ruthless, driven by Ludwig's assurances. But beneath the gilded veneer, the lunatic's throne is made of rotting timber. Now, the toybox demands that its people decide for themselves.

It is time to head back to Laplace for a final reckoning with the raven. At that moment, your assistant delivers crucial information: the great tower itself, the raven's very throne, is the core—the Proteus. Damn it! How could you have forgotten that it can change forms? Still, your goal is clearer now, is it not?
A suffocating yellow haze blankets the city. Everything looks grimy and gray. Where have you seen this before? The dust-choked air is deeply disturbing.

"No, this is a beautiful dusk. Gray conveys sophistication, and this dark yellow is a tribute to a master of cinema!" The painter enthusiastically explains his work in a booming voice, insisting that Dusk will fetch a fine price.
"Why won't it sell? Can't you see the singular vision in this glorious sunset?" the painter insists. "Or do you have data showing people hate my dusk?"
Another twilight landscape—this time painted in vivid yellow. It appears clearer, but carries a sense of unreality.
"You again?" The painter glances at you listlessly, then returns to his canvas.

Of course it's different. No one wanted to buy that painting. Tourists and critics alike failed to grasp my vision. All they talk about is value and profit. They do not understand art. Art is starvation, rejection, and transcendence!
That single sentence leaves you speechless. He's right: everyone has to eat—artists included.

Every shelf is crammed with books, each bearing a different title: xx Wanderer's Guide (Patched Edition) xx Wanderer's Guide (Revised Edition) xx Wanderer's Guide (No Revision Required Edition) xx Wanderer's Guide (A History of Nonexistent Revisions) xx Wanderer's Guide (I Swear This Is the Final Version)

You pull a book down at random and flip it open.
The pages are packed with dense text:
"The 'Storm,'" "Thought," "Epiphany," "The Unknown Sea." The tiny words spread like a virus, seeping into the depths of your mind.
It states: "This page is only a rough conceptual draft. Please continue reading and turn to the next page."
As you ponder the logic between the words, a loose page drifts down and lands at your feet. You pick it up in confusion.

Yet every page branches into more material:
Concepts, annotations, addenda, responses to addenda, and responses to those responses ...
You snap the book shut in frustration, sending a cloud of dust into the air and attracting the attention of a few Carbuncles. They fluff their fur, gather together, and silently stare at you.
You realize you are being pulled along by "useless" information, forced to move forward and forward again—yet this so-called "direction" is nothing more than another labyrinth.

At that moment, the page in your hand trembles. In the next instant, countless shelves collapse, and an endless flood of pages spills out, surging around your feet like a tide.
They murmur, debate, and feverishly argue for their respective editions.

Are Critters in top hats really any smarter than the rest? You stare in astonishment as they crowd around a cramped table. On it lies an aged book: A Study of 19th-Century Literature (Reversed Edition).
Grr-glr-glr. Incomprehensible Critter-Speech spills from their mouths. They bounce and flail, convinced they have uncovered some profound "metaphor."
One particularly large Critter taps a line of text with its paw and blinks at you expectantly, seemingly asking for "a meaningful interpretation."

The Critters immediately fall silent. They exchange looks, then erupt into discussion, gurgling loudly.
They rub their fur against the floor, generating crackling static. Some even shed tears of excitement as they emphatically circle a line of text with their paws.

You focus on the line of reversed words, recognizing just fragments of letters.
Together, they almost assemble a sentence—

You adopt a solemn tone and say slowly, "This is clearly a deconstruction of linear narrative."
Even you have no idea what you are talking about.
The Critters, however, are instantly elated. Some are even moved to tears.

You step into a corridor devoid of features. This isn't the Laplace Scientific Computing Center you're familiar with.
Pale green walls, pale green floors, and pale green ceilings.
The lights buzz softly.
A sign says, "Please proceed."
You proceed forward, only for a new corridor to extend beyond the end. You look up at the sign hanging from the wall—"Exit 9."

You glance behind you—nothing there, only flickering lights.
The sign has been updated:
"Anomalous activity detected. Please return to the entrance."

Ahead lies the same corridor. The color of the walls and floor, the flickering lights, and even the cracks in the ceiling are identical.
The sign is still there.
The only difference is that it now bears your signature.

You turn back, only to find the same walls, the same floors, and the same fluorescent lights at every corner.
In the dim glow, you spot a pair of twins walking arm in arm, smiling at you.

You walk faster and faster, growing increasingly uneasy.
The corridor collapses behind you and rebuilds ahead.
The "Exit 9" sign flickers—"9" becomes "8," then "10," then "0," before snapping back to "9."
A loud rumble erupts—you've stepped on a mechanism. A new corridor rises from below, as if pointing toward the way where you came.

The familiar "Exit 9" appears again.
From ahead, you hear coworkers from Laplace talking about experiment outcomes.
"Is he not out yet?"
"Out? He was never inside."

You turn around and see the sign still in place.
However, its message has completely changed.

A Klein Blue room stretches out before you, uniform in every direction.
You blink, unsettled, suspecting you have entered a play in which you were never meant to appear.
An aging TV and a remote control sit alone nearby.
Harsh static spills from the television. The image steadies, revealing a suited salesman holding something suspiciously familiar ... It's an hourglass.

You scan the room.
Klein Blue paintings hang on Klein Blue walls.
Twisted staircases, inverted shadows, folded skies, melting clocks.
You sense an artist striving to discover a style—their most refined version of one.

You turn and see several papers stacked on the table: The Application of Surrealism in Contemporary Society, Paradigm Conflicts and Their Underlying Social Logic, and Installation Art and Its Relationship with Klein Blue.

The salesman seems to notice your confusion.
He slightly leans out from the screen, studying you.
"Let me guess ... You think it's just an hourglass, don't you?"

You turn off the TV, but it flickers back on by itself.
The image freezes on the salesman's smug grin and gleaming teeth.
"You can run, but you can't hide!"

The salesman's expression stiffens.
"You—you actually called this an ... hourglass?"
"I remember you. You're the one who insisted on arguing whether it was an hourglass or a Klein bottle!"
"Do you know where the problem lies? The moment humans treat language as nothing but a tool, imagination dies!"

He fumes, his hands shaking.
"You people don't understand perfection in language at all, let alone the grace of metaphysics!"

"I only mean ... it resembles an hourglass."
He ignores you completely and launches into a rehearsed speech:
"You wouldn't get it."
"Educate yourself."
"The Klein bottle is pure symbolism—primitive, ancient—a piece of postmodern poetry!"
His voice grows shrill until the entire image begins to shake. With a sharp crack, the TV cuts to black.

The salesman holds the "Klein bottle" toward the screen.
His smile returns, unchanged.
"Honestly, I'm not entirely sure what it is."
"But when I call it a Klein bottle, people are usually willing to pay triple."

He finishes speaking and points the bottle's mouth at the camera.
The sand inside the "Klein bottle" flows backward. You see your reflection in the Klein Blue glass.
You notice that beyond the cover, only elaborate layouts and incomprehensible metaphors remain.
There's a Critter lying beneath the dome. It supposedly exists in a "superposition of sleep and wakefulness." One eye is shut tight, while the other stares straight at you.

"It is contemplating fate," the man explains. "I want to know whether it is considered awake or asleep."
He points to the dice scattered across the table. "An odd number means it's asleep. An even number means it's awake."

He grows impatient, wearing the same expression as those Laplace researchers who constantly suspect others of insulting their work.
"You know nothing about research. Who says an experiment must produce a definitive result?"

The man taps lightly on the glass casing. The Critter inside does not move.
"People demand cause and effect, answers, and flawless conclusions."
He smiles.
"What I pursue is an eternal suspense—one that stirs the heart."

"The dice symbolize the uncertainty of existence. Each roll produces a different result!"
He gestures wildly through the air, movements so elaborate they surpass any divination ritual you have ever seen.
Then, the die falls ... He rolled a 3.

You turn away, ending a conversation more absurd than the experiment itself.
Behind you, you hear glass shattering, followed by the chittering laughter of a Critter.

You arrive at a strange place. Like the retro-futuristic walls of the Laplace you know, everything is smooth, with outlines visible only on close inspection. It is a temporary room. You do not know its purpose—only that it exists, as if waiting for you.

The room is sparsely furnished: a round table, a cold light, and two transparent chairs.
A large mirror hangs on the wall; in it, you glimpse yourself—a blurred silhouette.
A notebook lies on the table. The cover reads, "Temporary Version: For Internal Discussion Only."

You see a notice tucked beside the door handle:
"Welcome to the Deep Thought Seminar."
Below, in small print:
"Please dress appropriately. Your attire represents your depth of thought."
You sigh inwardly. A welcome this "proper" can only signal a discussion just as "proper" and self-important.
You open the notebook. The pages feel as smooth as the walls. There is not a single word that could be called a "deep thought."

On the blank page, you casually write a single word—"Depth."
"Good. That is an excellent start. You already grasp the importance of depth."
A man has sat down across from you without you noticing. His hairline is ruler-straight, his face utterly smooth, and his clothing seemingly from the last century.

You move behind the mirror and find it covered in small cards, each bearing a phrase of supposed "intellectual depth":
"We search for the self across different eras."
"In a vast world, words occupy only a tiny fraction and hold no inherent meaning."
The cards are neatly arranged. The signatures at the bottom differ, yet the handwriting is identical.

"Depth of thought," he says slowly, "is the effective manipulation of language—using ornate, complex, unsustainable words, arranged in unpredictable sequences under atypical conditions, until you feel discomfort, confusion, and abandon independent thinking."

You begin to echo his ideas.
He smiles with satisfaction and continues at length:
"The mirror of consciousness, the projection of meaning, the duality of thought—these are all manifestations of depth ..."

You sigh. "You don't actually understand what 'depth of thought' is, do you?"
Silence falls. The "smooth" walls ripple with faint wrinkles.

It dawns on you: everything here is a magnified human cerebral cortex. The walls are neural pathways, the mirror a region regulating self-perception, and the "deep thinker" a projection of a thinking pattern.

Transparent light passes through its clear facets, refracting into countless colors. You feel dizzy watching it.
Cracks spider through the crystal; you can almost picture the tiny particles inside colliding and fracturing.
"You are walking inside a box."

The voice inside the crystal turns soft, tinged with sorrow.
"Look—you have already crossed these six layers and hexagonal grids countless times. Each time you believe you will reach the end, yet you never do. Those outside the box toy with you relentlessly, trapping you in an endless loop. This emptiness is called destiny."

"If destiny truly follows fixed rules, then were the words you just spoke also prewritten?"
The crystal replies in a lighter tone.
"Of course, the flow of destiny is set, but it sometimes branches, because we always make unexpected choices."

"Rules apply only to those who try to understand them. Destiny applies only to those who obey it."
The voice fades.
"Keep moving forward. If you lose your way, it means you have reached a place where fate has yet to arrive."
The hexagonal tiles beneath your feet rearrange themselves, drawn by some unseen force. A new pattern forms—and at the edge of the grid, a sea appears.

You approach the sea, only to find it absurdly shallow. At its far edge, a line of text reads:
"This scenery is a temporary resource. Please note that your thoughts may strand themselves in the Depths of Myth at any time."

Sounds rise from beneath the sea. Semi-transparent figures surface, like psychological archetypes—security robots, smoke, warped stars, an opera singer's spirit ...
One shadow coughs. "They're working us to death out here."

The shadows exchange a glance.
"I suppose we never considered what we wanted to express."
"The creator of this sea decided that for us."
"Without being told why, we were forced to play specific roles: primitive urges, fogs of war, harbingers of a new era ..."
The shadows collapse, resembling striking workers on the streets of Paris.

The shadows visibly relax.
"Someone finally said it out loud!"
"Do you get it? I've got three different names across all the places I've appeared—Vienna, Paris, a magazine, even a wanted poster!"
"Please ... All we want to do is rest quietly at the bottom of the sea."

"It's simple," the shadows say in unison. "We're not the sea, we're not orange juice, we're not the anima mundi."
"Someone keeps digging deep into the seabed. They even dug up that terrifying 'wailing whirl'!"
"They summon us to spare those who fall in from even worse mental torment!"
The sea stills, then begins to ripple again.
As you approach the door, it opens on its own, as though inviting—no, beckoning—you inside, like a pitcher plant luring in its prey with the sweetest nectar. But will you enter?
You enter the hall. Inside, the splendor of the lavish exterior vanishes, and only loneliness remains.

A white horse turns back to acknowledge you.
It appears calm, sorrowful, and resigned. Truly, any horse stuck looping through this broken toybox as a museum exhibit would feel the same.

You decide to explore first. It is pitch-dark here, yet everything remains perfectly visible thanks to the gleaming white horse following close behind. Wherever you go, it follows.
The cold lingers.

You try to approach it and are unsurprisingly brushed off. It keeps a certain distance from you.
Its hoofprints glow faintly, as though guiding your path.

You stop, and it stops, as though greeting an old acquaintance.
Only then do you realize it looks exactly like you.

The glowing footprints fade as mist rises around you.
Darkness overtakes your vision. When you come to, you are exactly where you began.
The space remains quiet still, yet subtle lights betray the existence of decidedly unscientific beings.

"Got a shirt to spare?"
A ragged ghost calls out to you.
He ignores your response and rambles on, "I was once a worker. I saved up my whole life just to have a shirt of my own."

He looks both confused and indignant.
"I don't know where the money went. I worked every day, pinched every penny, but I still died in these patched-up rags."
Whenever I tried to save, something came up—sickness, back taxes, family emergencies, those bizarre mandatory donations ...
You realize your own life works much the same. Just when you think things are getting better, reality hits you like a bucket of cold water.
You push the door open. As it gives way, dust rains down. Inside, the silence remains, but the human touch is gone—replaced by the smell of wilderness and overgrown weeds.
You spot an old farmer sowing seeds. Technically, this is the first actual person you've seen here. Should you say something?

"I'm growing lambs," he says. "Harvested a batch last week. Want a taste?" You hope this is merely a system error, not intentional design. The toybox's randomness is like that—logically sound, yet always ready to surprise you when your guard is down.
You discover the lamb plant tastes exactly like real lamb.
"What do you think? If a fake becomes convincing enough, it becomes real."
"What do you think? Even if a fake becomes convincing enough, it's still a fake."
The coffin holds a great man. He shielded the villagers when the Critters invaded. Now they honor him with a proper funeral.
You wait for the eulogy to begin.
"To our great, our truly great ..." The speaker falters, wipes his brow, and whispers to someone nearby—what was his name?
Everyone knew him, yet they only ever called him "you," "him," or "hey, you." No one had asked his name, and now, no one knows it.
You may be a stranger here, yet the locals appear just as oblivious. How curious.
What kind of beauty standards do Critters have? It starts explaining its regimen: grooming, deep repair, hyaluronic injections ...
You tell it that it already looks beautiful and needs no further cosmetic work. The Critter scoffs, clearly unimpressed by your lack of taste.
A Critter has called you ignorant. Wonderful. Keeping your temper, you play along and suggest where it could improve further.
Then it attacks you. Apparently, it believes you were mocking it.
You can't appease it, and you can't oppose it. It appears the perfect language remains a myth.
When you toss a stone into the water, it turns to gold and sinks instantly. So ... are those golden statues actually people?
As you prepare to leave, a stranger arrives, glancing between you and the gold at the bottom, eyes gleaming.
"Ha!" The stranger scoffs. "Of course you'd say that. Anyone can see that glint in your eyes! Are you trying to make a fool out of me?"
You have nothing to add. His gaze drifts between you and the pond. At last, he sighs and turns to leave.
You turn to leave—then "plunk!" Damn it. The pool has claimed yet another statue.
You prepare to give thanks as you leave, but the web reads, "Hurry up and save it."
You prepare to give thanks as you leave, but the web reads, "Please save it."
Cold air drifts from deep inside the cabinet. It might just be a refrigerator disguised as an antique wardrobe.

The wardrobe connects to another world.
A man with goat legs waits inside, asking you to save his world.

The goat-legged man shares a prophecy: "When the demon king falls, spring will return."
He says this world has been without sunlight for a long time.
Violence won't get rid of any problems, except maybe yourself.
The goat-legged man industrialized the world, caused global warming, and was elected the second demon king.
You see a tiny figure who has already reached the top and even built a house in the flower's heart.
Almost every tiny figure slips and falls once they reach the calyx.

You watch for a long time before another tiny figure finally reaches the top.
He returns to the ground carrying gifts from the one living in the house.
The others immediately crowd around him.
You see that he's holding nothing more than a clump of pollen, yet he claims it's the secret to wealth.
You see that he's holding nothing more than a clump of pollen, yet the crowd envies him as if he's obtained a priceless treasure.

Perhaps only by rewriting danger into a comforting tale can he hold onto it with a clear conscience.
He begins sharing the story of his climb, encouraging others to scale the tulip.

The little Critter seems delighted, spinning in place and admiring itself. Then it notices you.
"Hallo! You iz heer for me crow-nay-shun?"
When asked about its identity, the Critter grows visibly excited, as if it's been waiting for this very moment. After an extended bout of self-promotion, you finally understand who it is.

It calls itself the "Least Supreme Warlord," a noble of the Glory Carbuncle Kingdom. It dreams of becoming like their leader, the Most Supreme Warlord. Today is its coronation, and you are the only attendee.
Having finally found someone to confide in, it chatters excitedly in incomprehensible gurgles. In short, it feels it still falls short of the Most Supreme Warlord and wants advice.
Size ...? The Critter looks inspired and excitedly promises to name you Chief Minister.
Color ...? The Critter looks inspired and excitedly promises to name you Chief Minister.
Combat ability ...? The Critter looks inspired and excitedly promises to name you Chief Minister.

"Me minis-ter! You come at da rite time! Look, me BIG now!"
You're greeted enthusiastically by the little Critter—no, "large Critter" would be a more accurate descriptor. It tells you that it ate nonstop until it became a truly chunky fellow.
Clearly pleased with its size, it lays out the next steps in its plan: change colors, improve combat ability—and ultimately replace the Most Supreme Warlord as leader of the Glory Carbuncle Kingdom!

"Me minis-ter! You come at da rite time! Look at me COLORZ now!"
You're greeted enthusiastically by the little Critter, who has somehow managed to dye its fur with random splotches of color.
Clearly pleased with its colors, it lays out the next steps in its plan: grow bigger, improve combat ability—and ultimately replace the Most Supreme Warlord as leader of the Glory Carbuncle Kingdom!

"Me minis-ter! You come at da rite time! SPAR wif me!"
You're greeted enthusiastically by the little Critter, who seems eager for you to test its combat ability.
You defeat the Least Supreme Warlord without much effort. It isn't discouraged. After all, its leader can't beat you either.
Clearly pleased with its combat ability, it lays out the next steps in its plan: grow bigger, change colors—and ultimately replace the Most Supreme Warlord as leader of the Glory Carbuncle Kingdom!

"Happy New Year! Kung hei fat choi! Red packet, please!"
The child greets you with exaggerated enthusiasm.
After you respond, the scene freezes in silence. The child keeps winking and silently mouthing "red packet."
"Uh, red packets are ... an Eastern custom. If you say 'kung hei fat choi' at the right time of year, you get a red packet with money inside."
The child is delighted, though he keeps saying, "You shouldn't have" and "This isn't appropriate." Is refusal part of the ritual?
His smile freezes when you take the packet back. You can't help but laugh—it appears smiles don't vanish, they migrate from face to face.
Clutching the red packet, the child beams from ear to ear and rattles off a string of auspicious phrases—"may everything go your way," "may all your wishes come true" ...
The child freezes, clearly caught off guard. After a long silence, he hands you a red packet.
The tower is eerily quiet. As you move to enter, you hear a faint rustling.
As soon as you speak, the sound vanishes. You're not sure it was there in the first place.
"W-Wait!" Seeing you ready to demolish the tower, someone inside panics.
The man reveals himself—a member of the Crates Gang. He's been camping here to ambush people leaving.
In his opinion, ambushing victims beats scavenging; he just didn't expect to run into you.
"Of course! People can't resist places with loot. I've done this plenty of times," he says, pitching his scam confidently. "Wanna team up? We'll split the spoils."
The Crates Gang member reluctantly hands over his meager supplies.
"Haha! Finally!" Another Crates Gang member leaps out and attacks.
"Ow! I give up! Don't hit me!" Beaten, the Crates Gang member hands over his supplies.
You accept the Crates Gang member's proposal and lie in wait together inside the tower. Time ticks by, second after second—no one comes.

You accept the Crates Gang member's proposal and lie in wait together inside the tower. Time ticks by, second after second, until a faint sound suddenly breaks the silence—someone is actually approaching.
It turns out to be a curious Critter. Either way, the ambush counts as a success.
The Critter clearly never expected an ambush. Startled, it drops a pile of items while cursing and flees.
Text appears on the map: "This map compiles collective wisdom from successful journeys. Follow it and you won't go wrong."
The previous message fades. New text appears: "State your destination. All successful routes will be displayed for selection."

Dozens of crooked routes unfold before you.
Text appears: "Choose a route to follow, or proceed freely. If you successfully reach your destination, your route will be recorded."

By the time you've made it halfway in, you've already had to endure wind, frost, rain, and lightning.
The map updates: "User comment: This route gets very smooth later on."

You find a scenic hiking route—it's long, but it successfully leads to the destination. 
The map responds: "Congratulations. Route completed. Please leave a review."
For the latter half of your journey, you tumble from the mountaintop into the valley—reaching the destination in under ten minutes.
She says nothing, her gaze fixed squarely on you.
You wait, but she offers no reply, only that unblinking stare.
There's a hint of mockery in her eyes, and her silence leaves you deeply uneasy.
She continues staring, the prolonged silence growing increasingly aggravating.

The girl remains unresponsive.
As you step forward to lash out, you realize she's just a painting.

The lemonade kid flashes an eager smile, stacking cup after cup in front of you. "Buy more. Prices go up tomorrow."
You eye the shriveled lemon slices floating inside—small, pale, and unmistakably sour.

The kid explains, "The market decides. If prices go up, we follow."
You point at the withered slices. "So all lemons on the market look like this?"
"Of course! We're all peddling the same stuff."

"If prices rise, why buy it at all? Does lemonade even affect the research schedule?"
You walk away, lost in thought.

You pause by the cart, catching your cold reflection in the window.
Your ferrofluid trembles, registering emotional fluctuation.
Every cup of lemonade is identical—size, sweetness, ice, even the wilted lemon slices.

Back in the lab, you hand out identical lemonades to teammates working in eerie synchronicity.
"Lemonade prices go up tomorrow. Maybe we can try something else—coffee, milk, or black tea. Any preference?"

They all look up at once with vacant eyes and hollow expressions. Amid this chaos—of research, of the Pre-Storm Protocol, of everything—who cares about tomorrow's drink? Then someone laughs. Others follow. Soon the lab fills with unsettling laughter.

You look back at the lemonade and its floating slices.
Order is cold. Flavor is standardized. Time marches on, indifferent to individual will.

Then you decide to change something—anything.
You call out, "One lemonade. No lemon slices. Less ice. Regular sugar."

The Critters stagger.
The one at the very top clamps a cane in its mouth and stretches toward the fake moon, but it only manages to scratch faint ripples across the water.

"That isn't the real moon. It's just a perfect optical illusion."
The Critters ignore you and keep moving.
Ripples spread, and the moon's reflection shatters into meaningless fragments of light.

The Critter tower wobbles and slowly turns toward you.
A ridiculous realization dawns: they seem to have mistaken your head for a second moon—smooth, reflective, round, and, from their perspective, much closer than the fake one in the pool.

Your ferrofluid surges into the shape of an exclamation mark. Your irritation has peaked.
The Critters, unfazed, reach harder with their cane toward your head.

There's a loud bang, and a wave of dizziness hits you, despite the fact you have no eyes.
"I am not the moon!"
As your emotions overload, sparks crackle as the Critters collapse from electrocution.

The Critters circle you again. You realize that in their world, anything reflective is a moon—and any moon is worth risking everything for.
They resume tapping your glass head with their cane, still fishing for the fake moon below.
They don't move aside. This is their secret base, and they claim to be an army—duty-bound to guard it against all suspicious figures. Like you.
Once they learn you're carrying classified military materials, the child in front quickly clears a path. He assures you they'll resume their watch once you pass.

You clearly scare the children. Still, fantasies have to collide with reality sooner or later. They leave in frustration, hurling threats as they go—their leader, a powerful blood-sucking monster, will soon find you and take brutal revenge. She'll grab your shadow and kick it around like a ball!
At this point, it's best to leave.
You encounter someone hiding in a restroom. This time, you don't force the door open; you simply wait quietly for him to come out.
He can clearly hear you outside. He barely dares to breathe. A strange standoff ensues. A desperate attempt at hiding.
Eventually, he gives in. The door creaks open. A Laplace researcher emerges with wobbling footsteps, his legs clearly asleep. He looks at you with pleading eyes.

He's used to this sort of thing, but today, he has his reasons. It's department team-building day, and everyone knows it's an event meant to bring people closer, yet it always ends up making everyone feel awkward instead.

Those who enjoy crowds can't relax. Those who prefer quiet don't dare attend. Those happy to dine with leaders don't need this meal. Those who aren't gain only despair. He just wants to hide, wait until it's over, then go home alone and enjoy his quiet life. And now, once again, he runs into you.
You understand. You usher him back into the restroom and promise to message him once everyone's gone.

Picrasma Candy—stimulating, invigorating, and rumored to affect arcane skill output. For you, it simply keeps you awake at work. It guarantees efficiency in Laplace; it's the foundation of departmental progress.

Now you're holding a bag of it. You swear you've seen the logo somewhere before. There's a promotion beside it: "Chance to win a golden ticket to tour—and possibly inherit—the Picrasma Candy Factory!"
You tear it open to find a golden ticket. You aren't surprised. Ever since you picked it up, you knew your odd behavior had triggered another toybox event.
Just eating candy would be boring. There has to be more—like a factory tour.
As for the candy, you have a colleague who always struggles with sleep after machine repairs; they'll make good use of it.
A towering structure pierces the sky, its spire nearly touching the upper layer. This is the factory you might inherit? Should you start studying management right now?
Maybe hire some Critters to help produce the goods—sell 30% for funding, send 70% to the LSCC. Your thoughts drift. The future always feels pleasant when imagined.

While you are still lost in thought, the other winners arrive—a Laplace researcher who must eat ten packs of Picrasma Candy a day, a Foundation committee member obsessed with power struggles, a supremely confident Zeno soldier, and an ordinary civilian highly skilled with computers.

It's clear the competition is fierce. Compared to them, you seem painfully ordinary. You're not addicted to Picrasma Candy, you're not interested in power, you possess some combat skills but little real experience, and you're far from proficient with computers.

But in stories like this, the average Joe is usually the strongest of them all. As expected, during the tour the others fall into traps—bizarre machines, deceptive scenery. You nonchalantly walk through the entire route alone. The factory is yours now.

You wake in an unfamiliar room, staring at an unfamiliar ceiling.
You rise three minutes before your usual alarm. You don't remember ever needing one—alarms represent flawless order, and you've always disliked order.

You pass through the corridor, and as always, the "Outstanding 'Storm' Contribution Memorial Wall" greets you.
There are portraits of many researchers here, including your own.

You stare at your portrait. The person there feels like a stranger—wearing the expression of someone who's just completed a "great achievement."
Below the portrait, someone has added a label: "Psychological state under observation."

In your office, you notice your cup has been moved five centimeters. Yesterday, it sat ten centimeters from the desk corner. At some point, measuring that distance became your new pastime.
You take a sip. Cold, of course.
You deliberately push the cup farther out of alignment—beyond your recorded margin of error—then leave the office as if nothing happened, heading to the Laplace lounge to buy a pack of mints.
When you return, the cup is back—exactly five centimeters from the desk corner.
You stop fixating on the distance between the cup and the edge of the desk. You have always known that clinging too tightly to fixed rules is meaningless.

You open your familiar notebook, only to find a line written on the first page: "Current status: Acceptable."
You let out a dry chuckle and turn to the second page.
It reads, "Suspected behavior: Attempting escapism."

Three supervisors appear before you, stating that your "recent cognitive fluctuations are abnormal" and that your behavior must be "deconstructed."
You ask, "To what extent?"
They answer, "All behavioral patterns, including silence, must be standardized."
You reflect that if even silence requires a fixed pattern, then this world is already nearing collapse.

No matter what you choose, your day is archived by the supervisors.
You move through the six-layered map, stepping across familiar hexagonal tiles. Each choice appears different, yet leads to the same outcomes—combat, resources, and new events.

Reviewing the details, you sense the supervisors are reconstructing your past, crafting scenarios meant only for you.
Isn't it difficult for them, too? You look up and wave at someone beyond the screen.

You have always despised combat. To you, it is the least efficient activity in human history.
Yet you continue running through this unstable box, trading inefficient simulations for the promise of an efficient solution to the "Storm."

You cannot ignore what appears before you—
Three Critters stack themselves into a tower that defies physics, wobbling toward the water. The top one grips a cane, trying to reach for something.

The Critter tower lurches violently.
The top Critter pokes the fake moon with its clenched cane. The water ripples, and the reflection shatters.

"That isn't the real moon. It's just a perfect optical illusion."
You recognize the voice at once. Your colleague has voiced the thought before you could.
It's rare for you to agree.

As expected, the Critter tower enters a state of catastrophic instability.
After a brief struggle, the Critters collapse all at once.
Water splashes upward, shredding what remains of the fake moon, yet the Critters don't seem to care. The top one keeps fishing for scattered fragments of light.
All three Critters tip forward at once. Like dominoes, they crash toward your colleague, and the cane strikes his glass bowl of a head.

The ferrofluid churns violently. The symbols inside rearrange. You know what this means all too well: your colleague is about to lose control.
You step forward to try to stop what comes next.

You forcefully pull the Critters away from your colleague.
They grasp at empty air and tumble into a tangled heap, and as your hand clips his glass head, electricity crackles violently through you.
A short circuit? Ha. Maybe you should ask the Laplace equipment administrator to inspect this body of yours—chances are a wire's been crossed somewhere it shouldn't be.
A staff member approaches, wearing a perfectly calibrated smile: "You only need to answer one question."
He hands you a form. Printed clearly at the top, you see: "Do you agree with the current statement?"
The staff member nods. "Very good. You remembered."

He hesitates, then pushes the form back toward you.
The question has been freshly reprinted.
The people around you begin answering on your behalf.

As you walk away, the street signs appear sharper than before.
However, you can't quite recall what they used to say.
The staff member adds a note to the record: "Inconsistent attitude. Further conditioning required."

You quicken your pace.
However, the crowd on the street begins chasing after you, shouting answers like vendors hawking their wares.
No matter where you turn, it positions itself squarely in front of you.
Just as you reach for the apple, it speaks: "What do you see?"
It slowly turns, revealing itself to be only half an apple.
It suddenly bolts away. You scowl and roll your eyes.

"This is Whitepest Grass," the old man says. "Sweet-tasting. Makes you immune to all poisons. Care to try?"
He immediately performs an entire martial arts routine, as if to prove that eating the stuff is good for you.

The grass is indeed sweet. Then your limbs go numb and your head buzzes loudly ...
This plant is anything but a simple weed. You should at least try to do something before you collapse.

Some time later, you crawl back to your feet.
The world spins. Beside you lies a bottle of seeds labeled "Whitepest Grass."
The medicine keeps you barely conscious, though your limbs remain numb, and the world keeps spinning.
After several failed tests, you notice a second label beneath the first: "Whiterest Grass," accompanied by a smiley face with its tongue poking out.
A sentence surfaces in your mind: never eat strange things from strangers.

Inside the box is yet another box, just slightly smaller.
Printed neatly on the surface are the words: "You'd be better off not opening this."

As expected, the box contains another box.
The warning remains unchanged: "You'd be better off not opening this."

Predictably, there are boxes again—but this time, there are two of them.
Both have writing on them.
The first reads, "You'd be better off not opening this," and the other also reads, "You'd be better off not opening this."

Inside, there is only a crumpled note.
It reads: "You'd be better off not opening this."

On second thought, this is hardly unusual.
Research often ends in "nothing gained," "wasted effort," "total failure," or "no results at all."
But dialectically speaking, even having no answer can still count as a result.

You wake from troubled dreams to the familiar ceiling of Laplace.
Your body feels strangely light. You touch your arm. It's covered in coarse black fur.
When you lift your head a little, you find you've transformed into a massive Critter.

Was it something you ate last night? Your mind races through the possibilities.
Candy-machine byproducts? Improvised compounds? Experimental drugs? Or that bottle of lab waste you drank?
A melancholy sigh interrupts your thoughts, coming from a small dog prone to pondering the meaning of the universe.

You try to shout, but your throat only produces a distinctive Critter-esque gurgle.
The sound attracts the Most Supreme Warlord.
He invites you to join the Independent State of Critters.

The dog looks at you and says calmly, "Avoidance won't resolve your current existential dilemma."
You realize you can now understand it directly.

"If existence is a concept," the dog continues, "I see it as a river."
You disagree, but all you can manage is a gurgle.
"You've been cast into a tributary entirely separate from your past," the dog says. "Eventually, the streams will converge. We'll all become Critters, citizens of the Independent State of Critters."

You try to explain yourself in Critter-Speech. The little dog thinks for a moment before saying, "Whether it was an accident or a symbol, it all points to the same ending—nothingness. No matter what we do, the river's course cannot be changed."
A hollow feeling washes over you, and at that moment, you desperately need a chew toy.

You try again to explain in Critter-Speech.
Silence follows—long, unbroken silence.
"I see," the dog finally says. "So this is your true nature." It turns and walks away, leaving behind a clean chew toy.
"By the way," he adds, "I saw someone knock over your reagents and dump in a generous amount of Dr. Papper."

Three penguins suddenly appear in front of you.
They wear sunglasses and top hats, and clearly ought to symbolize something, but your distaste for symbolism rivals the difficulty of swallowing an oversized vitamin tablet.

They wheel over a massive machine, a strange phonograph that emits unsettling noises.
You recognize it immediately—you once left several bite marks on its surface.
The penguins proudly announce that they are admirers of Institutum Lorentz and firmly believe that "to study chaos, one must first immerse oneself in chaos."
You pat the phonograph's casing, sending a small cloud of dust drifting down, along with several black hairs. Its overall state of disrepair is far worse than the damage caused by your teeth.

The penguins squawk nervously, afraid that any additional force from you would prove their theory flawed from the very start.
"Those old fools actually approved funding for this kind of research?"

The penguins excitedly explain that the sounds coming from the phonograph's speakers are themselves "a part of chaos."
They twist the knobs, lights flicker, tracks overlap, and the machine spews out a "chaotic melody," like weather forecasts, stock reports, and astrology shows chopped together at random.
"Look! A tiny disturbance is enough to trigger an irreversible chain reaction!"

"To study chaos, one must immerse oneself in chaos," you reply calmly. "By that logic, to study fire you'd have to set yourself on fire, and to study financial crime you'd first have to embezzle public funds."

You continue your point, "I understand now—chaos isn't your research subject, it's simply your workflow."
As you finish speaking, the phonograph conveniently plays a cheerful tune.

"If you really want to make chaos tangible, you might start with a more basic issue," you suggest. "For instance, how to turn your budget from 'a chaotic concept' into something tangible—actual funds. That's more relevant to our world than the flap of a butterfly's wings and far more likely to cause a chain reaction."
The penguins lapse into extended silence, and eventually, the phonograph powers off.

Your colleagues eagerly show you their invention.
"Watch closely! It can read emotions, synchronize brainwaves, and resolve difficult interpersonal conflicts!"
They invite you to be the first test subject and promise that "nothing dangerous will happen."

You've seen this scenario too many times before.
If you approach, any mishap will be blamed on you. But if you keep your distance, the worst outcome is a destroyed lab—and that has nothing to do with you.

You poke the sphere, and it immediately begins spinning wildly.
Your colleagues erupt with excitement, as if witnessing a miracle.
"You've formed a deep psychic connection with it!"
Meanwhile, the sphere plays a voice message: "Target emotion detected: mania, excitement, and a substantial level of hatred."

The sphere spins faster and faster as the machine hums loudly. "Emotional overload detected. Evacuate immediately."
Your colleagues panic and scatter, running faster than you've ever seen them move during fire drills.
The lab is instantly empty.
The voice fades away, the sphere slows to a stop, and it rolls to your feet.

You prepare to dismantle it.
The moment you pry open the casing, you discover that its core is built from your past research—your ideas, discarded drafts, and formulas, all crudely stitched together into one chaotic whole.
Hey, Medicine Pocket, there's something really bothering me, and I wanted to share it with you! No, nothing's on fire.

Your refusal is treated as though it were never heard at all, and he mercilessly continues with his noisy gossip. You don't mind—when it comes to absorbing complaints, your brain is polished enough that every word slips away without sticking.

After half an hour of uninterrupted complaining, you finally extract a sliver of useful information—the position they were hiring for was "Arcanum Theorist," but due to a communication error, they ended up recruiting a "Theoretical Arcanist" instead.
A chill runs through you, and your reaction clearly isn't what he was hoping for. He clicks his tongue in disappointment and walks away.
These fragments appear to be debris caused by a malfunction within the toybox itself. They only manifest in affected zones, present extreme danger, and look strangely familiar.
Let's go. It's time to meet the highest authority inside this toybox.
Knowledge is wealth—and at this very moment, it finally takes on a tangible form.
It sits quietly, modest and mute, brimming with possibility.
There's luggage scattered across the ground and a very lost traveler.
A green wooden crate containing all manner of goods, remembered only when it's finally needed.
A single venue packed with pieces, each locked in open conflict.
A makeshift camp, dilapidated and barely able to house more than a handful of people.
A swarm of Critters suddenly bursts out from nowhere, blocking your path.
Overexcited Critters crowd around you, chattering uncontrollably.
You are attacked. Apparently, the Critter believes you were mocking it.
There's a loud signboard yelling warnings at all those who pass by.
"A pack of Gadgets specially made for novice field trainees." Signed by Musae III.
A familiar old friend stands quietly here, patiently waiting for you to arrive.
A small cave that appears to serve as the resistance's secret base within the toybox.
The Leader of the Crates Gang
The leader of the Crates Gang glares at you with unmistakable hostility.
A team of Foundation field investigators. You recognize them.
A Zeno military officer with a hardened, disciplined look.
A Laplace researcher whose eyes appear hollow and distant.
A Critter from the "Glory Carbuncle Kingdom," noticeably sharper than its peers.
A raven gazes down from above, like an emperor surveying his domain.
An adorable little squirrel who claims, quite seriously, to be an officer of Zeno.
You see a painter working hard. He visibly brightens after spotting you and immediately shows you his painting.
The painter is here once more, working as intensely as ever, but with a visible air of melancholy.

You climb the steps and arrive at a strangely designed library, formed from countless hexagonal corridors.
Endless bookshelves tilt at unnatural angles, as though bowing toward some invisible central point.

You recognize them. They have appeared everywhere—on Ford automobiles, in Viennese street cafés, on a newspaper's bounty page, and inside the box carried by a merchant who insists his collecting is "a study of artistic essence."
Naturally, they appear here as well.
See what they are doing this time#You've seen them many times in the lab already
A green building that looks clearly unsafe.
You stop in front of a tent. A faint rustling sound comes from within ...

"Do you believe in the existence of a creator?"
A melancholy man blocks your path. "Don't you ever feel like we're living inside a box?"
His hand gently strokes an object beneath a glass cover, as if re-enacting a famous thought experiment.
Look under the glass#Is he insane?
A strangely shaped building that faintly radiates light.

"Fate is a predetermined rule."
As you move through endless hexagonal maps and tiles, the crystal's glow catches your eye.
Take the crystal#Avoid it before it starts lecturing you

A concept proposed by a psychologist, one of your dear colleagues' favorite research topics, frequently invoked by so-called "deep thinkers" both inside and outside the toybox, and now thoroughly overused.
It is an ocean, a can of orange juice, your dream—or the shared dream of the entire universe.
Do you believe in it? A pure, empty, monistic utopia, no different from the illusory tower inside the toybox.
Believe#Refuse to play this game of metaphors

Why would there be such an extravagantly decorated museum in the wilderness? Golden gates, marble walls, stained glass windows ... If the surroundings did not resemble a deserted wasteland, you might genuinely consider buying a ticket and immersing yourself in art.
The same museum again, though it has lost some of its former splendor and gained a sense of decay. Should you enter once more?

This is the third time you have seen the museum, and its deterioration has worsened. Rust and vines creep across its golden doors, cracks spread through its marble walls, and the entire structure teeters on the brink of collapse.
You find a group of people gathered around a coffin, arguing fiercely.
A Critter in a formal gown spins anxiously in place.
Huh?#I must be imagining things, time to leave

You walk to the edge of a pond.
The water is crystal clear, revealing numerous golden statues resting at the bottom.

You step into a barn and encounter a spider that can write.
On her web, she has written: Hello.
The Demon King in the Wardrobe
You discover an antique wardrobe colder than any of your colleagues, yet noticeably expensive.
You see a group of tiny people climbing a tulip.
Take a look#I should take a nap
It's a chubby little carbuncle that shows no sign of aggression.
This Critter resembles the "Most Supreme Warlord," at least in terms of size.
This Critter resembles the "Most Supreme Warlord," at least in terms of color.
This Critter resembles the "Most Supreme Warlord," at least in terms of hostility.
A child looks at you with hopeful eyes.
You spot a tower hidden in dense foliage before you. All is quiet.
You receive a bizarre map. Its cover boldly declares: Follow This and You Will Not Fail.
Take a look#Must be a prank
A girl wearing pearl earrings glances over her shoulder, her gaze fixed firmly on you.
A mobile food stand is parked here, apparently offering lemonade.
Three Critters are stacked atop one another, wobbling as they inch toward the water. The top one grips a cane and strikes a pose as though reaching for something with its ... hands? Paws?
A group of children blocks your path. You have no intention of engaging with them—you have more pressing matters—but they clearly have no intention of letting you pass.
Another restroom appears, completely out of place.

A bag of Picrasma Candy, exquisitely packaged.
You locate the Picrasma Candy factory marked on the golden ticket. It's just as grand as you imagined.
A building resembling staff dormitories stands here. Just looking at it induces instant exhaustion.
A table stands by the roadside, bearing a sign that reads: "Free Unified Narrative Registration."
An apple falls from the sky and lands squarely on your face.
You see an elderly man eating grass.

There's a message on top: "You'd be better off not opening this."

Supposedly, this "breakthrough" exists solely to prove that they can invent something impressive without you.

Tezcatlipoca Location: A museum in Mexico City Exhibition Hall: Tezcatlipoca Gallery The Aztec god Tezcatlipoca, the "smoking mirror," ruled as the First Sun. A trickster god, Tezcatlipoca embodied conflict and change. He often changed his appearance and summoned illusions to beguile, test, or destroy people. He was known to play tricks on royalty, bringing entire dynasties to their end. This capricious god of the first sun emitted only a dim light, up until he was struck from the sky by Quetzalcoatl. In anger, Tezcatlipoca transformed into a jaguar to devour the people. This relief is a replica of the original wall carving. Note that the obsidian mirror replacing his right foot is not an error; depictions of Tezcatlipoca use symbolic imagery in place of his foot, which he used as bait to subdue the giant monster Cipactli.

Did your history begin with myths or with agriculture?
The second sun rose. But then the wind came. A storm devoured the sun and blew Quetzalcoatl from the sky.
The wind stopped. No longer trapped in the wind, you became bound to agriculture instead.
Yes, the storm destroyed a blazing sun, but it also anchored you to this scorching land. Crops became not only your food but also the foundation of calendars and metaphors for society itself. You and your brothers and sisters lived and died by these crops.
Your mind absorbed knowledge of weaving, refining, and writing. Your body learned to farm, to battle, and to innovate. Your soul planted a civilization both glorious and heavy.

"I'm so glad you accepted my invitation to this important academic exchange. How should I address you ...?"
"Why do you ask? You're not my people! I am who I am, the rain and life—"
"All right. A rain of fire destroyed the world you nourished. Does this mean there was a critical failure in your career as manager of the eras?"
"While the rain of fire burnt my people's flesh and crops, it was merely part of the cycle of balance."
"So you accept destruction as the price for maintaining the balance?"
"Perhaps."
"An interesting perspective. What advice would you give to the people who became butterflies and were reborn?"
"I would advise them to become creatures that can hold water—whether it be tears, blood, or molten metal—and accept the cycle once more."

Day after 4-Ātl.
I may be the last chronicler of this world.
That goddess in the jade skirt and shawl, deity of all rivers and lakes ... Her tears from the past have become today's flood. Temples, cornfields, stone houses—everything was swallowed in an instant by the deluge of water rushing into the valley.
I was lucky. The goddess left me a canoe; although wave after wave has tried to engulf this little boat, it remains afloat.
Night has fallen. On the water's surface, there's something glimmering in the moonlight. As I look closer, I realize they're people—no, fish. Their skin shimmers with scales, their hands flattened into fins, their feet fused into tails. The people have transformed into fish. They leap from the water, offering their respects to the living.
I raise my hand in return. The fourth sun destroyed the world, but I was spared in the end. Tremble, tremble before Her sorrow.

When I saw you, you were standing on a road carpeted with marigolds. The stained-glass window overhead reflected the warm light of countless homes. Children danced around you with sugar skulls in hand. You held a brush dipped in glaze, painting an image of Tōnatiuh onto your beloved bajo quinto.
You and I live beneath the fifth sun. The world's movement continues tearing old rifts open and creating new fractures. The earthquakes may never stop. But will they be this world's end? It's hard to say. In truth, the world exists in eternal chaos, forever constructing and deconstructing, gathering and splitting apart.
Perhaps your mission is to keep walking this road toward destruction, praying the glaze never dries. For the world is still growing, and we must leave behind more unfinished works to keep creating joy in our lives.

"Those who crave war believe they sit high atop the cannons. Those who dread war see only the dark muzzles aimed at their faces. It tempts you, it terrifies you. Yet that power was never yours. It exists only to destroy." As long as humanity draws breath, conflict will never end—not until all turns to ash.

Something's been going on with Endless Stream lately, and I need to get this off my chest. I'm an old-timer here—been around since '92, back when the site first launched and you still had to queue up for a dial-up connection. Then in '94, L decided (he wasn't even the admin yet, haha) to upgrade the forum to what it is today. I was so excited I pulled an all-nighter helping him get it done. First, the technical side. Alt accounts have surged lately, especially spammers flooding the board with ads. If this keeps up, it'll put unnecessary strain on the server. Second, the people. Internet forums today are what the agora was to ancient Greece and what salons and cafés were to 18th-century Paris. I urge everyone to write quality posts and support the good ones. If we don't, Endless Stream will end up shallow and worthless!

I walked past the stadium today and noticed the woods out back have been fenced off with sheet metal. Someone told me it's a construction site now. I used to pick pinecones there with my classmates when I was a kid. Seeing it like that got me feeling a little sentimental, so I wanted to share a true story from my family.
My great-grandfather was a traveling merchant when he was young—he only came home for the New Year. One winter, heavy snowfall buried the roads. He couldn't tell which direction was which. By the time he'd eaten through all his rations, he still hadn't found the main road. He figured that was it for him: time to hide his goods in a thicket, then try to find some way to get word to his family. But just then, a chipmunk darted out of the brush, chattered at him a few times, and took off running.
Something told him to follow it. The chipmunk led him to a tree, hurried up the trunk, and vanished. He looked around and found a huge stash of pine nuts tucked beneath the roots. As soon as he'd gathered them up, another chipmunk appeared and led him to a cache of peanuts. Three chipmunks in all—and thanks to the food they led him to, he held out until the snow stopped. Eventually, a fellow traveler passed by, and my great-grandfather followed him home.
Now, this was nearly a hundred years ago. I'm definitely not saying people should go raiding a wild animal's winter stockpile. But because of what happened, our family started a tradition: every year after the winter solstice, we grab a handful of nuts, like peanuts, cashews, and almonds, and leave them out for the chipmunks in the nearest patch of woods. No incense, no prayer—just bury the nuts by the roots. I went with my grandfather once as a kid, and I swear I saw a chipmunk watching us from behind a branch.
Zhu County is booming these days, and new construction is a good thing. But there are way fewer groves and fields than when I was little. Where are the chipmunks, the hedgehogs, and the birds supposed to go? So if you don't mind me saying—if any of you have a chance, scatter a little millet on your balcony, and hang up a birdhouse. It might just help a few small lives. Not every animal is going to "repay the favor," but who knows? You might end up with a wonderful story of your own someday.
All things truly do have spirits. Who knows—maybe the next commenter will be an arcane chipmunk in disguise!

In fact, Qi is always in flux, just like the seasons—spring gives way to autumn, and the cycle never stops. You've all learned the 24 Solar Terms song in school, right? Each solar term is divided into three pentads, which means the climate shifts 72 times in a single year. Sound like a familiar number? That's exactly how many transformations Sun Wukong can perform!
And whether we're talking about Sun Wukong's 72 transformations or the 72 pentads of the year, from the perspective of Qi, they're really the same thing. The Qi that makes up all physical matter is constantly shifting. When the flow of Qi changes, the things it constitutes change with it. The third pentad of Awakening of Insects says, "hawks transform into cuckoos." The second pentad of Pure Brightness says, "field mice transform into quails." The climate shifts, so the animals shift along with it. It's the same principle behind trees budding in spring and bearing fruit in autumn. Nothing mysterious about it!
Unfortunately, the arcane energy in the world today is far weaker than it was in ancient times. So phenomena the ancients described, like the great Kun fish transforming into the Peng bird, aren't commonly seen these days. (Though if you're lucky, you might still catch withered grass spawning fireflies.) And lifespans like those of Dachun, the ancient tree, or Pengzu, the legendary elder, are long gone. But the transformations of Qi still act on every living thing. Sun Wukong originally sought out Master Puti to learn the 72 transformations because he sought longevity. If you can learn to regulate the flow of Qi within yourself, you may not be able to shapeshift like the Monkey King, but you can still achieve the goal of a longer, healthier life!

4.3.2 Commander
A commander was charged with the protection of a single city or fortress. Stationed at the city garrison, he commanded the local constables and answered to the Corps Leader and the Provincial Governor. The commander managed all military affairs within his city, including provisions, pay, and the administration of garrison farmland. Huanzhou frequently encountered trouble from Yaos, so the commander bore an additional duty: Yao disaster mitigation. This meant keeping them from infiltrating the county and stamping out any that caused trouble in the countryside. Working with the local soldiers, the commander investigated Yao-related incidents, arrested those who damaged farmland, and exterminated any violent Yao.

4.5.1 Constable
Patrol Bureaus were typically established in county towns and at key roads and river crossings. They answered to the local magistrate and the commander, and they followed military dispatch orders.
The head of a Patrol Bureau was the chief constable, a rank of the lowest ninth grade. The constable led a force of archer-conscripts drawn from local farmers. His primary duties were interrogating travelers, apprehending bandits, and guarding against Yao. The rank of constable was a humble one—most were promoted from minor clerks, as scholars and degree holders considered the post beneath them. Performance reviews were held every three years, with a full evaluation at nine. The standards were harsh, and promotions were rare.

First, I'd like to thank everyone for their help. I'm a history graduate student currently researching the family history of the Lis of Huanzhou—a gentry family that produced many Imperial Scholars throughout the Ming Dynasty. The Lis originally settled in Zhu County but relocated to Chun Town sometime after the seventeenth century. Their family rule states this was to escape a "disaster" in Zhu County. They received reliable advance warning and evacuated several days before it struck, sparing the family from casualties. The Lis weren't alone—the Lu, Chen, and Lee families of Huanzhou all have records of departing Zhu County around the same time, and cross-referencing their accounts confirms the timing aligns: all of them left in the period surrounding the "disaster." The Huanzhou Prefectural Gazette records only official reassignments after the disaster. The county magistrate and the commander were both transferred elsewhere, and the fates of many other officials remain unknown. Stories from Huanzhou has a more specific and unsettling record: "At that time, the sun and the moon hung together in the sky. The earth split in two from the gate of the School of Mei, opening a rift miles long that swallowed souls. When the governor had it investigated, they couldn't find a single human dead or alive, only clothes, dead plants, and animals." I suspect the Zhu County Annual may have more detailed records. Ming Dynasty annuals aren't easy to come by, though. Does anyone have access?
